title: מבנה הסוגיות – Menachot
note: חלוקה לסוגיות ולשלבי הדיון שנוצרה בבינה מלאכותית באתר talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).
note_de: KI-erzeugte Einteilung in Sugjot und Argumentationsschritte von talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum); englisch, hebräisch wo dort vorhanden.
note_en: AI-generated sugya sections and argument steps from talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all meal-offerings whose handful was taken not for their own sake are valid but do not fulfill the owner's obligation, except for the sin-offering and jealousy-offering, which are invalid if performed with mixed intentions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all meal-offerings whose handful was taken not for their own sake are valid but do not fulfill the owner's obligation, except for the sin-offering and jealousy-offering.
The Mishnah specifies that for the sin-offering and jealousy-offering, if the handful was taken not for its own sake, or with mixed intentions, the offering is invalid.
The Mishnah clarifies the mixed-intention cases: performing the act for the sin-offering and then for the free-will offering, or vice versa.

items.text: Gemara's question on the word 'except'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the word 'except'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the word 'except' (אֶלָּא) to introduce the exception, suggesting it could have simply said 'and they do not fulfill the obligation'. It answers that the word teaches that while the offering does not fulfill the owner's obligation, the offering itself is valid, and it is prohibited to change its designation, as per Rava's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah uses the word 'אֶלָּא' (except) instead of simply stating that the offerings do not fulfill the owner's obligation.
The Gemara answers that the word 'אֶלָּא' teaches that while the offering is valid, it is forbidden to deviate from the intended purpose, as per Rava's principle regarding the burnt-offering.

items.text: Two explanations for the prohibition
items.text_en: Two explanations for the prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative explanations for the prohibition against changing the offering's designation: one based on logic (that one should not change the offering's purpose) and one based on a biblical verse (Deuteronomy 23:24), which teaches that if one fulfills his vow as promised it is a vow, otherwise it is a freewill offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative rationales for the prohibition: first, a logical argument that one should not change the offering's designation repeatedly.
The Gemara offers a second rationale from a verse: if one fulfills the vow as promised, it remains a vow; otherwise, it becomes a free-will offering.

items.text: Gemara's initial question
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a voluntary meal-offering (נדבה) can be changed from its intended designation, based on the Mishnah's discussion of offerings brought for the wrong name.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a voluntary meal-offering (נדבה) can be changed from its intended designation.

items.text: Proposing the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Proposing the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah might not align with Rabbi Shimon, who holds that all meal-offerings are valid even if their kemitzah was not for their proper name, because the distinctive actions of meal-offerings make the intention recognizable, unlike animal sacrifices where all actions are identical.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah does not align with Rabbi Shimon, who holds that all meal-offerings whose kemitzah was performed not for their proper name are valid.
The baraita explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: the distinctive actions of each meal-offering type make the intention recognizable, unlike animal sacrifices where all actions are identical.

items.text: Refuting the proposal with Rav Ashi, Rabbah, and Rava
items.text_en: Refuting the proposal with Rav Ashi, Rabbah, and Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the positions of Rav Ashi, Rabbah, and Rava. Rav Ashi distinguishes between a change in the type of offering (e.g., griddle to deep-pan) and a change in the specific meal-offering; Rabbah distinguishes between a change in sanctity and a change in owner; Rava distinguishes between a meal-offering offered for another meal-offering and for an animal sacrifice. Ultimately, the Mishnah's case involves a change in sanctity, so it does not align with Rabbi Shimon according to Rabbah and Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's case fits Rav Ashi's distinction between a change in type and a change in offering, but questions how it aligns with Rabbah and Rava.
Rabbah distinguishes between a change in sanctity (שינוי קודש) and a change in owner (שינוי בעלים).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's case is a change in sanctity, not a change in owner, so Rabbah's distinction does not apply.
Rava distinguishes between a meal-offering offered for another meal-offering and for an animal sacrifice.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah involves a meal-offering for another meal-offering, so according to Rabbah and Rava it does not align with Rabbi Shimon's lenient position.

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Shimon's statements
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Shimon's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction within Rabbi Shimon's own statements: in one baraita he says all meal-offerings are valid when kemitzah is not for their name, but in another he distinguishes between a sin-offering meal (invalid if not for its name) and a voluntary meal (valid but does not fulfill the obligation), based on the verse comparing meal-offerings to a sin-offering and a guilt-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction within Rabbi Shimon's own statements by citing a baraita where he distinguishes between a sin-offering meal and a voluntary meal based on the verse 'קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים הִיא כְּחַטָּאת וּכְאָשָׁם'.

The baraita explains that a sin-offering meal-offerings is like a sin-offering (invalid if not for its name), while a voluntary meal-offering is like a guilt-offering (valid but does not fulfill the obligation).
The Gemara elaborates that just as a guilt-offering is valid but does not bring atonement if offered not for its name, so too a voluntary meal-offering is valid but does not fulfill the obligation.

items.text: Rabbah's resolution and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rabbah's resolution and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a change in sanctity (שינוי קודש) and a change in owner (שינוי בעלים). Abaye objects that since intention is derived from a biblical analogy, there should be no difference. Rabbah responds that Rabbi Shimon relies on logic: the distinctive actions of meal-offerings make the intention recognizable, and the Torah only invalidates unrecognizable intentions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a change of sanctity (שינוי קודש) and a change of owner (שינוי בעלים).
Abaye objects that since the disqualification of improper intent is derived from a biblical analogy (היקש), there should be no difference between a change of sanctity and a change of owner.
Rabbah answers that Rabbi Shimon's principle that the actions prove the intent is based on logical reasoning (סברא), and the Torah only disqualifies unrecognizable intent, not recognizable intent.
The Gemara provides a mnemonic (סימן) listing the topics for the upcoming challenges to Rabbah's position.

items.text: Testing the principle with bird offerings
items.text_en: Testing the principle with bird offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara tests Rabbi Shimon's principle by considering bird offerings: if one performs melikah or sprinkling of a burnt-offering above the altar for the sake of a sin-offering, would it be valid? The Gemara argues that the distinctive actions (melikah above vs. below, sprinkling above vs. below) make the intention recognizable, so it should be valid, but notes that sin-offering birds also have a valid placement above, complicating the test.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Shimon's principle: if one performs melikah of a bird burnt-offering above the altar for the sake of a sin-offering, the distinctive action (above vs. below) should make the intention recognizable and thus valid, yet Rabbi Shimon agrees it is invalid.
The Gemara rejects the challenge: a sin-offering bird also has a valid melikah placement above the red line, so the action does not make the intention recognizably false.

The Gemara raises another challenge: if one squeezes the blood of a bird burnt-offering above the red line for the sake of a sin-offering, the distinctive action (squeezing vs. sprinkling) should make the intention recognizable and thus valid.

items.text: Gemara's answer to the bird-offering objection
items.text_en: Gemara's answer to the bird-offering objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara responds to the earlier objection about bird offerings: the case of a bird sin-offering whose blood was sprinkled below for the sake of a burnt-offering is valid because the actions (sprinkling below, not above) prove it is a sin-offering. The same logic applies to meal-offerings, but the Mishnah only compared them to animal sacrifices, not bird offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers the bird-offering objection by arguing that the bird sin-offering's actions (sprinkling below, not above) prove its identity, and the Mishnah only compared meal-offerings to animal sacrifices, not to bird offerings.

items.text: Applying the principle to holy-of-holies slaughtered in the south
items.text_en: Applying the principle to holy-of-holies slaughtered in the south
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that if one slaughters a most holy sacrifice in the south for the sake of a lesser holy sacrifice, it should be valid because the act of slaughtering in the north (which is required for most holy sacrifices) proves its true status. However, the Gemara objects: the Torah permits slaughtering lesser holy sacrifices anywhere in the courtyard, including the north, so the location does not prove anything.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that if one slaughters a most holy sacrifice (קׇדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים) in the north for the sake of a lesser holy sacrifice (קָדָשִׁים קַלִּים), the act should be valid because the location (north) proves its true status as a most holy sacrifice.
The Gemara objects that the location does not prove anything, because the Torah permits slaughtering lesser holy sacrifices anywhere in the courtyard, including the north.

items.text: Applying the principle to lesser holy sacrifices slaughtered in the north
items.text_en: Applying the principle to lesser holy sacrifices slaughtered in the north
items.desc_en: The Gemara then considers the reverse: lesser holy sacrifices slaughtered in the north for the sake of most holy sacrifices. The act of slaughtering in the south (where lesser holy sacrifices are normally slaughtered) should prove their true status. But the Gemara objects: one might say they are actually most holy sacrifices, and the slaughterer merely erred by slaughtering them in the south.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that lesser holy sacrifices slaughtered in the south for the sake of most holy sacrifices should be accepted, because their actions prove they are lesser holy sacrifices, since most holy sacrifices would have been slaughtered in the north.
The objection counters that one might say they are actually most holy sacrifices, and the slaughterer merely erred by slaughtering them in the south.

items.text: Challenge from the case of a pan and a deep-pan
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of a pan and a deep-pan
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle by citing the case of a person who vows to bring a meal-offering in a pan (מחבת) but brings it in a deep-pan (מרחשת). According to the Mishnah, if he said 'this is for a pan' and brought it in a deep-pan, it is invalid, even though the vessel type should prove his intent. The Gemara distinguishes between a vow (עלי) and a designated offering (זו), and notes that Rabbi Shimon holds that the vessel's identity is insignificant, so the principle fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle by analogizing to a pan (מחבת) offered for a deep-pan (מרחשת), arguing that the vessel's identity could be mistaken.
The Gemara distinguishes: in the case of a vow (עלי), the vessel type is determined by what is actually brought, not by intent.
The Gemara cites a baraita: one who vows to bring a meal-offering in a pan (מחבת) but brings it in a deep-pan (מרחשת) has not fulfilled his vow, per the Tanna Kamma.
The Gemara cites another baraita: if one designated a specific offering (זו) for a pan but brought it in a deep-pan, it is invalid, per the Tanna Kamma.
The Gemara resolves that for Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the vessel's identity is insignificant, the principle of 'deeds prove intent' applies equally to both vows and designated offerings.

items.text: Challenge from gender differences (male vs. female)
items.text_en: Challenge from gender differences (male vs. female)
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle further: if one slaughters a burnt-offering (male) for the sake of a sin-offering (female), it should be valid because the gender difference proves intent. But the Gemara objects that a male goat can be a sin-offering (e.g., the prince's sin-offering), so gender is not decisive. Even for a private sin-offering (female), the fat tail might obscure the gender. The Gemara concludes that people are not generally attentive to gender differences.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if one slaughters a burnt-offering (male) for the sake of a sin-offering (female), it should be valid because the gender difference proves intent, but the objection is raised that a male goat can be a prince's sin-offering, so gender is not decisive.
The Gemara objects: even if one specifies a private sin-offering (female), the fat tail of a female sheep might obscure the gender difference.
The Gemara objects further: even if a female goat (without a fat tail) is brought, people are not generally attentive to gender differences between males and females.

items.text: Challenge from age differences (one year vs. two years)
items.text_en: Challenge from age differences (one year vs. two years)
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle with age: a Paschal lamb (one year old) slaughtered for the sake of a guilt-offering (two years old) should be valid, but there are guilt-offerings of one year (Nazirite, leper). Even for specific guilt-offerings (theft, misuse), the reverse case (guilt-offering for Paschal lamb) fails because the Paschal lamb is one year old. The Gemara concludes that people are not attentive to age differences, as a one-year-old can appear two and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: a Paschal lamb (one year old) slaughtered for the sake of a guilt-offering (two years old) should be valid, but since there are guilt-offerings of one year (Nazirite, leper), the age difference is not decisive.

An objection is raised: even for specific guilt-offerings (theft, misuse), the reverse case (guilt-offering slaughtered for Paschal lamb) fails because the Paschal lamb is one year old and the guilt-offerings are two years old.
The Gemara concludes that people are not attentive to age differences, as a one-year-old can appear two and vice versa.

items.text: Challenge from wool vs. hair and the case of a calf and ox
items.text_en: Challenge from wool vs. hair and the case of a calf and ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle with a goat (hair) slaughtered for a guilt-offering (wool), but the objection is that a black ram might be mistaken for a goat. Finally, the Gemara notes that a calf or ox slaughtered for a Paschal lamb or guilt-offering would be valid because those offerings never come from a calf or ox, so the physical difference is clear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that a goat (שעיר) slaughtered for a guilt-offering (אשם) should be valid because the goat has hair (שער) while the guilt-offering requires wool (צמר), but the objection is that a black ram (דיכרא אוכמא) might be mistaken for a goat.
The Gemara concludes that a calf or ox slaughtered for a Paschal lamb or guilt-offering would be valid because those offerings never come from a calf or ox, so the physical difference is clear.

items.text: Opening question: What are 'most sacrifices'?
items.text_en: Opening question: What are 'most sacrifices'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's phrase 'רוב זבחים' (most sacrifices), explaining that it refers to the majority of sacrifices, not all.

items.text: Rava's resolution: Distinction between intent for a meal-offering vs. for a sacrifice
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: Distinction between intent for a meal-offering vs. for a sacrifice
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between intent for a meal-offering (מנחה לשם מנחה) and intent for a sacrifice (מנחה לשם זבח). The former is valid due to 'תורה אחת לכל המנחות', while the latter is invalid because 'תורה אחת למנחה וזבח' is not written. The Gemara then addresses the Mishnah's statement about 'מעשיה מוכיחין עליה' and explains that even though the intent is recognizable, the verse teaches a single Torah for all meal-offerings. It concludes by explaining why sacrifices are different.

items.text: Challenge from sin-offerings and resolution for Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Challenge from sin-offerings and resolution for Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's logic by applying it to sin-offerings (חטאת), arguing that if 'תורה אחת' applies, then all sin-offerings should be valid regardless of intent. It then distinguishes between Rabbi Shimon's view and the Rabbis: for the Rabbis, a sin-offering for fat offered for a sin-offering for blood is valid, but for a Nazirite's or leper's sin-offering it is invalid because those are essentially burnt-offerings. Rav Acha bar Rava teaches that all such cases are invalid based on the verse 'ושחט אותה לחטאת'.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution: Distinction between intent regarding the vessel vs. the offering type
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution: Distinction between intent regarding the vessel vs. the offering type
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi offers a different resolution: intent for a griddle-cake offering (מחבת) in the name of a deep-pan offering (מרחשת) is invalid because it is intent regarding the vessel, which does not disqualify; but intent for a griddle-cake offering in the name of a deep-pan offering-type (מנחת מרחשת) is invalid because it is intent regarding the offering type, which does disqualify. He then explains the Mishnah's statement about 'מעשיה מוכיחין' and why sacrifices are different due to multiple common actions.

items.text: Rav Acha's objection to Rav Ashi and the distinction regarding 'belulah'
items.text_en: Rav Acha's objection to Rav Ashi and the distinction regarding 'belulah'
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava objects to Rav Ashi's explanation, asking why Rabbi Shimon would invalidate a meal-offering intended for 'belulah' (mixed) if it is merely intent regarding a vessel. Rav Ashi responds that the intent is for 'belulah' in a general sense. The Gemara then questions why the same logic wouldn't apply to 'shelamim' (peace-offerings), and explains that 'shelamim' is a name for the sacrifice itself, whereas 'belulah' is not a name for the meal-offering itself but only a description.

items.text: Summary of rejected opinions: Rabbah, Rava, and Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Summary of rejected opinions: Rabbah, Rava, and Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why each Amora's opinion is rejected: Rabbah's view is rejected because the Torah only disqualifies recognizable intent; Rava's view is rejected because 'וזאת תורת' does not imply a single Torah for all; Rav Ashi's view is rejected due to Rav Acha's objection.

items.text: Rav Hoshaya's dilemma: Meal-offering intended for a sacrifice
items.text_en: Rav Hoshaya's dilemma: Meal-offering intended for a sacrifice
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that what was simple for Rabbah and Rava was a dilemma for Rav Hoshaya, who asked Rabbi Asi: what is the law for a meal-offering intended for a sacrifice (מנחה לשם זבח)?

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon's ruling is due to recognizable intent not disqualifying, or because the Torah wrote 'this is the Torah of the meal-offering' but not of a sacrifice. The Gemara then notes that this cannot be resolved according to Rabbah, Rava, or Rav Ashi due to various difficulties.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Shimon's ruling is because recognizable intent does not disqualify, or because the Torah wrote 'וזאת תורת המנחה' (this is the Torah of the meal-offering) but not for a sacrifice.
The Gemara responds that we have not reached the end of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning.
The Gemara notes that the question cannot be resolved according to Rabbah due to Abaye's difficulty.
The Gemara notes that the question cannot be resolved according to Rava due to the difficulty from the verse 'וזאת תורת החטאת' (this is the Torah of the sin-offering).
The Gemara notes that the question cannot be resolved according to Rav Ashi due to the difficulty of Rav Acha bar Rava.

items.text: Source for meal-offering of jealousy
items.text_en: Source for meal-offering of jealousy
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the meal-offering of jealousy is also disqualified when not offered for its own sake, given that the sin-offering is explicitly called a 'sin-offering' in the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the meal-offering of jealousy (מנחת קנאות) is also disqualified when not offered for its own sake, given that the sin-offering is explicitly called a 'sin-offering' in the verse.

items.text: Derivation from sin-offering via verbal analogy
items.text_en: Derivation from sin-offering via verbal analogy
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav Nachman that the surplus of the meal-offering of jealousy is a freewill offering. Rav Nachman confirms this, deriving from the word 'iniquity' written in both the sin-offering and the jealousy offering that just as the sin-offering's surplus is a freewill offering, so too for the jealousy offering, and just as the sin-offering is disqualified when not for its own sake, so too the jealousy offering.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav Nachman that the surplus of the meal-offering of jealousy is a freewill offering.

Rav Nachman confirms the baraita, deriving from the word 'עָוֹן' (iniquity) written in both the sin-offering and the jealousy offering that just as the sin-offering's surplus is a freewill offering and it is disqualified when not for its own sake, so too for the jealousy offering.

items.text: Challenge and rejection of extending the analogy to guilt-offering
items.text_en: Challenge and rejection of extending the analogy to guilt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if we derive from 'iniquity', then a guilt-offering should also be disqualified when not for its own sake. The Gemara responds that we derive 'iniquity' from 'iniquity' but not 'his iniquity' from 'iniquity'. However, the Gemara then questions this distinction, citing a teaching that 'return' and 'come' are the same, and suggests deriving 'his iniquity' from the 'iniquity' of hearing the voice. The Gemara concludes that the verbal analogy is only for the surplus being a freewill offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if we derive from 'עָוֹן' (iniquity), then a guilt-offering (אשם) should also be disqualified when not for its own sake, since it shares the same verbal analogy with the sin-offering.

The Gemara responds that we derive the general term 'עָוֹן' (iniquity) from 'עָוֹן', but we do not derive the specific phrase 'עֲוֹנוֹ' (his iniquity) from the general 'עָוֹן', thus excluding the guilt-offering.

The Gemara objects that this distinction is meaningless, citing the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael that 'וְשָׁב הַכֹּהֵן' (and the priest shall return) and 'וּבָא הַכֹּהֵן' (and the priest shall come) are the same, implying that different forms can be equated.

The Gemara further objects that we could derive 'עֲוֹנוֹ' (his iniquity) from the 'עָוֹן' (iniquity) of hearing the voice (שמיעת הקול), where the verse says 'וְנָשָׂא עֲוֹנוֹ' (and he shall bear his iniquity).
The Gemara concludes that the verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) is only applied for the surplus being a freewill offering (מותר נדבה), not for disqualification when not for its own sake.

items.text: Limitation of the verbal analogy
items.text_en: Limitation of the verbal analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the verbal analogy is only for the surplus being a freewill offering. If one argues that a verbal analogy cannot be partial, the Gemara explains that the Torah revealed regarding the sin-offering that it is only disqualified when not for its own sake, but all other offerings are valid whether for their own sake or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the objection that a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) cannot be applied partially.

The Gemara resolves that the Torah revealed regarding the sin-offering (חטאת) that it is only disqualified when not for its own sake, but all other offerings are valid whether for their own sake or not.

items.text: Source for disqualification of meal-offerings not for their sake
items.text_en: Source for disqualification of meal-offerings not for their sake
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the meal-offering of a sinner and of jealousy are disqualified when not for their own sake. It answers that just as the sin-offering is disqualified because 'it' is written, so too 'it' is written regarding these offerings. The Gemara then addresses the guilt-offering, where 'he' is written, but explains that 'he' is written only after the burning of the sacrificial parts, meaning the offering itself is valid even if the parts were not burned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that the meal-offering of a sinner and the meal-offering of jealousy are disqualified when performed not for their own sake.
The Gemara answers that just as the sin-offering is disqualified because the word 'הִיא' (it) is written regarding it, so too 'הִיא' is written regarding these meal-offerings.
The Gemara objects that the guilt-offering also has the word 'הוּא' (he) written, but that 'הוּא' is written only after the burning of the sacrificial parts.
A baraita supports that the word 'הוּא' for the guilt-offering applies only after the burning of the parts, meaning the offering itself is valid even if its parts were not burned.

items.text: Alternative use of 'he' for guilt-offering
items.text_en: Alternative use of 'he' for guilt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word 'he' in the guilt-offering is used for a teaching of Rav Huna citing Rav: a guilt-offering that was designated for pasture and then slaughtered without specification is valid as a burnt-offering. This applies only if it was designated for pasture, as the verse says 'he' – it should remain in its current state.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the word 'הוּא' in the guilt-offering is not used to exclude the case after the burning of the fats, then what is its purpose?
Rav Huna citing Rav answers: The word 'הוּא' teaches that a guilt-offering designated for pasture and then slaughtered without specification is valid as a burnt-offering.
The Gemara clarifies the scope: only if the animal was designated for pasture does the rule apply, as the verse says 'הוּא' – it should remain in its current state.

items.text: Rav's ruling on the omer offering
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on the omer offering
items.desc_en: Rav states that the omer meal-offering, if its handful was taken not for its own sake, is disqualified because it came to permit and did not permit. The same applies to the guilt-offering of a nazirite.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the omer meal-offering taken not for its own sake is disqualified because it came to permit and did not permit, and the same applies to the guilt-offering of a nazirite.

items.text: Opening statement: guilt-offerings of a leper slaughtered not for their name are invalid
items.text_en: Opening statement: guilt-offerings of a leper slaughtered not for their name are invalid
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that the guilt-offering of a leper slaughtered not for its name is invalid because it comes to qualify (the leper) but does not qualify.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that a leper's guilt-offering slaughtered not for its name is invalid because it comes to qualify (the leper) but does not qualify.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: why isn't the omer meal-offering excluded from the rule?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: why isn't the omer meal-offering excluded from the rule?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah listing meal-offerings invalid if not for their name excludes the omer, but the omer is a communal offering that comes to permit the new grain. The Gemara answers that the mishnah only lists individual offerings, not communal ones, and only those that come for their own sake, not for the sake of a sacrifice.

items.text: Mar's statement: the same applies to guilt-offerings of a nazirite and a leper
items.text_en: Mar's statement: the same applies to guilt-offerings of a nazirite and a leper
items.desc_en: Mar states that the guilt-offering of a nazirite and a leper slaughtered not for their name are invalid, because they come to qualify but do not qualify.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: why aren't these guilt-offerings excluded from the general rule?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: why aren't these guilt-offerings excluded from the general rule?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the mishnah listing all sacrifices slaughtered not for their name as valid except for the paschal and sin-offerings should also exclude the guilt-offerings of a nazirite and a leper. The Gemara answers that since there are other guilt-offerings (for theft and misuse) that come for atonement, the mishnah does not list them all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the mishnah listing all animals slaughtered not for their name as valid except for the pesach and sin-offerings should also explicitly exclude the guilt-offerings of a nazirite and a leper, which come to enable and did not enable.
The Gemara answers that since there are other guilt-offerings (for theft and misuse) that come for atonement, the category is not uniform, so the mishnah does not list them all.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's distinction: atonement offerings can come after death, qualification offerings cannot
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's distinction: atonement offerings can come after death, qualification offerings cannot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the guilt-offerings of a nazirite and a leper (which come to qualify) from other guilt-offerings (which come to atone). Rabbi Yirmeya answers that we find a scriptural distinction: atonement offerings can be brought after the owner's death, but qualification offerings cannot, as taught in a mishnah about a woman who dies after bringing her sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the guilt-offerings of a nazirite and a leper are singled out as coming to qualify, while other guilt-offerings also come for atonement and fail to atone.

Rabbi Yirmeya answers that Scripture distinguishes between atonement offerings, which can be brought after the owner's death, and qualification offerings, which cannot, citing a mishnah about a woman who dies after bringing her sin-offering.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's objection: qualification offerings can also come after death
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's objection: qualification offerings can also come after death
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi, objects that qualification offerings can also come after death, citing a mishnah about a nazirite who dies: the money designated for his burnt-offering and peace-offerings (which qualify him) are brought after his death.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi challenges: qualifying-offerings also have some that come after death? For we learned: one who sets aside money for his nazirite offering — they may not benefit nor misuse, because they are all fit to come as shelamim.

Rabbi Yehuda objects that qualification offerings can also come after death, citing a mishnah about a nazirite who dies: the money designated for his burnt-offering and peace-offerings (which qualify him) are brought after his death.

The Gemara cites the baraita: if the nazir died and he had unspecified money, it falls to nedava; specified money: chatat money goes to the Dead Sea, no benefit or misuse; olah money — bring an olah, and misuse applies.

The mishnah details the disposition of a nazirite's funds after death: unspecified funds go to nedava, while specified funds for the burnt-offering and peace-offerings are brought after death, proving that qualification offerings can come posthumously.
Rabbi Papa answers: Rabbi Yirmeya meant we find no fixed qualifying-offering that comes after death, and nazir is a non-fixed qualifying-offering.
Rav Pappa clarifies Rabbi Yirmeya's position: no fixed qualification offering comes after death, and the nazirite's offerings are a non-fixed qualification, thus not a counterexample.

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution: fixed vs. non-fixed qualification
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution: fixed vs. non-fixed qualification
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that Rabbi Yirmeya meant that we do not find a fixed qualification that comes after death, and the nazirite's qualification is not fixed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the objection by clarifying that Rabbi Yirmeya meant we do not find a fixed qualification (הכשר קבוע) that comes after death, and the nazirite's qualification is not fixed.

items.text: Opening statement: the rule of shaving on one of three
items.text_en: Opening statement: the rule of shaving on one of three
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the principle that if a nazirite shaved for one of three reasons, he has fulfilled his obligation, setting the stage for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: Mar states the principle that a nazirite who shaved for one of three specified reasons has fulfilled his obligation.

items.text: Challenge to Rav from the leper's guilt-offering
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav from the leper's guilt-offering
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that a leper's guilt-offering slaughtered not for its sake is valid but requires another guilt-offering to permit the leper, which contradicts Rav's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a leper's guilt-offering slaughtered not for its own name, which requires another guilt-offering, contradicting Rav's position.

items.text: Reish Lakish's view on the Omer offering
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's view on the Omer offering
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that the Omer offering performed not for its sake is valid, but its remnants cannot be eaten until another Omer is brought to permit them. The Gemara questions how the second Omer can be offered if its flour must come from permitted grain.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that the Omer offering performed not for its sake is valid, but its remnants cannot be eaten until another Omer is brought to permit them.
The Gemara questions how the second Omer can be offered if its flour must come from grain permitted to Israel, given that the first Omer's remnants are still forbidden.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's explanation: no lack of time on the same day
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's explanation: no lack of time on the same day
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah explains that Reish Lakish holds that there is no concept of 'lack of time on the same day' for the Omer, so the second Omer is not considered to have been offered before its time.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah explains that Reish Lakish holds the principle that a sacrifice lacking time (מחוסר זמן) does not apply to the same day (אין מחוסר זמן לבו ביום).

items.text: Challenge from bird offerings and the Omer's permissibility
items.text_en: Challenge from bird offerings and the Omer's permissibility
items.desc_en: Rav Adda the son of Rav Yitzchak challenges Reish Lakish from a baraita listing differences between bird and meal offerings, including that those lacking atonement (like zavim) are permitted in the sanctuary, which would apply to the Omer if it were permitted. The Gemara responds that since there is no lack of time, it is not considered prohibited.

sub.text: Rav Adda the son of Rav Yitzchak's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Adda the son of Rav Yitzchak's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda challenges Reish Lakish by citing a baraita that lists differences between bird and meal offerings, including that those lacking atonement (מחוסרי כפרה) are permitted in the sanctuary, which would apply to the Omer if it were permitted.
Rav Adda infers that if Reish Lakish were correct, the Omer offering would also be permitted in the sanctuary despite lacking atonement.
The Gemara answers that since the Omer has no lack of time (אין מחוסר זמן לבו ביום), it is not considered prohibited, so the baraita's rule does not apply.

items.text: Challenge from the leper's oil application
items.text_en: Challenge from the leper's oil application
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishet challenges Reish Lakish from the law of the leper: if oil was applied before blood, one must repeat the oil application, implying that order matters even on the same day, contradicting 'no lack of time'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects from a baraita about a leper's anointing: if oil was applied before blood, one must refill and reapply; if the principle of 'no מחוסר זמן' applied, why would one need to redo it?
Rav Sheishet objects: if there is no lack of time on the same day, why must one repeat the oil application? The act should be valid בדיעבד (after the fact).

items.text: Rav Pappa's distinction: the leper's laws require 'being'
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's distinction: the leper's laws require 'being'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that the leper's laws are different because the verse 'This shall be the law of the leper' implies the process must remain in its proper sequence, unlike the Omer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that the laws of a leper are different because the Torah writes a 'הויה' (existence) requirement: 'זאת תהיה תורת המצורע' — the procedure must be in its proper sequence.

items.text: Final challenge and resolution: the Omer's time is fixed by sunrise
items.text_en: Final challenge and resolution: the Omer's time is fixed by sunrise
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges his own distinction from the law of the leper's sin-offering and guilt-offering, then resolves that Reish Lakish holds that the Omer is permitted by sunrise, not by the offering itself, so there is no issue of time.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges his own distinction from the leper's sin-offering and guilt-offering, arguing that if there is no issue of time (אין מחוסר זמן לבו ביום), then one should be able to stir the blood of the sin-offering and offer the guilt-offering first.

Rav Pappa resolves that Reish Lakish holds the Omer is permitted by sunrise (האיר מזרח מתיר), not by the offering itself, so there is no issue of time, and both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish agree on this even when the Temple stands.

items.text: Opening principle: 'When the east lights up' permits
items.text_en: Opening principle: 'When the east lights up' permits
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that the omer offering becomes permitted when the eastern sky lights up (dawn).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that the omer offering becomes permitted when the eastern sky lights up (dawn).

items.text: Reish Lakish's statement derived from a mishnah
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's statement derived from a mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish's statement was not explicit but inferred from a mishnah about first-fruit offerings and the omer. He rules that if one brought such offerings on the 16th of Nisan, they are valid, implying that 'when the east lights up' permits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Reish Lakish's statement was not explicit but derived from a mishnah about first-fruit offerings and the omer.
The mishnah states that before the two loaves one may not bring first-fruit offerings, but if brought they are valid.
Rabbi Yitzchak reports that Reish Lakish ruled that on the 16th of Nisan such offerings are valid, implying that 'when the east lights up' permits.

items.text: Rava's ruling on the omer offering and improper intent
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on the omer offering and improper intent
items.desc_en: Rava states that if one performed the kemitzah of the omer offering not for its sake, it is valid and does not require another omer to permit it, because improper intent only applies to one fit for service, with a fit item, and in a fit place.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the omer offering whose kemitzah was performed not for its sake is valid, because improper intent only applies to a fit priest, a fit item, and a fit place.
Rava elaborates that the three conditions exclude a blemished priest, the omer itself (a novelty), and a damaged altar.

items.text: Baraita: Deriving terefah from 'from the cattle'
items.text_en: Baraita: Deriving terefah from 'from the cattle'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the phrase 'from the cattle' (lower) excludes a terefah animal. A logical argument is presented: a blemished animal is forbidden for the altar, so a terefah should certainly be forbidden. The argument is challenged and defended with various analogies (chelev, melikah), and concludes with the verse itself.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the phrase 'from the cattle' (lower) comes to exclude a terefah animal.

The gemara raises a logical argument: if a blemished animal, permitted to a commoner, is forbidden for the altar, then a terefah, forbidden to a commoner, should certainly be forbidden for the altar; but this is challenged by chelev and blood, which are forbidden to a commoner yet permitted for the altar.
The first answer distinguishes chelev and blood as coming from a permitted source, whereas a terefah is entirely forbidden, so it should not be permitted for the altar.
An objection is raised: melikah (the pinching of a bird's neck) is entirely forbidden to a commoner yet permitted for the altar, challenging the previous distinction.
The second answer distinguishes melikah because its sanctity (at the time of melikah) caused its prohibition to a commoner, whereas a terefah's prohibition is not due to sanctity.
The resolution concludes that the verse itself ('from the cattle' lower) excludes the terefah, overriding the logical arguments.

items.text: Siman for the following disputes
items.text_en: Siman for the following disputes
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic sign for the subsequent Amoraitic statements: 'Rekich, Mar, Adda, le-Sheisheih'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic sign for the subsequent Amoraitic statements: 'Rekich, Mar, Adda, le-Sheisheih'.

items.text: Rav's refutation: The omer offering as a counterexample
items.text_en: Rav's refutation: The omer offering as a counterexample
items.desc_en: Rav argues that the omer offering is a counterexample: it is forbidden to a commoner but permitted to the altar. The Gemara attempts to distinguish it because it permits new grain, and then extends the argument to the Sabbatical year (permitinng sefichin according to Rabbi Akiva). Further challenges are raised and resolved.

sub.desc_en: Rav opens by proposing the omer offering as a counterexample: it is forbidden to a commoner but permitted to the altar, though the objection is raised that it permits new grain.
The Gemara extends the argument to the Sabbatical year, noting that the omer permits sefichin (volunteer growth) according to Rabbi Akiva.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Abba to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Abba to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Abba objects to Rav Ashi that even according to Rabbi Akiva one could refute the argument because the omer permits new grain outside the Land of Israel.
The Gemara responds that even for those who hold that new grain outside the Land is not a Torah prohibition, the omer comes to permit the negative commandment inherent in it.
Rav Acha mi-Difti resolves the argument by noting that if the omer's unique feature is that its mitzvah is precisely to permit, then a treifa cannot be compared, as its mitzvah is not to permit.

items.text: Reish Lakish's refutation: The compounding of incense
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's refutation: The compounding of incense
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish argues that the compounding of incense is a counterexample: it is forbidden to a commoner but permitted to the altar. The Gemara corrects the phrasing and notes that its distinguishing feature is that its mitzvah is in that very act.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish objects that the compounding of incense (מפטם הקטורת) is a counterexample: forbidden to a commoner but permitted to the altar.
The Gemara rejects the phrasing, noting that 'מפטם' refers to a person, not the incense itself.
The Gemara corrects the term to 'פיטום הקטורת' (the compounding of incense) and notes that its distinguishing feature is that its mitzvah is in that very act.

items.text: Mar bar Ravina's refutation: Shabbat
items.text_en: Mar bar Ravina's refutation: Shabbat
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina argues that Shabbat is a counterexample: it is forbidden to a commoner but permitted to the altar (for sacrifices). The Gemara initially suggests that Shabbat is permitted to a commoner through circumcision, but rejects that because circumcision is a mitzvah, not a personal need. It concludes that Shabbat's distinguishing feature is that its mitzvah is in that very act.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina proposes Shabbat as a counterexample to the argument, asserting that Shabbat is forbidden to a commoner but permitted to the Temple for the sake of offerings.

sub.text: Gemara's first refutation of the distinction
sub.text_en: Gemara's first refutation of the distinction
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Shabbat is partially permitted to a commoner for the mitzvah of circumcision, thus the comparison is flawed.
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that circumcision is a mitzvah, not a personal need of the commoner, so it does not count as a leniency for common use.
The Gemara concludes that Shabbat's defining feature for the argument is that its very essence is a mitzvah (sanctity of the day), unlike a substantive prohibition such as treifa.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Abba's refutation: Kilayim
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Abba's refutation: Kilayim
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Abba argues that kilayim (forbidden mixtures) is a counterexample: they are forbidden to a commoner but permitted to the altar (e.g., in the Temple curtain). The Gemara initially suggests that kilayim is permitted to a commoner through tzitzit, but rejects that because tzitzit is a mitzvah. The text breaks off mid-argument.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Abba proposes that kilayim (forbidden mixtures) serves as a counterexample: it is forbidden to a commoner but permitted to the altar.
The Gemara objects that kilayim is permitted to a commoner through the mitzvah of tzitzit, but the text breaks off mid-argument.

items.text: Initial refutation of the binyan av from kilayim
items.text_en: Initial refutation of the binyan av from kilayim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous attempt to prove tereifah is valid from kilayim fails because kilayim's mitzvah is specifically with that prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the binyan av from kilayim fails because kilayim's mitzvah is specifically with that prohibition.

items.text: Rav Shisha's proposed binyan av and its refutation
items.text_en: Rav Shisha's proposed binyan av and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi suggests a binyan av from melikah and chelev/dam, but the Gemara refutes it because the common element (they are forbidden to a non-priest but permitted to the altar) is not shared: melikah's mitzvah is specifically with that act.

sub.text: Rav Shisha son of Rav Idi's proposal
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha son of Rav Idi's proposal
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha proposes to reconstruct the argument using a מה הצד (analogy from shared features) with melikah, chelev, and blood.
The Gemara objects that chelev and blood come from a permitted state, unlike melikah.
The Gemara resolves that the common feature is that all are forbidden to commoners but permitted to the altar, yet the analogy fails because each has its own unique mitzvah.

items.text: Rav Ashi's binyan av from ba'al mum and yotzei dofen
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's binyan av from ba'al mum and yotzei dofen
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi proposes a binyan av from ba'al mum and yotzei dofen to prove tereifah is invalid. Rav Acha Saba objects that the common element (permitted to non-priests but forbidden to the altar) is not shared because ba'al mum was permitted in some cases. The Gemara then refutes the common element further.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proposes to derive the law from a ba'al mum (blemished animal).
The Gemara objects that ba'al mum has the unique feature that it allows substitutes to be offered.
Rav Acha Saba objects that a yotzei dofen (caesarean-born animal) is permitted to commoners but forbidden to the altar, breaking the analogy.
The Gemara objects that yotzei dofen is not sanctified as a firstborn.
The Gemara notes that ba'al mum and yotzei dofen each have unique features that prevent a clean analogy.
The Gemara resolves that the common feature is that all are permitted to commoners and forbidden to the altar, so tereifah should also be forbidden.
The Gemara objects that the common feature fails because tereifah has a permitted category within its class (melikah).

items.text: Rav Acha's challenge and final resolution
items.text_en: Rav Acha's challenge and final resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava challenges Rav Ashi's claim that tereifah was permitted in some cases, and the Gemara concludes that the real distinction is that the common element's defect is visible, unlike tereifah, so a verse is needed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava challenges Rav Ashi's claim that tereifah was permitted in some cases, questioning the meaning of 'permitted from its category' and rejecting the example of melikah of a bird burnt-offering.
Rav Ashi clarifies that the permitted case is melikah of a bird sin-offering for the priests, who eat from the table of the Most High.
The Gemara concludes that the real distinction is that the common element's defect is visible, unlike tereifah, so a verse is needed to exclude tereifah.

items.text: Source verses for tereifah disqualification
items.text_en: Source verses for tereifah disqualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites two verses that exclude tereifah from sacrifices: 'mimashkeh Yisrael' and 'kol asher ya'avor tachat hashavet'. It explains why both are necessary, covering cases where the animal was never fit or became tereifah after consecration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether tereifah is derived from here, and cites the verse 'מִמַּשְׁקֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל' (from what is permitted to Israel).
The Gemara cites the verse 'כֹּל אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבוֹר תַּחַת הַשָּׁבֶט' (all that passes under the rod) to exclude a tereifah that cannot pass.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution of the need for both verses
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the need for both verses
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both verses are needed: 'מִמַּשְׁקֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל' excludes an animal that never had a kosher moment, while 'כֹּל אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבוֹר' excludes one that became tereifah after sanctification.

The Gemara adds that if only 'כֹּל אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבוֹר' were written, one might think to exclude only an animal tereifah before sanctification, so 'מִן הַבָּקָר' is needed to exclude one tereifah after sanctification.

items.text: Mishnah: Disqualifications for kemitzah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Disqualifications for kemitzah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various invalidating conditions for the kemitzah of all meal-offerings, including improper personnel, improper state, improper position, and improper quantity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists invalidating factors for kemitzah (taking the handful) of all meal offerings.
The Mishnah states that kemitzah with the left hand is invalid, but Ben Beteira says he may return it and take again with the right.
The Mishnah lists invalidating conditions for extraneous items in the handful and defines excess and deficient kemitzah.

items.text: Gemara: Why mention minchat chotei separately?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why mention minchat chotei separately?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'one minchat chotei and all meal-offerings' instead of just saying 'all meal-offerings'. It answers that it is necessary for Rabbi Shimon's view, who holds that minchat chotei should logically require oil and frankincense but is exempted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'one minchat chotei and all meal offerings' instead of just saying 'all meal offerings'.
The Gemara answers that the specification is needed for Rabbi Shimon, who holds that minchat chotei differs in its requirement for oil and frankincense.

items.text: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah rules that a non-priest's kemitzah invalidates the offering, considering Rabbi Shimon's view that the sinner should not benefit. It suggests that even if the kemitzah is invalid, the offering might still be valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah rules that a non-priest's kemitzah invalidates the offering, given Rabbi Shimon's principle that the sinner should not benefit, and suggests that even invalid kemitzah might be acceptable.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah only needed to teach about Rabbi Shimon's view, it would have said 'except' rather than 'all'. Since it says 'all', it includes all disqualifications, not just Rabbi Shimon's case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah's ruling is only for Rabbi Shimon, it should have stated so explicitly in the parallel case of blood reception.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's use of 'כל' (all) implies it applies to all cases, not just Rabbi Shimon's view.

items.text: Refinement of the necessity
items.text_en: Refinement of the necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling is still necessary because one might think the first clause is not according to Rabbi Shimon, and therefore the latter clause also is not. The Mishnah teaches that it is indeed according to Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's ruling is necessary to prevent the assumption that the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Rav's ruling on a non-priest who performed kemitzah
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a non-priest who performed kemitzah
items.desc_en: Rav rules that if a non-priest performed kemitzah, he should return the handful. The Gemara questions the Mishnah's use of 'invalidated', and Rav explains it means 'invalidated until he returns it'.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that if a non-priest performed kemitzah, he should return the handful, and explains that 'invalidates' in the Mishnah means it is invalid until he returns it.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah says 'invalidated', not 'return'.
Rav explains that 'invalidated' means invalidated until he returns it.

items.text: Comparison with Ben Betera's ruling
items.text_en: Comparison with Ben Betera's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares Rav's ruling to Ben Betera's, who allows returning the handful if taken with the left hand. It clarifies that the dispute is only when the handful is lacking, and Rav's ruling applies to all disqualifications, not just the left hand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If Rav's ruling is that a זר (non-priest) who performed קמיצה (the handful removal) returns the handful, then this is identical to Ben Betera's ruling about the left hand — so what is Rav adding?
The Gemara clarifies: The dispute between the Rabbis and Ben Betera is only when the handful is lacking (חסר קומץ); if the handful is intact, even the Rabbis agree it may be returned.

The Gemara objects: If Rav's ruling is like Ben Betera, then Ben Betera requires returning and then re-performing the קמיצה with the right hand — Rav's ruling does not mention this, so they are not identical.
The Gemara resolves: Rav's ruling is indeed in line with Ben Betera, but it teaches that Ben Betera's leniency applies not only to the left hand but to all disqualifications, not just the left hand.

items.text: Distinction between left hand and non-priest
items.text_en: Distinction between left hand and non-priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the left hand is different, noting it is valid on Yom Kippur. It argues that a non-priest is also valid for slaughter. The Gemara responds that slaughter is not considered service, and cites Rabbi Zeira's ruling about the red heifer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the left hand is singled out for disqualification, given that it is valid on Yom Kippur, and notes that a non-priest is also valid for slaughter.
The Gemara answers that slaughter is not considered a service, so the non-priest's validity there does not apply to kemitzah.
The Gemara objects, citing Rabbi Zeira quoting Rav that slaughter of the red heifer by a non-priest is invalid, implying slaughter is a service.
The Gemara distinguishes the red heifer as קדשי בדק הבית (sanctified for Temple maintenance), which requires priesthood, unlike ordinary sacrifices.
The Gemara objects that if קדשי בדק הבית require priesthood, then קדשי מזבח (altar sanctified items) should certainly require it, undermining the distinction.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi answers that the red heifer is like the inspection of leprous signs, which is not a service but still requires priesthood, so the parallel fails.

items.text: Learning from the bamah (private altar)
items.text_en: Learning from the bamah (private altar)
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests learning from the bamah that a non-priest's kemitzah might be valid. It cites a baraita about one who leaves the Temple courtyard, and concludes that the Torah's verse 'This is the law of the burnt-offering' teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes learning from the bamah (private altar) that a non-priest's kemitzah might be valid.
The Gemara cites a baraita that a non-priest who left the courtyard may ascend the altar, proving that the bamah validates invalid persons.
The Gemara rejects the analogy, noting that the verse 'This is the law of the burnt-offering' is adjacent, teaching that the bamah's leniency does not apply to the Temple.

items.text: Ben Betera's leniency for all disqualifications
items.text_en: Ben Betera's leniency for all disqualifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav's novelty, citing a baraita that Ben Betera validates all disqualifications. It also cites a verse teaching that kemitzah can be done where a non-priest stands, and that the verse implies any disqualification is treated like the left hand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether without Rav's teaching, Ben Betera would have disqualified other disqualifications, citing a baraita that Ben Betera actually validates all disqualifications.
A baraita is cited stating that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon report that Ben Betera validates all disqualifications.
Another baraita is cited, teaching that the verse 'וְקָמַץ מִשָּׁם' (and he shall take a handful from there) indicates that kemitzah can be performed where a non-priest stands.
Ben Betera derives from the same verse that if one performed kemitzah with the left hand, he must return the handful and perform kemitzah again with the right hand.
The Gemara concludes that since the verse is written in a general manner, the same logic applies to the left hand and to all other disqualifications.

items.text: Rav's actual teaching: kemitzah even with sanctification
items.text_en: Rav's actual teaching: kemitzah even with sanctification
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rav's teaching is that even if the non-priest sanctified the handful in a vessel, it is valid. This excludes the view of Rabbi Yosei ben Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda the baker, who distinguish between kemitzah alone and kemitzah with sanctification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rav's teaching is that kemitzah is valid even if the non-priest sanctified the handful in a vessel, excluding the view of Rabbi Yosei ben Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda the baker who distinguish between kemitzah alone and kemitzah with sanctification.

items.text: Rav Nachman's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to the distinction between kemitzah and sanctification, arguing that if kemitzah by a non-priest is service, then even without sanctification it is invalid; if not, then sanctification does not matter. He resolves that kemitzah is service, but its completion requires sanctification in a vessel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to the Tannaim's position, arguing that if kemitzah by a non-priest is considered service, then even without sanctification in a vessel it should be invalid; if it is not service, then sanctification should not matter.
Rav Nachman resolves that kemitzah is indeed service, but its completion requires the act of sanctification in a vessel.
The Gemara objects that if kemitzah requires sanctification to complete it, then even without sanctification the kemitzah should be invalid, contradicting the Tannaim's distinction.

items.text: Opening question: returning the kometz to its place
items.text_en: Opening question: returning the kometz to its place
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the priest returns the kometz to its original vessel, does it sanctify the vessel and become invalid?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether returning the kometz to its original vessel sanctifies the vessel and invalidates the offering.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and Resh Lakish's query
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and Resh Lakish's query
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that service vessels only sanctify with intention. The Gemara objects from Resh Lakish's query: if service vessels can sanctify invalid offerings initially? Rabbi Yochanan answered they do not sanctify for sacrifice but do sanctify to become invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that service vessels (כלי שרת) only sanctify with intention (מדעת).
The Gemara objects: if intention is required, why did Resh Lakish ask whether vessels sanctify invalid offerings לכתחילה (the ideal standard), and Rabbi Yochanan answered they do not sanctify?
Rabbi Yochanan resolves: vessels do not sanctify invalid offerings for sacrifice (ליקרב), but they do sanctify them to become invalid (ליפסל).

items.text: Rav Amram's resolution and the mechanics of kemitzah
items.text_en: Rav Amram's resolution and the mechanics of kemitzah
items.desc_en: Rav Amram explains the case as returning the kometz to a heaped base. The Gemara questions how the kemitzah was performed, and resolves that it was a heaped base; after taking the handful, a depression is formed. When returning, the priest places it on the vessel's rim and tilts it so it falls by itself, like a monkey returning it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram explains the case as one where the priest returned the handful (קומץ) to a heaped base (ביסה גדושה), resolving the earlier difficulty.
The Gemara questions how the kemitzah (taking the handful) was performed in this scenario, since the base was heaped.
The Gemara answers that the case is actually one where the handful was returned to a heaped base (ביסה טפופה), clarifying the mechanics.
The Gemara resolves that after taking the handful, a depression is formed; when returning, the priest places it on the vessel's rim and tilts it so it falls by itself, like a monkey returning it.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's challenge and the story of Avimi
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's challenge and the story of Avimi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya suggests the case could be a vessel on the ground, but that raises the question of kemitzah from a vessel on the ground. Rabbi Zeira notes this touches on a known dilemma. The Gemara then recounts that Avimi studied Menachot in Rav Chisda's house, but his tractate was uprooted; he came to Rav Chisda to recall his learning, and Rav Chisda thought it more effective to go to him.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya proposes that the case could be a vessel on the ground, and then infers that this raises the question of whether one may perform kemitzah (קְמִיצָה) from a vessel on the ground.
Rabbi Zeira notes that Rabbi Yirmeya's question touches on a known dilemma, and mentions that Rabbi Avimi taught Menachot in Rav Chisda's house.

The Gemara objects that Avimi could not have taught in Rav Chisda's house, because Rav Chisda himself said he learned many 'sticks' (קוּלְפֵי) from Avimi regarding the ruling about announcing 'רצופין' (continuous days) for thirty or sixty days.

The Gemara resolves that Avimi's tractate was uprooted (he forgot his learning), so he came to Rav Chisda to recall it; Rav Chisda thought it more effective for Avimi to come to him rather than sending for him.

items.text: Rav Nachman's interrogation of Avimi
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's interrogation of Avimi
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Avimi how the kemitzah is performed and how the meal-offering is sanctified. Avimi answers that the priest lifts the vessel. Rav Nachman objects that this would require three priests; Avimi retorts that even thirteen would be needed, like the daily tamid offering.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Avimi how the kemitzah is performed, and Avimi answers that the priest lifts the vessel.
Rav Nachman asks how the meal-offering is sanctified, and Avimi again answers that the priest lifts the vessel.
Rav Nachman objects that this would require three priests, and Avimi retorts that even thirteen would be needed, like the daily tamid offering.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from the Mishnah's rule listing kemitzah, placing in a vessel, etc., but not mentioning lifting. The Gemara resolves that the Tanna lists the order of services, not the order of priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the Mishnah's rule listing kemitzah, placing in a vessel, conveying, and burning, but omitting lifting.
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna lists the order of services (סדר עבודות), not the order of priests (סדר כהנים), so lifting is not mentioned.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's practical ruling
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's practical ruling
items.desc_en: When asked whether one may take the handful from a vessel on the ground, Rav Sheshet says to go see what is done in practice: four priests enter with two loaves and two bowls, and four precede them to take them.

sub.desc_en: The questioners ask Rav Sheshet whether one may take the handful from a vessel placed on the ground.
Rav Sheshet tells them to observe the Temple practice: four priests enter with two loaves and two bowls, and four precede them to take them, implying the vessel is lifted.

items.text: Gemara's inference: kemitzah from a vessel on the ground
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: kemitzah from a vessel on the ground
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not mention lifting the table, implying that the kemitzah can be taken from a vessel resting on the ground. It rejects the counter-argument that the Mishnah only lists the order of services, because here it does list the number of priests. The conclusion is that the kemitzah is taken from a vessel on the ground.

items.text: Rava's certainty on kemitzah and sanctification from a vessel on the ground
items.text_en: Rava's certainty on kemitzah and sanctification from a vessel on the ground
items.desc_en: Rava states that it is obvious that the kemitzah can be taken from a vessel on the ground, as we find with the removal of the showbread pans. Similarly, sanctifying the meal-offering in a vessel on the ground is obvious from the arrangement of the showbread pans.

items.text: Rava's query on sanctification of the handful and his retraction
items.text_en: Rava's query on sanctification of the handful and his retraction
items.desc_en: Rava questions whether the sanctification of the handful is learned from the meal-offering or from blood. He resolves it from blood. However, this contradicts his earlier ruling that a handful divided between two vessels is sanctified, since if it were like blood, it would not be sanctified. Therefore, Rava retracts that earlier ruling.

items.text: Source that blood is not sanctified in halves and the query on its halakhic status
items.text_en: Source that blood is not sanctified in halves and the query on its halakhic status
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rav Tachlifa ben Shaul that blood sanctified in two vessels for less than a full sprinkling is not sanctified. It then raises a query: is this a halakha from which we cannot learn, or is it derived from the verse 'and dip in the blood'?

items.text: Rabbi Zerika's ruling and the derivation from verses
items.text_en: Rabbi Zerika's ruling and the derivation from verses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika quoting Rabbi Elazar rules that even blood is not sanctified in halves. Rava cites a supporting baraita: 'And dip' implies no wiping. The verse 'in the blood' requires that there be sufficient blood for dipping from the start, and 'from the blood' means from the blood of the matter.

items.text: Exegesis of 'and dip' and 'in the blood', and the exclusion of remnants on the finger
items.text_en: Exegesis of 'and dip' and 'in the blood', and the exclusion of remnants on the finger
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both 'and dip' and 'in the blood' are necessary: 'and dip' alone would imply even without sufficient blood for multiple dippings, so 'in the blood' requires initial sufficiency; 'in the blood' alone would imply even with wiping, so 'and dip' prohibits wiping. 'From the blood' excludes remnants on the finger, supporting Rabbi Elazar's view that remnants on the finger are invalid.

items.text: Discussion on remnants on the finger and wiping after sprinkling
items.text_en: Discussion on remnants on the finger and wiping after sprinkling
items.desc_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda reports a baraita about sprinkling where if the sprinkling was not yet completed, the garment requires washing; if completed, it does not. The Gemara debates whether this refers to before or after the act. Abaye cites a baraita that after finishing sprinkling, one wipes his hand on the cow's body, implying that before finishing, he wipes his finger. The Gemara concludes that the finger does not require wiping, and Abaye suggests wiping on the rim of the bowl, as per the verse 'golden bowls'.

items.text: Contradiction regarding Rabbi Elazar's view on the High Priest's griddle-cakes
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding Rabbi Elazar's view on the High Priest's griddle-cakes
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Elazar ruled that blood is not sanctified in halves, but elsewhere he ruled that the High Priest's griddle-cakes are sanctified in halves because they are offered in halves. This suggests a different principle.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Elazar learn from blood to meal-offering?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Elazar learn from blood to meal-offering?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Elazar would derive laws from blood to a meal-offering, given that he learns from the showbread arrangement. It answers that he learns from meal-offering to meal-offering, not from blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Elazar would learn from blood to a meal-offering, and answers that he learns from meal-offering to meal-offering, not from blood.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about showbread and Rabbi Elazar's explanation
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about showbread and Rabbi Elazar's explanation
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if the showbread was broken before the time of removal, the bread is invalid and the frankincense is not offered; after the time, the bread is invalid but the frankincense is offered. Rabbi Elazar explains that once the time for removal arrives, it is considered as if removed. The Gemara objects that this should be like a meal-offering that lacked a handful before the kemitzah, but resolves that the handful is designated, and once the time arrives, it is as if removed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Elazar's method of learning from one meal-offering to another, citing a baraita that seems to contradict it.

The baraita rules that if showbread was broken before the time of removal, the bread is invalid and the frankincense is not offered; after the time, the bread is invalid but the frankincense is offered.
Rabbi Elazar explains that once the time for removal arrives, it is considered as if the bread was already removed, even if not physically removed.
The Gemara objects that this should be like a meal-offering that lacked a handful before the kemitzah (handful removal), which would invalidate the offering.
The Gemara resolves that the handful is designated, and once the time for removal arrives, it is considered as if removed, unlike a meal-offering where the handful is not yet designated.

items.text: Further objection: Should it be like remnants that were lost?
items.text_en: Further objection: Should it be like remnants that were lost?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case should be like remnants that were lost between kemitzah and burning, where the handful is not offered. It notes that this is a dispute, and Rabbi Elazar follows the opinion that the handful is offered even if remnants are lost.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the showbread is different because its handful (the frankincense) is already designated, unlike a regular meal-offering where the handful is not yet selected.
The Gemara answers that this is a dispute, and Rabbi Elazar follows the opinion that the handful is offered even if remnants are lost.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar on half-offerings of the High Priest's griddle-cakes
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar on half-offerings of the High Priest's griddle-cakes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says the High Priest's griddle-cake offering is not sanctified in halves; Rabbi Elazar says it is. Rabbi Acha explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning from the verse 'mincha machatzitah' — bring a complete offering and then halve it. A baraita supports this, teaching that one must bring a full tenth-ephah and halve it, not bring half from home.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says the High Priest's griddle-cakes (חֲבִיתֵּי כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל) are not sanctified in halves, while Rabbi Elazar says they are sanctified in halves because they are offered in halves.

Rabbi Acha explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: the verse 'מִנְחָה מַחֲצִיתָהּ' (a meal-offering, its half) teaches that one must bring a complete offering and then halve it, not bring half from the start.

A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan: the griddle-cakes were not brought in halves; one brings a full tenth-ephah and halves it, and the verse 'מַחֲצִיתָהּ בַּבֹּקֶר' teaches that he brings half from a complete offering, not half from home.

items.text: Clarification: The requirement is only for the mitzvah
items.text_en: Clarification: The requirement is only for the mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rav Geviha from Bei Katil tells Rav Ashi that the requirement to bring a full tenth-ephah is only for the mitzvah, not for validity, because the verse 'chukah' is written. Rav Ashi explains that the verse is needed to require bringing it whole from home.

sub.desc_en: Rav Geviha miBei Ketil asks Rav Ashi: since the verse says 'חוקה' (a statute), doesn't that imply the requirement is essential for validity, not just for the mitzvah?
Rav Ashi answers that the verse 'חוקה' is only needed to require bringing the tenth-ephah whole from home, not to make the requirement essential for validity.

items.text: Contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan's view on half-tenth-ephah with intent to add
items.text_en: Contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan's view on half-tenth-ephah with intent to add
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan said that if one set aside half a tenth-ephah with intent to add, it is sanctified, but here he requires a full tenth-ephah. The Gemara answers that the case of intent to add is different, based on a baraita about 'male'im' (full) and Rabbi Yosei's distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's consistency, citing a case where he ruled that half a tenth-ephah set aside with intent to add is sanctified, contradicting his requirement of a full tenth-ephah for the High Priest's griddle-cakes.

The Gemara rejects the possibility that Rabbi Yochanan does not learn one case from another, citing his own ruling that peace-offerings slaughtered in the Temple courtyard are valid, derived from the principle that the secondary should not be stricter than the primary.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the case of intent to add, citing a baraita that interprets 'מלאים' (full) and Rabbi Yosei's ruling that when one intends to add, each half-tenth-ephah is sanctified individually.

items.text: Rav's position: Does he follow Rabbi Elazar or Rabbi Yochanan?
items.text_en: Rav's position: Does he follow Rabbi Elazar or Rabbi Yochanan?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav follows Rabbi Elazar, who would learn from the griddle-cakes that half is sanctified. But Rav learns from other offerings that a meal-offering is sanctified without oil or frankincense, so he must follow Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which authority Rav follows regarding the griddle-cakes, and notes that if he follows Rabbi Elazar, he should learn from the griddle-cakes that half is sanctified.
