The Gemara begins to challenge this logic with a baraita, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Opening case: kilayim and the kal vachomer challenge
items.text_en: Opening case: kilayim and the kal vachomer challenge
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes a case where one planted another's vineyard with immature vines, and the Sages prohibited the seeds but permitted the vines. The Gemara questions why a kal vachomer argument is not applied: if the one who prohibits (the planter) is not prohibited, then the one who comes to prohibit and did not prohibit (the vineyard owner) should certainly not be prohibited. The Gemara answers that the case involves kambos and luf, which are Torah-prohibited, while other seeds are Rabbinically prohibited; the Sages penalized the one who committed the transgression but not the one who did not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one planted another's vineyard with immature vines, and the Sages prohibited the seeds but permitted the vines.

The Gemara questions why a kal vachomer argument is not applied: if the one who prohibits (the planter) is not prohibited, then the one who comes to prohibit and did not prohibit (the vineyard owner) should certainly not be prohibited.

The Gemara answers that the case involves kambos and luf, which are Torah-prohibited, while other seeds are Rabbinically prohibited; the Sages penalized the one who committed the transgression but not the one who did not.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's question about piggul with the lambs and bread
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question about piggul with the lambs and bread
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rav: if one slaughters the lambs of the Nazirite's offering with intent to eat an olive's bulk from them and from their bread the next day, what is the law? He clarifies that he is not asking about the lambs becoming piggul (since if intent on the bread alone does not piggul the lambs, certainly intent on both does not), but rather whether the lambs combine with the bread to piggul the bread. Rav answers that in this case, the bread is piggul and the lambs are not. The Gemara then questions why a kal vachomer is not applied: if the one who pigguls (the bread) is not pigguled, then the one who comes to piggul and did not piggul (the lambs) should certainly not be pigguled.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rav: if one slaughters the lambs of the Nazirite's offering with intent to eat an olive's bulk from them and from their bread the next day, what is the law?

Rabbi Elazar clarifies that he is not asking about the lambs becoming piggul (since if intent on the bread alone does not piggul the lambs, certainly intent on both does not), but rather whether the lambs combine with the bread to piggul the bread.
Rav answers that in this case, the bread is piggul and the lambs are not.

The Gemara objects: why not apply a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) — if the one who pigguls (the bread) is not pigguled, then the one who comes to piggul and did not piggul (the lambs) should certainly not be pigguled?

items.text: Gemara's objection: kal vachomer is not applied in such cases
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: kal vachomer is not applied in such cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: do we apply a kal vachomer of this type? It cites the earlier case of kilayim where the kal vachomer was rejected. The Gemara repeats the distinction: there, kambos and luf are Torah-prohibited, while other seeds are Rabbinically prohibited; the Sages penalized the one who transgressed but not the one who did not. But here (regarding piggul), the kal vachomer should apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) of this type is applied, citing a baraita about kilayim (mixed seeds) where such an argument was rejected.

The Gemara distinguishes the kilayim case: there, kambos and luf are Torah-prohibited while other seeds are Rabbinically prohibited, so the Sages penalized the transgressor but not the non-transgressor; but here (regarding piggul), the kal vachomer should apply.

items.text: Distinction between the versions: lambs vs. todah
items.text_en: Distinction between the versions: lambs vs. todah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the one who teaches the kal vachomer regarding the todah offering would certainly apply it to the lambs, but the one who teaches it regarding the lambs holds that only lambs, which are bound to each other for waving, are subject to the kal vachomer, but the todah, whose components are not bound for waving, is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute between the two versions of the kal vachomer: the one who teaches it regarding the todah (תודה) would apply it all the more so to the lambs (כבשים), but the one who teaches it regarding the lambs limits it to lambs because they are bound to each other for waving (תנופה), unlike the todah whose components are not bound for waving.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's second question: intent on the fellow lamb
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's second question: intent on the fellow lamb
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba Zuti presents a version where Rabbi Elazar asks Rav: if one slaughters the lamb with intent to eat an olive's bulk from its fellow lamb the next day, what is the law? Does 'its fellow' mean the lamb, and thus not piggul, or does it mean the bread, and thus piggul? Rav answers that they have already learned a baraita: if one slaughtered one of the lambs to eat from it the next day, it is piggul and its fellow is valid; if to eat from its fellow the next day, both are valid. This shows that 'its fellow' means the lamb. The Gemara questions whether this is conclusive, perhaps he specified 'its fellow lamb'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rav: if one slaughters the lamb with intent to eat an olive's bulk from its fellow the next day, does 'its fellow' mean the lamb (so no piggul) or the bread (so piggul)?
Rav cites a baraita: if one slaughtered one lamb to eat from it the next day, it is piggul and its fellow is valid; if to eat from its fellow, both are valid, proving 'its fellow' means the lamb.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the baraita refers to a case where the slaughterer explicitly specified 'its fellow lamb', so it does not prove the general meaning of 'its fellow'.

items.text: Mishnah: the offering pigguls its libations, but not vice versa
items.text_en: Mishnah: the offering pigguls its libations, but not vice versa
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the offering pigguls its libations once they are sanctified in a vessel, according to Rabbi Meir, but libations do not piggul the offering. Examples are given: if one slaughters the offering to eat from it the next day, it and its libations are piggul; if one intends to offer the libations the next day, only the libations are piggul. The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir says libations are subject to piggul because the blood of the offering permits them to be offered. The Sages object that one can bring the offering today and its libations up to ten days later. Rabbi Meir responds that he only meant when they come with the offering. The Sages counter that one can change them to another offering. Rava explains that Rabbi Meir holds that libations are fixed by the slaughter, like the bread of the todah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the offering pigguls its libations once sanctified in a vessel, according to Rabbi Meir, but libations do not piggul the offering, and gives examples.
A baraita cites Rabbi Meir's position that libations are subject to piggul because the blood of the offering permits them to be offered.

The Sages object that one can bring the offering today and its libations up to ten days later, and Rabbi Meir responds that he only meant when they come with the offering, but the Sages counter that one can change them to another offering.
Rava explains that Rabbi Meir holds that libations are fixed by the slaughter, like the bread of the todah.

items.text: Parallel case: the log of oil of the metzora
items.text_en: Parallel case: the log of oil of the metzora
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the log of oil of the metzora is subject to piggul because the blood of the guilt-offering permits it for the thumb and big toe, according to Rabbi Meir. The Sages object that one can bring the guilt-offering today and the log up to ten days later. Rabbi Meir responds that he only meant when it comes with the guilt-offering. The Sages counter that one can change it to another guilt-offering. Rava again explains that Rabbi Meir holds that the log is fixed by the slaughter, like the bread of the todah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the log of oil of the metzora is subject to piggul because the blood of the guilt-offering permits it for the thumb and big toe, according to Rabbi Meir.
The Sages object that one can bring the guilt-offering today and the log up to ten days later.
Rabbi Meir responds that he only meant when it comes with the guilt-offering, and the Sages counter that one can change it to another guilt-offering.
Rava explains that Rabbi Meir holds that the log is fixed by the slaughter, like the bread of the todah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on partial piggul
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on partial piggul
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: if one had piggul intent for the handful (קומץ) but not the frankincense (לבונה), or vice versa, Rabbi Meir holds it is piggul and one is liable for karet, while the Sages require piggul intent in all permitting factors. They agree that in the case of a sin-offering meal offering or a jealousy offering, the handful alone is the permitting factor. Additional cases involve the two loaves and the showbread.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding piggul intent for the handful or frankincense alone.
The Mishnah notes that the Sages agree with Rabbi Meir regarding the sin-offering meal offering and jealousy offering, where the handful alone is the permitting factor.
The Mishnah presents a second case: slaughtering one lamb with intent to eat two loaves the next day, with the same dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages.
The Mishnah concludes with a ruling on slaughtering one lamb with intent to eat from it the next day, where it is piggul but the companion is valid, and intent for the companion leaves both valid.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel on the dispute's scope
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel on the dispute's scope
items.desc_en: Rav limits the Mishnah's dispute to a case where the handful was given in silence and the frankincense with intent, but if the handful was given with intent and the frankincense in silence, all agree it is piggul because one acts based on initial intent. Shmuel holds the dispute remains even in that case.

sub.desc_en: Rav limits the Mishnah's dispute to a case where the handful was given in silence and the frankincense with intent; but if the handful was given with intent and the frankincense in silence, all agree it is piggul because one acts based on initial intent.
Shmuel holds that the dispute remains even in the case where the handful was given with intent and the frankincense in silence.

items.text: Rava's teaching challenged and resolved
items.text_en: Rava's teaching challenged and resolved
items.desc_en: Rava teaches this tradition, and Rav Acha bar Rav Huna challenges him with a baraita that explicitly states a dispute when the handful is given with intent and the frankincense in silence. The Gemara initially suggests the baraita refers to a case where the frankincense was already given in silence beforehand, but two refutations are raised, including that the baraita says 'afterwards'. Rav Chanina resolves it by interpreting the baraita as referring to two separate opinions (שתי דיעות).

sub.desc_en: Rava sits and teaches the tradition about the dispute regarding intent in the handful and frankincense.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna challenges Rava by citing a baraita that explicitly states a dispute when the handful is given with intent and the frankincense in silence, contradicting Rava's position.
The Gemara initially suggests that the baraita refers to a case where the frankincense was already given in silence beforehand, so the later intent on the handful is not affected.

The Gemara raises two refutations: first, that this is the same as the earlier case, and second, that the baraita explicitly says 'afterwards', indicating the frankincense was given after the handful.
Rav Chanina resolves the difficulty by interpreting the baraita as referring to two separate opinions (שתי דיעות), not a single sequence of actions.

items.text: Challenge from inner altar blood cases
items.text_en: Challenge from inner altar blood cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about blood placed on the inner altar (e.g., Yom Kippur, anointed priest's bull, community bull). There, Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute even when piggul occurs in only one of the three applications. The Gemara tries to apply the 'two opinions' explanation, but questions it for the view that 'בְּפַר' means the bull itself, not its blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that distinguishes between blood placed on the outer altar and blood placed on the inner altar.
The baraita states that for inner altar blood (Yom Kippur, anointed priest's bull, community bull), Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute piggul even when it occurs in only one of the three applications.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that the dispute applies even when piggul occurs in only one application, challenging the 'two opinions' explanation.

The Gemara objects that the 'two opinions' explanation works only for the view that 'בְּפַר' includes the bull's blood, but not for the view that 'בְּפַר' excludes the blood, leaving the challenge unresolved.

items.text: Rava and Rav Ashi's resolutions
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Ashi's resolutions
items.desc_en: Rava explains the baraita as a case where one had piggul intent in the first and third applications but was silent in the second, arguing that if all actions follow initial intent, the third piggul is unnecessary. Rav Ashi objects that the baraita does not mention silence, and instead explains it as piggul in all three, questioning why multiple piggul intents are needed if all follow the first.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains the baraita as a case where one had piggul intent in the first and third applications but was silent in the second, arguing that if all actions follow initial intent, the third piggul is unnecessary.
Rav Ashi objects that the baraita does not mention silence, and instead explains it as piggul in all three, questioning why multiple piggul intents are needed if all follow the first.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that Rabbi Meir holds piggul and liability for karet, noting that karet only applies when all the permitting factors have been offered. It explains that once the handful is invalidated by improper intent inside the Sanctuary, any subsequent sprinkling of water in the Sanctuary is meaningless.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's phrase 'בין בין' (whether inside or outside) implies a contradiction, and declares it a difficulty.
Mar explains that Rabbi Meir's ruling of piggul and karet applies only when all the permitting factors (מתכירין) have been offered, as karet requires that.
Mar cites the principle that the term 'יֵרָצֶה' (it shall be accepted) applies equally to valid and invalid offerings, requiring all permitting factors to be offered in both cases.
The Gemara resolves that since the improper intent (מחשבה) invalidated the handful inside the Sanctuary, the subsequent sprinkling of water in the Sanctuary is merely meaningless water.

items.text: Rabbah and Rava's resolutions regarding the number of bulls and goats
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rava's resolutions regarding the number of bulls and goats
items.desc_en: Rabbah suggests the Mishnah can be found with four bulls and four goats, while Rava argues it can even be with one bull and one goat. The Gemara then addresses contradictions in the numbers of bulls and goats (43, 47, 48) by attributing them to disputes about mixing horns and whether the remnants (shirayim) are essential.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah proposes that the Mishnah's case can be found with four bulls and four goats.
Rava argues that even one bull and one goat suffice for the Mishnah's case.
The Gemara raises a contradiction between 43 and 47 bulls and goats, resolving it by attributing the difference to a dispute about mixing horns.
The Gemara raises another contradiction with 48 bulls and goats, resolving it by attributing the difference to a dispute about whether the remnants (שיריים) are essential.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on holakhah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on holakhah
items.desc_en: An inquiry is raised: if one had improper intent during the carrying (holakhah) of the handful, what is the law? Rabbi Yochanan holds that holakhah is like kemitzah (taking the handful), while Reish Lakish holds it is like haqtarah (offering). Rava explains that Rabbi Yochanan considers any service that is not a permitting factor to be a significant service that can cause piggul on its own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: if one had improper intent during the carrying (holakhah) of the handful, what is the law?
Rabbi Yochanan rules that holakhah is like kemitzah (taking the handful), while Reish Lakish rules it is like haqtarah (offering).
The Gemara objects: for Reish Lakish, there is also the holakhah of frankincense, but what is Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning?
Rava explains that Rabbi Yochanan considers any service that is not a permitting factor to be a significant service that can cause piggul on its own.

items.text: Abaye's objection and Rava's response regarding the slaughter of one lamb
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and Rava's response regarding the slaughter of one lamb
items.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing a Mishnah where slaughtering one of the lambs for the two loaves is a non-permitting service, yet Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute whether piggul applies. Rava responds that the bread is not sanctified in the oven; rather, the slaughter of the lambs sanctifies it, so the one who comes to sanctify is like one who comes to permit.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing a Mishnah where slaughtering one of the lambs for the two loaves is a non-permitting service, yet Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute whether piggul applies.
Abaye cites the Mishnah detailing the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding piggul from slaughtering one lamb.
Rava responds that the bread is not sanctified in the oven; rather, the slaughter of the lambs sanctifies it, so the one who comes to sanctify is like one who comes to permit.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's objection and Rava's response regarding circumcised and uncircumcised
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's objection and Rava's response regarding circumcised and uncircumcised
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi cites a baraita where others say that if one offered the circumcised before the uncircumcised, it is valid, but the reverse is invalid. The Gemara notes they dispute about half a permitting factor. Rava responds that the blood is not sanctified in the animal's neck; rather, the knife sanctifies it, so the one who comes to sanctify is like one who comes to permit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects by citing a baraita where 'Others' rule that offering circumcised before uncircumcised is valid, but the reverse is invalid.
Rava responds that the blood is not sanctified in the animal's neck; rather, the knife sanctifies it, so the one who comes to sanctify is like one who comes to permit.

items.text: Gemara's attempt to resolve the dispute from a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's attempt to resolve the dispute from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that lists kemitzah, placing in a vessel, and holakhah as services where piggul applies. It attempts to interpret holakhah as that of the offering, but is rejected. It then suggests holakhah of placing in a vessel, but notes a textual issue. Finally, it raises a difficulty from the phrase 'came to offer' instead of 'came to carry', and from 'placed in silence' instead of 'carried', concluding with a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing kemitzah, placing in a vessel, and holakhah as services where piggul applies.
The Gemara asks whether 'holakhah' in the baraita refers to the carrying of the offering to the altar for burning (הקטרה).
The Gemara rejects this interpretation, suggesting 'holakhah' refers to carrying the vessel containing the handful to the altar.
The Gemara objects that if 'holakhah' means carrying the vessel, the baraita should list 'placing in a vessel and carrying' rather than 'carrying and placing in a vessel'.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita simply teaches the order in this way, and the textual order is not a problem.
The Gemara objects that the baraita says 'came to offer' (הקטרה) instead of 'came to carry' (הולכה).
The Gemara resolves that since carrying is necessary for offering, the baraita calls it 'offering'.
The Gemara objects that the baraita says 'placed the handful in silence' instead of 'carried in silence'.
The Gemara concludes that the difficulty remains unresolved.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Chisda, Rav Hamnuna, and Rav Sheshet regarding offering a sesame-sized portion
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Chisda, Rav Hamnuna, and Rav Sheshet regarding offering a sesame-sized portion
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: if one offered a sesame-sized portion with intent to eat a sesame-sized portion until the whole handful is consumed, one says piggul, one says invalid, and one says valid. It attempts to align these with Rabbi Meir, the Sages, and Rabbi Eliezer, but rejects each alignment. It concludes that each opinion is the view of all, based on whether the action is a normal way of eating or offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute of Rav Chisda, Rav Hamnuna, and Rav Sheshet regarding offering a sesame-sized portion with intent to eat a sesame-sized portion: one says piggul, one says invalid, one says valid.
The Gemara proposes aligning each opinion with a known Tanna: piggul with Rabbi Meir, invalid with the Sages, valid with Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara rejects the alignment with Rabbi Meir, arguing that Rabbi Meir's position there applies only when he thought about the full measure, but here he did not think about the full measure.

The Gemara rejects the alignment with the Sages, arguing that their position there applies only when he did not think about the entire permitting factor, but here he did think about the entire permitting factor, so they would agree it is piggul.

The Gemara rejects the alignment with Rabbi Eliezer, arguing that his position there applies only when he did not complete the offering from that same service, but here he did complete it from that same service, so he would agree it is invalid.
The Gemara concludes that each opinion is the view of all, based on whether the action is a normal way of eating or offering.

The Gemara explains: the one who says piggul holds that this is a normal way of eating and offering; the one who says invalid holds that it is not a normal way of eating or offering, so it is like a meal-offering that was not offered; the one who says valid holds that it is a normal way of offering but not a normal way of eating.

items.text: Opening statement: The sharp ones of Pumbedita assert that הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה even for Rabbanan
items.text_en: Opening statement: The sharp ones of Pumbedita assert that הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה even for Rabbanan
items.desc_en: The sharp scholars of Pumbedita claim that the act of offering (הקטרה) can cause piggul for another offering (הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה), and this applies even according to the Rabbanan who hold that one cannot cause piggul with a half-permitter. They distinguish this case because here the thought was about the frankincense (לבונה), which is considered as if thought about the entire permitter.

sub.desc_en: The sharp scholars of Pumbedita assert that the act of offering (הקטרה) can cause piggul for another offering (הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה), even according to the Rabbanan who deny piggul with a half-permitter, because here the thought was about the frankincense (לבונה), which is considered as if thought about the entire permitter.

items.text: Rava cites a Mishnah to support the claim, but is rejected
items.text_en: Rava cites a Mishnah to support the claim, but is rejected
items.desc_en: Rava cites a Mishnah (the general rule about piggul) to support the idea that הקטרה can cause piggul for both eating and offering. The Gemara initially assumes the Mishnah implies this, but then rejects the proof, distinguishing between the cases: the Mishnah's rule applies to both eating and offering, but the case of הקטרה only applies to eating, not to offering.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a Mishnah (the general rule about piggul) to support the claim that הקטרה can cause piggul for both eating and offering.
The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah implies that הקטרה (offering) is analogous to the other acts, applying to both eating and offering.
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing that the Mishnah's rule applies to both eating and offering, but the case of הקטרה only applies to eating, not to offering.

items.text: Rav Menashya bar Gadda cites Rav Chisda: אין הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה even for Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda cites Rav Chisda: אין הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה even for Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda, sitting before Abaye, reports in the name of Rav Chisda that there is no concept of הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה, and this applies even according to Rabbi Meir who holds that one can cause piggul with a half-permitter. The reason is that the handful (קומץ) is not the permitter for the frankincense (לבונה), so one cannot cause piggul through it.

sub.text: Rav Menashya bar Gadda citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda, sitting before Abaye, reports in Rav Chisda's name that there is no concept of הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה (offering piggul through offering), and this applies even according to Rabbi Meir.

He explains that Rabbi Meir's principle of מפגלין בחצי מתיר (piggul with a half-permitter) applies only where the thought is about the leftovers (שיריים), whose permitter is the handful (קומץ), but here the handful is not the permitter for the frankincense (לבונה), so one cannot cause piggul through it.

items.text: Abaye asks if this is from Rav, and it is confirmed
items.text_en: Abaye asks if this is from Rav, and it is confirmed
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Menashya bar Gadda if he heard this from Rav himself. He confirms yes, and it is also stated that Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav: אין הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Menashya bar Gadda whether the statement he just made was heard from Rav himself, and Rav Menashya confirms it.
The gemara adds that it was also stated explicitly: Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav that 'no burning (הקטרה) can render another burning piggul (מפגלת).'

items.text: Rav Yaakov bar Idi cites a Mishnah about the two lambs, but is rejected
items.text_en: Rav Yaakov bar Idi cites a Mishnah about the two lambs, but is rejected
items.desc_en: Rav Yaakov bar Idi cites a Mishnah in the name of Abaye: if one slaughtered one of the two lambs (of the Shavuot offering) with intent to eat from it the next day, it is piggul but its fellow is valid; if he intended to eat from its fellow the next day, both are valid. The Gemara suggests this proves that one cannot cause piggul through something that is not its permitter. However, the Gemara rejects this: there the two lambs are not established in one vessel, but here the frankincense and the handful are in one vessel, so they are considered one.

sub.text: Rav Yaakov bar Idi citing Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Yaakov bar Idi citing Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov bar Idi cites a Mishnah in Abaye's name: if one slaughtered one of the two Shavuot lambs with intent to eat from it the next day, it is piggul but its fellow is valid; if he intended to eat from its fellow, both are valid, implying that one cannot cause piggul through something that is not its permitter.
The Gemara rejects the proof: there the two lambs are not established in one vessel, but here the frankincense and the handful are in one vessel, so they are considered one entity.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna reports a difficult ruling from Rabbi Chanina, and Rav Adda bar Ahava resolves it
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna reports a difficult ruling from Rabbi Chanina, and Rav Adda bar Ahava resolves it
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna reports that Rabbi Chanina taught him a difficult ruling: if one offered the handful (קומץ) with intent to offer the frankincense (לבונה) the next day, and the frankincense with intent to eat the remainder (שיריים) the next day, it is piggul. The Gemara questions what new teaching this provides. Rav Adda bar Ahava resolves that the case is unique because the thought (מחשבה) spreads over the entire minchah, even though generally there is no הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה and no piggul with a half-permitter.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna reports a difficult ruling from Rabbi Chanina: if one offered the handful (קומץ) with intent to offer the frankincense (לבונה) the next day, and the frankincense with intent to eat the remainder (שיריים) the next day, it is piggul.

The Gemara questions what new teaching this ruling provides, noting that it could be teaching either that הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה (offering pigguls offering) or that one can be liable for piggul with a half-permitter (חצי מתיר), but the case combines both elements.

Rav Adda bar Ahava resolves that the case is unique because the thought (מחשבה) spreads over the entire minchah, even though generally there is no הקטרה מפגלת הקטרה and no piggul with a half-permitter.

items.text: A Tanna teaches before Rav Yitzchak bar Abba: according to all, it is invalid, and the text is corrected
items.text_en: A Tanna teaches before Rav Yitzchak bar Abba: according to all, it is invalid, and the text is corrected
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav Yitzchak bar Abba: if one offered the handful with intent to eat the remainder, according to all it is piggul. The Gemara objects: but they disagree? Rather, say: according to all it is invalid (פסול). The Gemara then questions why the Tanna did not simply say 'this is piggul and it is Rabbi Meir's view,' and explains that the Tanna confused the terms 'piggul' and 'pasul' but did not confuse 'this is' with 'according to all.'

sub.text: Tanna before Rav Yitzchak bar Abba
sub.text_en: Tanna before Rav Yitzchak bar Abba
sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav Yitzchak bar Abba that if one offered the handful with intent to eat the remainder, according to all it is piggul.
The Gemara objects: but the rabbis and Rabbi Meir disagree on this point?
The Gemara resolves: rather, say 'according to all it is invalid (פסול).'
The Gemara asks: why not simply say 'this is piggul and it is Rabbi Meir's view'?
The Gemara answers: the Tanna confused the terms 'piggul' and 'pasul' but did not confuse 'this is' with 'according to all.'

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter: הדרן עלך הקומץ את המנחה
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter: הדרן עלך הקומץ את המנחה
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך הקומץ את המנחה' (we return to you, chapter 'The one who takes a handful of the minchah').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך הקומץ את המנחה' (we return to you, chapter 'The one who takes a handful of the minchah').

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of intent for non-standard items and less than a kezayit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of intent for non-standard items and less than a kezayit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If one takes a handful of the minchah with intent to eat something not normally eaten or to offer something not normally offered, it is valid; Rabbi Eliezer invalidates. If one intends to eat something normally eaten or to offer something normally offered but less than a kezayit, it is valid. If one intends to eat half a kezayit and offer half a kezayit, it is valid, because eating and offering do not combine.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of intent for non-standard items: the handful is valid, but Rabbi Eliezer invalidates.
The Mishnah continues with cases of intent for standard items less than a kezayit and half a kezayit each, all valid.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Asi cites Rabbi Yochanan explaining Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning from a verse
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Asi cites Rabbi Yochanan explaining Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning from a verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is from the verse 'ואם האכל יאכל מבשר זבח שלמיו' – the verse speaks of two eatings: one is human eating and the other is altar eating (offering). This teaches that just as one can cause piggul through human eating, so too through altar eating; and just as one can cause piggul from human eating to human eating and from altar eating to altar eating, so too from human eating to altar eating and from altar eating to human eating. The reason is that the Torah expressed offering (הקטרה) in the language of eating. The Rabbis, however, explain the verse differently.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan asks what is Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning, and explains that the verse 'ואם האכל יאכל מבשר זבח שלמיו' speaks of two eatings: human eating and altar eating.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that just as one can cause piggul from human eating to human eating and from altar eating to altar eating, so too from human eating to altar eating and from altar eating to human eating.
The gemara explains that the reason is because the Torah expressed offering (הקטרה) in the language of eating.
The gemara notes that the Rabbis explain the same verse differently.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the comparison between eating and burning
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the comparison between eating and burning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the comparison between eating and burning is consistent whether one thinks in terms of eating for the altar or burning for the altar, and that just as eating requires an olive's bulk, so too burning requires an olive's bulk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the comparison between eating and burning is consistent whether one thinks in terms of eating for the altar or burning for the altar, and that just as eating requires an olive's bulk, so too burning requires an olive's bulk.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's inference from the doubled verb
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's inference from the doubled verb
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that the Torah's use of the doubled form 'הֵאָכֹל יֵאָכֵל' teaches two things: both eating and burning, and the measure of an olive's bulk.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer infers from the doubled verb 'הֵאָכֹל יֵאָכֵל' that the Torah teaches two things: both eating and burning, and the measure of an olive's bulk.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's question and Rav Asi's answer about karet
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question and Rav Asi's answer about karet
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Asi: if Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is based on this, should he also impose karet? Rav Asi responds that there is a dispute among Tannaim regarding Rabbi Eliezer's view, with some holding the disqualification is biblical and others rabbinic.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Asi: if Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is based on the double language, should he also impose karet (excision), despite Rav Asi's earlier statement that Rabbi Eliezer concedes there is no karet penalty?

Rav Asi responds that the matter is disputed among Tannaim regarding Rabbi Eliezer's view: some hold the disqualification is biblical (דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא) and would impose karet, while others hold it is rabbinic (דְּרַבָּנַן) and carries no karet.

items.text: Baraita about slaughtering with improper intent
items.text_en: Baraita about slaughtering with improper intent
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who slaughters a sacrifice with intent to drink its blood, burn its flesh, or eat its fats the next day is valid, but Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies. Rabbi Yehuda disqualifies intent to leave its blood for the next day, and Rabbi Elazar adds that Rabbi Eliezer also disqualifies this while the Sages validate.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that slaughtering a sacrifice with intent to drink its blood, burn its flesh, or eat its fats the next day is valid.
Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies the sacrifice in all these cases.
Rabbi Yehuda disqualifies intent to leave the blood for the next day.
Rabbi Elazar adds that Rabbi Eliezer also disqualifies intent to leave the blood, while the Sages validate.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's position and the dispute about karet
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's position and the dispute about karet
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's view: if he follows the Sages, his ruling is redundant; if he follows Rabbi Eliezer, then Rabbi Elazar's statement is identical. The Gemara suggests that the difference between them is whether karet applies, but then rejects this, concluding that there is no karet and the dispute is about three positions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to whose position does Rabbi Yehuda rule? If it is according to the Sages, then his ruling is redundant, since they permit even explicit thought of eating.
The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Eliezer, but then objects that Rabbi Elazar's statement would be identical to Rabbi Yehuda's.

The Gemara proposes that the difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar is whether karet applies: Rabbi Yehuda holds that there is liability for karet, while Rabbi Elazar says there is no karet.
The Gemara rejects this, stating that everyone agrees there is no karet, and instead explains that there are three positions in the dispute.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's position on leaving blood
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's position on leaving blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages is specifically about intending to leave blood until the next day, but all agree that actually leaving it disqualifies. This is based on a decree comparing partial blood to all blood, and a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda argues that if leaving blood until tomorrow disqualifies, then intending to do so also disqualifies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds the dispute is about intending to leave blood, but actually leaving it disqualifies by Torah law due to a decree comparing partial blood to all blood.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda argues that if leaving blood until tomorrow disqualifies, then intending to do so also disqualifies.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's statement about the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's statement about the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar comes to say that in this case as well, Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies and the Sages validate.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that in this case as well, Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies and the Sages validate.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about Yosef HaBavli
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about Yosef HaBavli
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that Rabbi Yehuda holds that all agree leaving blood disqualifies, citing a baraita where Rabbi Elazar ben Shmuel and Yosef HaBavli discuss the matter. Yosef initially learned from Rabbi Yehuda that it is disqualified, but Rabbi Elazar ben Shmuel repeatedly says it is valid, except that Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies. Yosef rejoices at recovering his 'lost' tradition, and Rabbi Elazar ben Shmuel explains that Rabbi Yehuda transmitted Rabbi Eliezer's view because he was his disciple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda really holds that leaving blood overnight is universally disqualified, citing a baraita that seems to contradict this.
The baraita recounts that Rabbi Elazar ben Shmuel repeatedly ruled that the sacrifice is valid, except that Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies it.
Yosef HaBavli rejoices, explaining that Rabbi Yehuda taught him it is disqualified, and he now recovers his 'lost' tradition.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shmuel explains that Rabbi Yehuda transmitted Rabbi Eliezer's disqualifying view because he was his disciple, resolving the apparent contradiction.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the baraita: if Rabbi Yehuda taught that all agree it is disqualified, why would Yosef say he recovered his 'lost' tradition? It was a dispute. Alternatively, if he taught that it is valid except Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies, then why mention 'because of the dispute'? The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yehuda indeed taught 'all agree it is disqualified', and Yosef meant that he at least recovered some disqualification in the world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: if Rabbi Yehuda taught that all agree it is disqualified, why would Yosef say 'you returned my lost object' when the matter was actually a dispute?
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Yehuda taught that it is valid except Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies, then why does the baraita say 'because of the dispute' — we also teach a dispute!
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yehuda indeed taught 'all agree it is disqualified', and Yosef meant that he at least recovered some disqualification in the world.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on meal-offering procedures
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on meal-offering procedures
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists actions that, if omitted, do not disqualify a meal-offering. The Gemara questions the meaning of 'did not pour' – if it means no pouring at all, the Torah requires it; rather it means a non-priest poured. Similarly, 'did not mix' means a non-priest mixed, but if not mixed at all, it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists actions that, if omitted, do not disqualify a meal-offering.
The Gemara questions the meaning of 'did not pour' – if it means no pouring at all, the Torah requires it and omission would disqualify.
The Gemara explains that 'did not pour' means a non-priest poured, not that pouring was omitted entirely.
The Gemara concludes that if mixing was not done at all, the offering is invalid, but if a non-priest mixed, it remains valid.

items.text: Contradiction from the mishnah and Rabbi Zeira's principle
items.text_en: Contradiction from the mishnah and Rabbi Zeira's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a mishnah states that sixty (log) are mixed but sixty-one are not, and asks what if they are not mixed—the mishnah says 'he did not mix'—it is valid. Rabbi Zeira then states a general principle: for something fit for mixing, mixing is not indispensable; for something unfit, mixing is indispensable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a mishnah: sixty (log) are mixed, sixty-one are not, and if they are not mixed, the mishnah says 'he did not mix'—it is valid.
Rabbi Zeira states a general principle: for something fit for mixing, mixing is not indispensable; for something unfit, mixing is indispensable.

items.text: Resolution: each case stands on its own
items.text_en: Resolution: each case stands on its own
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the two cases are distinct: 'he did not pour' means a non-priest poured, but 'he did not mix' means he did not mix at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the contradiction by asserting that each clause refers to a different situation: 'he did not pour' means a non-priest poured, while 'he did not mix' means he failed to mix at all.

items.text: Clarification of 'many crumbs' in the mishnah
items.text_en: Clarification of 'many crumbs' in the mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's phrase 'or if he crumbled them into many crumbs—it is valid,' asking: if he did not crumble at all it is valid, why mention many crumbs? It answers that 'many crumbs' means he increased the crumbs, and alternatively, it teaches that even with many crumbs the form of loaves is not required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah mentions 'many crumbs' as valid, since even without crumbling it is valid.
The Gemara answers that 'many crumbs' means he increased the number of crumbs, not that he crumbled them into many pieces.
The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the mishnah teaches that even with many actual crumbs, the form of loaves (תורת חלות) is not required.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon on priestly service
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon on priestly service
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who taught that any priest who does not acknowledge a service has no share in the priesthood, listing fifteen services including pouring and mixing, derived from the verse 'from the sons of Aaron.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah is not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Shimon.
A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Shimon states that any priest who does not acknowledge a sacrificial service has no portion in the priesthood, based on the verse regarding the priestly gifts.
The baraita asks: from where is it derived that this principle applies to fifteen additional services, including pouring, mixing, and breaking?

The baraita lists the fifteen services: pouring, mixing, breaking, salting, waving, bringing, removal of the handful, burning, pinching, receiving, sprinkling, the sotah water, the heifer's neck, the leper's purification, and the Priestly Benediction.
The baraita answers that the verse 'from the sons of Aaron' teaches that any service entrusted to the sons of Aaron requires acknowledgment for a priest to have a share in the priesthood.

items.text: Rav Nachman's distinction: priestly vs. Israelite offerings
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's distinction: priestly vs. Israelite offerings
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: here (the mishnah) refers to an Israelite's meal offering, which requires kemitzah, so from kemitzah onward is a priestly duty, teaching that pouring and mixing are valid by a non-priest; there (Rabbi Shimon) refers to a priest's meal offering, which does not require kemitzah, so from the start it requires a priest.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: here (the mishnah) refers to an Israelite's meal offering, which requires קמיצה (kemitzah), so from קמיצה onward is a priestly duty, teaching that pouring and mixing are valid by a non-priest; there (Rabbi Shimon) refers to a priest's meal offering, which does not require קמיצה, so from the start it requires a priest.

items.text: Rava's objection to Rav Nachman's distinction
items.text_en: Rava's objection to Rav Nachman's distinction
items.desc_en: Rava objects: since the priest's offering derives the requirement of pouring from the Israelite's offering, just as there it is valid by a non-priest, so too here it should be valid by a non-priest.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Nachman's distinction: since the priest's offering derives the requirement of pouring from the Israelite's offering, just as there it is valid by a non-priest, so too here it should be valid by a non-priest.

items.text: Alternative version and Rava's conclusion
items.text_en: Alternative version and Rava's conclusion
items.desc_en: Some say Rav Nachman distinguished between offerings that are subject to kemitzah and those that are not. Rava again objects, and concludes that the mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports that Rav Nachman distinguished between offerings that are subject to kemitzah (קמיצה) and those that are not.
Rava objects: since the non-kemitzah offerings derive their requirement for pouring (יציקה) from the kemitzah offerings, they should likewise be valid when performed by a non-priest (זר).
Rava concludes that the mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who requires a priest for all service-related actions.

items.text: Rabbis' scriptural basis and Rabbi Shimon's derivation
items.text_en: Rabbis' scriptural basis and Rabbi Shimon's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Rabbis' reasoning from the verse: 'and he shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it and bring it to the sons of Aaron the priest and take a handful'—from kemitzah onward is a priestly duty, teaching that pouring and mixing are valid by a non-priest. Rabbi Shimon derives from 'sons of Aaron' that all services assigned to Aaron's sons require a priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Rabbis who hold that pouring and mixing are valid by a non-priest.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive from the verse that from the kemitzah onward is a priestly duty, teaching that pouring and mixing are valid by a non-priest.
The Gemara states that Rabbi Shimon derives from 'sons of Aaron' that all services assigned to Aaron's sons require a priest.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Shimon's principle of 'Mikra Nidrash Lefanav Ule'acharav'
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Shimon's principle of 'Mikra Nidrash Lefanav Ule'acharav'
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Shimon holds that a verse is interpreted by both its preceding and following context, specifically regarding the requirement that only priests perform the service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Shimon's principle that a verse is interpreted by both its preceding and following context, specifically regarding the requirement that only priests perform the service.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Shimon from a baraita on blood application
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Shimon from a baraita on blood application
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Shimon's view by citing a baraita where he argues that since the word 'hand' is not stated for receiving the blood, receiving with the left hand is valid, implying he does not interpret the verse by its preceding context. Abaye explains that the dispute is about whether the verse is interpreted by its preceding context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Shimon by citing a baraita that derives from the verse that both receiving and applying blood must be done with the right hand, implying he interprets the verse by its preceding context.
Rabbi Shimon responds that since the word 'hand' is not stated for receiving the blood, receiving with the left hand is valid, showing he does not interpret the verse by its preceding context.
Abaye resolves the challenge by explaining that the dispute is about whether the verse is interpreted by its preceding context, and Rabbi Shimon holds it is interpreted only by its following context.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Shimon's use of 'Vav Mosif Al Inyan Rishon'
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Shimon's use of 'Vav Mosif Al Inyan Rishon'
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative reason for Rabbi Shimon's position: the 'vav' in 'vehevi'ah' adds to the previous subject, connecting the meal-offering to the priestly service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides an alternative reason for Rabbi Shimon's position: the 'vav' in 'vehevi'ah' adds to the previous subject, connecting the meal-offering to the priestly service.

items.text: Challenge to 'Vav Mosif' from slaughter by a non-priest
items.text_en: Challenge to 'Vav Mosif' from slaughter by a non-priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the 'vav mosif' principle by citing the verse about slaughter, which would then require slaughter by a priest. The Gemara resolves this by noting that the verse 'vesamach...veshachat' teaches that slaughter is valid by a non-priest, and a kal vachomer from sprinkling shows it does not require the owner, and Yom Kippur proves slaughter does not require a priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Shimon's principle of 'vav mosif' by citing the verse about slaughter, which would then require slaughter by a priest, contradicting the known halacha that slaughter is valid by a non-priest.
The Gemara resolves that the verse 'vesamach...veshachat' teaches that slaughter is valid by a non-priest, just as semicha is performed by non-priests.
The Gemara objects that semicha requires the owner, so a kal vachomer from sprinkling shows that slaughter does not require the owner.
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Yom Kippur, where the verse 'veshachat et par hachatat asher lo' implies that ordinary slaughter does not require the owner.

items.text: Rav's principle: 'Torah' and 'Chukah' indicate indispensability
items.text_en: Rav's principle: 'Torah' and 'Chukah' indicate indispensability
items.desc_en: Rav states that wherever 'Torah' and 'Chukah' are written, they indicate that the ritual is indispensable, as in the verse 'Zot Chukat HaTorah'.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that wherever the words 'Torah' and 'Chukah' appear together, they indicate that the ritual is indispensable, citing the verse 'Zot Chukat HaTorah'.

items.text: Siman (mnemonic)
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic)
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is provided for the following examples.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic (נת״ץ יקמ״ל) to organize the following examples.

items.text: Testing Rav's principle with examples: Nazir, Todah, Metzora, Yom Kippur, other sacrifices, Minchah, Lechem Hapanim
items.text_en: Testing Rav's principle with examples: Nazir, Todah, Metzora, Yom Kippur, other sacrifices, Minchah, Lechem Hapanim
items.desc_en: The Gemara tests Rav's principle by examining cases where only 'Torah' or only 'Chukah' is written, and whether the rituals are indispensable. It addresses each case: Nazir (tenufah is indispensable due to 'ken ya'aseh'), Todah (four loaves are indispensable due to connection to Nazir), Metzora (four species are indispensable due to 'zot tihyeh torat hametzora'), Yom Kippur (two goats are indispensable with only 'Chukah'), other sacrifices (require both 'Torah' and 'Chukah'), Minchah (only 'Chukah' on eating, but the verse 'migirsah umishamnah' teaches otherwise), and Lechem Hapanim (the 'Chukah' on eating applies to the whole matter).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's principle by citing the Nazir, where only 'תורה' is written, yet Rav himself rules that the tenufah (wave-offering) is indispensable.
The Gemara distinguishes the Nazir case because the verse 'כֵּן יַעֲשֶׂה' (so shall be done) is written, which is equivalent to having 'חוקה' (a statute) written.
The Gemara raises the Todah (thanksgiving offering), where only 'תורה' is written, yet the Mishnah rules that the four loaves are indispensable.

The Gemara answers that the Todah is different because it is linked (הוקש) to the Nazir by the verse 'עַל זֶבַח תּוֹדַת שְׁלָמָיו', and the master taught that 'שְׁלָמָיו' includes the peace-offerings of the Nazir.
The Gemara challenges with the Metzora (leper), where only 'תורה' is written, yet the Mishnah rules that the four species are indispensable.
The Gemara answers that the Metzora is different because the verse 'זֹאת תִּהְיֶה תּוֹרַת הַמְּצֹרָע' (this shall be the law of the leper) is written, which is equivalent to having 'חוקה' written.
The Gemara raises Yom Kippur, where only 'חוקה' is written, yet the Mishnah rules that the two goats are indispensable.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's principle means that either 'תורה' or 'חוקה' alone suffices for indispensability.
The Gemara asks about other sacrifices, where 'תורה' is written, yet they are not indispensable.
The Gemara explains that 'תורה' requires 'חוקה' to be written as well; if only 'תורה' is written without 'חוקה', it does not indicate indispensability.
The Gemara challenges with the Minchah (meal-offering), where 'חוקה' is written, yet Rav himself rules that only where the verse repeats (מחזיר) does it indicate indispensability.
The Gemara distinguishes the Minchah case because the 'חוקה' there is written specifically regarding the eating (אכילה), not the entire offering.
The Gemara raises the Lechem Hapanim (showbread), where 'חוקה' is also written regarding eating, yet the Mishnah rules that the two rows and the two bowls are indispensable.
The Gemara answers that wherever 'חוקה' is written regarding eating, it applies to the entire matter (the whole ritual).

The Gemara further distinguishes the Minchah case because the verse 'מִגִּרְשָׂהּ וּמִשַּׁמְנָהּ' (from its fine flour and its oil) teaches that the repetition applies only to the ingredients, not the entire offering.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the fine flour and oil are indispensable (me'akev) for the meal-offering, but nothing else is indispensable.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel dispute the scope of 'me'akev'
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute the scope of 'me'akev'
items.desc_en: Rav holds that wherever the Torah repeats the word 'minchah', it indicates that the item is indispensable. Shmuel limits indispensability to fine flour and oil. The Gemara clarifies that their dispute actually concerns the interpretation of 'melo kumtzo' and 'bekumtzo'—whether a measure for the handful is prohibited—and they argue about learning from the dedication of the Tabernacle (dorot mish'ah).

items.text: Objection from Shmuel's own ruling on vessels
items.text_en: Objection from Shmuel's own ruling on vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Shmuel himself learns from the dedication of the Tabernacle (the verse 'shneihem mele'im solet') that sprinkling vessels (mizrakot) sanctify dry items, contradicting his principle. The Gemara answers that there the verse is repeated twelve times, making it a special case.

items.text: Challenge from the law of hagashah (bringing near)
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of hagashah (bringing near)
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenge Rav: the law of hagashah (bringing the offering near the altar) is explicitly stated in the Torah yet is not indispensable. The Gemara explains that the verse 'lifnei Hashem' comes only to establish the location—the southwest corner of the altar—not to make it indispensable.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's resolution of the two verses
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's resolution of the two verses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer explains how to reconcile the two verses 'lifnei Hashem' and 'el pnei hamizbe'ach' to determine the exact location for hagashah. Rav Ashi adds that this Tanna holds the entire altar stood in the north.

items.text: Challenge from the law of salt
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of salt
items.desc_en: Rav Huna objects that salt is not explicitly mentioned in the Torah as indispensable for the meal-offering, yet it is indispensable, as derived from the verse 'brit melach olam hi'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Salt as a covenant
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Salt as a covenant
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon regarding the source for the requirement of salt in offerings. Rabbi Yehuda states that a covenant of salt is mentioned, while Rabbi Shimon derives it from a verbal analogy with the covenant of priesthood.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda states a covenant of salt is mentioned, while Rabbi Shimon derives the requirement of salt from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) with the covenant of priesthood.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is the salt requirement on the offering or the priest?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is the salt requirement on the offering or the priest?
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests that the Tanna of our Mishnah holds that if one did not salt, the offering is still valid. Abaye objects, comparing it to pouring, and proposes that the requirement is that a priest must salt, not a non-priest. Rav Yosef counters that a non-priest cannot approach the altar. An alternative answer is given: since the verse says 'covenant', it is as if the verse itself requires salt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests that the Tanna of our Mishnah holds that if one did not salt, the offering is still valid.
Abaye objects, comparing salting to pouring, and proposes that the requirement is that a priest must salt, not a non-priest.
Rav Yosef counters that a non-priest cannot approach the altar.
An alternative answer is given: since the verse says 'covenant', it is as if the verse itself requires salt.

items.text: Derivation of items requiring salt from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of items requiring salt from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for the verse 'and every meal-offering of yours you shall salt', and explains it is needed for a derivation: it excludes wood and blood, then includes only items that others come as an obligation for them, like the meal-offering. It then derives that only the handful requires salt, but then includes frankincense, and through further verses includes all other items listed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a verse is needed for the salt requirement, pointing out that the verse 'and every meal-offering of yours you shall salt' already exists.
The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for a derivation: without the word 'minchah', one might think even wood and blood, which are called 'korban', require salt.
The baraita teaches that the word 'minchah' limits salt to items for which others come as an obligation, like the meal-offering itself.
The Gemara objects that if the comparison is to the meal-offering which permits, one might include blood which permits; the verse 'from your meal-offering' excludes blood.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'korban' teaches that only the handful of the meal-offering requires salt, not the entire meal-offering.
The Gemara asks how we include frankincense that comes with the meal-offering in the same vessel, and answers that it is included because it comes together.
The Gemara asks how we include frankincense that comes alone, frankincense in bowls, incense, meal-offerings of priests, the anointed priest, libations, and various sacrificial parts.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'upon all your offerings you shall offer salt' includes all these items.

items.text: Analysis of the derivation: general and particular
items.text_en: Analysis of the derivation: general and particular
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the earlier derivation, noting a contradiction: if the principle is that only items that others come as an obligation for them require salt, then frankincense should not be included. It resolves by applying the hermeneutic principle of general and particular, concluding that the general and particular and general includes all items that others come as an obligation for them, like wood. The Gemara then debates whether blood should be included, and concludes that the verse 'from your meal-offering' excludes blood, and all the other items are included by one side.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier derivation: if the principle is that only items that others come as an obligation for them require salt, then why is frankincense included, since it does not fit that description?

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by applying the hermeneutic principle of כלל ופרט וכלל (general, particular, and general), concluding that the general includes all items that others come as an obligation for them, like wood.
The Gemara objects: if the principle is that others come as an obligation for the item, then only wood fits, not frankincense or other items.
The Gemara rejects the objection by considering whether blood could be included via libations, but notes that libations accompany sacrificial portions, and the debate is between atonement and joy.
The Gemara resolves that frankincense is included because it comes with the meal-offering in one vessel, while wood is included because it enables all offerings.

The Gemara objects further: if the particular is both that others come as an obligation for it and that it permits, then only frankincense in bowls (which permits the showbread) would be included, excluding other items.
The Gemara concludes that since the verse 'from your meal-offering' was needed to exclude blood, it implies that all the other items are included by one side (i.e., they all require salt).

items.text: Why limbs are included and not blood
items.text_en: Why limbs are included and not blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse 'from your meal-offering' excludes blood but not limbs. It answers that limbs are more similar to the meal-offering in several respects: others come as an obligation for them, they are consumed by fire, they are offered outside, they have leftover, they are susceptible to impurity, and they have misuse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse 'from your meal-offering' excludes blood but not limbs, asking why limbs are not also excluded.

The Gemara answers that limbs are more similar to the meal-offering than blood is, listing six shared characteristics: others come as an obligation for them, they are consumed by fire, they are offered outside, they have leftover, they are susceptible to impurity, and they have misuse.

items.text: Gemara's objection to the previous argument
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to the previous argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that blood should be more comparable to the minchah than wood, since blood permits the minchah like the minchah itself and is invalidated at sunset like the minchah. It concludes that the differences (between blood and wood) are more numerous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that blood should be included in the exclusion (מעוט) rather than wood, because blood permits the minchah (מתכפר) like the minchah itself and is invalidated at sunset like the minchah, concluding that the differences between blood and wood are more numerous.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi's statement about wood
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi's statement about wood
items.desc_en: Mar's statement that wood is called a korban is attributed to Rabbi. The Gemara notes that Rabbi would require salt for wood, as taught in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Who is the Tanna who holds that wood is called a korban (קרבן)? It answers that it is Rabbi (רבי), and then questions whether Rabbi would require salt for wood.
The Gemara asks: Who is the authority who holds that wood is called a korban?
The Gemara answers: It is Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi).
The Gemara concludes that according to Rabbi, wood requires salt (מלח).

items.text: Baraita on wood as a korban
items.text_en: Baraita on wood as a korban
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'korban minchah' indicates that one may donate wood, specifically two logs, and Rabbi says wood is a korban minchah requiring salt and being brought near the altar.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: The verse 'קרבן מנחה' teaches that one may donate wood for the altar, and Rabbi says that wood is considered a minchah offering (קרבן מנחה), requiring salt (מלח) and presentation (הגשה).
The baraita adds a supporting verse from Nehemiah about the lottery for the wood-offering.
Rabbi rules that wood is a korban minchah, requiring salt (מלח) and being brought near the altar (הגשה).

items.text: Rava and Rav Papa's extensions of Rabbi's view
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Papa's extensions of Rabbi's view
items.desc_en: Rava says that according to Rabbi, wood requires kemitzah (taking a handful). Rav Papa says that according to Rabbi, wood requires other wood (for the fire).

sub.desc_en: Rava adds that according to Rabbi, wood requires kemitzah (קמיצה, the priestly scooping of the flour), and Rav Papa adds that wood requires other wood (for burning).
Rav Papa adds that according to Rabbi, wood requires other wood (for the fire).

items.text: Gemara's conclusion about the verse's exclusion
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion about the verse's exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that wood is excluded from the law of me'ilah, and asks what the verse comes to exclude. It answers that if it were to exclude blood, that would already be derived from 'al minchatecha'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If wood is excluded (from the verse), then what does the verse come to exclude? It answers that if it were to exclude blood, that would already be derived from the phrase 'על מנחתך' (upon your minchah).

items.text: Exclusion of wood and incense from salting requirement
items.text_en: Exclusion of wood and incense from salting requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a baraita that states wine, blood, wood, and incense do not require salting, asking whose opinion it follows. It then cites Rabbi Yishmael's principle that only items which can become impure, go up in fire, and are on the outer altar require salting, thereby excluding wood (not susceptible to impurity), blood and wine (not consumed by fire), and incense (not on the outer altar).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that excludes wood and incense from the salting requirement and includes libations.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the baraita follows, noting that if it follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, wood is problematic, and if it follows the Sages, incense is problematic.

The Gemara identifies the baraita as following Rabbi Yishmael, who derives that only items susceptible to impurity, consumed by fire, and placed on the outer altar require salting, thereby excluding wood, blood, wine, and incense.

items.text: Blood's exemption from salting and the effect of salting on blood
items.text_en: Blood's exemption from salting and the effect of salting on blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even without the verse excluding blood, one might think blood requires salting, but since salting removes its status as blood (as per Ze'iri quoting Rabbi Chanina that cooked blood is not subject to the prohibition, and Rav Yehuda that salted blood is not), the verse teaches that salting is not needed. Rav Yehuda adds that roasted limbs brought up have no 'pleasant aroma' requirement, but the verse still teaches that a little salt is needed for the mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the verse had not excluded blood, would we have thought blood requires salting?

sub.text: Gemara's answer citing Ze'iri and Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing Ze'iri and Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: since salting removes blood from its halachic category (as per Ze'iri quoting Rabbi Chanina that cooked blood is not prohibited, and Rav Yehuda that salted blood is not), the verse teaches that salting is unnecessary.
Rav Yehuda adds that roasted limbs brought up have no 'pleasant aroma' requirement, reinforcing that salting is not needed for blood.
The Gemara concludes: one might think a little salt is needed for the mitzvah, but the verse teaches that even that is not required.

items.text: Congealed blood: cooked vs. sun-dried
items.text_en: Congealed blood: cooked vs. sun-dried
items.desc_en: Rava states Ze'iri's ruling that cooked blood is not subject to the prohibition. Abaye objects from a baraita that one who congeals blood and eats it is liable. The Gemara resolves: if congealed by fire, it does not revert to its original state, so it is not considered blood; if by the sun, it does revert, so it is still blood.

sub.desc_en: Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina states that cooked blood is not subject to the prohibition of eating blood.
Abaye objects to Rava's citation of Ze'iri's ruling by citing a baraita that one who congeals blood and eats it is liable.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: if congealed by fire (cooked), it does not revert to its original state and is not considered blood; if by the sun, it does revert and remains blood.

items.text: Congealed blood: once rejected, rejected?
items.text_en: Congealed blood: once rejected, rejected?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether congealed blood, even if it reverts, is considered rejected. Rabbi Mani asked Rabbi Yochanan about congealed blood that was eaten, and he replied that since it was rejected, it remains rejected. Rabbi Mani was silent, but then suggested that perhaps the distinction is between outer and inner sin-offerings. Rav Chisda clarifies: for outer sin-offerings, congealed blood is still fit for 'taking and giving', so eating it is liable; for inner sin-offerings, it is not fit for 'dipping and sprinkling', so one is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether congealed blood that reverted should be considered rejected, citing Rabbi Mani's inquiry to Rabbi Yochanan.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that since the blood was rejected, it remains rejected, and Rabbi Mani is silent.
Rabbi Mani suggests a distinction between outer sin-offerings and inner sin-offerings.

Rav Chisda clarifies that for outer sin-offerings, congealed blood is fit for 'taking and giving' (לקיחה ונתינה), so eating it incurs liability; for inner sin-offerings, it is not fit for 'dipping and sprinkling' (טבילה והזאה), so one is exempt.

items.text: Rava's and Rav Pappa's rulings on congealed blood
items.text_en: Rava's and Rav Pappa's rulings on congealed blood
items.desc_en: Rava himself rules that even for inner sin-offerings, eating congealed blood is liable because it is fit for its counterpart in outer sin-offerings. Rav Pappa concludes that therefore, congealed donkey's blood is also liable because it is fit for its counterpart in outer sin-offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that even for inner sin-offerings, eating congealed blood is liable because it is fit for its counterpart in outer sin-offerings.
Rav Pappa concludes that congealed donkey's blood is also liable because it is fit for its counterpart in outer sin-offerings.

items.text: Blood as an interposition (chatzitzah)
items.text_en: Blood as an interposition (chatzitzah)
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel quoting Ze'iri states that blood, whether wet or dry, interposes (for immersion). An objection is raised from a baraita that dry blood interposes but wet blood does not. The Gemara resolves: if it is sticky, it interposes; if not, it does not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel in the name of Ze'iri states that blood, whether wet or dry, constitutes a interposition (חוצץ) for immersion.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists dry blood as interposing but wet blood as not interposing.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: if the blood is sticky (סָרֵיךְ) it interposes; if not, it does not.

items.text: Derivation of salting method from verses
items.text_en: Derivation of salting method from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verses 'with salt' and 'you shall salt' to teach that one must salt the offering, not just season it, and not with brine. The verse 'do not omit the salt' teaches to bring salt that does not spoil, i.e., Sodomite salt, and if unavailable, any salt. The word 'takriv' teaches that it can be brought even on Shabbat or in impurity. The meaning of 'tevonenu' is debated: Rava bar Ulla says it means to mix like straw in mud, Abaye says to make it like a structure, Rava says to give it flavor like understanding, and Rav Ashi says to give it a taste like understanding. The practical method: bring the limb, put salt on it, turn it over, put salt again, and bring it up.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'תִּמְלָח' (you shall salt) comes to teach.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verses 'בַּמֶּלַח' (with salt) and 'תִּמְלָח' (you shall salt) that one must salt the offering, not just season it, and not with brine.

The baraita continues: the verse 'וְלֹא תַשְׁבִּית מֶלַח' (do not omit the salt) teaches to bring salt that does not spoil, i.e., Sodomite salt, and if unavailable, any salt; the word 'תַּקְרִיב' (you shall bring) teaches that it can be brought even on Shabbat or in impurity.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the word 'תְּבוֹנֵהוּ' (you shall season it) in the baraita.
Rava bar Ulla explains that 'תְּבוֹנֵהוּ' means to mix the salt with the offering like straw in mud.
Abaye objects that if the meaning were 'mix like straw,' the verb should be 'יִתְבּוֹנֶנּוּ' (it will be mixed), not 'תְּבוֹנֵהוּ' (you shall season it).
Abaye explains that 'תְּבוֹנֵהוּ' means to make the salt into a structure on the offering.
Rava objects that if the meaning were 'make a structure,' the verb should be 'יִבְנֶנּוּ' (he will build it), not 'תְּבוֹנֵהוּ'.
Rava explains that 'תְּבוֹנֵהוּ' means to give it flavor like understanding (תְּבוּנָה).
The Gemara asks the meaning of Rava's term 'תְּבוּנֵהוּ' (give it understanding).
Rav Ashi explains that 'תְּבוּנֵהוּ' means to give it a taste like understanding (בִּינָה).
The Gemara concludes that the verse 'תִּמְלָח' (you shall salt) teaches that the salt must give taste, not just be a structure or mixture.
The Gemara describes the practical method: bring the limb, put salt on it, turn it over, put salt again, and bring it up to the altar.

items.text: Abaye's extension to a pot
items.text_en: Abaye's extension to a pot
items.desc_en: Abaye says that the same salting method applies to a pot (for cooking the offering).

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that the same salting method applies to a pot used for cooking the offering.

items.text: Opening baraita and Rav Mattana's prooftext
items.text_en: Opening baraita and Rav Mattana's prooftext
items.desc_en: The baraita distinguishes between salt on the limb (subject to me'ilah) and salt on the ramp or top of the altar (not subject to me'ilah). Rav Mattana cites a verse to support this distinction.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that salt on the limb is subject to me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property), but salt on the ramp or top of the altar is not.
Rav Mattana cites a verse (Ezekiel 43:24) to support the distinction: salt is thrown on the limb before it is offered, but not on the ramp or altar top.

items.text: Shmuel's distinction regarding salt for priests
items.text_en: Shmuel's distinction regarding salt for priests
items.desc_en: Shmuel explains that the Mishnah's allowance for priests to benefit from salt and wood applies only to their sacrifices, not for ordinary eating.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel distinguishes that the Mishnah's allowance for priests to benefit from salt and wood applies only to their sacrifices, not for ordinary eating.

items.text: Gemara's initial understanding and correction
items.text_en: Gemara's initial understanding and correction
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes 'for their sacrifice' means for salting sacrifices, and 'for eating' means eating sacred meat, but objects that if salt is given for salting hides, it should certainly be given for eating sacred meat.
