It then cites a baraita listing three places for salt, and reinterprets Shmuel: 'for their sacrifice' means for eating the sacrifice, and 'for eating' means eating non-sacred food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that Shmuel's phrase 'for their sacrifice' refers to salting sacrifices, and 'for eating' refers to eating sacred meat, then objects that if salt is given for salting hides it should certainly be given for eating sacred meat.
The Gemara cites a baraita that lists three places where salt is placed for sacrifices, including the Chamber of Salt for salting hides.
The Gemara reinterprets Shmuel: 'for their sacrifice' means for eating the sacrifice, and 'for eating' means eating non-sacred food.

items.text: Clarification of the need for the ruling
items.text_en: Clarification of the need for the ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the ruling is necessary, since non-sacred food is obvious, and explains that even though the court decreed that priests should eat sacred food with non-sacred food and terumah to be satiated, they still do not give them salt from sacred property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's ruling about non-sacred food is necessary, since it is obvious.
The Gemara explains that even though the court decreed that priests eat sacred food with non-sacred food and terumah to be satiated, they still do not give them salt from sacred property.

items.text: Ravina's proof and the source for communal salt
items.text_en: Ravina's proof and the source for communal salt
items.desc_en: Ravina argues to Rav Ashi that if Shmuel meant salting, then only the court's decree would prevent giving salt to priests, but logically priests should receive salt even more than Israelites. A baraita then debates whether a donor brings salt from home or from communal funds, concluding from a verse that salt comes from communal funds.

sub.desc_en: Ravina argues to Rav Ashi that if Shmuel's statement referred to salting, then only the court's decree would prevent giving salt to priests, but logically priests should receive salt even more than Israelites.
A baraita raises the possibility that a donor brings salt from home, analogous to frankincense.
The baraita counters that salt might come from communal funds, like wood.
The baraita resolves that salt, which applies to all sacrifices, is compared to wood (also universal), not to frankincense (which is not universal).
The baraita objects that salt, which comes with the meal offering in one vessel, should be compared to frankincense, not to wood.
The baraita concludes from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'ברית מלח עולם' and 'מאת בני ישראל ברית עולם' that salt comes from communal funds.

items.text: Rav Mordechai's resolution regarding Ben Bukhri
items.text_en: Rav Mordechai's resolution regarding Ben Bukhri
items.desc_en: Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi said the ruling is needed only for the case of Ben Bukhri, who testified that any priest who contributes to the Temple treasury does not sin. The Gemara explains that since Ben Bukhri holds that priests are not obligated to contribute initially, bringing salt would be a sin of bringing non-sacred items into the Temple courtyard.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi said the ruling is needed only for the case of Ben Bukhri.

The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Ben Bukhri testified that any priest who contributes does not sin, while Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai argued the opposite, and the priests derive their exemption from a verse.

The Gemara explains that since Ben Bukhri holds priests are not obligated to contribute לכתחילה (the ideal standard), bringing salt would be a sin of bringing non-sacred items into the Temple courtyard.

items.text: Unfinished thought
items.text_en: Unfinished thought
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new line of reasoning but does not complete it in this segment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins an unfinished thought, introducing a hypothetical assumption that it does not complete.

items.text: Conclusion of earlier discussion: wood for the altar from communal funds
items.text_en: Conclusion of earlier discussion: wood for the altar from communal funds
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the earlier teaching that wood comes from communal funds applies only to Israel, who have a chamber (lishkah), but not to priests, who lack one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the earlier teaching about wood from communal funds applies only to Israel, who have a chamber (lishkah), but not to priests, who lack one.

items.text: Source for wood from communal funds and dispute
items.text_en: Source for wood from communal funds and dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita deriving that wood and fire must be from communal funds, like the altar. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon learns from a verse, while Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua argues that wood and fire must not have been used by a private individual. The difference between them is new wood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that wood must come from communal funds, which is obvious to the Tanna?

A baraita is cited: one might think a person who vows a burnt-offering could bring wood from home, but a verse teaches that just as the altar is from communal funds, so too wood and fire are from communal funds — the words of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua offers a different derivation: just as the altar was never used by a private individual, so too wood and fire must never have been used by a private individual.
The Gemara clarifies the practical difference between the two opinions: new wood that has never been used by a private individual.

items.text: Clarification about old wood and the term 'morigim'
items.text_en: Clarification about old wood and the term 'morigim'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether old wood is invalid, citing David's use of old wood from Arvnah. It answers that even there it was new. Then it explains the term 'morigim' (threshing sledges) with definitions from Ulla, Rav Yehuda, and Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether old wood is invalid for the altar, citing David's use of old wood from Arvnah.
The Gemara answers that even David's wood was new, not old.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the term 'morigim' (threshing sledges).
Ulla defines 'morigim' as a 'bed of turbel' (a threshing sledge).
The Gemara asks for further clarification of Ulla's definition.
Rav Yehuda explains it as a 'goat of cork' (a threshing board) used for treading grain.
Rav Yosef cites the verse 'Behold I have made you into a new sharp threshing sledge with teeth; you shall thresh mountains' to support the definition.

items.text: Mishnah: Mixed handfuls of meal-offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Mixed handfuls of meal-offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the handful of one meal-offering mixes with another, it is valid, even with priest's or anointed priest's offerings. Rabbi Yehuda rules that with the anointed priest's or drink-offerings it is invalid because their batter differs in consistency and they absorb each other.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if the handful of one meal-offering mixes with another, including priest's or anointed priest's offerings, it is valid.
Rabbi Yehuda objects that for the anointed priest's offering or drink-offerings it is invalid because their batter differs in consistency and they absorb each other.

items.text: Gemara: Comparison to blood mixtures and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.text_en: Gemara: Comparison to blood mixtures and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about blood mixed with water, wine, or other blood, where Rabbi Yehuda says blood does not nullify blood. Rabbi Yochanan explains that both sides derive from the same verse about the bull and goat's blood, with the Rabbis holding that the majority blood is nullified by the minority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about blood mixed with water, wine, or other blood, concluding with Rabbi Yehuda's statement that blood does not nullify blood.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that both Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis derive their positions from the same verse about the bull and goat's blood, with the Rabbis holding that the majority blood is nullified by the minority.

items.text: Statement of the dispute
items.text_en: Statement of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the two positions: the Rabbis derive from the verse that offerings do not nullify each other, while Rabbi Yehuda derives that a substance of its own kind is not nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the two positions: the Rabbis derive from the verse that offerings do not nullify each other, while Rabbi Yehuda derives that a substance of its own kind is not nullified.

items.text: Challenge to the Rabbis' position
items.text_en: Challenge to the Rabbis' position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Rabbis: perhaps the verse only teaches about like substances, not about offerings in general. The Rabbis respond that since the verse mentions offerings, it teaches about offerings. The Gemara then raises a difficulty: perhaps both conditions are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Rabbis: perhaps the verse only teaches about like substances (מִין בְּמִינוֹ), not about offerings in general (עוֹלִין).
The Rabbis respond: if the verse only taught about like substances, you would be right, but since it also mentions offerings (עוֹלִין), it teaches about offerings.
The Gemara objects: perhaps both conditions — like substance and offering — are needed, leaving the Rabbis' position unresolved.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda: perhaps the verse only teaches about offerings, not about like substances. Rabbi Yehuda responds that since the verse mentions like substances, it teaches about like substances. The Gemara then raises the same difficulty: perhaps both conditions are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda: perhaps the verse only teaches about offerings (עולין), not about like substances (מין במינו).

Rabbi Yehuda responds: if the verse only taught about offerings (עולין) in non-like substances, your challenge would stand; but since it also mentions like substances (מין במינו), it teaches about like substances.
The Gemara objects: perhaps both conditions—like substances (מין במינו) and offerings (עולין)—are needed together, leaving the difficulty unresolved.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yehuda from a Mishnah
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yehuda from a Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda rules that certain meal-offerings are invalid because they absorb from each other, and comments that this is a case of like substances, supporting his view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda rules that certain meal-offerings are invalid because they absorb from each other, and comments that this is a case of like substances, supporting his view.

items.text: Rava's principle about nullification of mixtures
items.text_en: Rava's principle about nullification of mixtures
items.desc_en: Rava states Rabbi Yehuda's view: when a type is mixed with its own kind and another substance, the type is considered nullified, and the non-type overrides and nullifies it.

sub.desc_en: Rava states Rabbi Yehuda's principle: when a type is mixed with its own kind and another substance, the type is considered nullified, and the non-type overrides and nullifies it.

items.text: Debate about a kometz of a sin-offering that was oiled
items.text_en: Debate about a kometz of a sin-offering that was oiled
items.desc_en: It was stated: a kometz of a sin-offering that was oiled. Rabbi Yochanan says it is invalid, while Reish Lakish says one can stir it in the remaining oil and offer it. The Gemara clarifies that the verse 'do not put oil on it' only prohibits fixing oil for it like its counterparts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a dispute: a kometz of a sin-offering that was oiled — Rabbi Yochanan says it is invalid, Reish Lakish says one can stir it in the remaining oil and offer it.
The Gemara objects: but it is written 'do not put oil on it' (Leviticus 5:11), implying any oil invalidates the sin-offering.
The Gemara answers: that verse only prohibits fixing oil for it like its counterparts (other meal-offerings), not removing oil already mixed in.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection and clarification
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection and clarification
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish with a baraita about a dry offering mixed with a moist one, where Rabbi Yehuda says it may not be offered. The Gemara initially thinks this refers to a kometz of a sin-offering mixed with a kometz of a free-will offering, but then clarifies it is about different types of meal-offerings (for bulls/rams vs. lambs).

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish by citing a baraita: a dry meal-offering (חָרֵב) mixed with a moist one (בָּלוּל) may be offered, but Rabbi Yehuda says it may not.
The Gemara asks: does this not refer to a קומץ (handful) of a sin-offering mixed with a קומץ of a free-will offering?
The Gemara rejects the initial interpretation and clarifies: it refers to meal-offerings of bulls and rams mixed with those of lambs.
The Gemara notes that the baraita explicitly states 'meal-offering of bulls and rams with meal-offering of lambs,' and that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling is explicitly about that case.

items.text: Rava's query about oil on wood and the parallel debate
items.text_en: Rava's query about oil on wood and the parallel debate
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if one squeezed the oil of a kometz onto wood, is it considered attached for offering? Ravina suggests this is the same as the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about a limb without an olive's bulk completed by a bone. The Gemara explores whether the oil case differs, concluding with teiku (undecided).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether oil squeezed from a kometz (handful) onto wood is considered attached for the purpose of offering, or not.
Ravina suggests to Rav Ashi that Rava's query is identical to the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.
The Gemara cites the debate about a limb without an olive's bulk completed by a bone, where Rabbi Yochanan holds one is liable and Reish Lakish holds one is exempt.

The Gemara raises a possible distinction: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling there applies only to bone, which is of the same type as flesh, but oil is not of the same type as the kometz, so perhaps he would not apply it here.
The Gemara raises another possibility that even Reish Lakish might distinguish bone from oil, but concludes with teiku (undecided).

items.text: Mishnah: mixtures of meal-offerings and kometz
items.text_en: Mishnah: mixtures of meal-offerings and kometz
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses cases where two meal-offerings that were not yet scooped are mixed, or a kometz is mixed with an unscoped offering or with its remnants. It rules on validity and whether the offering is credited to the owner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of two meal-offerings that were not yet scooped and became mixed; if each can be scooped separately they are valid, otherwise invalid.
The Mishnah rules on a kometz mixed with an unscoped meal-offering: do not burn it; if burned, the scooped offering is credited but the unscoped one is not.
The Mishnah concludes with the case of a kometz mixed with its own remnants or another's remnants: do not burn it, but if burned it is credited to the owner.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina on nullification
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina on nullification
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that a neveila is nullified in a properly slaughtered animal, but not vice versa. Rabbi Chanina generalizes: anything that can become like the other is not nullified. The Gemara questions whose opinion this aligns with, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that a neveila (unslaughtered animal carcass) is nullified in a properly slaughtered animal because the slaughtered animal cannot become a neveila.
Rav Chisda adds that a slaughtered animal is not nullified in a neveila because the neveila can become like a slaughtered animal when it rots and loses its impurity.
Rabbi Chanina generalizes: anything that can become like the other is not nullified, and anything that cannot become like the other is nullified.
The Gemara questions whose opinion Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina follow, considering the views of the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's principle: following the appearance
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's principle: following the appearance
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yehuda follows the appearance, and that both items are of the same kind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yehuda follows the appearance, and that both items are of the same kind.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya's baraita and the debate over nullification of same kinds
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya's baraita and the debate over nullification of same kinds
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Chiyya's teaching that neveilah and shechutah nullify each other, and questions whether this aligns with the Rabbis or Rabbi Yehuda. It resolves that Rabbi Yehuda only says same kinds do not nullify when it is possible to have the same kind, but not when impossible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Chiyya's baraita that neveilah and shechutah nullify each other.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Chiyya's baraita aligns with the Rabbis or Rabbi Yehuda, noting that both positions seem to contradict it.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chiyya's baraita aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who only says same kinds do not nullify when it is possible to have the same kind, but not when impossible.

items.text: The dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina: following the nullifier or the nullified
items.text_en: The dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina: following the nullifier or the nullified
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rav Chisda holds that we follow the nullifier, while Rabbi Chanina holds that we follow the nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina.
Rav Chisda holds that we follow the nullifier (the substance that causes nullification).
Rabbi Chanina holds that we follow the nullified (the substance that is nullified).

items.text: First proof: two meal offerings mixed before kemitzah
items.text_en: First proof: two meal offerings mixed before kemitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about two meal offerings that were mixed before kemitzah, and analyzes whether it aligns with Rabbi Yehuda. It then explains the difficulty for Rav Chisda's view and resolves it using Rabbi Zeira's principle that kemitzah and shirayim do not nullify each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about two meal offerings mixed before kemitzah, showing that shirayim do not nullify the untithed portion.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the mishnah follows, and concludes it must be Rabbi Yehuda, since the Rabbis would allow nullification of like substances.
The Gemara notes that the mishnah works for the view that we follow the nullified item, but objects that for Rav Chisda's view (following the nullifier), the shirayim would not be untithed.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by invoking Rabbi Zeira's principle that just as the kemitzah does not nullify its fellow, so too the shirayim do not nullify the kemitzah.

items.text: Second proof: kometz mixed with an unkemitzah meal offering
items.text_en: Second proof: kometz mixed with an unkemitzah meal offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a kometz that became mixed with a meal offering that had not yet had its kemitzah performed, and analyzes the difficulty for Rabbi Chanina's view, again resolving with Rabbi Zeira's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a kometz that became mixed with a meal offering that had not yet had its kemitzah performed, and notes that the untithed portion does not nullify the kometz.
The Gemara asks who authored the baraita, concluding it must be Rabbi Yehuda, since the Rabbis would hold that like-types nullify each other.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis for Rav Chisda's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis for Rav Chisda's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rav Chisda, who follows the nullifier, the kometz is like the nullified substance, and since any particle is fit for kemitzah, it is a like-type mixture that does not nullify.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution with Rabbi Zeira's principle
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution with Rabbi Zeira's principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty for Rabbi Chanina, who follows the nullified substance, by invoking Rabbi Zeira's principle that the kometz and the remnants do not nullify each other.

items.text: Third proof: kometz mixed with shirayim of another offering
items.text_en: Third proof: kometz mixed with shirayim of another offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a kometz that became mixed with the shirayim of another meal offering, and again invokes Rabbi Zeira's principle to explain why the shirayim do not nullify the kometz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a kometz that became mixed with the shirayim of another offering, showing that the shirayim do not nullify the kometz.
The Gemara asks whose position this baraita follows, suggesting it cannot be the Rabbis who hold that like-types are nullified.
Rabbi Zeira invokes his principle that just as the kometz does not nullify its fellow, so too the shirayim do not nullify the kometz, explaining why nullification does not apply.

items.text: Fourth proof: matzah mixed with spices
items.text_en: Fourth proof: matzah mixed with spices
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about matzah mixed with spices, and analyzes the difficulty for Rav Chisda's view. It concludes that the case involves a minority of spices, so the matzah is not nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about matzah mixed with spices, which is still called matzah, and initially assumes the spices are a majority.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraita against Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraita against Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Chanina (who follows the nullified item), the matzah is nullified by the majority spices, but according to Rav Chisda (who follows the nullifier), the spices cannot become matzah, posing a difficulty.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita deals with a minority of spices, so the matzah is not nullified, and the baraita's language confirms this.

items.text: Transition: Rav Kahana's ascent and the sons of Rabbi Chiyya
items.text_en: Transition: Rav Kahana's ascent and the sons of Rabbi Chiyya
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new narrative: when Rav Kahana ascended, he found the sons of Rabbi Chiyya discussing a case of an isaron that was divided.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara narrates that when Rav Kahana ascended, he found the sons of Rabbi Chiyya discussing a case of an isaron that was divided.

items.text: First question: טבול יום touches one portion in a basket
items.text_en: First question: טבול יום touches one portion in a basket
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a טבול יום touches one of two portions of a meal-offering placed in a basket (ביסa), does the basket combine them so that both become impure? The question hinges on whether the principle 'כלי מצרף מה שבתוכו לקודש' applies only when the portions touch each other, or even when they do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a basket (ביסa) combines two portions of a meal-offering for impurity when a טבול יום touches one, questioning if the principle 'כלי מצרף מה שבתוכו לקודש' applies only when the portions touch each other or even when they do not.

items.text: Answer: 'כלי מצרף' vs 'כלי מחבר'
items.text_en: Answer: 'כלי מצרף' vs 'כלי מחבר'
items.desc_en: The questioner responds: the Mishna says 'כלי מצרף' (combines), not 'כלי מחבר' (connects), implying it always combines. He then asks a new case: what if one inserted a utensil between the portions?

sub.desc_en: The rabbi responds that the Mishna teaches 'כלי מצרף' (a vessel combines), not 'כלי מחבר' (a vessel connects), implying it combines even without contact, then asks a new question about inserting an object between the portions.

items.text: Answer: Distinction based on need for utensil
items.text_en: Answer: Distinction based on need for utensil
items.desc_en: The questioner answers his own question: a utensil combines only when it is necessary for the contents (e.g., for the service), but if not needed, it does not combine.

sub.desc_en: The rabbi answers that a vessel combines only when the portions need the vessel to hold them together, but not when they are independent.

items.text: Question: טבול יום inserts his finger between portions
items.text_en: Question: טבול יום inserts his finger between portions
items.desc_en: The questioner asks: what if a טבול יום inserts his finger between the portions? The answer: only an earthenware vessel conveys impurity through its airspace, not a finger.

sub.desc_en: The rabbi asks about a טבול יום inserting his finger between the portions, and answers that only a clay vessel (כלי חרס) transmits impurity through its airspace, not a finger.
The answerer responds: nothing conveys impurity through its airspace except an earthenware vessel, so a finger does not.

items.text: Question: קמיצה from one portion on behalf of another
items.text_en: Question: קמיצה from one portion on behalf of another
items.desc_en: The questioner now asks: may one perform קמיצה from one portion of a meal-offering on behalf of another? The issue is whether צירוף is biblical or rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: The rabbi asks whether one may take a handful (קומץ) from one portion on behalf of another, questioning if the combining (צירוף) is biblical (דאורייתא) or rabbinic (דרבנן).

items.text: Response: A similar case from a Mishna
items.text_en: Response: A similar case from a Mishna
items.desc_en: The sages respond: we have not heard about this, but we have heard a similar case: two meal-offerings that were not yet קמץ and became mixed. If one can take a קמץ from each separately, they are valid; otherwise invalid. Rava explains that the case involves separate lumps like a comb.

sub.desc_en: The sages respond that they have not heard about this case, but they have heard a similar case from a Mishna: two meal-offerings that were not yet קמץ (handful taken) and became mixed; if one can take a קמץ from each separately they are valid, otherwise invalid.
The gemara questions: if one can take a קמץ from each separately, why are they valid? The mixed portion was not touched by the other's קמץ.
Rava answers that the Mishna's case involves separate lumps (גושין) arranged like a comb, so the קמץ from each does not touch the other's portion.

items.text: Rava's proof from a baraisa and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rava's proof from a baraisa and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraisa: 'והרים ממנו' – from the connected part, meaning one may not bring an עשרון in two vessels and take a קמץ. But in one vessel that is like two vessels, one may take a קמץ. Abaye objects: two vessels means like a קפיזא in a קב, where partitions separate below; one vessel like two vessels means like a chicken trough, where partitions are above but the contents touch. Here, where they do not touch at all, it remains a question.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraisa that derives from the verse 'והרים ממנו' that the taking of the קמץ must be from the connected part, implying that in one vessel that is like two vessels, one may take a קמץ.

Abaye objects that the baraisa's case of two vessels involves partitions below (like a קפיזא in a קב), and one vessel like two vessels involves partitions above but with contact (like a chicken trough), whereas here the portions do not touch at all, so the question remains unresolved.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question: combination of utensil and water connection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question: combination of utensil and water connection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks: what is the law regarding the combination of a utensil and the connection of water? Does the principle of 'כלי מצרף' apply only to what is inside, or also to what is outside via water? And if a טבול יום touches from outside, does the utensil combine? The Gemara concludes with תיקו.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks: what is the law regarding the combination of a utensil (כלי מצרף) and the connection of water (חיבור מים)?

The Gemara clarifies the question: does the principle of 'כלי מצרף' apply only to what is inside the utensil (דְּגַוַּאי), or also to what is outside (דְּבָרַאי) via the water connection, since the water connects them?
Rabbi Yirmeya further asks: if we assume the water connection combines, what if a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) touches from outside (מבחוץ) — does the utensil still combine?
The Gemara concludes with תיקו (the question stands unresolved): does the rule of 'כלי מצרף' apply only when the touch is from inside (מגוואי), or is there no difference even from outside (מבראי)?

items.text: Rava's question: impurity of a divided עשרון
items.text_en: Rava's question: impurity of a divided עשרון
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if an עשרון was divided, one part became impure, and a טבול יום touched the impure part while both were in a basket, does the impurity 'satiate' itself (i.e., is the impure part considered fully impure so that it does not transmit further)? Abaye objects, citing a Mishna about a טמא סדין.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: if an עשרון was divided, one part became impure, and a טבול יום touched the impure part while both were in a basket, does the impurity 'satiate' itself (i.e., is the impure part considered fully impure so that it does not transmit further)?
Abaye objects, citing a Mishna about a טמא סדין (impure sheet) to argue that impurity does not 'satiate' itself.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rabbi Yossi's statement
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rabbi Yossi's statement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a garment used as a midras (pressure-impurity) and then made into a curtain is pure from midras but impure with magga midras (contact impurity). Rabbi Yossi objects, arguing that the concept of 'midras contact' is meaningless; rather, if a zav touches it, it is impure with the impurity of zav-contact.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution on the sequence of impurities
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution on the sequence of impurities
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why, if the zav touches the garment after it was already a midras, it should be impure with zav-contact, given the principle of 'שבע ליה טומאה' (saturation of impurity). It suggests that Rabbi Yossi's statement might refer to the zav touching before the midras, where a severe impurity (zav) overrides a light one (midras). However, the Gemara concludes that in a case where both impurities are light, the principle applies.

items.text: Proof from the case of two folded sheets
items.text_en: Proof from the case of two folded sheets
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from a case where a zav sits on two folded sheets: the upper sheet is impure with midras, and the lower sheet is impure with both midras and magga midras. The Gemara asks why the lower sheet is not saturated with impurity, and answers that there the impurities occur simultaneously, whereas here they occur sequentially.

items.text: Rava's case of the divided tenth-ephah
items.text_en: Rava's case of the divided tenth-ephah
items.desc_en: Rava presents a case: a tenth-ephah (עשרון) was divided, one part was lost, another was separated to replace it, and then the original was found, leaving three portions in a basket. He rules that if the lost portion becomes impure, the lost and original combine, but the separated one does not; if the separated one becomes impure, it and the original combine, but the lost does not; if the original becomes impure, both combine.

items.text: Abaye's objection to Rava
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rava
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that even if one of the portions becomes impure, both combine, because all are considered 'בני ביקתא דהדדי' (part of the same batch).

items.text: Application to kemitzah (handful-taking)
items.text_en: Application to kemitzah (handful-taking)
items.desc_en: The same principle is applied to kemitzah: if the kohen takes the handful from the lost portion, its remnants and the original are eaten, but the separated one is not; if from the separated, its remnants and the original are eaten, but the lost is not; if from the original, neither is eaten.

items.text: Abaye's extension to kemitzah
items.text_en: Abaye's extension to kemitzah
items.desc_en: Abaye extends his view to kemitzah: even if the handful is taken from one of the portions, neither is eaten, because all are part of the same batch.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Yitzchak's objections, and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Yitzchak's objections, and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects: how can the remnants be eaten if there is a handful that was not offered? Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya objects: how can the handful itself be offered if it contains three non-sacred parts? Rav Ashi resolves: the handful is determined by the kohen's intent, and when he takes it, he intends for the tenth-ephah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the ציץ atones for impurity but not for offering outside the courtyard (יוצא).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the ציץ (frontlet) atones for impurity but not for offering outside the courtyard (יוצא).

items.text: Gemara's initial deduction from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's initial deduction from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta that derives from the verse 'וְנָשָׂא אַהֲרֹן אֶת עֲוֹן הַקֳּדָשִׁים' that the ציץ atones only for impurity, not for piggul or notar, which are already excluded by other verses.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta cites the verse 'וְנָשָׂא אַהֲרֹן אֶת עֲוֹן הַקֳּדָשִׁים' and argues that the עון (sin) borne by the ציץ cannot be piggul or notar, as those are already excluded by other verses.
The Tosefta concludes that the ציץ atones only for the sin of טומאה (ritual impurity), which was permitted in its general category for communal offerings.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's challenge and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's challenge and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges that the verse could refer to the sin of יוצא, which is permitted in a private altar (במה). Abaye responds that the verse says 'לִפְנֵי ה׳', excluding יוצא which is outside the camp.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects that the verse could refer to the sin of יוצא (an offering taken outside the Temple), which is permitted in a private altar (במה).
Abaye responds that the verse says 'לִפְנֵי ה׳' (before the Lord), excluding יוצא which is outside the camp.

items.text: Rabbi Ila'a's challenge and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a's challenge and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a challenges that the verse could refer to the sin of offering with the left hand (שמאל), which is permitted on Yom Kippur. Abaye answers that the verse says 'עָוֹן', implying a sin that was originally present and then pushed aside, but on Yom Kippur the left hand is the primary mode of offering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a objects that the verse could refer to the sin of offering with the left hand (שמאל), which is permitted on Yom Kippur.
Abaye answers that the verse says 'עָוֹן', implying a sin that was originally present and then pushed aside, but on Yom Kippur the left hand is the primary mode of offering.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi derives from the verse 'עֲוֹן הַקֳּדָשִׁים' that the ציץ atones for the sin of the offerings, not the sin of the offerers (המקדישים).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi derives from the verse 'עֲוֹן הַקֳּדָשִׁים' that the ציץ atones for the sin of the offerings, not the sin of the offerers (המקדישים).

items.text: Rav Sima's challenge and Rav Ashi's answer
items.text_en: Rav Sima's challenge and Rav Ashi's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Sima challenges that the verse could refer to the sin of a blemished animal (בעל מום), which is permitted in bird offerings. Rav Ashi answers that the verse says 'לֹא יֵרָצֶה' and 'כִּי לֹא לְרָצוֹן יִהְיֶה לָכֶם', excluding blemished animals.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sima challenges Rav Ashi that the verse could refer to the sin of a blemished animal (בעל מום), which is permitted in bird offerings.
Rav Ashi answers that the verse says 'לֹא יֵרָצֶה' and 'כִּי לֹא לְרָצוֹן יִהְיֶה לָכֶם', excluding blemished animals.

items.text: Baraita on blood that became impure
items.text_en: Baraita on blood that became impure
items.desc_en: A Baraita teaches that if blood became impure and was sprinkled unintentionally, it is accepted; if intentionally, it is not. For communal offerings, it is always accepted; for non-Jews, it is always accepted regardless of intent.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the law of blood that became impure: if sprinkled unintentionally it is accepted, if intentionally it is not; for communal offerings and non-Jews it is always accepted regardless of intent.

items.text: Opening statement: לא הורצה
items.text_en: Opening statement: לא הורצה
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a brief statement that the offering was not accepted, setting up the contradiction to follow.

items.text: Contradiction from a baraita about the ציץ
items.text_en: Contradiction from a baraita about the ציץ
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that the ציץ effects acceptance for blood, flesh, and fat that became impure, regardless of intent or community status, contradicting the previous statement.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution: Rabbi Yossi vs. Rabbis
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution: Rabbi Yossi vs. Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing the first statement to Rabbi Yossi and the baraita to the Rabbis, citing a Tosefta about תרומה where Rabbi Yossi does not penalize intentional transgression.

items.text: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yossi hold that the ציץ works for eating?
items.text_en: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yossi hold that the ציץ works for eating?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Yosef, noting that a baraita explicitly states Rabbi Yossi says the ציץ does not effect acceptance for eating, unlike Rabbi Eliezer. The Gemara then suggests reversing the attributions.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection: The baraita about impurity and acceptance
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection: The baraita about impurity and acceptance
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects to reversing the attributions, citing a baraita that derives from verses that only meat permitted to the pure incurs liability for impurity, and that the ציץ effects acceptance for meat that became impure before blood sprinkling. The baraita concludes that Rabbi Eliezer holds the ציץ works for eating.

items.text: Proof that Rabbi Eliezer holds the ציץ works for eating
items.text_en: Proof that Rabbi Eliezer holds the ציץ works for eating
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that if meat became impure before sprinkling, liability for impurity after sprinkling is because the ציץ effects acceptance. It then notes that only Rabbi Eliezer holds that sprinkling does not help for meat that left the courtyard, and he also holds the ציץ works for eating.

items.text: Rav Chisda's resolution: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Rabbis
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's resolution: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda resolves the original contradiction by attributing the first statement to the Rabbis and the baraita to Rabbi Eliezer. The Gemara then questions whether Rabbi Eliezer also does not penalize intentional transgression, and after a back-and-forth about תרומה and קדשים, concludes that the baraita must be attributed to Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Ravina and Rav Sheila's alternative resolutions
items.text_en: Ravina and Rav Sheila's alternative resolutions
items.desc_en: Ravina and Rav Sheila offer different resolutions: Ravina distinguishes between impurity (intentional or not) and sprinkling (only unintentional), while Rav Sheila reverses the distinction. The Gemara explains Rav Sheila's view in light of the baraita.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah on impure blood
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah on impure blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies a baraita about blood that became impure and was sprinkled: if done unintentionally, it is accepted; if intentionally, it is not. It explains that the statement refers to the blood becoming impure, not the sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about blood that became impure and was sprinkled, distinguishing between unintentional and intentional cases.

items.text: Mishnah: Status of remnants
items.text_en: Mishnah: Status of remnants
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the remnants (שיירים) of a sacrifice become impure, are burned, or are lost, according to Rabbi Eliezer the sacrifice is valid, but according to Rabbi Yehoshua it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the remnants of a sacrifice become impure, are burned, or are lost, according to Rabbi Eliezer the sacrifice is valid, but according to Rabbi Yehoshua it is invalid.

items.text: Gemara: Rav's limitation and analysis
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav's limitation and analysis
items.desc_en: Rav limits the Mishnah to cases where all remnants are impure, not just some. The Gemara questions whether the same applies to lost or burned remnants, and resolves that the Mishnah's mention of impurity is just an example; the same rule applies to loss or burning, as remnants are significant.

sub.desc_en: Rav limits the Mishnah's ruling to a case where all remnants became impure, not just some of them.
The Gemara questions whether Rav's limitation applies only to impurity, or also to lost or burned remnants, analyzing the underlying logic of whether remnants matter (שיורא מילתא היא).
The Gemara resolves that Rav considers remnants significant (שיורא מילתא היא), so the same rule applies for loss or burning, and the Mishnah simply mentioned impurity as its primary case.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling on remnants
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling on remnants
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling: for any sacrifice, if an olive's bulk of meat or fat remains, the blood may be sprinkled; for a burnt offering, even half an olive of each suffices; for a meal-offering, even if all remains, the blood is not sprinkled. Rav Pappa explains this refers to the meal-offering of libations.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yehoshua's general rule: for any sacrifice, an olive's bulk of remaining meat or fat permits the blood to be sprinkled.

The baraita completes Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling: half an olive of each does not suffice for most sacrifices, but for a burnt offering it does, while for a meal-offering even if all remains the blood is not sprinkled.
Rav Pappa explains that the meal-offering in question is the accompanying meal-offering of libations, teaching that it is not treated as part of the sacrifice itself.

items.text: Source for sprinkling blood without meat
items.text_en: Source for sprinkling blood without meat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verse 'and he shall burn the fat for a pleasing aroma' that the fat alone suffices even without meat. This is extended to the diaphragm and kidneys, and a meal-offering is excluded. The need for both 'fat' and 'pleasing aroma' is explained.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that blood is sprinkled even when only fat remains, and cites Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael (with some attributing to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya).
The verse 'and he shall burn the fat for a pleasing aroma to the Lord' is cited, proving that fat alone suffices for the sprinkling even without meat.
The Gemara asks where the diaphragm and two kidneys (also offered on the altar) are included, and infers from the Mishnah that a meal-offering is excluded but these are included.

sub.text: Gemara's answer — Rabbi Yochanan's own derivation
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer — Rabbi Yochanan's own derivation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan himself derives from the phrase 'לְרֵיחַ נִיחֹחַ' (for a pleasing aroma) that anything you offer for a pleasing aroma is valid, including the diaphragm and kidneys.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of why both terms are needed
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of why both terms are needed
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both 'חֵלֶב' (fat) and 'לְרֵיחַ נִיחֹחַ' (for a pleasing aroma) are needed: 'חֵלֶב' alone would exclude diaphragm and kidneys, and 'לְרֵיחַ נִיחֹחַ' alone would include even a meal-offering, so both are written to indicate that only items brought for a pleasing aroma (fat, diaphragm, kidneys) are valid, not a meal-offering.

items.text: Mishnah: Offering without a sacred vessel
items.text_en: Mishnah: Offering without a sacred vessel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the kemitzah (handful) is offered without a sacred vessel, it is invalid, but Rabbi Shimon validates it. If the kemitzah is offered in two acts, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a meal-offering not in sacred vessels is invalid, but Rabbi Shimon validates it; if one offered its handful in two stages it is valid.

items.text: Gemara: Reasons for Rabbi Shimon's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara: Reasons for Rabbi Shimon's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiya explains Rabbi Shimon's view: the verse 'holy of holies' compares the meal-offering to a sin-offering (requiring right hand) and a guilt-offering (requiring a vessel). Rabbi Yannai says that once the kemitzah is taken from a sacred vessel, it may be offered even in one's belt or an earthenware pot. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes all agree the kemitzah requires sanctification.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiya asks for the reason behind Rabbi Shimon's ruling that the kemitzah (handful) may be offered without a sacred vessel.

He explains that the verse 'קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים הִיא כַּחַטָּאת וְכָאָשָׁם' (holy of holies, like a sin-offering and like a guilt-offering) teaches that the meal-offering is performed by hand (right hand) like a sin-offering, and in a vessel (left hand) like a guilt-offering.
Rabbi Yannai states that once the kemitzah is taken from a sacred vessel, it may be offered even in one's belt or an earthenware pot.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes that all agree the kemitzah requires sanctification (קידוש) in a sacred vessel.

items.text: Challenges and resolutions regarding Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Challenges and resolutions regarding Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings objections from baraitot that seem to contradict Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiya's explanation. He responds by reinterpreting the baraita. Further challenges are raised about the requirement for a sacred vessel, and the Gemara concludes with a discussion about the right hand and left hand in kemitzah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists kemitzah and incense as valid whether done by hand or with a vessel, in right or left hand, which contradicts Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiya's distinction.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiya's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiya's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiya responds that the baraita is teaching two separate cases: by hand in the right hand, and with a vessel in either hand.
The Gemara brings another baraita stating that kemitzah without a sacred vessel is invalid, and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon only validate from the point of placing in a vessel onward.
The Gemara resolves the objection by reinterpreting the baraita: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon only validate from the point of placing in a vessel onward, not the initial kemitzah.
The Gemara brings a baraita where the Sages require a sacred vessel for the entire process, while Rabbi Shimon only requires it for the initial kemitzah.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon requires both kemitzah and kiddush in a sacred vessel, but then allows the offering without a vessel.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about kemitzah with the right hand and placing in the left, requiring return to the right hand.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between improper place and improper time
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between improper place and improper time
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one intends to eat the sacrifice outside its proper place or time, it is invalid, but only improper time incurs karet. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon hold that improper place renders it invalid without karet, while improper time makes it pigul with karet. The Sages argue that placing the blood on the left side invalidates it entirely, as if the blood was spilled and collected.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if one intends to eat the sacrifice outside its proper place or time, it is invalid but does not incur karet.
Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon specify that improper place renders it invalid without karet, while improper time makes it pigul (פיגול) with karet.
The Sages argue that placing the blood on the left side invalidates it entirely, as if the blood was spilled and collected.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rav Nachman and support for Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rav Nachman and support for Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon do not require the blood to be placed in a vessel, which contradicts Rav Nachman's position. It then questions whether this is also a refutation of Rabbi Yannai, but Rabbi Yannai defends himself by claiming he follows the Tanna of the burning, not the one of the sides.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon do not require the blood to be placed in a vessel, and declares this a refutation of Rav Nachman.
The Gemara notes that this supports Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya, and questions whether it also constitutes a refutation of Rabbi Yannai.
Rabbi Yannai defends himself by claiming he follows the Tanna of the burning, not the Tanna of the sides.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan on 'twice'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan on 'twice'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one burned the handful twice, it is valid. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets 'twice' as exactly two times, not multiple times, while Rabbi Yochanan says it can be even multiple times. Rabbi Zeira explains the practical difference: whether there can be a handful less than two olive-bulks and a burning less than an olive-bulk.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one burned the handful twice, it is valid.
רבי יהושע בן לוי (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) interprets 'twice' as exactly two times, not multiple times.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) says it can be even multiple times.
The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two opinions.
רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) explains the dispute hinges on whether there can be a handful less than two olive-bulks and a burning less than an olive-bulk.

The Gemara clarifies that רבי יהושע בן לוי (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) holds there is no significance to a handful less than two olive-bulks or a burning less than an olive-bulk, while רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) holds there is significance.

items.text: When does the handful permit the remainder?
items.text_en: When does the handful permit the remainder?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks when the handful permits the remainder to be eaten. Rabbi Chanina says from the time the fire takes hold of it, while Rabbi Yochanan says from the time the fire catches most of it. Rav Yehuda explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning with a verse about the smoke of a furnace, which only rises when the fire catches most of it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From when does the handful permit the remainder to be eaten?
רבי חנינא (Rabbi Chanina) says: From the time the fire takes hold of it.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) says: From the time the fire catches most of it.

רב יהודה (Rav Yehuda) explains to רבה בר רב יצחק (Rabba bar Rav Yitzchak) the reasoning of רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan), citing the verse about the smoke of a furnace, which only rises when the fire catches most of it.

items.text: Baraita on burning times and resolution of contradiction
items.text_en: Baraita on burning times and resolution of contradiction
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that items normally burned at night, like limbs and fats, can be offered from sunset and burn all night. For items normally burned by day, like the handful and frankincense, the verse 'This is the law of the burnt-offering' includes them to be offered at sunset. The Gemara notes that at sunset the fire has not caught most of it, and resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between 'absorbing' (to begin burning) and 'permitting' (to allow eating).

sub.text: Ravin bar Rav Adda to Rava
sub.text_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda to Rava
sub.desc_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda reports to Rava a baraita taught by Rav Amram, beginning with items normally burned at night.
The baraita lists items normally burned by day, such as the handful and frankincense, and asks whether they can be offered at sunset.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita means 'with sunset' (not after), and derives from the verse 'This is the law of the burnt-offering' that these items are included to burn all night.
The Gemara objects that at sunset the fire has not caught most of the item, and resolves by distinguishing between 'absorbing' (to begin burning) and 'permitting' (to allow eating).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's version and contradiction with Rabbi Yannai on scattered incense
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's version and contradiction with Rabbi Yannai on scattered incense
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches the baraita with 'at sunset' and interprets it as referring to coals that have scattered. Rabbi Yannai agrees. However, this contradicts Rabbi Yannai's earlier statement that incense that scattered from the altar cannot be returned, even its crumbs, based on a verse about the fire consuming the burnt-offering. The Gemara concludes that incense is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Elazar teaches the baraita with the phrase 'at sunset' and interprets it as referring to coals that have scattered, and Rav Dimi confirms that Rabbi Yannai agrees.

The Gemara objects: Did Rabbi Yannai really say that? He earlier ruled that incense that scattered from the altar cannot be returned, even its crumbs, citing a baraita from Rabbi Chanina bar Minyomi in the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov that derives from the verse 'which the fire consumes the burnt-offering' that only the consumed parts of a burnt-offering are returned, not those of incense.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by concluding that incense is different from the coals of the altar, so Rabbi Yannai's ruling on scattered incense does not conflict with his interpretation of the baraita regarding scattered coals.

items.text: Three unresolved questions about arranging limbs on the altar
items.text_en: Three unresolved questions about arranging limbs on the altar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi reports that Rabbi Elazar asked: if one arranged the handful and then arranged the woodpile on top of it, is that a valid method of burning? The question remains unresolved. Chizkiyah asked about limbs arranged with the woodpile on top: must they be directly on the wood, or can they be under it? Also unresolved. Rabbi Yitzchak the smith asked about limbs arranged on the sides of the woodpile, but the text breaks off.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether arranging the handful (קומץ) and then placing the woodpile on top of it is a valid method of burning.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).
Chizkiyah asks whether limbs arranged with the woodpile on top must be directly on the wood (על העצים) or if they can be under it, given another verse.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).
Rabbi Yitzchak the smith asks about limbs arranged on the sides of the woodpile, but the text breaks off before a resolution.

items.text: Gemara's unresolved question about 'על'
items.text_en: Gemara's unresolved question about 'על'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the word 'על' in the context of the wood for the altar means 'near' or 'directly on', and leaves the matter unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Mishnah: Components that require full measure
items.text_en: Mishnah: Components that require full measure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a handful (קומץ), a tenth of an ephah (עשרון), wine, and oil each require their full measure; the flour and oil of a meal-offering, and the handful and frankincense, mutually impede each other.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural sources for the Mishnah's rules
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural sources for the Mishnah's rules
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives each rule from a verse: the handful from 'מלא קמצו' repeated, the tenth from 'מסלתה', wine and oil from 'ככה', and the mutual impediment of flour and oil from 'מסלתה ומשמנה' and 'מגרשה ומשמנה', and of the handful and frankincense from 'על כל לבונתה' and 'ואת כל הלבונה'.

items.text: Mishnah: Pairs and groups that mutually impede
items.text_en: Mishnah: Pairs and groups that mutually impede
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists pairs and groups that must all be present: the two goats of Yom Kippur, the two lambs of Shavuot, the two loaves, the two rows of showbread, the two bowls of frankincense, the two species for the nazirite, the three for the red heifer, the four for the thanksgiving offering, the four for the lulav, the four for the metzora, and the seven sprinklings for various rites.

items.text: Gemara: Sources for the Mishnah's pairs and groups
items.text_en: Gemara: Sources for the Mishnah's pairs and groups
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides scriptural sources: the goats of Yom Kippur and the rows and bowls from 'חוקה', the lambs and loaves from 'הויה', the nazirite species from 'כן יעשה', the red heifer from 'חוקה', the thanksgiving from an analogy to the nazirite, the metzora from 'זאת תהיה תורת המצרע', and the lulav from 'ולקחתם' implying a complete taking.

items.text: Debate about binding the lulav and the requirement of an 'agudah'
items.text_en: Debate about binding the lulav and the requirement of an 'agudah'
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava limits the Mishnah's rule to when one lacks the species, but if one has them, they do not impede. A challenge is raised from a baraita requiring the four species to be bound together. The Gemara resolves that this is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, and explains that the mitzvah to bind is for beautification, not validity.

items.text: Gemara: Sources for the seven sprinklings and other rites
items.text_en: Gemara: Sources for the seven sprinklings and other rites
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the mutual impediment of the seven sprinklings of the red heifer from 'חוקה', those of Yom Kippur from 'חוקה', and those of the anointed priest's bull, the congregation's bull for an unwitting sin, and the goats for idolatry from a verse that doubles the sprinklings.

items.text: Opening statement about missing one sprinkling
items.text_en: Opening statement about missing one sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general rule: if one omitted even one of the required sprinklings, the entire procedure is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general rule: if one omitted even one of the required sprinklings, the entire procedure is invalid.

items.text: Baraita on sprinklings for the red heifer, inner sin-offerings, and the leper
items.text_en: Baraita on sprinklings for the red heifer, inner sin-offerings, and the leper
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: the seven sprinklings of the red heifer are invalid if done not for their own sake or not directed toward the Tent of Meeting. For inner sin-offerings and the leper, not for their own sake invalidates, but not directed is valid.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the rules for the red heifer's seven sprinklings and for inner sin-offerings and the leper: not for their own sake invalidates all, but not directed toward the Tent of Meeting invalidates only the red heifer.

items.text: Reconciliation of the contradiction
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: another baraita says that for the red heifer, not for their own sake invalidates, but not directed is valid. Rav Chisda resolves: the first baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, the second follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita states that for the red heifer, not for their own sake invalidates, but not directed is valid.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction: the first baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, the second follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Baraita on entering the Temple while impure
items.text_en: Baraita on entering the Temple while impure
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the penalties for those lacking atonement who enter the Temple courtyard: unintentionally brings a sin-offering, intentionally is liable to karet. It also distinguishes between entering the Sanctuary (40 lashes) and entering the Holy of Holies (death). Rabbi Yehuda argues that the entire Sanctuary and the area before the Parochet are punishable by lashes, only the area before the Ark cover by death.

sub.desc_en: The baraita is cited to support the distinction between intentional and unintentional entry into the Temple courtyard for those lacking atonement.
The baraita continues with the penalties for pure individuals entering beyond their boundary: the Sanctuary carries lashes, the area before the Ark cover carries death.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that the entire Sanctuary and the area before the Parochet are punishable by lashes, only the area before the Ark cover by death.

items.text: The dispute's scriptural basis
items.text_en: The dispute's scriptural basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: the Rabbis interpret the verse to mean that entering the Sanctuary is prohibited under penalty of 'do not come', while entering from the Parochet to the Ark cover is under penalty of death. Rabbi Yehuda holds that the Sanctuary and the area before the Parochet are both under 'do not come', and only the area before the Ark cover is under death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what scriptural basis do the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda disagree?
The Gemara cites the verse from Leviticus 16:2 as the basis of the dispute.
The Rabbis hold that entering the Sanctuary is under the prohibition of 'do not come', while entering from the Parochet to the Ark cover is under the penalty of death.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that the Sanctuary and the area before the Parochet are both under the prohibition of 'do not come', and only the area before the Ark cover is under the penalty of death.

items.text: Reasoning of the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.text_en: Reasoning of the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the Rabbis' reasoning: if the verse meant as Rabbi Yehuda says, it would not need to mention 'from before the Parochet' separately. Rabbi Yehuda counters that without that phrase, one might think 'Kodesh' refers only to the Holy of Holies. The Rabbis respond that the entire Sanctuary is called 'Kodesh' as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the Rabbis' reasoning and explains that if the verse meant as Rabbi Yehuda says, the phrase 'מבית לפרוכת' (from within the Curtain) would be superfluous, proving that entering there incurs death.
Rabbi Yehuda counters that without 'מבית לפרוכת' (from within the Curtain), one might think 'קודש' (the holy place) refers only to the Holy of Holies, and the Sanctuary would not even be prohibited.

The Rabbis reject Rabbi Yehuda's concern, arguing that the entire Sanctuary is called 'קודש' (the holy place), as proven by the verse 'והבדילה הפרכת לכם בין הקדש ובין קדש הקדשים' (And the Curtain shall divide for you between the holy place and the Holy of Holies).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and the Rabbis' response
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and the Rabbis' response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues that if the verse meant as the Rabbis say, it would not need to mention 'to the face of the Ark cover'. The Rabbis respond that indeed it is not necessary, and it comes to exclude the 'crawling path' (entering sideways).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning, presenting his argument that if the verse meant as the Rabbis say, it would not need to mention 'אל פני הכפרת' (to the face of the Ark cover).
The Rabbis respond that indeed the phrase is not necessary, and it comes to exclude the 'crawling path' (entering sideways).

items.text: Support for the Rabbis from the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: Support for the Rabbis from the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a teaching: 'to the face of the Ark cover eastward' establishes a general principle that 'face' always means east. Then it discusses whether the word 'to' (אל) is precise. Rabbi Yehuda holds that 'to' is precise, and similarly 'toward' (נֹכַח) is precise. The Rabbis argue that since in the red heifer case 'toward' is not precise, here too it is not precise.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov establishes a general principle (בנין אב) that wherever 'face' is stated, it means eastward, based on the verse 'אֶל פְּנֵי הַכַּפֹּרֶת קֵדְמָה'.
The Gemara asks Rabbi Yehuda: since the verse could have said just 'פְּנֵי', why does it add 'אֶל'? This implies that 'אֶל' is precise (דווקא).
The Rabbis respond that 'אֶל' is not precise (לאו דווקא).
Rabbi Yehuda holds that both 'אֶל פְּנֵי הַכַּפֹּרֶת' and 'הִזָּה אֶל נֹכַח' are precise (דווקא).
The Rabbis argue that since in the red heifer case 'toward' (נֹכַח) is not precise, here too 'אֶל' is not precise.

items.text: Rav Yosef's challenge and Rabba bar Ulla's answer
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's challenge and Rabba bar Ulla's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rabbi Yehuda: if 'to' is precise, then in the Second Temple where there was no Ark, would there be no sprinklings? Rabba bar Ulla answers with a verse: 'and he shall atone for the holy sanctuary' – the place sanctified for the holy (i.e., the location itself).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rabbi Yehuda: if 'אֶל' (toward) is precise, then in the Second Temple where there was no Ark and no kaporet, would there be no sprinklings?

Rabba bar Ulla answers by citing the verse 'וְכִפֶּר אֶת מִקְדַּשׁ הַקֹּדֶשׁ' (and he shall atone for the holy sanctuary), interpreting it as the place sanctified for the holy (the location itself), not the physical Ark.

items.text: Rava's statement
items.text_en: Rava's statement
items.desc_en: Rava says: both baraitot follow the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that both the baraita about the red heifer and the baraita about the Temple entry follow the opinion of the Rabbis, resolving the apparent contradiction.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about the log offerings
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about the log offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between a statement that inner and leper's log offerings done not for their sake are invalid, while unintentional ones are valid, and a baraita that says both are valid. Rav Yosef resolves it by attributing the first to Rabbi Eliezer, who compares the log to the guilt offering via a hekesh, and the second to the Rabbis. Rava offers an alternative resolution: both views are the Rabbis, but one refers to qualifying the offering and the other to effecting atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction between a statement that inner and leper's log offerings done not for their sake are invalid while unintentional ones are valid, and a baraita that says both are valid.

Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing the first statement to Rabbi Eliezer, who compares the log to the guilt offering via a hekesh (verbal analogy), and the second to the Rabbis who do not make such a comparison.
The Gemara objects that a matter learned through a hekesh (verbal analogy) cannot in turn teach another matter through a hekesh.

Rava offers an alternative resolution: both views are the Rabbis, but one refers to qualifying the offering (הכשר הקרבן) and the other to effecting atonement (הרצוי), where the latter does not count for the owner's obligation.

items.text: Mishnah: Items whose parts must all be present
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items whose parts must all be present
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items where each component is indispensable: the seven branches of the menorah, its seven lamps, the two portions of the mezuzah, the four portions of tefillin, and the four tzitzit. Rabbi Yishmael argues that the four tzitzit are four separate commandments.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing items whose parts are indispensable: the seven branches of the menorah, its seven lamps, the two portions of the mezuzah, and even a single letter invalidates them.
The Mishnah continues: the four portions of tefillin and the four tzitzit each require all their parts, as the four tzitzit are one commandment.
Rabbi Yishmael argues that the four tzitzit are four separate commandments, not one.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the components of these items are all indispensable, and answers that the Torah uses the term "הֲוָיָה" (existence) regarding them, implying they must all be present.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the components of the items listed in the Mishnah are all indispensable, and answers that the Torah uses the term "הֲוָיָה" (existence) regarding them, implying they must all be present.

items.text: Deriving the menorah's material requirements
items.text_en: Deriving the menorah's material requirements
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the menorah can be made from a solid block or from gold; if made from scraps it is invalid, but from other metals it is valid. The Gemara questions this distinction, deriving from verses that "מִקְשָׁה" (hammered work) and "זָהָב" (gold) are required, but "תֵּיעָשֶׂה" (it shall be made) includes other metals. The discussion concludes that the term "הִיא" in "מִקְשָׁה הִיא" excludes trumpets from the requirement of hammered work.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rules for the menorah: it can be made from a solid block or gold; from scraps it is invalid, but from other metals it is valid.

The Gemara questions the distinction: why are scraps invalid due to the requirement of 'מִקְשָׁה' (hammered work) and 'הֲוָיָה' (creation), while other metals should also require 'זָהָב' (gold) and 'הֲוָיָה'?
The Gemara answers that the verse 'תֵּיעָשֶׂה' (it shall be made) includes other metals, but scraps are excluded because 'מִקְשָׁה' (hammered work) requires a creation process.
The Gemara objects that 'תֵּיעָשֶׂה' is also written in the context of 'מִקְשָׁה', and the repetition of 'מִקְשָׁה' is for invalidation, so why not include scraps?
The Gemara further objects that the repetition of 'זָהָב' (gold) also indicates invalidation, so why are other metals valid?
The Gemara resolves that the baraita's distinction is logical: if scraps were valid and other metals invalid, the repetitions of 'זָהָב' and 'מִקְשָׁה' would have no application.
A baraita is cited to show that the repetition of 'זָהָב' teaches that if the menorah is made of gold, it requires a talent of gold and its ornaments; if not, it does not require those.

The Gemara questions why the baraita does not also require the branches (קנים) to be made of gold, and answers that the branches are called 'פָּמוֹט' (a type of holder) and are not subject to the same rule.
Another baraita is cited to show that the verse 'וְזֶה מַעֲשֵׂה הַמְּנֹרָה מִקְשָׁה זָהָב' teaches that if the menorah is made of gold, it requires hammered work; if not, it does not.

The Gemara concludes that the final 'מִקְשָׁה' in the verse comes to exclude trumpets from the requirement of hammered work, as the term 'הִיא' (it) in 'מִקְשָׁה הִיא' specifies that only the menorah requires hammered work, not trumpets.

items.text: Question on the trumpets' exclusivity
items.text_en: Question on the trumpets' exclusivity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the trumpets made by Moses were valid for him but invalid for future generations, while the ark was valid for all. It explores the possible derivation from the phrase 'עשה לך' and rejects a simple analogy, concluding that the double 'לך' in the trumpets' verses indicates exclusivity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the trumpets made by Moses were valid for him but invalid for future generations, while the ark was valid for all, and proposes that the phrase 'עשה לך' might indicate exclusivity, but then objects that the same phrase appears regarding the ark.
The Gemara rejects the simple analogy and explains that the trumpets' exclusivity derives from the double occurrence of 'לך' in their verses: 'עשה לך' and 'והיו לך'.

items.text: Baraita on menorah materials and initial dispute
items.text_en: Baraita on menorah materials and initial dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Rav Chanin cites a baraita before Rav Yosef: a menorah made of silver is valid, but if made of wood, bone, or glass, all agree it is invalid. For metal alloys (e.g., lead, tin), Rabbi invalidates and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda validates. Rav Yosef asks for the reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Rav Chanin cites a baraita before Rav Yosef listing the rules for menorah materials: silver is valid, alloys are disputed between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, and wood/bone/glass are universally invalid.
Rav Yosef asks Rav Pappa bar Rav Chanin for the reasoning behind the dispute, and Rav Pappa responds that both sides interpret using the hermeneutic principle of כלל ופרט (general and specific).

items.text: Hermeneutical principles: כללי ופרטי vs. ריבויי ומיעוטי
items.text_en: Hermeneutical principles: כללי ופרטי vs. ריבויי ומיעוטי
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda disagree on the menorah's material because they apply different hermeneutical rules. Rabbi uses כלל ופרט וכלל, limiting the menorah to metal. Rabbi Yosei uses ריבה ומיעט וריבה, including all materials except earthenware. A supporting baraita is cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda disagree because Rabbi applies the rule of כלל ופרט (general and particular) limiting the menorah to metal, while Rabbi Yosei applies the rule of ריבויי ומיעוטי (amplifications and restrictions) including all valuable materials.

A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda disagree generally about Temple vessels made of wood, with Rabbi disqualifying them using כלל ופרט (general and particular) and Rabbi Yosei permitting them using ריבויי ומיעוטי (amplifications and restrictions).
The Gemara details Rabbi's application of כלל ופרט וכלל (general, particular, general) to the verses about the menorah, concluding that only metal is permitted.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara details Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's application of ריבה ומיעט וריבה (amplification, restriction, amplification) to the verses, including all materials except earthenware.

items.text: Supporting baraitot and the Hasmonean precedent
items.text_en: Supporting baraitot and the Hasmonean precedent
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one stating that if one lacks gold, he may use silver, copper, etc., and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda permits even wood. Another baraita prohibits making a menorah with seven branches from any material, but Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda adds a prohibition for wood, citing the Hasmoneans' iron spits coated with tin. The Sages reject this proof.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that if one lacks gold for the menorah, he may use silver, copper, etc., and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda permits even wood.
Another baraita prohibits making a seven-branched menorah even from other metals, but permits menorahs with five, six, or eight branches.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's objection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda adds that even a wooden menorah is prohibited, citing the precedent of the Hasmonean kings who made a menorah from iron spits coated with tin.
The Sages reject the proof, explaining that the Hasmoneans' menorah was originally iron spits coated with tin, and later upgraded to silver and gold, so it was not made of wood.

items.text: Dimensions and components of the menorah
items.text_en: Dimensions and components of the menorah
items.desc_en: Shmuel reports in the name of Sava the detailed measurements of the menorah: its total height (18 handbreadths), the arrangement of its base, flower, cups, knobs, and branches. It describes the pattern of three sets of two branches each, and the final three handbreadths containing three cups, a knob, and a flower. The cups, knobs, and flowers are each compared to specific shapes, and their mutual indispensability is stated.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel reports in the name of Sava the total height of the menorah (18 handbreadths) and the initial breakdown of its base, flower, and decorative sections.
The description details the three sets of two branches each, their spacing, and the final three handbreadths containing three cups, a knob, and a flower.
The cups, knobs, and flowers are each compared to specific shapes (Alexandrian cups, Cretan apples, and pillar flowers), and their total counts are given (22 cups, 11 knobs, 9 flowers).
The cups, knobs, and flowers each mutually impede one another, and all three categories together also mutually impede one another, establishing their indispensability.

items.text: Scriptural derivation for the cups
items.text_en: Scriptural derivation for the cups
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to explain the scriptural basis for the 22 cups, citing verses from the Torah that mention cups on the menorah and its branches.
