sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the 22 cups are easily derived from the verses, citing the four cups on the menorah itself and the three cups on each of the six branches.

items.text: Calculation of the Menorah's flowers
items.text_en: Calculation of the Menorah's flowers
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the number of flowers on the Menorah, finding a discrepancy: there should be nine flowers, but the count from the base and branches yields only eight. Rav Shalman resolves this by citing a verse that includes the base itself as a flower.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the number of flowers on the Menorah, noting that the count from the base and branches yields only eight flowers instead of the expected nine.

Rav Shalman resolves the discrepancy by citing the verse 'עַד יְרֵכָהּ עַד פִּרְחָהּ מִקְשָׁה הִיא' (from its base to its flower it is hammered out), which includes the base itself as a flower, bringing the total to nine.

items.text: Height of the Menorah
items.text_en: Height of the Menorah
items.desc_en: Rav states that the Menorah's height was nine handbreadths. Rav Shimi bar Chiya challenges this from a baraita about a stone with three steps before the Menorah. Rav responds that he was referring to the height from the top of the branches upward.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the height of the Menorah was nine handbreadths.
Rav Shimi bar Chiya challenges Rav from a baraita about a stone with three steps before the Menorah, implying a greater height.
Rav responds that he was referring to the height from the top of the branches upward.

items.text: Solomon's gold for the Menorah
items.text_en: Solomon's gold for the Menorah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the phrase 'מִכְלוֹת זָהָב' as referring to the fact that Solomon's gold was consumed by the Menorah. Rav Ami says that Solomon made ten menorahs, each requiring a thousand talents of gold, which was refined a thousand times. The Gemara questions this from a verse about Solomon's abundant gold, and answers that it refers to 'זָהָב סָגוּר' (closed gold). A baraita from Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda is cited about the Menorah of the Temple being slightly heavier than Moses' by a gold dinar, refined eighty times.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'מִכְלוֹת זָהָב' (consuming gold) means in the context of the Menorah.

Rav Ami explains that the Menorah consumed all of Solomon's closed gold (זָהָב סָגוּר), citing Rav Yehuda's tradition that Solomon made ten menorahs, each requiring a thousand talents of gold refined a thousand times to a single talent.
The Gemara objects from a verse that Solomon's abundant gold was not considered significant, implying he had vast amounts of gold beyond what the Menorah consumed.
The Gemara resolves that the verse refers to ordinary gold, while the Menorah consumed only the rare closed gold (זָהָב סָגוּר).
The Gemara objects that such a vast amount of gold could not have been consumed by the Menorah.

A baraita from Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda is cited, stating that the Temple Menorah was only slightly heavier than Moses' by a gold dinar, and was refined only eighty times to a talent, contradicting the notion of consuming a thousand talents.
The Gemara concludes that once the Menorah was made, it remained as it was, and the earlier tradition about Solomon's gold refers to the process of refining, not the final weight.

items.text: The pure Menorah
items.text_en: The pure Menorah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains the verse 'עַל הַמְּנֹרָה הַטְּהֹרָה' to mean that its work came down from a pure place. The Gemara questions this by comparing to 'עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן הַטָּהוֹר', and concludes that 'טָהוֹר' implies it could be impure, but for the Menorah, since it is made of metal which can become impure, the verse must mean that its work came from a pure place.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani (Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani) in the name of Rabbi Yonatan (Rabbi Yonatan) explains that the verse 'עַל הַמְּנֹרָה הַטְּהֹרָה' (upon the pure Menorah) teaches that its work came down from a place of purity.
The Gemara (Gemara) questions this interpretation by comparing to the verse 'עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן הַטָּהוֹר' (upon the pure Table), asking if it also means its work came from a pure place.
The Gemara (Gemara) answers that regarding the Table, 'טָהוֹר' (pure) implies it can become impure, and similarly for the Menorah, 'טְהוֹרָה' (pure) implies it can become impure.

The Gemara (Gemara) supports this with Reish Lakish (Reish Lakish), who explains that the Table, though a wooden vessel designated for rest, is called 'טָהוֹר' (pure) to imply impurity because it was lifted to show the shewbread to pilgrims.

sub.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's answer
sub.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's answer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara (Gemara) asks what 'חִיבַּתְכֶם' (your affection) means, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) explains that a miracle occurred with the shewbread, as it remained hot when removed.

The Gemara (Gemara) concludes that for the Menorah, which is made of metal and can become impure, the verse 'טְהוֹרָה' (pure) cannot imply impurity; rather, it must mean that its work came from a place of purity.

items.text: Heavenly origin of the vessels
items.text_en: Heavenly origin of the vessels
items.desc_en: A baraita states that an ark, table, and menorah of fire descended from heaven, and Moses saw and made them accordingly. The Gemara distinguishes this from the Mishkan, where the verse says 'כְּמִשְׁפָּטוֹ' (according to its judgment). Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says that Gabriel was girded like a linen garment and showed Moses the work of the Menorah. The school of Rabbi Yishmael lists three things that were difficult for Moses until God showed him with His finger: the Menorah, the New Moon, and the creeping things.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
sub.desc_en: A baraita states that an ark, table, and menorah of fire descended from heaven, and Moses saw and made them accordingly.
The Gemara asks whether the same reasoning applies to the Mishkan, where the verse says 'כְּמִשְׁפָּטוֹ' (according to its judgment).

The Gemara distinguishes: regarding the Mishkan it says 'כְּמִשְׁפָּטוֹ' (according to its judgment), while regarding the vessels it says 'כְּתַבְנִיתָם' (after their pattern), indicating a model was shown.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says that Gabriel was girded like a linen garment and showed Moses the work of the Menorah.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael lists three things that were difficult for Moses until God showed him with His finger: the Menorah, the New Moon, and the creeping things; some add the halakhot of slaughtering.

items.text: Laws of mezuzah writing
items.text_en: Laws of mezuzah writing
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses that two paragraphs of the mezuzah invalidate each other, and even one letter can invalidate them. Rav Yehuda said Rav clarified that this refers to the crown of a yod. The Gemara then cites another statement of Rav Yehuda said Rav that any letter not surrounded by parchment on all four sides is invalid. Ashyan bar Nadvak in the name of Rav Yehuda discusses the letter hei: if its interior is punctured it is valid, but if its leg is punctured it is invalid. Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Yaakov clarify that if the leg remains with the size of a small letter, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the two paragraphs of the mezuzah invalidate each other, and even a single letter can invalidate them.
The Gemara objects that this ruling is obvious.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav clarifies that the ruling refers to the crown of a yod (the small decorative stroke on the letter).
The Gemara again objects that even this clarification is obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling actually refers to another statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: any letter not surrounded by parchment on all four sides is invalid.

sub.text: Ashyan bar Nadvak in the name of Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Ashyan bar Nadvak in the name of Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Ashyan bar Nadvak reports in the name of Rav Yehuda that if the interior of the letter hei is punctured it is valid, but if its leg is punctured it is invalid.
Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Yaakov clarify that if the leg of the hei remains with the size of a small letter, it is valid; otherwise it is invalid.

items.text: Two cases of broken letter legs in Torah scrolls
items.text_en: Two cases of broken letter legs in Torah scrolls
items.desc_en: Two incidents are reported where the leg of a letter (heh in 'ha'am' and vav in 'vayaharog') broke off. Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Zeira rule on the validity based on whether the remaining stroke resembles a small letter or whether a child can still read it as the intended word.

items.text: Moses sees Rabbi Akiva's Torah and reward
items.text_en: Moses sees Rabbi Akiva's Torah and reward
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav relates that Moses found God tying crowns to letters and was told about Rabbi Akiva. Moses was allowed to see Rabbi Akiva's academy but could not understand the discussion until Akiva cited a law from Sinai. Moses then saw Akiva's flesh being weighed in a market and questioned the justice, but God silenced him.

items.text: Seven letters require three crowns
items.text_en: Seven letters require three crowns
items.desc_en: Rava states that seven letters (שעטנ"ז ג"ץ) require three crowns (tagin). Rav Ashi adds that the scribes of Rav's house would make a stroke on the roof of the chet and hang the leg of the heh.

items.text: The meaning of the heh's leg and the creation of the worlds
items.text_en: The meaning of the heh's leg and the creation of the worlds
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the symbolism: the stroke on the chet signifies that God lives forever, and the hanging leg of the heh alludes to the verse 'Bitchu baHashem adei ad' and the two worlds created with yod and heh. Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Ila'i expounds that this world was created with heh (like an open porch) and the world to come with yod (with few righteous). The hanging leg allows penitents to enter, and the crown on the heh is a knot God ties for those who return.

items.text: Rav's rule on errors in a Torah scroll and its refutation
items.text_en: Rav's rule on errors in a Torah scroll and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rav ruled that a Torah scroll with two errors per page should be corrected, three should be hidden. A baraita refutes him: three should be corrected, four hidden. Abaye asks about three errors on one page, and Rav Kahana explains that missing letters are problematic because they look like spots, but extra letters are not an issue. The case of Agra's father-in-law with extra letters is brought to Rabbi Abba.

items.text: Where to end a book in a Torah scroll
items.text_en: Where to end a book in a Torah scroll
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses Rav's ruling that one may finish a Torah scroll even in the middle of a page, and clarifies that this applies only to the individual books (Chumashim) within the scroll. A baraita is cited that seems to contradict Rav, but the Gemara resolves the contradiction by limiting Rav's statement to the Chumashim. The discussion concludes with a dispute between the Rabbis and Rav Ashi about whether the final verse 'before the eyes of all Israel' must be written in the middle of a line or specifically in the middle of a line.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that regarding extra (books) we have no concern.
The Gemara cites Rav's ruling that one finishing a Torah scroll may complete it even in the middle of a page.
A baraita is cited that contradicts Rav, stating one must not finish in the middle of a page but shorten to the page's end.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's statement applies specifically to the Chumashim (individual books) within the scroll.
The Gemara objects that Rav explicitly said 'Torah scroll,' not 'Chumashim.'
The Gemara clarifies that Rav meant the Chumashim within a Torah scroll.
The Gemara objects further, citing a tradition that the verse 'before the eyes of all Israel' is written in the middle of the page.
The Gemara resolves that the tradition referred to the middle of a line, not the middle of a page.
The Rabbis state that the verse may be written even in the middle of a line.
Rav Ashi insists it must be specifically in the middle of a line, and the halacha is decided accordingly.

items.text: The final eight verses of the Torah
items.text_en: The final eight verses of the Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua bar Abba in the name of Rav Giddel citing Rav states that the last eight verses of the Torah (describing Moses' death) are read by a single individual in the synagogue. The Gemara explains that this ruling is not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who holds that Moses wrote the entire Torah from God's dictation. According to Rabbi Yehuda (or Rabbi Nechemya), Joshua wrote these verses after Moses' death. Rabbi Shimon argues that the Torah cannot be missing even one letter, so Moses must have written them while crying. The Gemara concludes that even according to Rabbi Shimon, since these verses are different in nature, they are treated differently.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the final eight verses of the Torah are read by a single individual in the synagogue.
The Gemara asks whose opinion this ruling follows, concluding it is not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda (or Rabbi Nechemya) who argues that Joshua wrote the final eight verses after Moses' death, since Moses could not have written about his own death.
Rabbi Shimon objects that the Torah cannot be missing even one letter, citing the verse about placing the Torah scroll.
Rabbi Shimon explains that Moses wrote the entire Torah from God's dictation, but the final eight verses were written with tears, citing a parallel from Baruch.
The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Shimon, since these verses are different in nature, they are treated differently and read by a single individual.

items.text: The merit of writing or acquiring a Torah scroll
items.text_en: The merit of writing or acquiring a Torah scroll
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua bar Abba in the name of Rav Giddel citing Rav states that one who buys a Torah scroll from the market is like one who snatches a mitzvah from the market, but one who writes it himself is considered as if he received it from Mount Sinai. Rav Sheishet adds that even if one merely corrects a single letter, it is considered as if he wrote the entire scroll.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that buying a Torah scroll from the market is like snatching a mitzvah, but writing it oneself is credited as receiving it from Sinai.
Rav Sheishet adds that even correcting a single letter is considered as if one wrote the entire scroll.

items.text: Dimensions and spacing for a Torah scroll
items.text_en: Dimensions and spacing for a Torah scroll
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a parchment sheet (yeri'ah) should have between three and eight columns (dappin). One should not have too many or too few columns. If a sheet has nine columns, they should be divided as four and five, not three and six. At the beginning of a book, one must start a new sheet, but at the end, even a single verse on a single column suffices. The baraita then specifies the measurements for margins, spacing between columns, lines, words, and letters, and rules that one should not reduce the size of the writing to fill space. Finally, if a word has five letters, one should not write two inside the page and three outside.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the rule that a parchment sheet (יריעה) should have between three and eight columns (דפין), and one should not make fewer or more.
The baraita explains the reason: too many columns look like a letter, too few cause the eyes to wander, and gives the example of the repeated phrase 'למשפחותיכם' three times.
The baraita rules that if a sheet has nine columns, they should be divided as four on one side and five on the other, not three and six.

The baraita qualifies: this rule applies at the beginning of a book, but at the end even a single verse on a single column suffices, and the gemara corrects the wording to 'a single verse on a single column'.
The baraita specifies the measurements for margins, spacing between columns, and the differences for חומשין (the Five Books).
The baraita gives the spacing between lines, words, and letters: a line's height, a small letter's width, and a hair's breadth respectively.
The baraita rules that one should not reduce the size of the writing to fill space, whether from top, bottom, between lines, or between paragraphs.
The baraita concludes that if a word has five letters, one should not write two inside the page and three outside.

items.text: Mishnah: Correcting errors in a Torah scroll
items.text_en: Mishnah: Correcting errors in a Torah scroll
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the basic rules for writing a Torah scroll: three columns per page, two outside. If a two-letter word is available, it should not be placed between columns but written at the start of a line. For a mistake in writing God's name, Rabbi Yehuda says to erase the name, write it on the erased spot, and suspend the erased material. Rabbi Yosei says one may even suspend the name itself. Rabbi Yitzchak says one may erase and rewrite. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says one may suspend the entire name but not part of it. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Meir says one may not write the name on an erased or erased spot, nor suspend it; instead, one must remove the entire sheet and store it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule for Torah scroll layout: three columns per page, two outside, and a two-letter word must be written at the start of a line, not between columns.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that if one errs in writing God's name, he must erase the name, suspend the erased material, and rewrite the name on the erased spot.
Rabbi Yosei permits even suspending the name itself (without erasing).
Rabbi Yitzchak permits erasing and rewriting the name.
Rabbi Shimon Shezuri rules that one may suspend the entire name but not part of it.

sub.text: Mishnah (Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Meir)
sub.text_en: Mishnah (Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Meir)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Meir forbids writing the name on an erased or erased spot, or suspending it; instead, one must remove the entire sheet and store it.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute over the halacha
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute over the halacha
items.desc_en: The Gemara records two conflicting traditions about the halacha: Rav Chananel said in the name of Rav that the halacha is to suspend the name, while Rabbah bar bar Chanah said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel that the halacha is to erase and rewrite. The Gemara questions why each did not simply state the halacha according to the other, and explains that they reversed the attributions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records two conflicting traditions: Rav Chananel said in the name of Rav that the halacha is to suspend the name (תולין את השם), while Rabbah bar bar Chanah said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel that the halacha is to erase and rewrite (מוחק וכותב).
The Gemara asks: why did each master not simply state the halacha according to the other (i.e., why did they not agree)?
The Gemara resolves: because they reversed the attributions (i.e., each tradition actually attributed the opposite ruling to the same authority, so they are not in conflict).

items.text: Ravina bar Chinana's ruling: Halacha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
items.text_en: Ravina bar Chinana's ruling: Halacha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
items.desc_en: Ravina bar Chinana said in the name of Ulla, who said in the name of Rabbi Chanina, that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, and moreover, wherever Rabbi Shimon Shezuri taught a ruling, the halacha follows him.

sub.text: Ravina bar Chinana citing Ulla citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Ravina bar Chinana citing Ulla citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Ravina bar Chinana transmits a tradition in the name of Ulla and Rabbi Chanina that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, and moreover, wherever Rabbi Shimon Shezuri taught a ruling, the halacha follows him.

items.text: Gemara's question: Which ruling of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri is this principle applied to?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Which ruling of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri is this principle applied to?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: To which ruling of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri does this principle refer? It first suggests it refers to his ruling about suspending the name, but notes that a halachic ruling was already stated about that case, so the principle would be redundant. The Gemara concludes that it cannot refer to that case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: To which ruling of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri does this principle apply? It first suggests it refers to his ruling about suspending the name, but notes that a halachic ruling was already stated about that case, so the principle would be redundant.
The Gemara rejects this suggestion: If the principle applied there, the earlier statement would have said 'הלכה (the binding law) is like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri' explicitly, but it did not.

items.text: Second suggestion: The ruling about a five-year-old animal
items.text_en: Second suggestion: The ruling about a five-year-old animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the principle refers to Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's ruling that even a five-year-old animal that plows in the field is purified by its mother's slaughter. But again, a halachic ruling was already stated about that case by Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina, so the principle would be redundant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the principle 'halacha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri' applies to his ruling about a five-year-old animal being purified by its mother's slaughter.
The Gemara objects that Ze'iri already stated in Rabbi Chanina's name that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri in this case, so the general principle would be redundant.

items.text: Third suggestion: The ruling about a person in danger writing a get
items.text_en: Third suggestion: The ruling about a person in danger writing a get
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the principle refers to Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's ruling that even a person in danger (sick) can instruct that a get be written. But again, a halachic ruling was already stated about that case by Rabbi Yochanan, so the principle would be redundant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the principle 'halacha like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri' refers to his ruling that even a person in danger (מסוכן) can instruct that a get be written.
The Gemara offers an alternative: the principle might refer to Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's ruling about terumat ma'aser of demai that one may ask and eat on his word even on a weekday.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan already ruled halacha like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri regarding the sick person and terumat ma'aser of demai, so the general principle would be redundant.

items.text: Fourth suggestion: The ruling about Egyptian beans
items.text_en: Fourth suggestion: The ruling about Egyptian beans
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the principle refers to Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's ruling about Egyptian beans that took root before and after Rosh Hashanah, that one cannot tithe from one on the other. But again, a halachic ruling was already stated about that case by Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, so the principle would be redundant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the principle 'הלכה כרבי שמעון שזורי' refers to Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar's ruling in the name of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri about Egyptian beans that took root before and after Rosh Hashanah, that one cannot tithe from one on the other.
The baraita explains the practical solution: one gathers the entire pile and then tithes from the new on the new and from the old on the old.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani already stated in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri regarding this case, so the general principle would be redundant.

items.text: Conclusion: The principle applies to a different case
items.text_en: Conclusion: The principle applies to a different case
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the principle must apply to a different case, and records a dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak about which case it is, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the principle applies to a different case, and begins to record a dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak about which case it is, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening Mishnah about measuring a chest
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah about measuring a chest
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding how to measure a chest, with Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri offering additional opinions about measuring the thickness of legs and rims.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on measuring a chest, with both agreeing that the thickness of legs and rims is not measured.
Rabbi Yosei states that the thickness of legs and rims is measured, but the space between them is not.
Rabbi Shimon Shezuri adds a condition: if the legs are a handbreadth high, the space between them is not measured; otherwise, it is measured.

items.text: Gemara's citation of another Mishnah about oil and honey
items.text_en: Gemara's citation of another Mishnah about oil and honey
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir, the Sages, and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri dispute the order of libations, and the Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Shimon Shezuri includes wine.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir, the Sages, and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri dispute the order of libations, with Rabbi Shimon Shezuri adding wine.
The Gemara questions whether the first Tanna (Rabbi Meir) excludes wine entirely from the libation order.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah should be read as 'Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says: wine' (not 'also wine'), implying the first Tanna does include wine but not as a separate category.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's story about mixed produce
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's story about mixed produce
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Shimon Shezuri asked Rabbi Tarfon about untithed produce mixed with permitted food, and Rabbi Tarfon advised buying from the market and tithing on it, reasoning that most people tithe, making it like tithing from exempt on exempt.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's story of untithed produce (טבל) mixed with permitted food (חולין), and Rabbi Tarfon's instruction to buy from the market and tithe on it.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Tarfon's reasoning: the mixture is nullified by the majority (רוב), most common people (עמי הארץ) tithe, so it is like tithing from exempt on exempt (מן הפטור על הפטור).

items.text: Gemara's question about buying from a gentile
items.text_en: Gemara's question about buying from a gentile
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Tarfon did not advise buying from a gentile, and explains that he holds a gentile has no acquisition in the Land of Israel to exempt from tithes, so it would be like tithing from obligated on exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Tarfon did not advise buying from a gentile, and explains that he holds a gentile has no acquisition in the Land of Israel to exempt from tithes, so it would be like tithing from obligated on exempt.

items.text: Alternative version and further question
items.text_en: Alternative version and further question
items.desc_en: An alternative version says Rabbi Tarfon did advise buying from a gentile, holding that a gentile does have acquisition to exempt produce, making it like tithing from exempt on exempt. The Gemara then asks why he didn't just say 'buy from the market,' and explains he holds most amei ha'aretz do not tithe.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports that Rabbi Tarfon told the inquirer to buy from a gentile, holding that a gentile has acquisition in the Land of Israel to exempt produce from tithes, making it like tithing from exempt on exempt.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Tarfon did not simply tell the inquirer to buy from the market instead of from a gentile.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Tarfon holds most amei ha'aretz (common people) do not tithe, so buying from the market would not provide reliably tithed produce.

items.text: Inquiry about the halacha following Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
items.text_en: Inquiry about the halacha following Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
items.desc_en: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya asks Rav Pappa whether the principle that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri applies even in the case of mixed produce. Rav Ashi reports that Mar Zutra said Rabbi Chanina from Sura considered it obvious.

sub.text: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya's question to Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya's question to Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya asks Rav Pappa whether the principle that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri applies even in the case of mixed produce (טבל וחולין).
Rav Pappa answers affirmatively, confirming that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri even in that case.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's report of Mar Zutra
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's report of Mar Zutra
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that Mar Zutra said Rabbi Chanina from Sura considered the answer obvious, implying the principle applies universally.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'in every place that he taught' refers to a specific context, not a general rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's phrase 'in every place that he taught' refers to a specific context rather than a general rule.

items.text: Tear in a Torah scroll: stitching rules
items.text_en: Tear in a Torah scroll: stitching rules
items.desc_en: Rav states that a tear spanning two lines may be sewn, but three lines should not be sewn. Rava qualifies this: it applies only to old scrolls where the text is not widely spread, and only for stitching with sinews, not with threads.

sub.text: Rav Z'eira citing Rav Chananel citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Z'eira citing Rav Chananel citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav states the rule: a tear spanning two lines in a Torah scroll may be sewn, but a tear spanning three lines should not be sewn.

sub.text: Rabbah Zuti to Rav Ashi citing Rabbi Yirmeya from Difti citing Rava
sub.text_en: Rabbah Zuti to Rav Ashi citing Rabbi Yirmeya from Difti citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Rava qualifies that the prohibition against sewing a three-line tear applies only to old scrolls where the text is not widely spread, but for new scrolls it is permitted.

The gemara clarifies that 'old' means scrolls where the text is not widely spread (i.e., the lines are close together), and 'new' means scrolls where the text is widely spread; additionally, the leniency applies only to stitching with sinews (גידין), not with threads (גרדין).

items.text: Unresolved question: between pages and lines
items.text_en: Unresolved question: between pages and lines
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Abba asks about a tear between pages or between lines, but the question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Abba asks about the status of a tear between pages or between lines in a Torah scroll.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Mezuzah written in two-line columns
items.text_en: Mezuzah written in two-line columns
items.desc_en: Rav rules that a mezuzah written in two-line columns is valid. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak extends this to a pattern of two, three, and one lines. An objection is raised from a baraita that invalidates a mezuzah written like a shirah, but it is deflected: that baraita refers to a Torah scroll.

sub.text: Rav via Rabbi Z'eiri and Rav Chananel
sub.text_en: Rav via Rabbi Z'eiri and Rav Chananel
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a mezuzah written in two-line columns is valid.
The Gemara asks about the validity of a mezuzah written in a pattern of two, three, and one lines.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak extends Rav's ruling, stating that such a pattern is certainly valid, even if it resembles a shirah (poetic line format).
An objection is raised from a baraita that invalidates a mezuzah written like a shirah (poetic line format).
The objection is deflected: that baraita refers to a Torah scroll, not a mezuzah.

items.text: Mezuzah in a non-standard pattern: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.text_en: Mezuzah in a non-standard pattern: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a mezuzah written in a pattern of two, three, and one lines is valid, provided it is not made like a box (kubah) or like a tail (zanav).

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a mezuzah written in a two-three-one pattern is valid.
An alternative tradition attributes the same statement to Rav Acha bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that a mezuzah written in a two-three-one pattern is valid, provided it is not made like a box (קובה) or like a tail (זנב).

items.text: Placement of 'על הארץ' in the last line of Shema
items.text_en: Placement of 'על הארץ' in the last line of Shema
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda reports a dispute: some say 'על הארץ' should be at the end of the last line, others at the beginning. Each opinion is supported by a biblical verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda reports a dispute about whether the phrase 'על הארץ' (upon the earth) should be placed at the end or the beginning of the last line of the Shema.

The Gemara explains that each opinion is supported by a biblical verse: the first opinion cites 'גְּבֹהַּ שָׁמַיִם עַל הָאָרֶץ' (as high as the heavens are above the earth), and the second opinion cites 'כִּי הֵיכִי דִּמְרַחֲקָא שָׁמַיִם מֵאֶרֶץ' (as the heavens are distant from the earth).

items.text: Rabbi Meir's practice for writing a mezuzah
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's practice for writing a mezuzah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo describes Rav Huna's practice: rolling the mezuzah from 'אחד' toward 'שמע' and making its paragraphs closed. An objection is raised from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who says Rabbi Meir wrote it on a parchment like a page.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo reports that he saw Rav Huna roll the mezuzah from 'אחד' toward 'שמע' and make its paragraphs closed.
An objection is raised from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says Rabbi Meir wrote the mezuzah on a parchment like a page, contradicting Rav Huna's practice.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling on mezuzah
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling on mezuzah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one must leave a space above and below and make the paragraphs open. The speaker asks Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar for the reason, and he answers because there is no requirement for adjacency from the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the halacha for writing a mezuzah: one must leave space above and below and make the paragraphs open.
The speaker asks Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar for the reason behind the mishnah's ruling.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar answers that the reason is because there is no requirement for adjacency (סמיכות) from the Torah.

items.text: Gemara's question and clarification on Rav's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question and clarification on Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Chananel quotes Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. The Gemara asks whether this refers to open paragraphs, and answers that it refers to the spaces. Rav Menashya bar Yaakov defines the space as the width of a bookbinder's tool.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chananel reports in Rav's name that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
The Gemara asks whether Rav's ruling refers to open paragraphs (פתוחות).
The Gemara answers that Rav's ruling refers to the spaces (ריוח) between paragraphs, not the open paragraphs themselves.
Rav Menashya bar Yaakov defines the required space as the width of a bookbinder's tool (אטבא דספרי).

items.text: Abaye's challenge and resolution regarding custom
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge and resolution regarding custom
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef: if Rav's ruling is about spaces, why does Rav himself follow a custom, and the world practices with closed paragraphs? The Gemara brings two versions of Rav's statement about chalitzah with a shoe versus a sandal, showing that custom overrides Elijah's opinion. The Gemara concludes that the dispute is about the initial permissibility of a shoe, and this supports that Rav's ruling is about spaces.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef: if Rav's ruling is about spaces (רווח), why does Rav himself follow a custom, and the world practices with closed paragraphs (סתומות)?

sub.text: Rabbah citing Rav Kahana citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah citing Rav Kahana citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah reports Rav's first version: if Elijah says to perform חליצה (levirate release) with a shoe (מנעל) we listen, but not with a sandal (סנדל) because the people have already adopted the custom of using a sandal.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Kahana citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Kahana citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports Rav's second version: if Elijah says not to perform חליצה with a shoe we listen, but not with a sandal, because the people have already adopted the custom of using a sandal.

The Gemara asks what difference exists between the two versions, answers that the dispute is about the initial permissibility (לכתחילה) of a shoe, and concludes that this supports the interpretation that Rav's ruling is about spaces (רווח).

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the mitzvah is to make them closed, but if one makes them open it is valid. He interprets Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's 'open' as meaning 'even open'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the mitzvah is to make them closed (סתומות), but if one makes them open (פתוחות) it is valid, and interprets Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's 'open' as meaning 'even open'.

items.text: Supporting baraitot and objections regarding downgrading sanctity
items.text_en: Supporting baraitot and objections regarding downgrading sanctity
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak with a baraita about not downgrading sanctity from a Torah scroll to a mezuzah, implying that if downgrading were allowed, one could make a mezuzah from a Torah scroll. However, the Gemara raises objections: the baraita might refer to completing the number of paragraphs, and other baraitot discuss the material (klaf vs. duchsustus) and the rule that changing invalidates tefillin. The Gemara concludes that the discussion is about tefillin, and the distinction is about writing on the hair side.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak by citing a baraita that forbids downgrading sanctity from a Torah scroll to a mezuzah, implying that if downgrading were allowed, one could make a mezuzah from a Torah scroll.
The Gemara objects that the baraita might refer to completing the number of paragraphs, not to the issue of open vs. closed sections.

The Gemara raises another objection from a baraita that specifies the material for tefillin (קְלָף) and mezuzah (דּוּכְסוּסְטוֹס), which is only a preferred practice (לְמִצְוָה), not a strict requirement.
The Gemara objects further with baraitot stating that changing the material invalidates tefillin, and that changing between the two materials invalidates both tefillin and mezuzah.
The Gemara resolves that both baraitot discuss tefillin, and the distinction is about writing on the hair side of the parchment.

items.text: Dispute about changing the order of parashiyot in mezuzah
items.text_en: Dispute about changing the order of parashiyot in mezuzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a tannaitic dispute about whether changing the order of the parashiyot in a mezuzah invalidates it. Rabbi Acha (or Rabbi Akiva bar Chanina) validates it, while the first opinion invalidates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about writing the parashiyot on a parchment strip in the place of flesh (i.e., reversing the order of the sheets).

The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the dispute about changing the order in both cases is a tannaitic dispute, with Rabbi Acha (or Rabbi Akiva bar Chanina) validating and the first opinion invalidating.

items.text: Requirement for ruling lines on mezuzah
items.text_en: Requirement for ruling lines on mezuzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a mezuzah requires ruling lines, citing Rav Minyomi bar Chilkiah who says it does. It resolves this as a tannaitic dispute, with Rabbi Yirmeyah saying tefillin and mezuzot do not need ruling. The halakha concludes that tefillin do not need ruling but mezuzah does, and both may be written without a base text.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a mezuzah requires ruling lines, citing Rav Minyomi bar Chilkiah's statement that any mezuzah not ruled is invalid.
The Gemara resolves the dispute as a tannaitic disagreement, citing Rabbi Yirmeyah who says in the name of his teacher that tefillin and mezuzot do not require ruling lines.
The Gemara rules that tefillin do not require ruling lines but mezuzah does, and both may be written without a base text, explaining the reason as 'מִיגְרָס גְּרִיסִין' (a mnemonic for the ruling).

items.text: Sitting on a bed with a Torah scroll
items.text_en: Sitting on a bed with a Torah scroll
items.desc_en: Rav Chelbo reports that Rav Huna forbade sitting on a bed with a Torah scroll on it. Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan permits it, and explains a story about Rabbi Elazar as referring to a scroll on the ground.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chelbo reports that he saw Rav Huna forbid sitting on a bed with a Torah scroll on it by first removing the scroll to the ground.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan permits sitting on a bed with a Torah scroll on it, contradicting Rav Huna.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction from the story of Rabbi Elazar by explaining that in that case the scroll was on the ground, not on the bed.

items.text: Invalid forms of mezuzah: written as a letter or hung on a stick
items.text_en: Invalid forms of mezuzah: written as a letter or hung on a stick
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel rules that a mezuzah written as a letter (without proper format) is invalid, derived from a verbal analogy with a Torah scroll. Similarly, one hung on a stick is invalid because it must be affixed to the doorpost. A baraita supports this, adding that it is dangerous and lacks mitzvah.

sub.text: Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel rules that a mezuzah written as a letter (without proper format) is invalid, deriving this from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'כתיבה' (writing) from a Torah scroll.

sub.text: Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel (second ruling)
sub.text_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel (second ruling)
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel further rules that a mezuzah hung on a stick is invalid, because the verse requires it to be affixed 'בשעריך' (in your gates).
A baraita supports the ruling, stating that a mezuzah hung on a stick or placed behind the door is dangerous and lacks the fulfillment of the מצוה (commandment).

items.text: Placement of the mezuzah and the practice of the house of Monbaz
items.text_en: Placement of the mezuzah and the practice of the house of Monbaz
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the house of King Monbaz would place mezuzot in their inns as a reminder. Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel states that the mitzvah is to place the mezuzah within the doorway's space, which is obvious from the verse. The Gemara begins to consider a potential counterargument from Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the practice of the house of King Monbaz, who would place mezuzot in their inns as a reminder.
Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel states that the mitzvah is to place the mezuzah within the doorway's space.
The Gemara objects that this ruling is obvious from the verse 'בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ' (in your gates).
The Gemara considers a potential counterargument from Rava that might have suggested a different placement.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's statement about a handbreadth near the public domain teaches how far one must distance the mezuzah from the doorpost.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's mention of a handbreadth near the public domain that it teaches how far one must distance the mezuzah from the doorpost.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on writing the mezuzah on two pages
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on writing the mezuzah on two pages
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that if one wrote the mezuzah on two pages, it is invalid. A challenge is raised from a baraita that says it is invalid only if placed on two doorposts, implying it is valid on one doorpost. The Gemara resolves that the baraita means it is fit for two doorposts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that if one wrote the mezuzah on two separate sheets, it is invalid.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if one wrote it on two sheets and placed it in two doorposts it is invalid, implying that on one doorpost it is valid.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a mezuzah fit for two doorposts, not one actually placed in two.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on following the hinge side
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on following the hinge side
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that for mezuzah, one follows the hinge side. Rav Adda explains that 'heiker tzir' means the socket. An example is given of a doorway between two houses, between a men's and women's house.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that for the mezuzah, one follows the hinge side of the door.
The Gemara asks what is meant by 'the hinge side'.
Rav Adda explains that it refers to the socket (אבקתא) where the hinge fits.
The Gemara gives an example: a doorway between two houses, such as between the men's and women's quarters.
The Gemara answers that it is like a doorway between two houses, such as between the men's and women's quarters.

items.text: Rav Nachman's instruction to the Exilarch
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's instruction to the Exilarch
items.desc_en: The Exilarch built a house and asked Rav Nachman to affix a mezuzah. Rav Nachman told him to hang the doors first, implying the mezuzah is placed on the right side of the entrance.

sub.text: Story of Reish Galuta and Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Story of Reish Galuta and Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Reish Galuta built a house and asked Rav Nachman to affix a mezuzah; Rav Nachman told him to hang the doors first.
Rav Nachman instructed him to hang the doors first, so the hinge side would be identifiable.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav on the shape of the mezuzah
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav on the shape of the mezuzah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that if one made the mezuzah like a bolt, it is invalid. A contradiction is raised from Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef who said all mezuzot in Rabbi's house were made like a bolt, and the doorway Rabbi used to enter the study hall had no mezuzah. The Gemara resolves that one case is made like a stick (invalid) and the other like a lintel (valid).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that if one made the mezuzah like a bolt (a horizontal bar), it is invalid.
The Gemara objects: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reported that all mezuzot in Rabbi's house were made like a bolt, and the doorway Rabbi used to enter the study hall had no mezuzah.
The Gemara resolves: no contradiction — one case is where it was made like a simple stick (invalid), the other like a column (valid).
The Gemara resolves: no contradiction — one case is a bolt-shaped mezuzah (like a simple bar), the other is a column-shaped one (like a pillar).

items.text: Rav Huna's doorway and the rule of following the regular entrance
items.text_en: Rav Huna's doorway and the rule of following the regular entrance
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised from Rav Huna's doorway to the study hall which had a mezuzah, contradicting the previous resolution. The Gemara answers that Rav Huna's doorway was the regular entrance, as Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that for mezuzah one follows the regular entrance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects further: the doorway through which Rav Huna entered the study hall had a mezuzah.
The Gemara resolves: that doorway was regularly used, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that for the mezuzah, one follows the regularly used entrance.

items.text: Dispute on the height of the mezuzah
items.text_en: Dispute on the height of the mezuzah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Mattana citing Shmuel says the mitzvah is to place the mezuzah at the beginning of the upper third. Rav Huna says to raise it a handbreadth from the ground and distance it a handbreadth from the lintel, and the entire doorway is fit for a mezuzah.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Matna citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Matna citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Matna in the name of Shmuel rules that the mitzvah is to place the mezuzah at the beginning of the upper third of the doorpost.
Rav Huna rules that one must raise it a handbreadth from the ground and distance it a handbreadth from the lintel, and the entire doorpost is fit for the mezuzah.
Rav Huna adds that the entire height of the doorway is valid for placing a mezuzah.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Huna's view, attributed to Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Yosi derives from a gezerah shavah that the mezuzah must be placed at a height. The Gemara questions Shmuel's position, as it aligns with neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosi. Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan resolves that Shmuel actually holds like Rabbi Yosi, and the baraita's statement about the entire doorway being fit is Rabbi Yehuda's view, not Shmuel's.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Huna's view: Rabbi Yehuda says the mezuzah may be placed anywhere in the doorway, while Rabbi Yosi derives from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) that it must be placed at a height.
The Gemara questions Shmuel's position, noting that it aligns with neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosi, unlike Rav Huna who follows Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan resolves that Shmuel actually holds like Rabbi Yosi, and the baraita's statement about the entire doorway being fit is Rabbi Yehuda's view, not Shmuel's.

items.text: Clarification of the earlier statement about the upper third
items.text_en: Clarification of the earlier statement about the upper third
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies what is meant by 'the beginning of the upper third' in the earlier Mishnah: it means to distance the mezuzah no more than one third from the top beam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by 'the beginning of the upper third' and clarifies that it means to distance the mezuzah no more than one third from the top beam.

items.text: Rava's ruling on placing the mezuzah within a handbreadth of the public domain
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on placing the mezuzah within a handbreadth of the public domain
items.desc_en: Rava states that the mitzvah is to place the mezuzah within the handbreadth closest to the public domain. Two reasons are given: so that one immediately encounters the mezuzah, and for protection.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the mitzvah is to place the mezuzah within the handbreadth closest to the public domain.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rava's ruling.
The Rabbis explain that the reason is so that one immediately encounters the mezuzah upon entering.
Rav Chanina of Sura gives an alternative reason: so that the mezuzah protects the house.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's homily on God's protection
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's homily on God's protection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina contrasts the ways of God with those of flesh and blood: a mortal king sits inside while his guards protect him from outside, but God's servants sit inside while He protects them from outside, as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina contrasts the ways of God with those of flesh and blood: a mortal king sits inside while his guards protect him from outside, but God's servants sit inside while He protects them from outside, as per the verse.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a recessed doorway and the supporting baraita
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a recessed doorway and the supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Rava cites Rava: if one recessed the doorway a handbreadth deep, the mezuzah is invalid. The Gemara attempts to support this from a baraita about a door behind a door, but clarifies that the baraita refers to a different case.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Rava citing Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Rava citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Rava cites Rava's ruling that if one recessed the doorway a handbreadth deep, the mezuzah is invalid.
The Gemara proposes that a baraita about a door placed in a frame or covered with a brick, requiring a separate mezuzah if there is a handbreadth, supports Rava's ruling.
The Gemara rejects the support, explaining that the baraita refers to a door behind a door, not a recessed doorway.
The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly states 'a door behind a door,' so how could it be cited as supporting Rava's case?

items.text: Rav Acha bar Rava on the order of making a doorpost of reeds
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava on the order of making a doorpost of reeds
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if one made a doorpost of reeds, he cuts a reed and places the mezuzah inside. Rav Acha bar Rava limits this to when he first erected the doorpost and then cut and placed the mezuzah, but not if he cut and placed first and then erected, as that would be 'made' and not 'from the made'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that if one made a doorpost of reeds, he cuts a reed and places the mezuzah inside.

Rav Acha bar Rava limits the baraita to when he first erected the doorpost and then cut and placed the mezuzah, but not if he cut and placed first and then erected, as that would violate the principle of 'תַּעֲשֶׂה (you shall make) and not from the already made'.

items.text: Rava on doorways of blind alleys
items.text_en: Rava on doorways of blind alleys
items.desc_en: Rava states that doorways of blind alleys are exempt from mezuzah. A dispute between Rav Richumi and Abba Yosei defines such doorways: one says they lack a roof, the other says they lack a lintel.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that doorways of blind alleys are exempt from mezuzah.
The Gemara asks what defines doorways of blind alleys.

sub.text: Dispute between Rav Richumi and Abba Yosei
sub.text_en: Dispute between Rav Richumi and Abba Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rav Richumi and Abba Yosei dispute the definition: one says they lack a roof, the other says they lack a lintel.

items.text: Rabba bar Sheila and Abaye on the exedra
items.text_en: Rabba bar Sheila and Abaye on the exedra
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Sheila cites Rav Chisda: an exedra is exempt from mezuzah because it has no doorposts. The Gemara questions whether having doorposts would obligate it, and clarifies that they are only for strengthening the roof. Abaye testifies that the exedras of the house of Mar have doorposts but no mezuzah, as they are only for strengthening.

sub.text: Rabba bar Sheila citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Sheila citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Sheila (Rabba bar Sheila) cites רב חסדא (Rav Chisda) that an אכסדרה (exedra) is exempt from מזוזה (mezuzah) because it lacks doorposts.
The Gemara questions whether having doorposts would obligate the exedra in a מזוזה (mezuzah).
The Gemara objects that the doorposts are only made to strengthen the roof, not for an entrance.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Chisda meant even if it has doorposts, it is exempt because they are only for strengthening the roof.
אביי (Abaye) testifies that the exedras of the house of Mar have doorposts but no מזוזה (mezuzah), as they are only for strengthening the roof.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that a gatehouse, exedra, and porch are obligated in mezuzah. The Gemara resolves that this refers to the exedra of Rav's house, which is like a proper hall, or to a Roman-style exedra.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states a gatehouse, exedra, and porch are obligated in mezuzah, contradicting the earlier ruling that an exedra is exempt.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to the exedra of Rav's house, which is like a proper hall, or to a Roman-style exedra, which is more enclosed.

items.text: Rachava on the gatehouse requiring two mezuzot
items.text_en: Rachava on the gatehouse requiring two mezuzot
items.desc_en: Rachava cites Rav Yehuda: a gatehouse (bei harzikei) requires two mezuzot. Rav Pappa Saba defines it as a gatehouse open to a courtyard, with houses opening into the gatehouse.

sub.desc_en: Rachava reports in the name of Rav Yehuda that a gatehouse (בי הרזיקי) requires two mezuzot.

sub.text: Rav Pappa Saba defining the term
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa Saba defining the term
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa Saba explains in the name of Rav that 'בי הרזיקי' refers to a gatehouse (בית שער) that opens to a courtyard, with houses opening into the gatehouse.

items.text: Dispute about a gatehouse open to a garden and a small room
items.text_en: Dispute about a gatehouse open to a garden and a small room
items.desc_en: The Sages taught a dispute between Rabbi Yosi and the Sages about a gatehouse open to a garden and a small room. Rav and Shmuel agree that from the garden to the house all agree it is obligated, as it is an entrance to the house. The dispute is from the house to the garden. Rabba and Rav Yosef reverse the dispute: from the house to the garden all agree it is exempt, and the dispute is from the garden to the house.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute between Rabbi Yosi and the Sages about whether a gatehouse open to a garden and a small room is obligated in mezuzah.

Rav and Shmuel explain that all agree the gatehouse is obligated when entering from the garden to the house, but the dispute is about entering from the house to the garden, where one side considers the small room primary and the other considers the garden primary.

Rabba and Rav Yosef reverse the dispute: all agree that from the house to the garden the gatehouse is exempt, and the dispute is about from the garden to the house, where one side considers it an entrance to the house and the other considers the entire structure as a gatehouse.

items.text: Summary of earlier rulings and final halakha
items.text_en: Summary of earlier rulings and final halakha
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Abaye and Rava follow the lenient opinion of Rabbah and Rav Yosef, while Rav Ashi follows the stringent opinion of Rav and Shmuel, and the halakha is in accordance with Rav and Shmuel for stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara summarizes that Abaye and Rava follow the lenient opinion of Rabbah and Rav Yosef, while Rav Ashi follows the stringent opinion of Rav and Shmuel, and the halakha is in accordance with Rav and Shmuel for stringency.

items.text: Laws of a skylight and multiple entrances
items.text_en: Laws of a skylight and multiple entrances
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a skylight (lul) open from the house to the attic requires one mezuzah if it has one door, and two if it has two doors. Rav Pappa infers that a portico with four doors requires four mezuzot, even if one entrance is used regularly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a ruling: for a skylight open from the house to the attic, Rav Huna says if it has one opening it requires one mezuzah, and if two openings, two mezuzot.
Rav Pappa infers from Rav Huna that a portico with four entrances requires four mezuzot.
The Gemara objects that this is obvious, but clarifies that the ruling is necessary even if one entrance is the main one.
The gemara resolves that the inference is needed even if one entrance is regularly used.

items.text: A doorway in the corner
items.text_en: A doorway in the corner
items.desc_en: Ameimar rules that a doorway in the corner requires a mezuzah. Rav Ashi objects that it has no doorposts, and Ameimar replies that the corners themselves serve as doorposts.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar rules that a doorway at a corner requires a mezuzah.
Rav Ashi objects that such a doorway lacks doorposts, and Ameimar responds that it has doorposts.
Ameimar responds that the corners themselves serve as the doorposts (פַּצִּימִין).

items.text: Mezuzah on the left side
items.text_en: Mezuzah on the left side
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa visits the house of Mar Shmuel and sees a mezuzah placed on the left doorpost. He questions whether this follows Rabbi Meir, who requires a mezuzah even with one doorpost, but only on the right side.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa visits Mar Shmuel's house, sees a doorway with only one doorpost on the left and a mezuzah, and questions whether this follows Rabbi Meir, who only requires a doorpost on the right.
Rav Pappa questions whether the placement follows Rabbi Meir, who requires a mezuzah even with one doorpost but only on the right side, not the left.

items.text: Source that mezuzah is on the right
items.text_en: Source that mezuzah is on the right
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'your house' that the mezuzah is placed on the right side upon entering. Rabbah explains that a person naturally steps with their right foot first. Rav Shmuel bar Acha cites a verse from Kings about the collection chest placed on the right.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the source is for placing the mezuzah on the right, and cites a baraita that derives it from the verse 'בֵּיתֶךָ' (your house) interpreted as 'בִּיאָתְךָ' (your entry) from the right.
Rabbah explains that the right side is the natural way of entry because a person first steps with their right foot.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Acha citing Rava bar Ulla
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Acha citing Rava bar Ulla
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Acha, in the presence of Rav Pappa, cites a verse from Kings (II Kings 12:10) about the collection chest placed on the right side upon entering the Temple, as additional support for the right-side placement.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding one doorpost
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding one doorpost
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: Rabbi Meir requires a mezuzah even if there is only one doorpost, while the Sages exempt. Rabbi Meir's reasoning is based on a ריבוי אחר ריבוי from the word 'mezuzot', while Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse 'on the two doorposts' that 'mezuzot' alone means one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding a house with only one doorpost, noting the Sages' reasoning from the plural 'mezuzot'.
Rabbi Yishmael explains Rabbi Meir's position: the double occurrence of 'mezuzot' creates a ריבוי אחר ריבוי (repetition after repetition) that limits to one mezuzah.
Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse 'on the two doorposts' that the word 'mezuzot' alone means one, establishing a בנין אב (general principle) for all occurrences.

items.text: Derivation that mezuzah must be written on parchment
items.text_en: Derivation that mezuzah must be written on parchment
items.desc_en: A baraita uses a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'writing' to teach that the mezuzah must be written on a scroll, not on stones. Rav Acha bar Rava questions Rav Ashi why a גזירה שווה is needed when the verse says 'and you shall write them' implying complete writing, and the Gemara explains that without the גזירה שווה one might think to write on a stone and affix it to the doorpost.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'writing' to teach that the mezuzah must be written on a scroll, not on stones.
The baraita raises an alternative possibility: the גזירה שווה could instead teach that the mezuzah must be written on stones, like the writing of the stones of the altar.
The baraita resolves the ambiguity by comparing the nature of the writing: the mezuzah's writing is perpetual (for generations), like the scroll of Baruch, not the temporary writing on stones.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava questions Rav Ashi: since the verse says 'on the doorposts,' why is a גזירה שווה needed at all? Rav Ashi answers that the verse 'וכתבתם' implies complete writing, and then 'על המזוזות' specifies the location.
The Gemara explains that without the גזירה שווה, one might have thought to write the mezuzah on a stone and affix it to the doorpost, so the גזירה שווה teaches that it must be written on a scroll.

items.text: The four sections of tefillin and the letter yud
items.text_en: The four sections of tefillin and the letter yud
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the four sections of tefillin are interdependent, and even one letter invalidates them. Rav Yehuda says this was necessary only for the serif of the yud, and further, for the rule that any letter not surrounded by parchment on all four sides is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the four sections of tefillin are interdependent, and even one letter invalidates them, then notes that this is obvious.
Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that the statement was necessary only for the serif of the letter yud, but the Gemara objects that this too is obvious.
The Gemara resolves that the statement was actually needed for Rav Yehuda's other ruling: any letter not surrounded by parchment on all four sides is invalid.

items.text: Derivation of four parshiyot from the word 'totafot'
items.text_en: Derivation of four parshiyot from the word 'totafot'
items.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yishmael who derives the requirement for four parshiyot from the three spellings of 'totafot' in the Torah. Rabbi Akiva argues that this derivation is unnecessary, as the word itself implies two in Katpi and two in Afriki.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Yishmael's derivation of four parshiyot from the three spellings of 'totafot' in the Torah.
Rabbi Akiva argues that the derivation is unnecessary, as the word 'totafot' itself implies two in Katpi and two in Afriki.

items.text: Writing on four parchments and placing in four compartments
items.text_en: Writing on four parchments and placing in four compartments
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one might think to write the parshiyot on four separate parchments and place them in four separate compartments, but the verse 'for a memorial between your eyes' indicates a single memorial, so they must be placed in four compartments made from one piece of leather. Rabbi and the Sages disagree about whether space is needed between the compartments, but they agree that a thread or sinew should be placed between each.

sub.desc_en: The baraita raises a hypothetical: could one write the four parshiyot on four separate parchments and place them in four separate compartments?

The baraita answers by citing the verse 'ולזכרון בין עיניך' (and for a memorial between your eyes), teaching that one must write them on four parchments but place them in four compartments made from one piece of leather.
Rabbi states that if one wrote them on one parchment and placed them in four compartments, it is valid, but there must be space between them.
The Sages argue that no space is needed, but both agree that one places a thread or string between each compartment, and if the indentations are not recognizable, the tefillin are invalid.
The Sages hold that space is not needed between the compartments.
Rabbi and the Sages agree that a thread or sinew is placed between each compartment, and if the indentations are not visible, the tefillin are invalid.

items.text: Writing tefillin shel yad on one parchment
items.text_en: Writing tefillin shel yad on one parchment
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses how to write tefillin shel yad: it should be written on one parchment, but if written on four and placed in one compartment, it is valid. Rabbi Yehuda requires that the four parshiyot be attached, based on the verse 'and it shall be a sign upon your hand', while Rabbi Yosei disagrees.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the question of how to write the tefillin, stating that the tefillah shel yad is written on one parchment, but if written on four parchments and placed in one compartment, it is valid.
Rabbi Yehuda requires gluing them together, citing the verse 'והיה לך לאות על ידך' (and it shall be a sign upon your hand), comparing the internal unity to the external single sign.
Rabbi Yosei argues that gluing is not required.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's claim and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's claim and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei claims that Rabbi Yehuda agrees with him that if one has two tefillin shel rosh and no tefillin shel yad, he can cover one and use it as shel yad. The Gemara questions this, noting their dispute, and Rava explains that Rabbi Yehuda retracted based on Rabbi Yosei's words.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei claims that Rabbi Yehuda agrees with him that if one lacks tefillin shel yad but has two tefillin shel rosh, one may attach leather to one and use it as shel yad.
The gemara objects: 'Agrees? That is their dispute!' — implying that Rabbi Yosei's claim is self-contradictory.
Rava resolves the contradiction: from Rabbi Yosei's words, Rabbi Yehuda retracted his earlier position.

items.text: The rule of not downgrading sanctity
items.text_en: The rule of not downgrading sanctity
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a statement from Rav Chananya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that tefillin shel yad can be made into shel rosh, but not vice versa, because one may not downgrade from a higher sanctity to a lower one. The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction by distinguishing between old and new tefillin, and according to the opinion that designation is significant.

sub.text: Rav Chananya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Chananya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Chananya reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a tefillah shel yad may be made into shel rosh, but not vice versa, because one may not downgrade from a higher sanctity to a lower one.

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between old tefillin (עתיקתא) and new ones (חדתתא), and according to the opinion that designation (הזמנה) is significant, since they were designated from the start.

items.text: Order of the parshiyot in tefillin shel rosh
items.text_en: Order of the parshiyot in tefillin shel rosh
items.desc_en: A baraita states the order: 'Kadesh Li' and 'VeHaya Ki Yevi'acha' on the right, 'Shema' and 'VeHaya Im Shamoa' on the left. The Gemara notes a contradiction with another baraita, and Abaye resolves it by distinguishing between the reader's right and the wearer's right, as the reader reads them in order.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states the order of the parshiyot in tefillin shel rosh: 'Kadesh Li' and 'VeHaya Ki Yevi'acha' on the right, 'Shema' and 'VeHaya Im Shamoa' on the left.
The Gemara objects that another baraita states the opposite order.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the reader's right and the wearer's right, as the reader reads them in order.

items.text: Invalidation if parshiyot are switched
items.text_en: Invalidation if parshiyot are switched
items.desc_en: Rav Chananel said in the name of Rav that if one switched the parshiyot, they are invalid. Abaye adds a qualification, but the text is cut off.

sub.text: Rav Chananel in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chananel in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chananel quotes Rav: if one interchanged the parshiyot, they are invalid.
Abaye begins to qualify the ruling, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Discussion of the arrangement of tefillin compartments
items.text_en: Discussion of the arrangement of tefillin compartments
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially states that the inner compartment faces outward and the outer inward, but not inner to inner or outer to outer. Rava questions this, arguing that the same issue of seeing the airspace applies. The Gemara concludes that there is no difference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the inner compartment faces outward and the outer inward, but not inner to inner or outer to outer.
Rava objects that the same problem of seeing the wrong airspace applies to the alternative arrangement as well.
The Gemara concludes that there is no difference between the arrangements.

items.text: Halakhot le-Moshe mi-Sinai regarding tefillin
items.text_en: Halakhot le-Moshe mi-Sinai regarding tefillin
items.desc_en: Rav Chananel quotes Rav that the 'titura' (the box) of tefillin is halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai. Abaye adds that the 'ma'avarta' (the passageway) and the shin of tefillin are also halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chananel quotes Rav that the 'titura' (the box) of tefillin is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai (law given to Moses at Sinai).
Abaye adds that the 'ma'avarta' (the passageway) of tefillin is also a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai.
Abaye further states that the shin (the letter Shin) on tefillin is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai.

items.text: Requirement for the slit to reach the stitching
items.text_en: Requirement for the slit to reach the stitching
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the slit must reach the stitching. Rav Dimi from Nehardea says that if it is recognizable, it is not necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the slit must reach the stitching.
Rav Dimi from Nehardea says that if the slit is recognizable, it is not necessary to reach the stitching.

items.text: Checking the parchment of tefillin
items.text_en: Checking the parchment of tefillin
items.desc_en: Abaye says the parchment of tefillin must be checked for defects, as otherwise the writing may not be perfect. Rav Dimi from Nehardea says it is not necessary, as the quill will test it.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that the parchment (קילפא) of tefillin must be checked for defects, lest a flaw prevent perfect writing.
Rav Dimi from Nehardea objects that checking is unnecessary, because the quill (קולמוס) itself will test the parchment as it writes.

items.text: Color of tefillin straps
items.text_en: Color of tefillin straps
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that black straps are halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai. A baraita is cited that permits green, black, or white straps but not red due to disgrace. A story about Rabbi Akiva's student using blue straps is discussed, and the Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the inside and outside of the straps.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that black tefillin straps are a law from Moses at Sinai.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that permits green, black, or white straps, contradicting the exclusive requirement for black.
Rabbi Yehuda cites a story about a student of Rabbi Akiva who used blue straps, and Rabbi Akiva did not object.
The Gemara questions how it is possible that Rabbi Akiva saw his student and did not protest.
The Gemara answers that either Rabbi Akiva did not see him, or if he had seen him, he would not have allowed it.
A similar story is cited about Hurkanos, son of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hurkanos, who used purple straps and his father did not object.
The Gemara again questions how it is possible that Rabbi Eliezer saw his son and did not protest.
The Gemara answers similarly that either he did not see him, or if he had seen him, he would not have allowed it.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the inside (where any color is permitted) and the outside (where only black is required).
The Gemara objects that if the baraita refers to the inside, why mention disgrace? It answers that sometimes the straps turn over, exposing the inside.

items.text: Square shape of tefillin
items.text_en: Square shape of tefillin
items.desc_en: A baraita states that square tefillin are halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai. Rav Pappa specifies that this applies to their stitching and diagonal. The Gemara considers a supporting baraita about round tefillin being dangerous and not a mitzvah, and Rav Pappa clarifies that the baraita refers to a round shape like a nut.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that square tefillin are a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai (law given to Moses at Sinai).
Rav Pappa specifies that the requirement of squareness applies to the stitching and the diagonal of the tefillin.
The Gemara attempts to support Rav Pappa by citing a baraita that round tefillin are dangerous and not a mitzvah.
Rav Pappa clarifies that the baraita refers to a round shape like a nut, not merely non-square tefillin.

items.text: Tefillin with cracks in the box
items.text_en: Tefillin with cracks in the box
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says tefillin are valid as long as the face of the tablet remains. Rav Chisda says if two cracks appear they are valid, but three invalidate. Rava qualifies that two cracks are invalid if they are opposite each other, and only in new tefillin. Abaye asks how to distinguish new from old, and Rav Yosef explains that old tefillin are those that heal when scratched.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that tefillin are valid as long as the face of the tablet remains intact; Rav Chisda adds that two cracks are valid but three invalidate.
Rava qualifies that two cracks are valid only if not opposite each other, and only in new tefillin; in old ones, even opposite cracks are valid.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef how to distinguish new tefillin from old ones.
