Rav Yosef explains that old tefillin are those that heal when scratched with a knife, while new ones do not.

items.text: Alternative explanation of the earlier Mishnah
items.text_en: Alternative explanation of the earlier Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation of the earlier Mishnah regarding the order of the parshiyot in the tefillin, suggesting that the new ones are placed on one side and the old on the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation of the Mishnah: the new parshiyot are placed on one side and the old on the other.

items.text: Tying a torn tefillin strap
items.text_en: Tying a torn tefillin strap
items.desc_en: Abaye, sitting before Rav Yosef, had his tefillin strap cut. He asked Rav Yosef if he could tie it, and Rav Yosef answered based on the verse 'And you shall bind them' that the binding must be complete.

sub.desc_en: Abaye, sitting before Rav Yosef, had his tefillin strap cut and asked if he could tie it; Rav Yosef answered based on the verse 'וּקְשַׁרְתָּם' (and you shall bind them) that the binding must be complete.

items.text: Sewing a torn strap into the tefillin
items.text_en: Sewing a torn strap into the tefillin
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef asked Rav Ashi if one can sew a torn strap into the tefillin. Rav Ashi told him to go see what the people do, implying that the custom is authoritative.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yosef's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef asks Rav Ashi whether one may sew a torn strap into the tefillin.
Rav Ashi tells him to go see what the people do, implying that the custom is authoritative.

items.text: Shortened straps are valid
items.text_en: Shortened straps are valid
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa initially said that shortened straps are valid, but then retracted, distinguishing between items used for a mitzvah (like tzitzit and hyssop) and items of sanctity (like tefillin), where shortened straps are invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa initially states that shortened straps are valid, but then immediately retracts this statement as insignificant.
Rav Pappa cites the tradition of Bnei Rabbi Chiyya that shortened tekhelet (תכלת) and shortened hyssop (אזוב) are valid, which would seem to support his original position.

Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between items used for a mitzvah (מצוה), like tzitzit (ציצית) and hyssop, which are valid even shortened, and items of sanctity (קדושה), like tefillin (תפילין), which are invalid when shortened.

items.text: Minimum length of tefillin straps
items.text_en: Minimum length of tefillin straps
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the minimum length of tefillin straps. Rami bar Chama said in the name of Reish Lakish that it is until the finger joint. Various Amoraim demonstrated different ways of measuring, and others had their own practices for tying and hanging the straps.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: given that straps have a required minimum, what is that minimum length?

sub.text: Rami bar Chama citing Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rami bar Chama citing Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama reports Reish Lakish's ruling: the minimum strap length reaches until the finger joint (אצבע צרדה).

sub.text: Demonstrations by Rav Kahana and Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Demonstrations by Rav Kahana and Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana would show the measure with a bent finger, while Rav Ashi showed with an extended finger, demonstrating two ways of visualizing the finger joint.

sub.text: Stam: practices of Rabbah, Rav Acha bar Yaakov, and Mar brei d'Ravna
sub.text_en: Stam: practices of Rabbah, Rav Acha bar Yaakov, and Mar brei d'Ravna
sub.desc_en: Various Amoraim had their own customs for tying and hanging the tefillin straps: Rabbah tied, straightened, and let them hang; Rav Acha bar Yaakov tied and let them hang; Mar brei d'Ravna followed the practice of 'our' tradition.

items.text: The knot of tefillin and their beauty
items.text_en: The knot of tefillin and their beauty
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that the knot of tefillin is a halakha from Moses at Sinai. Rav Nachman added that their beauty should be outward. Rav Ashi, whose strap turned over, was reminded by Mar Zutra that the beauty should be outward.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in Rav's name that the knot of tefillin is a halakha from Moses at Sinai.
Rav Nachman adds that the beauty of tefillin should be outward.

sub.text: Story about Rav Ashi and Mar Zutra
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Ashi and Mar Zutra
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra rebukes Rav Ashi when his strap turns over, citing the principle that beauty should be outward, and Rav Ashi admits he forgot.

items.text: The tefillin knot and its placement
items.text_en: The tefillin knot and its placement
items.desc_en: A baraita identifies the tefillin of the head as the 'name of God' called upon Israel. Rav Chana bar Bizna said God showed Moses the knot of tefillin. Rav Yehuda taught that the knot must be on top and facing forward, symbolizing Israel's superiority and forward position.

sub.desc_en: A baraita identifies the tefillin of the head as the 'name of God' called upon Israel, citing Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol.

sub.text: Rav Chana bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.text_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna reports that God showed Moses the knot of tefillin, as derived from the verse about seeing God's back.
Rav Yehuda rules that the tefillin knot must be on top and facing forward, symbolizing Israel's superiority and forward position.

items.text: When to recite the blessing on tefillin
items.text_en: When to recite the blessing on tefillin
items.desc_en: A dispute is recorded about when to recite the blessing on tefillin. One opinion says from the time of placing them, but another says all blessings are recited before performing the mitzvah. Abaye and Rava reconcile: from the time of placing until the time of tying.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Beidarei quoting Rav (or alternative tradents)
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Beidarei quoting Rav (or alternative tradents)
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Beidarei (or alternative tradents) states that the blessing on tefillin is recited from the time of placing them.
The gemara objects: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel says that all blessings are recited before performing the mitzvah (עובר לעשייתן), contradicting the idea of blessing at the time of placing.
Abaye and Rava both resolve the contradiction: the blessing is recited from the time of placing until the time of tying, so one may bless before the final act of tying.

items.text: Blessings for tefillin and talking between them
items.text_en: Blessings for tefillin and talking between them
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that if one talks between putting on the arm and head tefillin, he must recite a blessing again. Abaye and Rava clarify that if he did not talk, he recites one blessing; if he talked, he recites two blessings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that if one talks between putting on the arm and head tefillin, he must recite a blessing again.

The Gemara objects that Rav Chisda's statement implies that if one did not talk, he does not bless, contradicting a baraita sent by Rav Chiyya bar Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that requires a separate blessing for each tefillin.
Abaye and Rava resolve the contradiction: if one did not talk, he recites one blessing for both; if he talked, he recites two blessings.

items.text: Talking between tefillin is a transgression
items.text_en: Talking between tefillin is a transgression
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that talking between the arm and head tefillin is a transgression, and one who does so must return from the battle array.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that talking between the arm and head tefillin is a transgression, and one who does so must return from the battle array.

items.text: Order of putting on and removing tefillin
items.text_en: Order of putting on and removing tefillin
items.desc_en: A baraita states that when putting on tefillin, one puts on the arm tefillin first, then the head tefillin, based on the verse. When removing, one removes the head tefillin first, then the arm tefillin, derived from the requirement that both be on the head simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states the order of putting on tefillin: arm first, then head, citing the verse 'וקשרתם לאות על ידך' followed by 'והיו לטוטפות בין עיניך'.
The gemara asks: from where do we derive that when removing tefillin, one removes the head tefillin first, then the arm tefillin?

Rabbah says Rav Huna explained to him from the verse 'והיו לטוטפות בין עיניך' — as long as they are between your eyes, there should be two (so when removing, the head tefillin must be removed first to avoid having only the arm tefillin while the head is bare).

items.text: Time for blessing and wearing tefillin
items.text_en: Time for blessing and wearing tefillin
items.desc_en: The rabbis teach that one recites a blessing on tefillin at the time of putting them on, and if one puts them on early, he can touch them later and bless. The time for wearing tefillin is until sunset; Rabbi Yaakov says until the foot leaves the market, and the Sages say until bedtime. Rav Nachman rules like Rabbi Yaakov, but some say the halakha is not like him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that one recites a blessing on tefillin at the time of putting them on, and if one puts them on early, he can touch them later and bless.
The baraita asks until when one may wear tefillin, and the first opinion answers: until sunset.
Rabbi Yaakov gives a second opinion: until the foot leaves the market.
The Sages give a third opinion: until bedtime.
The Sages concede to Rabbi Yaakov that if one removed tefillin for a bathroom or bathhouse and the sun set, he does not put them back on.
Rav Nachman rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yaakov.
Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna would pray with tefillin at night, supporting a lenient view.
An alternative tradition states that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yaakov.

items.text: Challenge from Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier assertion that one may not wear tefillin at night, citing that Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna would pray with tefillin at night. It answers that this was a dispute, implying that not all agree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier assertion that one may not wear tefillin at night, citing that Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna would pray with tefillin at night.
The Gemara answers that this was a dispute, implying that not all agree.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbah bar Rav Huna's view
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbah bar Rav Huna's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbah bar Rav Huna actually held that view, citing his statement that if there is doubt about nightfall one does not remove tefillin, but if it is definitely night one removes them. The Gemara explains that this was said regarding the eve of Shabbat, and then analyzes the underlying logic: if night is a time for tefillin, so is Shabbat; if Shabbat is not, then night is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbah bar Rav Huna actually held that view, citing his statement that if there is doubt about nightfall one does not remove tefillin, but if it is definitely night one removes them.

The Gemara explains that Rabbah bar Rav Huna's statement was said regarding the eve of Shabbat, and then analyzes the underlying logic: if night is a time for tefillin, so is Shabbat; if Shabbat is not, then night is not.

items.text: Source for excluding nights and Shabbat from tefillin
items.text_en: Source for excluding nights and Shabbat from tefillin
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yossi HaGelili derives from the verse 'miyamim yamimah' that tefillin are not worn at night or on Shabbat and festivals. Rabbi Akiva derives the exclusion of Shabbat and festivals from the requirement for an 'ot' (sign), as those days themselves are signs.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yossi HaGelili's derivation from the verse 'מִיָּמִים יָמִימָה' (from days to days) that tefillin are not worn at night (יָמִים, not nights) nor on all days (מִיָּמִים, excluding Shabbat and festivals).
Rabbi Akiva rejects the derivation from the verse and states that the law of the 'חוקה' (statute) applies only to the Passover offering, not to tefillin.

The Gemara cites another baraita where Rabbi Akiva derives the exclusion of Shabbat and festivals from the requirement for an 'אות' (sign), as those days themselves are signs, so tefillin are not needed.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on the prohibition after sunset
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on the prohibition after sunset
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says one who wears tefillin after sunset violates a positive commandment, while Rabbi Yochanan says it is a negative commandment. The Gemara initially suggests they dispute the principle of Rabbi Avin citing Rabbi Ila, that 'hishamer', 'pen', and 'al' indicate a negative commandment. It then offers an alternative: both accept Rabbi Avin's principle, but disagree whether 'hishamer' of a positive commandment is a negative or positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that one who wears tefillin after sunset violates a positive commandment, while Rabbi Yochanan rules it violates a negative commandment.
The Gemara suggests the dispute hinges on whether they accept Rabbi Avin's principle that 'הִשָּׁמֶר' (guard), 'פֶּן' (lest), and 'אַל' (do not) always indicate a negative commandment.

The Gemara rejects the first explanation and offers an alternative: both accept Rabbi Avin's principle, but they disagree whether 'הִשָּׁמֶר' (guard) attached to a positive commandment is itself a negative or positive commandment.

items.text: Permissibility for safeguarding and Ravina's story
items.text_en: Permissibility for safeguarding and Ravina's story
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar adds that if one intends to safeguard the tefillin, it is permitted. Ravina recounts that he was sitting before Rav Ashi when it got dark, and Rav Ashi put on tefillin, claiming it was for safeguarding, but Ravina suspected he actually held that the law permits it but one should not instruct others to do so.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that if one intends to safeguard the tefillin, it is permitted to wear them after dark.
Ravina recounts that he was sitting before Rav Ashi when it got dark, and Rav Ashi put on tefillin, so Ravina asked if he was doing so for safeguarding.
Rav Ashi answers affirmatively that he is wearing them for safeguarding.
Ravina discerns that Rav Ashi actually held the law permits wearing tefillin at night but one should not instruct others to do so.

items.text: Obligation to touch tefillin frequently
items.text_en: Obligation to touch tefillin frequently
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna states that one must touch their tefillin frequently, derived via a kal vachomer from the tzitz: if the tzitz, which has only one mention of God's name, requires constant attention, then tefillin with many mentions certainly require it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that one must touch their tefillin frequently, deriving this obligation via a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from the tzitz (the high priest's headplate), which has only one mention of God's name yet requires constant attention, so tefillin with many mentions certainly require it.

items.text: Derivation that tefillin are worn on the left hand
items.text_en: Derivation that tefillin are worn on the left hand
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that 'yadcha' refers to the left hand, and they bring three verses where 'yad' is contrasted with 'yamin' to prove that 'yad' alone means the left hand.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach that 'יָדְךָ' (your hand) in the context of tefillin refers to the left hand, and they cite three verses where 'יָד' (hand) is contrasted with 'יָמִין' (right hand) to prove that 'יָד' alone means the left hand.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei HaChoram's proof from Joseph
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei HaChoram's proof from Joseph
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaChoram argues that the right hand is called 'yad' in the verse about Joseph, implying that 'yad' alone refers to the right. The Gemara notes that the other opinion holds that only 'yad yemino' is called 'yad', not 'yad' alone.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaChoram argues that the right hand is called 'יָד' (hand) based on the verse about Joseph placing his right hand.
The Gemara objects that the other opinion holds that only 'יַד יְמִינוֹ' (right hand) is called 'יָד', not 'יָד' alone.

items.text: Rabbi Natan's derivation from tying and writing
items.text_en: Rabbi Natan's derivation from tying and writing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Natan argues that just as writing is done with the right hand, so too tying (tefillin) is with the right, and therefore the placement is on the left. The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yosei HaChoram derives the left hand, and answers that he derives it from the same source as Rabbi Natan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Natan argues that just as writing (כְּתִיבָה) is done with the right hand, so too binding (קְשִׁירָה) of tefillin is with the right hand.
The Gemara notes that since binding is with the right hand, the placement (הַנָּחָה) of the tefillin is on the left hand.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yosei HaChoram derives that placement is on the left hand.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yosei HaChoram derives it from the same source as Rabbi Natan.

items.text: Rav Ashi's derivation from 'yadekhah'
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's derivation from 'yadekhah'
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi derives that tefillin are placed on the left arm from the word 'yadekhah' written with a weak hei. Rabbi Abba questions whether it could refer to the strong hand, and Rav Ashi responds that it is not written with a chet.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi says that the word 'יָדְכָה' is written with a weak 'הֵ״י' (heh), indicating the left hand.
Rabbi Abba objects to Rav Ashi, suggesting that 'יָדְךָ' might mean the strong hand (right hand).
Rav Ashi rejects the objection, noting that the word is not written with a 'חֵי״ת' (chet) which would indicate strength.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on 'yadekhah' and the amputee
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on 'yadekhah' and the amputee
items.desc_en: A baraisa presents a dispute: 'yadekhah' with a hei refers to the left, while 'Acherim' say it includes an amputee. Another baraisa states that one without an arm is exempt from tefillin, but Acherim say 'yadekhah' includes an amputee.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that 'יָדְכָה' with a 'הֵ״י' refers to the left hand.
Acherim says that 'יָדְךָ' includes a person with a stumped arm (גִּידֵּם).
A supporting baraita states that one without an arm is exempt from tefillin.
Acherim again says that 'יָדְכָה' includes a person with a stumped arm.

items.text: The ambidextrous person
items.text_en: The ambidextrous person
items.desc_en: A baraisa states that an ambidextrous person places tefillin on his right (which is his left). Another baraisa says he places on his left (which is everyone's left). Abaye resolves the contradiction by saying the latter refers to one who is ambidextrous.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis taught that a left-handed person (אִטֵּר) places tefillin on his right arm, which is his left.
The Gemara objects with another baraita that says a left-handed person places tefillin on his left arm, which is everyone's left.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by saying that the second baraita refers to a person who is ambidextrous (שׁוֹלֵט בִּשְׁתֵּי יָדָיו).

items.text: Location of tefillin on the head
items.text_en: Location of tefillin on the head
items.desc_en: The school of Menashe teaches that 'al yadecha' refers to the bicep, and 'bein einecha' refers to the crown. The school of Rabbi Yannai says it is the place where a baby's brain is soft.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Menasheh
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Menasheh
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Menasheh teaches that 'עַל יָדְךָ' refers to the bicep (קִיבּוֹרֶת) and 'בֵּין עֵינֶיךָ' refers to the crown of the head (קׇדְקֹד).
The Gemara asks where exactly the crown of the head is, and the school of Rabbi Yannai answers that it is the place where a baby's brain pulsates.

items.text: The person with two heads
items.text_en: The person with two heads
items.desc_en: Pleimo asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about a person with two heads on which to place tefillin. Rabbi Yehuda responds harshly. A man then arrives whose son was born with two heads, asking how much to give the priest for redemption. An elder cites a baraisa that he must give ten sela'im. The Gemara questions this based on a baraisa of Rami bar Chama.

sub.text: Pleimo's question to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
sub.text_en: Pleimo's question to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
sub.desc_en: Pleimo asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: a person with two heads — on which head does he place tefillin?
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi responds harshly: either leave or accept excommunication.

sub.text: A man arrives with a practical case
sub.text_en: A man arrives with a practical case
sub.desc_en: Meanwhile, a man arrives whose son was born with two heads, asking how much to give the priest for pidyon haben (redemption of the firstborn).
An elder cites a baraisa that the man must give ten sela'im (double the standard five) for the two-headed firstborn.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rami bar Chama's baraisa
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rami bar Chama's baraisa
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: does the baraisa of Rami bar Chama not teach that if the firstborn dies within thirty days, the redemption is not required, implying a limit?

items.text: Derivation of arm tefillin placement from 'ach'
items.text_en: Derivation of arm tefillin placement from 'ach'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word 'ach' in the verse divides the obligation, and the placement of arm tefillin is derived from the head tefillin by analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the word 'אך' (ach) divides the obligation, and the placement of arm tefillin is different because the Torah tied it to the head.

items.text: Source for arm tefillin on the bicep
items.text_en: Source for arm tefillin on the bicep
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that 'al yadecha' refers to the bicep, derived from a verbal analogy between arm and head tefillin.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that 'yadecha' (your hand) refers to the bicep (קיבורת).
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive this?
The baraita teaches that 'al yadecha' (upon your hand) means the height of the arm (bicep), derived via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from head tefillin, which are placed on the height of the head.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yitzchak's alternative derivations
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yitzchak's alternative derivations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer derives from 'vehaya lecha le'ot' that tefillin must be hidden from others, and Rabbi Yitzchak derives from 'vesamtem... al levavchem' that the placement must be opposite the heart.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that the verse 'וְהָיָה לְךָ לְאוֹת' (and it shall be for you as a sign) teaches that tefillin must be hidden from others.
Rabbi Yitzchak derives from 'וְשַׂמְתֶּם... עַל לְבַבְכֶם' (and you shall place these words upon your hearts) that the placement of tefillin must be opposite the heart.

items.text: Practice of placing arm tefillin opposite the heart
items.text_en: Practice of placing arm tefillin opposite the heart
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Acha bar Avya would place the tefillin opposite the heart. Rav Ashi's tefillin were visible, and Amemar explained that the requirement of 'lecha le'ot' applies only in the place of the sign.

sub.desc_en: Reports that Rabbi Chiyya and Rav Acha bar Avya would intentionally place the arm tefillin opposite the heart.
Describes that Rav Ashi was sitting before Amemar with a wound on his hand, and his tefillin were visible, prompting Amemar's question.
Amemar asks Rav Ashi: does the master not hold that the tefillin are 'for you as a sign' and not for others as a sign, so they should not be visible?
Rav Ashi answers that the requirement of 'for you as a sign' was stated only regarding the place of the sign (the arm), not that it must be hidden from others.

items.text: Source for head tefillin placement and Rabbi Yehuda's derivation
items.text_en: Source for head tefillin placement and Rabbi Yehuda's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that 'bein einecha' refers to the bicep of the head from a verbal analogy with the baldness prohibition. Rabbi Yehuda adds that it must be a place fit for a single plague mark, excluding the area between the eyes which has flesh and hair.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that head tefillin are placed on the bicep of the head, and answers with a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the baldness prohibition.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that the source is unnecessary, deriving from a verbal analogy with the hand that the place must be fit for a single plague mark.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda's exclusion applies to the area between the eyes, which has both flesh and hair and thus can show two types of plague marks.

items.text: Dispute whether four tzitzit are one mitzvah or four
items.text_en: Dispute whether four tzitzit are one mitzvah or four
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that four tzitzit are interdependent because they are one mitzvah. Rav Yosef, Rava bar Ahina, and Ravina offer different practical differences between the views. Rabbi Yishmael holds they are four separate mitzvot, and the halakha follows him but is not practiced.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that four tzitzit (ציציות) are interdependent because they constitute one mitzvah (מצוה).
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the view that they are one mitzvah and the view that they are four.
Rav Yosef answers that the difference concerns a linen sheet with tzitzit (סדין בציצית), which is exempt from tzitzit according to one view but obligated according to the other.
Rava bar Ahina answers that the difference concerns a tallit (טלית) with five corners, which requires tzitzit on four corners according to one view but on all five according to the other.

Ravina answers that the difference concerns Rav Huna's ruling that one who goes out on Shabbat (שבת) with a tallit not properly fringed is liable for a sin-offering (חטאת), which applies only if the tzitzit are one mitzvah.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's statement
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's statement
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi states that one who reduces his cloak (גלימא) to fewer than four corners accomplishes nothing, as it becomes a tallit with five corners requiring tzitzit on all.

Rav Mesharshiya states that one who ties his cloak (גלימא) in a knot accomplishes nothing, because it is considered as if untied, citing a Mishnah about tied water-skins (חמתות) being pure except for Arab ones.
Rav Dimi from Nehardea states that one who sews his cloak (גלימא) closed accomplishes nothing, and if it does not require tzitzit, he should cut it open and discard it.
Rabbi Yishmael holds that the four tzitzit are four separate mitzvot (מצוות), and Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules that the halakha (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yishmael but is not practiced.

items.text: Story of Ravina and Mar bar Rav Ashi about tzitzit
items.text_en: Story of Ravina and Mar bar Rav Ashi about tzitzit
items.desc_en: Ravina followed Mar bar Rav Ashi on Shabbat; a thread broke but Mar did not mention it until home. The Gemara questions why he did not act, citing the principle that human dignity overrides a negative commandment, and Rav bar Sheva explains.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Ravina was following Mar bar Rav Ashi on Shabbat of the festival; a thread of his tzitzit broke, but Mar did not mention it until they reached home, and then said he would have discarded it if told.
The Gemara questions why Mar bar Rav Ashi did not act immediately, citing the principle that human dignity (כבוד הבריות) overrides a negative commandment in the Torah.

sub.text: Rav bar Sheva's explanation before Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav bar Sheva's explanation before Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav bar Sheva explains the matter before Rav Kahana (the text breaks off, but the move serves as the resolution to the question).

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion: the prohibition of 'lo tasur'
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion: the prohibition of 'lo tasur'
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes a prior discussion about the prohibition of deviating from rabbinic decrees, citing the principle that human dignity overrides a negative commandment, and notes that the case here involves a rabbinic law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the prohibition of deviating from rabbinic decrees (לא תסור) applies, but here the case involves a rabbinic law (כרמלית), so human dignity overrides it.

items.text: Return to the chapter 'HaKometz'
items.text_en: Return to the chapter 'HaKometz'
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the main topic of the chapter, which deals with the meal offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the main topic of the chapter, which deals with the meal offering.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: techelet and white, head and arm tefillin
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: techelet and white, head and arm tefillin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the blue thread does not impede the white, nor the white the blue; similarly, the head tefillin does not impede the arm tefillin, nor vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the blue thread (תכלת) does not impede the white thread, and vice versa, and the hand tefillin does not impede the head tefillin, and vice versa.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is the Mishnah not like Rabbi?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is the Mishnah not like Rabbi?
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah, which says the fringes do not impede each other, contradicts Rabbi's view that they do, based on the verse 'and you shall see it' implying both together. The Sages interpret the verse as each separately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah, which says the fringes do not impede each other, contradicts Rabbi's view that they do.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi learns from the verse 'וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ' (and you shall see it) that the white and blue fringes impede each other.
The Sages interpret the same verse as meaning each fringe is seen separately, so they do not impede each other.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's resolution: the Mishnah can be like Rabbi, regarding precedence
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's resolution: the Mishnah can be like Rabbi, regarding precedence
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the Mishnah can even align with Rabbi, as it deals with the order of tying: the white should precede the blue, but if reversed, it is still valid, merely lacking the optimal mitzvah.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav resolves the challenge by asserting that the Mishnah can align even with Rabbi, as it deals only with the order of precedence (קדימה), not with invalidation.

A baraita is cited to support the resolution: it is a מצוה (commandment) to tie the white before the blue, but if reversed, the person has still fulfilled the obligation (יצא), merely lacking the optimal performance of the mitzvah.
The Gemara asks what exactly is meant by 'lacking the mitzvah' — i.e., what specific deficiency is incurred when the order is reversed.

items.text: Initial assumption about mutual indispensability
items.text_en: Initial assumption about mutual indispensability
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that if one omitted the white fringe but fulfilled the blue, Rabbi would hold they are mutually indispensable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that if one omitted the white fringe but fulfilled the blue, Rabbi would hold they are mutually indispensable.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's reinterpretation
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's reinterpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the case is not about omission but about performing the mitzvah in a non-optimal manner.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the case is where one omitted the ideal form of the commandment and performed it in a suboptimal way.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's answer for a blue garment
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's answer for a blue garment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the case where white does not impede blue and vice versa. Rami bar Chama answers that it refers to a garment entirely of blue, where the order of attachment matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted that white does not impede blue, but blue does not impede white — what is the case?
Rami bar Chama answers that the case is a garment entirely of blue, where the order of attaching white and blue matters.

items.text: Levi and Shmuel's discussion on a linen garment
items.text_en: Levi and Shmuel's discussion on a linen garment
items.desc_en: Levi asks Shmuel about the same issue, and Shmuel answers that it applies to a linen garment with tzitzit, where the white must be attached first based on the verse 'the corner' meaning the color of the garment.

sub.desc_en: It was also stated: Levi asked Shmuel about the same issue, and Shmuel answered that the case is a linen garment with fringes, where the ideal standard (מצוה) is to prioritize white first.
The Gemara explains the reason: the verse says 'the corner' (הכנף) meaning the color of the corner, so if one prioritizes blue over white, it is invalid.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's answer for a blue garment revisited
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's answer for a blue garment revisited
items.desc_en: The Gemara again asks about the case where blue does not impede white. Rami bar Chama answers that it refers to a garment entirely of blue, where blue must be attached first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Granted that white does not impede blue, but what about the case where blue does not impede white?
Rami bar Chama answers that the case is a garment entirely of blue, where the mitzvah is to attach blue first, and if one attached white first it is invalid.

items.text: Rava's answer about remnants and the measure
items.text_en: Rava's answer about remnants and the measure
items.desc_en: Rava rejects the color-based answer and explains that the case is about remnants (gardonim) where one color is frayed and the other remains. The measure for valid remnants is enough to tie them, as stated by Bar Hamdurei in the name of Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions whether the previous explanation about color order is relevant, implying the real issue is not about colors.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Bnei Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Bnei Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: The Bnei Rabbi Chiyya are cited to support that remnants of techelet are valid, analogous to remnants of hyssop.

sub.text: Bar Hamdurei's ruling in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Bar Hamdurei's ruling in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Bar Hamdurei in the name of Shmuel sets the measure for valid remnants as enough to tie them.

items.text: Unresolved inquiry about the measure and Rav Ashi's question
items.text_en: Unresolved inquiry about the measure and Rav Ashi's question
items.desc_en: An inquiry is raised whether the measure 'enough to tie' refers to all together or each individually, left unresolved (teiku). Rav Ashi asks about thick threads that could be tied if thinner, and Rav Acha bar Rava answers that it is even more recognizable as a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved inquiry (תיקו) whether the measure 'enough to tie' refers to tying all the fringes together or each one individually.
Rav Ashi asks about thick threads that cannot be tied now but could be tied if they were thinner, whether they are considered valid.
Rav Acha bar Rava answers that such thick threads are even more recognizable as a mitzvah (מצוה), implying they are valid.

items.text: The Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi and Rava's inference
items.text_en: The Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi and Rava's inference
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi as Rabbi Yitzchak citing a chain, who holds that without blue one may attach white. Rava infers from this that each loop must be tied, otherwise the remnants would be entirely permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna disagrees with Rabbi's position that blue and white are interdependent, and cites a baraita where Rabbi Yitzchak in a chain of tradition rules that one who lacks blue may attach white.
Rava infers from the baraita that each loop must be tied, otherwise the remnants of the blue thread would be entirely permitted.

items.text: The upper knot is biblical
items.text_en: The upper knot is biblical
items.desc_en: Rabbah infers from the fact that a linen garment requires tzitzit that the upper knot is biblical, because if it were rabbinic, why would one need to permit linen? The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling that a single loop is not a connection proves the knot is biblical.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the case of a linen garment that was tied (דִּלְמָא דְּאִיקְּטַר).

Rabbah infers that the upper knot is biblical (דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא), arguing that if it were rabbinic, there would be no need to permit linen tzitzit, and the Mishnah's rule that a single loop is not a connection proves the knot is biblical.

items.text: Thread torn from its root
items.text_en: Thread torn from its root
items.desc_en: Rav states that if the thread is torn from its root, the tzitzit is invalid. Rava challenges Rav Nachman with a baraita that distinguishes between the beginning and the end of the thread. The Gemara clarifies the terms 'sheyarav' and 'gardumav', concluding that they refer to the remnant needed for tying.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that if the thread is torn from its root, the tzitzit is invalid.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman with a baraita that distinguishes between the beginning and the end of the thread, implying that at the end even a remnant suffices.
The Gemara asks what the terms 'sheyarav' and 'gardumav' mean, suggesting they refer to remnants and torn ends respectively.
The Gemara rejects the distinction and explains that the baraita teaches one concept: we require a remnant of the gardumin for tying.

items.text: The winding thread counts in the minimum
items.text_en: The winding thread counts in the minimum
items.desc_en: Rabbah says in the name of Rav that the thread used for winding counts toward the minimum number of threads. Rav Yosef objects, saying it was Samuel who said this. A supporting tradition from Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha confirms this.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states in the name of Rav that the winding thread (חוט של כרך) counts toward the minimum number of threads required for ציצית.
Rav Yosef objects, asserting that the ruling was said by Samuel, not by Rav.
A supporting tradition is cited: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports that Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha also taught that the winding thread counts toward the minimum.

items.text: Blue thread that is mostly wound
items.text_en: Blue thread that is mostly wound
items.desc_en: Rava says in the name of Samuel that if most of the blue thread is wound, it is valid. Rav Yosef corrects him, saying it was Rav who said this. Multiple traditions confirm this, and Rav Chiya bar Rav Natan adds that even one winding is valid, and the beauty of the blue is one-third of the fringe and two-thirds of the branch.

sub.desc_en: Rava, sitting and teaching, reports in the name of Shmuel that blue thread (תכלת) that is mostly wound is valid.
Rav Yosef objects, correcting Rava that it was Rav, not Shmuel, who said this ruling.
A supporting tradition is cited: Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rav Sheshet in the name of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba in the name of Rav confirms that blue thread that is mostly wound is valid.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Rav Natan's tradition
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Natan's tradition
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Natan teaches a version of the tradition that adds: even one winding is valid, and the beauty of the blue thread is one-third of the fringe and two-thirds of the branch.

items.text: The measure of a winding and the number of windings
items.text_en: The measure of a winding and the number of windings
items.desc_en: Rabbi says a winding is the amount to wrap, repeat, and triple. A baraita states one should not reduce from seven windings nor add beyond thirteen, corresponding to the seven firmaments and the six spaces between them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the measure of a winding (חוליא).
Rabbi answers that a winding is the amount to wrap, repeat, and triple (כורך, שונה, משלש).
A baraita states one should not reduce from seven windings nor add beyond thirteen, corresponding to the seven firmaments and the six spaces between them.

items.text: Beginning and ending with white
items.text_en: Beginning and ending with white
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one begins and ends the winding with white, because 'the corner' implies the type of the corner, and one ascends in holiness, not descends.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one begins and ends the winding with white, because 'the corner' implies the type of the corner, and one ascends in holiness, not descends.

items.text: A garment entirely blue
items.text_en: A garment entirely blue
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah see a man wearing a garment entirely of blue, and the Gemara begins to discuss the requirement for a blue thread on such a garment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets the scene: Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah were sitting when a man passed by wearing a garment entirely of blue (תכלת), and they cast a blue thread upon him.

items.text: Opening dispute on wool vs. linen tzitzit
items.text_en: Opening dispute on wool vs. linen tzitzit
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbah bar bar Hannah argue over the meaning of 'gedil' vs. 'petil' in the tzitzit verse, with Rav favoring a single twisted thread and Rabbah requiring two distinct threads.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing Rav and Rabbah bar bar Hannah's dispute about the aesthetic preference for wool (גְּלִימָא) and tekhelet (תְּכֵלְתָּא) in tzitzit.
The Gemara asks: On what basis do they disagree?

The Gemara explains: Rabbah bar bar Hannah holds that the verse uses both 'גְּדִיל' and 'פְּתִיל', allowing either a twisted or untwisted thread; Rav holds that 'פְּתִיל' is always required, and 'גְּדִילִים' teaches the count of threads (two for 'גְּדִיל', four for 'גְּדִילִים'), and one must twist the thread from within.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on wool exempting linen
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on wool exempting linen
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that wool threads exempt linen ones from tzitzit, establishing a hierarchy of exemption.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules in the name of Levi that wool threads exempt linen ones from the obligation of tzitzit.

items.text: Inquiry on linen exempting wool
items.text_en: Inquiry on linen exempting wool
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether linen threads can exempt wool ones, considering the verse's prohibition of mixing wool and linen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: whether linen threads can exempt a wool garment, given that wool threads exempt linen but the reverse might not hold.
The Gemara suggests an alternative: since the verse permits mixing wool and linen for ציצית (ritual fringes), there should be no difference whether wool is on linen or linen on wool.
Raḥava citing Rav Yehuda resolves the dilemma: both wool threads on linen and linen threads on wool are valid, and such threads exempt even silk garments.

items.text: Rav Nachman's view on shiraim exemption
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's view on shiraim exemption
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman argues that shiraim (silk garments) are exempt from tzitzit, contradicting Rava who holds they are obligated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Nachman's ruling disagrees with the previous statement, as Rav Nachman says that שיראין (silk garments) are exempt from ציצית (ritual fringes).

Rava raises an objection against Rav Nachman from a ברייתא (baraita) that states that שיראין (silk garments), כלך (kalakh), and סריקין (serikin) are all חייב (obligated) in ציצית (ritual fringes), and the Gemara clarifies that this obligation is מדרבנן (by rabbinic law).

items.text: Clarifying the exemption rule for mixed materials
items.text_en: Clarifying the exemption rule for mixed materials
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes whether the exemption applies only to wool and linen together or to each individually, citing a tannaitic source that exempts both kinds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: if the obligation for silk garments is only rabbinic, how can the baraita permit mixing wool and linen (כלאים) in the fringes?
The Gemara resolves: the baraita means one may use either wool or linen strings, not both together.
The Gemara supports this interpretation by noting the baraita's later clause: strings of their own type exempt, but not of other types, which fits a rabbinic obligation.
The Gemara rejects the alternative that the obligation is Torah law, because then only wool or linen would exempt, not other fabrics.

items.text: Rava's resolution on the verse contradiction
items.text_en: Rava's resolution on the verse contradiction
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the apparent contradiction between 'kanaf' (wing) and 'tzemer ufishtim' (wool and linen) by explaining that wool and linen exempt both within and outside their kind, while other materials exempt only within their kind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous argument, noting that it is not conclusive, and introduces Rava's approach.

Rava raises a contradiction between the verse 'הכנף' (the corner) implying the fringe must be from the same type as the garment, and the verse 'צמר ופשתים' (wool and linen) indicating only these materials.
Rava resolves the contradiction: wool and linen strings exempt any garment, whether of their own type or not, while other materials exempt only garments of their own type.

items.text: Rav Nachman citing Tanna of Beit Yishmael
items.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Tanna of Beit Yishmael
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman supports his view by citing the Tanna of Beit Yishmael's rule that garments of wool and linen are exempt from tzitzit.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's citation of Tanna of Beit Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's citation of Tanna of Beit Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman supports his view by citing the Tanna of Beit Yishmael's rule that garments of wool and linen are exempt from tzitzit.

items.text: Tanna of Beit Yishmael's broader exemption
items.text_en: Tanna of Beit Yishmael's broader exemption
items.desc_en: The Tanna of Beit Yishmael expands the exemption to include camel wool, rabbit wool, goat hair, kalakh, serikin, and shiraim, based on the verse 'or beged'.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna of Beit Yishmael derives from the general mention of 'garments' in the Torah and the specific mention of 'wool and linen' in one place that all garments of wool and linen are included.

items.text: Abaye's critique of the Tanna's consistency
items.text_en: Abaye's critique of the Tanna's consistency
items.desc_en: Abaye notes that this Tanna of Beit Yishmael contradicts another Tanna of Beit Yishmael who limits exemption to wool garments only.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that this Tanna of Beit Yishmael contradicts another Tanna of Beit Yishmael, who limits the word 'בגד' (garment) to wool but then expands it to include other materials via the word 'או בגד' (or a garment).

items.text: Opening Tannaic dispute
items.text_en: Opening Tannaic dispute
items.desc_en: The Tannaim state the dispute: Beit Shammai exempts a linen garment from tzitzit, Beit Hillel obligates it, and the halakha follows Beit Hillel.

sub.desc_en: The Tannaim state the dispute: Beit Shammai exempts a linen garment from tzitzit, Beit Hillel obligates it, and the halakha follows Beit Hillel.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok's objection and Rabbi's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok's objection and Rabbi's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok objects that anyone who adds tekhelet in Jerusalem is merely one of the fools. Rabbi responds that the reason they forbade it is because people are not expert in the laws of tekhelet.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok's objection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok's objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok objects that anyone who adds tekhelet in Jerusalem is merely one of the fools.
Rabbi responds that the reason they forbade adding tekhelet is because people are not expert in the laws of tekhelet.

items.text: Rava bar Rav Chana's proposal and rejection
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chana's proposal and rejection
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chana suggests that they should throw ten sets of tzitzit into the marketplace to publicize the matter. The Gemara rejects this, saying it would only increase confusion. Another suggestion to teach it in the public lecture is rejected due to a decree because of the noise.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chana proposes to Rava that they throw ten sets of tzitzit into the marketplace to publicize the matter.
The Gemara rejects the proposal, arguing that it would only increase confusion.
The Gemara suggests teaching the matter in the public lecture.
The Gemara rejects this due to a decree because of the noise.

items.text: Objection from white tzitzit and Resh Lakish's principle
items.text_en: Objection from white tzitzit and Resh Lakish's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if tekhelet is not available, one could use white tzitzit. The response is that since it is possible with its own kind (white), it is not permitted. This is based on Resh Lakish's principle: wherever there is a positive and negative commandment, if you can fulfill both, do so; if not, the positive overrides the negative.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if tekhelet is unavailable, one could use white tzitzit, and the response is that since white is possible with its own kind, it is not permitted.
The Gemara cites Resh Lakish's principle that wherever there is a positive and negative commandment, if both can be fulfilled that is best, otherwise the positive overrides the negative.

items.text: Further proposals and Rava's conclusion
items.text_en: Further proposals and Rava's conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests checking the tzitzit, but this is rejected due to a decree because of tasting. Another proposal to write the halakha on a tablet is raised, but the Gemara questions whether the tablet would stand and be relied upon. Rava concludes with 'now' (the current situation).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes checking the tzitzit to verify their status.
The Gemara rejects this due to a decree because of tasting (טעימה).
The Gemara proposes writing the halakha on a tablet (דיסקי).
The Gemara questions whether the tablet would stand and be relied upon.
Rava concludes with 'now' (השתא), indicating the current situation.

items.text: Initial objection and Rashbam's answer
items.text_en: Initial objection and Rashbam's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: earlier it was said that one relies on the edges (diskei) for chametz on Pesach and Yom Kippur which are karet, so surely here, where it is only a positive commandment, we should rely?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: since we rely on the edges (דיסקי) for chametz on Pesach and Yom Kippur which carry the penalty of כרת (karet), surely here, where it is only a positive commandment, we should also rely?

items.text: Rava's answer: concern for tearing and the principle of taaseh velo min he'asui
items.text_en: Rava's answer: concern for tearing and the principle of taaseh velo min he'asui
items.desc_en: Rava answers that there is a concern that the garment might tear within three fingerbreadths and then be sewn, and the Torah said 'taaseh' – and not from that which is already made. This means the holes for the tzitzit must be made anew, not rely on the existing weave.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the concern is the garment might tear within three fingerbreadths and be sewn, and the Torah said 'תַּעֲשֶׂה' (you shall make) – and not from that which is already made (וְלֹא מִן הֶעָשׂוּי).

items.text: Rabbi Zeira permits his linen garment and a decree due to night garment
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira permits his linen garment and a decree due to night garment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira permitted his own linen garment (by not attaching tzitzit), and Rab Zeira said there is also a decree because of night garments (which are exempt, so one might come to think day garments are also exempt).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira permits his own linen garment (by not attaching tzitzit), establishing a practical ruling.
Rab Zeira adds a decree due to night garments (which are exempt from tzitzit), so one might mistakenly exempt day garments as well.

items.text: Rava: rule for garment made of cloth with leather corners
items.text_en: Rava: rule for garment made of cloth with leather corners
items.desc_en: Rava states a principle: if the main garment is cloth but its corners are leather, it is obligated; if the main garment is leather and its corners are cloth, it is exempt. The reason is that we require the essence of the garment to be of a material that takes tzitzit.

sub.desc_en: Rava states a principle: a garment whose main body is cloth but corners are leather is obligated in tzitzit, while one whose main body is leather and corners are cloth is exempt, because the essence of the garment must be of a material that takes tzitzit.

items.text: Rav Achai follows the corner
items.text_en: Rav Achai follows the corner
items.desc_en: Rav Achai holds that the determining factor is the material of the corner (kanaf) itself, not the main garment.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that Rav Achai follows the corner (kanaf) as the determining factor for the obligation of tzitzit, rather than the main garment.

items.text: Adding tzitzit to a 3-cornered garment to make 4; challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Adding tzitzit to a 3-cornered garment to make 4; challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Huna says: if one attached tzitzit to a garment that had three corners, and then completed it to four, it is invalid due to 'taaseh velo min he'asui'. This is challenged from the practice of the early pious ones who would attach tekhelet after weaving three. Rava answers that they made a hole (patzu) first, not woven. Rabbi Zeira's ruling about a mu'teletes (a garment with a slit) is also brought, and Rava distinguishes: there, since he is already within the prohibition of bal tosif, it is not considered an act of making.

sub.text: Rava citing Rav Sechorah citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rav Sechorah citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Huna rules that attaching tzitzit to a three-cornered garment and then completing it to four corners is invalid due to the principle of 'תַּעֲשֶׂה – וְלֹא מִן הֶעָשׂוּי' (you shall make, not from the already-made).
The Gemara challenges Rava's ruling from the practice of the early pious ones (חסידים הראשונים) who would attach tekhelet after weaving three corners, implying it is permitted.

The Gemara resolves the challenge by emending the baraita: it should read 'since they made a hole (פצעו) in it for three corners', not 'wove', so the tzitzit were attached before the garment was complete.

sub.text: Gemara's further objection from Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Gemara's further objection from Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects further: Rabbi Zeira ruled that attaching tzitzit to a mu'teletes (a garment with a slit) is valid, seemingly contradicting the principle of 'תַּעֲשֶׂה – וְלֹא מִן הֶעָשׂוּי'.

Rava answers that in the case of a mu'teletes, since the person is already within the prohibition of בל תוסיף (adding to a mitzvah), the act of attaching tzitzit is not considered a valid act of making (מעשה).

items.text: Rav Papa's objection: maybe he intends to nullify
items.text_en: Rav Papa's objection: maybe he intends to nullify
items.desc_en: Rav Papa objects to Rava's distinction: perhaps when one adds a fifth tzitzit, he intends to nullify the mitzvah, not to add. In that case there is no bal tosif, and the act of making (ma'aseh) exists, so the principle of 'taaseh velo min he'asui' should apply.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa objects to Rava's distinction: perhaps when one adds a fifth tzitzit, he intends to nullify the mitzvah, not to add, so there is no bal tosif (prohibition of adding) and the act of making (ma'aseh) exists, making the principle of 'taaseh velo min he'asui' applicable.

items.text: Tekhelet and kilayim; definition of a peturah garment
items.text_en: Tekhelet and kilayim; definition of a peturah garment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Matna citing Shmuel says: tekhelet is not subject to kilayim (the prohibition of mixing wool and linen), and this applies even to a 'tallit peturah' (exempt garment). The Gemara asks what 'tallit peturah' means – if it means one without the required size, that contradicts a baraitha which defines a tallit for a minor that covers his head and most of his body.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Matna citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Matna citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports in the name of Shmuel that the tekhelet (blue wool) thread is not subject to the kilayim (mixed wool-linen) prohibition, even when attached to a 'tallit peturah' (exempt garment).
The Gemara asks what 'tallit peturah' means — what kind of garment is considered exempt.

The Gemara objects: if 'peturah' means a garment lacking the minimum size (שיעור), this contradicts a baraitha that defines a valid tallit for a minor as one that covers his head and most of his body.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's phrase 'and likewise for kilayim'
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's phrase 'and likewise for kilayim'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'and likewise for kilayim' in the Mishnah, since there is no casual exemption for kilayim. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains it refers to a linen garment with tzitzit. The Gemara then clarifies that the exemption mentioned is for a garment that had tzitzit attached while folded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'and likewise for kilayim' means, noting that there is no casual exemption for kilayim.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the phrase refers to a linen garment with tzitzit, not to kilayim itself.
The Gemara clarifies that the exemption mentioned in the Mishnah refers to a garment that had tzitzit attached while it was folded.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Zeira already stated this principle, and resolves that it was stated as one of two related teachings.

items.text: The law of a folded garment
items.text_en: The law of a folded garment
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon disagree about whether a folded garment requires tzitzit. They agree that if it is sewn, it is obligated. The Gemara clarifies that the case is where it is held together with pins.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a folded garment (טלית כפולה) is obligated in tzitzit according to the Tanna Kamma, Rabbi Shimon exempts it, and both agree that if it is sewn it is obligated.
The Gemara objects: if it is sewn, the obligation is obvious — why does the baraita need to state it?
The Gemara resolves: the case is where the garment is held together with pins, not sewn, so the baraita clarifies that sewing makes it obligated.

items.text: Rabbah bar Huna's encounter with Rava bar Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Huna's encounter with Rava bar Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Huna sees Rava bar Rav Nachman wearing a folded garment with tzitzit on the fold. He objects, saying the corner is not the one specified by the Torah. Rava removes it and puts on another garment. Rabbah bar Huna then corrects himself, saying the obligation is on the garment, not the person, so he must attach tzitzit.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Huna visits Rava bar Rav Nachman and sees him wearing a folded garment with tzitzit attached to the fold, and the tzitzit string comes to rest near his head.
Rabbah bar Huna objects that this corner is not the one the Torah specified, so Rava removes the garment and puts on another.
Rabbah bar Huna corrects himself, explaining that the obligation is on the garment (חובת טלית), not the person, so Rava must attach tzitzit to that garment.

items.text: Support from the early pious ones and the angel's objection
items.text_en: Support from the early pious ones and the angel's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a support from the early pious ones who would attach tekhelet after weaving three fingers, but dismisses it as they were stringent. It then recounts an angel who found Rav Ketina wearing a linen garment and questioned the fate of the tekhelet tzitzit. Rav Ketina asks if they punish for a positive commandment, and the angel says they do when there is anger.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests a support from the early pious ones who would attach tekhelet after weaving three fingers of the garment.
The Gemara rejects the support, explaining that the pious ones were stringent upon themselves and do not reflect the standard law.
An angel finds Rav Ketina wearing a linen garment and questions what will become of the tekhelet tzitzit that should have been attached.
Rav Ketina asks the angel whether they punish for neglecting a positive commandment.
The angel answers that they do punish for positive commandments when there is divine anger.

items.text: Analysis of the obligation: person vs. garment
items.text_en: Analysis of the obligation: person vs. garment
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the dispute between Rabbah bar Huna and Rava bar Rav Nachman. If the obligation is on the person, one is liable for not attaching tzitzit when wearing a garment. If on the garment, the garment itself is not liable. The Gemara concludes that Rabbah bar Huna meant to say that Rava was trying to exempt himself from tzitzit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses a dilemma: if the obligation is on the person (חובת גברא), then one who wears a garment without tzitzit is liable; but if it is on the garment (חובת טלית), then the garment itself bears no liability.

The Gemara refines the position: even if the obligation is on the person, the Torah only obligates one when wearing a garment that is itself subject to the obligation (בת חיותא), not when wearing a garment that is exempt.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbah bar Huna's statement was actually a rebuke: 'Are you trying to exempt yourself from tzitzit?'

items.text: Garments for storage and the honor of the elderly
items.text_en: Garments for storage and the honor of the elderly
items.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Kisna says in the name of Shmuel that storage garments are obligated in tzitzit, but Shmuel admits that if an elder made it for his honor, it is exempt because it is not for covering. The Gemara notes that at the time of wearing, we do attach tzitzit to avoid shaming the elder.

sub.text: Rav Tovi bar Kisna in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Tovi bar Kisna in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Kisna reports Shmuel's ruling that storage garments (כלי קופסא) are obligated in tzitzit, but Shmuel concedes that if an elder made it for his honor it is exempt.
The Gemara explains the reason: the Torah said 'אשר תכסה בה' (which you cover yourself with), and this garment is not made for covering.
The Gemara resolves that at the time of wearing, we certainly attach tzitzit to avoid shaming the elder, citing the verse 'לועג לרש חרף עושהו' (he who mocks the poor insults his Maker).

items.text: The law of a torn garment and attaching tekhelet from elsewhere
items.text_en: The law of a torn garment and attaching tekhelet from elsewhere
items.desc_en: Rachbah says in the name of Rabbi Yehuda that a garment torn within three fingerbreadths of the corner cannot be sewn, but beyond that it can. A baraisa supports this, with Rabbi Meir and the Sages disagreeing about within three. They agree that one may not bring a piece of cloth with tekhelet from elsewhere and attach it, but they agree that one may bring tekhelet from elsewhere and attach it.

sub.desc_en: Rachbah states in the name of Rabbi Yehuda that a garment torn beyond three fingerbreadths from the corner may be sewn, but within three fingerbreadths it may not.
A baraita supports the distinction: beyond three fingerbreadths all agree one may sew; within three, Rabbi Meir forbids and the Sages permit.
All agree one may not bring a piece of cloth with tekhelet from elsewhere and attach it, but one may bring tekhelet from elsewhere and attach it.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's statement that the fringe must not be interrupted that one may transfer threads from one garment to another. It then questions this inference, suggesting it might only apply to a worn-out garment.

items.text: Baraita on a garment entirely of tekhelet
items.text_en: Baraita on a garment entirely of tekhelet
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that a garment entirely of tekhelet can be exempted with any colored threads except kala ilan. Another baraita contradicts this, saying only threads of the same type exempt, and for a tekhelet garment one must bring tekhelet and another material, but kala ilan is invalid though if used it is valid.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a garment with four threads and one with eight threads.

items.text: Return to the inference about transferring threads
items.text_en: Return to the inference about transferring threads
items.desc_en: The Gemara again raises the inference about transferring threads from one garment to another, but suggests it might only apply if one made the garment anew.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on transferring threads
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on transferring threads
items.desc_en: It is stated that Rav and Shmuel disagree on whether one may transfer threads from one garment to another, and similarly on lighting from one lamp to another and on the halakha regarding Rabbi Shimon's ruling on dragging. Abaye notes that the master (Rav Yehuda) follows Rav in all matters except these three, where he follows Shmuel. A baraita is cited explaining Rabbi Shimon's ruling.

items.text: Practices of the Amoraim
items.text_en: Practices of the Amoraim
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rav Yehuda gave his tzitzit to a weaver, Rav Chanina made a fringe, and Ravina sewed them.

items.text: Dispute on the number of threads and measurements
items.text_en: Dispute on the number of threads and measurements
items.desc_en: A baraita records the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the number of threads (four vs. three) and the length of the fringe (four vs. three fingerbreadths). Rav Pappa explains the biblical handbreadth. Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda argue about the placement and length, and Rav Pappa rules: four threads within three fingerbreadths, and the fringe length is four.

items.text: Challenge from the elders' ruling
items.text_en: Challenge from the elders' ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the notion that tzitzit has a fixed measurement, citing a tradition that the elders of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel ruled that tzitzit has no measurement. The Gemara initially assumes this means no measurement at all, but then rejects that interpretation.

items.text: Establishing that tzitzit has a minimum but no maximum length
items.text_en: Establishing that tzitzit has a minimum but no maximum length
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that just as a lulav has a minimum length (three handbreadths) but no maximum, so too tzitzit has a minimum length but no maximum. This is derived from a parallel with the lulav, which is explicitly stated to have a minimum but no maximum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that tzitzit has no maximum length but has a minimum length, drawing a parallel to the lulav which also has a minimum but no maximum.

items.text: Definition of tzitzit and requirement to separate the threads
items.text_en: Definition of tzitzit and requirement to separate the threads
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'tzitzit' means a lock of hair, and Abaye adds that one must separate the threads like the locks of hair of an Aramean (i.e., like a fringe).

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'ציצית' (tzitzit) means a branch-like tuft, and Abaye adds that one must separate the threads like the tufts of Aramaeans.

items.text: Placement of tzitzit on the corner
items.text_en: Placement of tzitzit on the corner
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if one attaches tzitzit to the corner of the garment or to the hem, it is valid, but Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov invalidates both. Rav Giddel cites Rav that tzitzit must hang on the corner, supporting Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: the Tanna Kamma validates tzitzit attached to the corner or hem, while Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov invalidates both.
The gemara identifies that Rav Giddel's statement in Rav's name — that tzitzit must hang on the corner — aligns with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position.

items.text: Distance from the edge for tzitzit
items.text_en: Distance from the edge for tzitzit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan states that one must distance the tzitzit from the edge by the full length of a thumb's knot. The Gemara explains that both Rav Pappa's ruling (about three fingerbreadths) and Rabbi Yaakov's ruling are necessary, as each teaches a different aspect: Rav Pappa's ruling sets a maximum distance, while Rabbi Yaakov's sets a minimum distance.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that one must distance the tzitzit from the edge of the garment by the full length of a thumb's knot.

The Gemara explains that both Rav Pappa's ruling (about three fingerbreadths as a maximum distance) and Rabbi Yaakov's ruling (about a thumb's knot as a minimum distance) are necessary, because without Rabbi Yaakov's ruling one might think that bringing the tzitzit closer is always better.

The Gemara concludes that without Rav Pappa's ruling one might think that distancing the tzitzit further is always better, so both rulings are needed to establish both a minimum and a maximum distance.

items.text: Incident about the distance requirement
items.text_en: Incident about the distance requirement
items.desc_en: Rav Sama saw that Ravina's garment had tzitzit less than a thumb's knot from the edge and questioned him. Ravina replied that the ruling was said only at the time of making the tzitzit. Rav Ashi comforted Rav Sama, saying that one of them is worth two of us.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sama sees that the corner of Ravina's garment has tzitzit less than a thumb's knot from the edge and asks Ravina if he does not hold by Rabbi Yaakov's ruling.
Ravina answers that Rabbi Yaakov's ruling was said only at the time of making the tzitzit, not after the fact.
Rav Ashi comforts Rav Sama, who is embarrassed, saying that one of them (Ravina) is worth two of us.

items.text: Methods of attaching tzitzit threads
items.text_en: Methods of attaching tzitzit threads
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov would insert four threads, fold them, and insert them into the garment, requiring eight threads on the garment to fulfill 'gedil' and 'gedilim' in place of 'petil'. Rav Yirmiyah from Difti would insert eight threads (sixteen total) without folding. Mar, son of Ravina, acted like us (the standard practice).

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov would insert four threads, fold them, and insert them into the garment, requiring eight threads on the garment to fulfill 'gedil' and 'gedilim' in place of 'petil'.
Rav Yirmiyah from Difti would insert eight threads (sixteen total) without folding them.
Mar, son of Ravina, acted like us (the standard practice).

items.text: Blessing for tzitzit
items.text_en: Blessing for tzitzit
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman found Rav Adda bar Ahavah reciting the blessing 'la'asot tzitzit' while attaching strings, and told him that Rav said tzitzit does not require a blessing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman finds Rav Adda bar Ahava attaching threads and reciting the blessing 'לַעֲשׂוֹת צִיצִית' (to make tzitzit), and asks what blessing he heard.
Rav Nachman reports that Rav ruled that tzitzit does not require a blessing.
Rav Nachman reports that Rav ruled tzitzit does not require a blessing.

items.text: Challenge to Rav's ruling and the principle of blessings for mitzvot
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav's ruling and the principle of blessings for mitzvot
items.desc_en: After Rav Huna's death, Rav Chisda challenged Rav's statement that tzitzit does not require a blessing, citing Rav's own ruling that tzitzit made by a non-Jew is invalid. Rav Yosef explained that Rav Chisda held a principle: a mitzvah valid when done by a non-Jew does not require a blessing when done by a Jew, while one invalid when done by a non-Jew does require a blessing. The Gemara challenges this principle with circumcision (valid by a non-Jew yet requires a blessing) and sukkah (valid by a non-Jew yet no blessing for making it), and tefillin (invalid by a non-Jew yet no blessing for making it is mentioned).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets the scene: after Rav Huna's death, Rav Chisda came to challenge Rav's statement against Rav's own ruling.
Rav Chisda questions Rav's statement that tzitzit does not require a blessing, citing Rav's own ruling that tzitzit made by a non-Jew is invalid.
Rav Yosef explains Rav Chisda's principle: a mitzvah valid when done by a non-Jew does not require a blessing when done by a Jew, while one invalid when done by a non-Jew does require a blessing.
The Gemara objects to the principle, citing circumcision which is valid when performed by a non-Jew yet requires a blessing.
The baraita records the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about who may circumcise, and the Gemara notes that a blessing is recited for circumcision.
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that Rav himself holds circumcision by a non-Jew is invalid, citing a verse.
Rabbi Yochanan derives the invalidity of circumcision by a non-Jew from the verse 'הִמּוֹל יִמּוֹל' (he shall surely be circumcised).
The Gemara notes that sukkah supports the principle (valid by a non-Jew yet no blessing for making it), but tefillin is a refutation.
The Gemara cites a baraita that a sukkah made by a non-Jew is valid, yet the blessing recited is only for sitting, not for making the sukkah.
The Gemara raises tefillin as a refutation: tefillin are invalid when made by a non-Jew, yet no blessing for making them is mentioned.

items.text: Opening baraita on invalid scribes
items.text_en: Opening baraita on invalid scribes
items.desc_en: A baraita from Mipashrunya lists who invalidates a Torah scroll, tefillin, or mezuzah: a heretic, Samaritan, gentile, slave, woman, minor, or apostate Jew. The verse 'and you shall bind them' and 'and you shall write them' implies that only those obligated in binding are obligated in writing.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists who invalidates a Torah scroll, tefillin, or mezuzah, deriving from the verse that only those obligated in binding (קשירה) are obligated in writing (כתיבה).

items.text: Gemara's inference about blessing for tefillin
items.text_en: Gemara's inference about blessing for tefillin
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for a Jew, no blessing is required when making tefillin, as per Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna citing Rabbi Yochanan: the blessing for donning tefillin is said, but not for making them. The reason is that a mitzvah whose performance completes the obligation (like circumcision) requires a blessing even if done by a gentile, but a mitzvah whose performance does not complete the obligation (like tefillin) does not require a blessing from a Jew.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a Jew does not need to recite a blessing when making tefillin, citing Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Yochanan who lists the blessings for donning tefillin but not for making them.

The Gemara explains the reason: for a mitzvah whose performance completes the obligation (like circumcision), a Jew must bless even if a gentile performs it; but for a mitzvah whose performance does not complete the obligation (like tefillin), a Jew does not bless.

items.text: Dispute about tzitzit: obligation of the garment or the person
items.text_en: Dispute about tzitzit: obligation of the garment or the person
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that regarding tzitzit, the dispute is whether it is an obligation of the garment (chovat talit) or an obligation of the person (chovat gavra).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute about tzitzit is whether it is an obligation of the garment (חובת טלית) or an obligation of the person (חובת גבר).

items.text: Rav Mordechai's version and Rav Yehuda's proof for tzitzit by a gentile
items.text_en: Rav Mordechai's version and Rav Yehuda's proof for tzitzit by a gentile
items.desc_en: Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that they teach the baraita differently. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: From where is it derived that tzitzit made by a gentile is valid? The verse says 'Speak to the children of Israel and they shall make for themselves tzitzit' — others may make for them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that they (the Babylonian academies) teach the baraita differently.

Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav that the source for the validity of tzitzit made by a gentile is the verse 'דַּבֵּר אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְעָשׂוּ לָהֶם צִיצִית' — others may make tzitzit for them.

items.text: Materials for tzitzit: Rav and Shmuel on sisin
items.text_en: Materials for tzitzit: Rav and Shmuel on sisin
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: If one made tzitzit from thorns, threads, or shreds, it is invalid; from sisin (flax stalks), it is valid. When Rav Yehuda said this before Shmuel, Shmuel said: Even from sisin it is invalid, because we require spinning for the sake of the mitzvah.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Rav's ruling: tzitzit made from thorns, threads, or shreds are invalid, but from sisin (flax stalks) they are valid.
When Rav Yehuda presented Rav's ruling before Shmuel, Shmuel rejected it, ruling that even sisin is invalid because spinning for the sake of the mitzvah (לשמה) is required.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on covering tefillin with gold or untanned hide
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on covering tefillin with gold or untanned hide
