items.desc_en: A baraita: If one covered tefillin with gold or with the hide of an unclean animal, they are invalid. With the hide of a clean animal, they are valid even if not tanned for their sake. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: Even with the hide of a clean animal they are invalid until tanned for their sake.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma rules that tefillin covered with gold or the hide of an unclean animal are invalid, but with the hide of a clean animal they are valid even if not tanned for their sake.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel objects, ruling that even with the hide of a clean animal the tefillin are invalid until the hide is tanned for their sake.

items.text: Abaye's question on tekhelet dyeing and Rav Ashi's explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's question on tekhelet dyeing and Rav Ashi's explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda how they dye tekhelet. The process involves taking the blood of the chilazon and other ingredients, boiling them, testing with an egg, and burning the egg. The Gemara infers three things: tasting invalidates, dyeing must be for its sake, and tasting invalidates. Rav Ashi explains that the reason tasting invalidates is because dyeing must be for its sake.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda how they dye tekhelet, and Rav Shmuel describes the process of taking chilazon blood and ingredients, boiling, testing with an egg, and burning the egg.
The Gemara infers three things from the described process: tasting invalidates, dyeing must be for its sake, and tasting invalidates.
The Gemara objects that the second and third inferences are redundant, as 'tasting invalidates' and 'dyeing for its sake' seem to be the same point.
Rav Ashi resolves the objection by explaining that the gemara's statement means: 'What is the reason tasting invalidates? Because we require dyeing for its sake.'

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on tasting and the second color
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on tasting and the second color
items.desc_en: A baraita: Tasting invalidates, as it says 'all of tekhelet' — the words of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel. Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai says: Even a second appearance in it is valid, as it says 'and scarlet wool'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's position that tasting the dye invalidates the tekhelet, based on the verse 'כְּלִיל תְּכֵלֶת' (all of tekhelet).
Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai argues that even a second appearance of color in the dye is valid, citing the verse 'וּשְׁנִי תוֹלָעַת' (and scarlet wool).

items.text: Baraita on inspection and purchase of tekhelet, tefillin, and scrolls
items.text_en: Baraita on inspection and purchase of tekhelet, tefillin, and scrolls
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught: Tekhelet has no inspection and is bought only from an expert. Tefillin have inspection and are bought only from an expert. Scrolls and mezuzot have inspection and are bought from anyone. The Gemara questions that tekhelet has no inspection, citing Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda who tested it with a certain process.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that tekhelet has no inspection and is bought only from an expert, tefillin have inspection and are bought only from an expert, and scrolls and mezuzot have inspection and are bought from anyone.
The Gemara objects that tekhelet does have inspection, citing Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda who tested it with a process involving a certain insect, water of a certain plant, and urine.

items.text: Opening discussion: validity of tekhelet that splits
items.text_en: Opening discussion: validity of tekhelet that splits
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case of a 40-day-old bird whose chest splits; if it splits it is invalid, if not it is valid. This is a preliminary statement about the test for tekhelet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the test for tekhelet: a 40-day-old bird whose chest splits is invalid, otherwise valid.

items.text: Rav Adda's alternative test with sourdough
items.text_en: Rav Adda's alternative test with sourdough
items.desc_en: Rav Adda in the name of Rav Avira proposes a test using sourdough made from barley; if the tekhelet improves it is valid, if it worsens it is invalid, with a mnemonic of 'change of falsehood, change of truth'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda in the name of Rav Avira proposes an alternative test for tekhelet using sourdough made from barley, with a mnemonic of 'change of falsehood, change of truth'.

items.text: Clarification of 'no examination'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'no examination'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by 'no examination' and explains it means to taste it (the tekhelet).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'no examination' means in the context of the tekhelet.
The Gemara answers that 'no examination' means to taste the tekhelet to test its quality.

items.text: Practical test and resolution of conflicting traditions
items.text_en: Practical test and resolution of conflicting traditions
items.desc_en: Mar brought tekhelet from Moshki in the years of Rav Achai; they tested it with Rav Yitzchak's method (split) and Rav Adda's method (sourdough). Rav Achai initially thought to invalidate it, but concluded that the two traditions were said in sequence: first test with Rav Yitzchak, then if it splits, test with Rav Adda. They sent from there that the traditions were said sequentially.

sub.desc_en: Mar brought tekhelet from Moshki in the years of Rav Achai; they tested it with Rav Yitzchak's method (split) and Rav Adda's method (sourdough).
Rav Achai initially thought to invalidate it, but argued that since it cannot be both not tekhelet and not indigo, the traditions must be sequential.

sub.text: Rav Achai's explanation and confirmation from there
sub.text_en: Rav Achai's explanation and confirmation from there
sub.desc_en: Rav Achai explains the sequential testing: first test with Rav Yitzchak (if no split, kosher; if split, test with Rav Adda); they sent from there confirming the traditions were said sequentially.

items.text: Rabbi Mani's strict practice
items.text_en: Rabbi Mani's strict practice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Mani was precise and bought according to the stringencies of the Mishnah; an elder told him that earlier generations did so and succeeded.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Mani was exacting and purchased sky-blue wool according to the stringencies of the Mishnah.
A certain elder told Rabbi Mani that his predecessors did the same and their businesses succeeded.

items.text: Baraita: buying a tallit with tzitzit from the market
items.text_en: Baraita: buying a tallit with tzitzit from the market
items.desc_en: The baraita rules: if bought from an Israelite, it is in its presumptive status; from a gentile, from a merchant it is valid, from a layman it is invalid. The Gemara explains the reason: here they translate it as due to a harlot (the gentile might sell it to a Jew who will use it for idolatry), while Rav Yehuda says it is lest the gentile accompany the Jew on the road and kill him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a tallit with tzitzit bought from an Israelite is in its presumptive status; from a gentile merchant it is valid, from a lay gentile it is invalid.
The baraita adds that one may not sell a tallit with tzitzit to a gentile unless the tzitzit are first untied.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind the baraita's distinction between a gentile merchant and a lay gentile.
The sages of here explain the reason is due to a harlot (the gentile might sell it to a Jew who will use it for idolatry).
Rav Yehuda gives an alternative reason: lest the gentile accompany the Jew on the road and kill him.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's practice and blessing on tzitzit
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's practice and blessing on tzitzit
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda would attach tekhelet to the garments of his household and bless every morning 'to wrap oneself in tzitzit'. The Gemara questions: since he attaches, he holds it is a time-bound positive commandment, so why bless every morning? It answers: like Rabbi, who says one blesses on tefillin each time he puts them on. Rav Yehuda was modest and did not remove his cloak all day, so he only blessed in the morning when changing from night to day clothing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda would attach tekhelet to his household's garments and recite the blessing 'to wrap oneself in tzitzit' every morning.
The Gemara questions: since Rav Yehuda attaches tekhelet, he holds tzitzit is a non-time-bound positive commandment, so why does he bless every morning?
The Gemara answers: Rav Yehuda follows Rabbi, who says one blesses on tefillin each time he puts them on.
The Gemara objects: if so, he should bless every time he puts it on, but Rav Yehuda was modest and did not remove his cloak all day.
The Gemara resolves: he only blessed in the morning when changing from night clothing to day clothing.

items.text: Baraita: who is obligated in tzitzit and exemptions
items.text_en: Baraita: who is obligated in tzitzit and exemptions
items.desc_en: The baraita states all are obligated: priests, Levites, Israelites, converts, women, and slaves. Rabbi Shimon exempts women because it is a time-bound positive commandment. The Gemara questions why priests are mentioned (obvious), and explains it is needed because one might think priests, who are permitted sha'atnez during service, are exempt; the baraita teaches that only during service is it permitted, not otherwise. Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is derived from 'and you shall see it' excluding night garments, and 'which you cover yourself with' includes a blind person's garment.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that all are obligated in tzitzit, listing priests, Levites, Israelites, converts, women, and slaves, and then records Rabbi Shimon's exemption for women because it is a time-bound positive commandment.
The Gemara questions why the baraita mentions priests, Levites, and Israelites, since it is obvious that they are obligated.

The Gemara explains that priests needed to be mentioned because one might think they are exempt due to their permission to wear sha'atnez during service; the baraita teaches that this permission applies only during service, not otherwise.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Shimon's exemption of women.
A baraita is cited deriving from the verse 'וּרְאִיתֶם אוֹתוֹ' (and you shall see it) that night garments are exempt from tzitzit, establishing the time-bound nature.
The baraita resolves the derivation by including a blind person's garment (since others see it) and excluding night garments (since they are not seen by others), reinforcing the time-bound exemption.

items.text: Derivation of four corners from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of four corners from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how the phrase 'אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ' is used to teach that a garment must have four corners, not three or five. It argues that a five-cornered garment is included because it contains four, while a three-cornered garment is excluded because it does not contain four.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ' (which you cover yourself with) teaches, and cites a baraita that the verse 'עַל אַרְבַּע כַּנְפוֹת כְּסוּתְךָ' (on the four corners of your garment) means four corners, not three.

The Gemara objects that the verse could be interpreted as excluding a five-cornered garment instead of a three-cornered one, and then resolves that the phrase 'אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ' includes a five-cornered garment, leaving 'עַל אַרְבַּע' to exclude a three-cornered one.
The Gemara explains the reasoning: a five-cornered garment is included because it contains four corners, while a three-cornered garment is excluded because it does not contain four.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon derives the requirement from the word 'אֲשֶׁר', while the Rabbis do not derive anything from 'אֲשֶׁר'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon derives the requirement from the word 'אֲשֶׁר', while the Rabbis do not derive anything from 'אֲשֶׁר'.

items.text: Multiple homiletical interpretations of 'וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ'
items.text_en: Multiple homiletical interpretations of 'וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents several baraitot that expound the verse 'וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ וּזְכַרְתֶּם', linking it to the recitation of Shema, the prohibition of kilayim, the acceptance of all mitzvot, the equivalence of tzitzit to all mitzvot, and the chain from seeing to remembering to doing. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai adds that one who is diligent in this mitzvot merits to receive the Divine Presence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the verse 'וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ' (and you shall see it), since Rabbi Shimon already used the word 'אֲשֶׁר' for his derivation.
The first baraita expounds that seeing the tzitzit (ציצית) reminds one of the mitzvah of reciting Shema (קריאת שמע), which is timed by the ability to distinguish between techelet (תכלת) and white.
The second baraita expounds that seeing the tzitzit reminds one of the adjacent mitzvah of kilayim (כלאים), as the verse about tzitzit follows the prohibition of mixing wool and linen.

The third baraita expounds that once a person is obligated in the mitzvah of tzitzit, he becomes obligated in all mitzvot, and this follows Rabbi Shimon's view that tzitzit is a time-bound positive mitzvah.
The fourth baraita expounds that the mitzvah of tzitzit is equivalent in weight to all the other mitzvot combined.

The fifth baraita expounds a chain: seeing leads to remembering, remembering leads to doing; Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai adds that one diligent in this mitzvah merits to receive the Divine Presence (שכינה), as derived from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'אֹתוֹ' here and 'אֹתוֹ' in the verse about fearing God.

items.text: The preciousness of Israel and the protective power of mitzvot
items.text_en: The preciousness of Israel and the protective power of mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that Israel is beloved because God surrounded them with mitzvot like tefillin, tzitzit, and mezuzah. David's experience in the bathhouse highlights the importance of the mitzvah of milah. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov states that one who has these mitzvot is fortified against sin.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by declaring that Israel is beloved because God surrounded them with mitzvot (commandments) — tefillin (תפילין) on head and arm, tzitzit (ציצית) on garments, and mezuzah (מזוזה) on doorposts — and cites David's verse 'שבע ביום הללתיך' (seven times a day I praise You).

The baraita recounts that when David entered the bathhouse and saw himself naked, he lamented being without a mitzvah, but was comforted by recalling the milah (מילה, circumcision) on his flesh, and upon exiting he composed a psalm about the eighth-day mitzvah.

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov states that whoever has tefillin on head and arm, tzitzit on garment, and mezuzah on doorpost is fortified against sin, citing the verse 'והחוט המשולש לא במהרה ינתק' (the threefold cord is not quickly broken) and 'חונה מלאך ה׳ סביב ליראיו ויחלצם' (the angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear Him and delivers them).

items.text: The significance of the blue thread (techelet)
items.text_en: The significance of the blue thread (techelet)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir explains why techelet is special: it resembles the sea, which resembles the sky, which resembles the Throne of Glory, as indicated by verses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir asks why the blue thread (תְּכֵלֶת) is distinguished from all other colors, and answers that it resembles the sea, which resembles the sky, which resembles the Throne of Glory, as supported by verses.

items.text: Greater punishment for neglecting a lesser mitzvah
items.text_en: Greater punishment for neglecting a lesser mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir uses a parable to teach that the punishment for neglecting a less valuable mitzvah (like white threads) is greater than for neglecting a more valuable one (like techelet), because the king's command was easier to fulfill.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir teaches that the punishment for neglecting the white threads is greater than for neglecting the techelet, using a parable of a king who commanded two servants to bring seals of clay and gold respectively.

items.text: The obligation to recite one hundred blessings daily
items.text_en: The obligation to recite one hundred blessings daily
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir derives from the verse 'מָה' (which numerically equals 100) that a person must recite one hundred blessings each day. Rav Chiyya bar Rav Avya would complete the count on Shabbat and festivals by using fragrant spices and delicacies.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir states the obligation to recite one hundred blessings daily, deriving it from the verse 'מָה' (which numerically equals 100).

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Avya's practice
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Avya's practice
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Avya would complete the count of one hundred blessings on Shabbat and festivals by using fragrant spices and delicacies.

items.text: The three daily blessings and the status of a slave
items.text_en: The three daily blessings and the status of a slave
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir teaches that one must recite three blessings daily: for not being made a gentile, a woman, or a boor. Rav Acha bar Yaakov questions his son's blessing, and the Gemara clarifies that the blessing for not being a slave is already included in the blessing for not being a woman.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir teaches that a person is obligated to recite three blessings daily: for not being made a gentile, a woman, or a boor.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov hears his son blessing 'who did not make me a boor' and questions whether such a blessing is warranted.
The son responds by asking what blessing he should recite instead, and suggests that the blessing for not being a slave is already included in the blessing for not being a woman.
The Gemara clarifies that a slave is indeed included in the category of a woman, resolving the son's question.

items.text: Gemara's directive to add to the dye
items.text_en: Gemara's directive to add to the dye
items.desc_en: The Gemara instructs to add more dye to the mixture, continuing the previous discussion.

items.text: Baraita about the chilazon
items.text_en: Baraita about the chilazon
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the chilazon, its appearance, its rarity, and that its blood is used for techelet.

items.text: Rabbi Natan on the reward for tzitzit
items.text_en: Rabbi Natan on the reward for tzitzit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Natan states that even the lightest mitzvah has reward in this world, and the reward in the World to Come is incalculable, using tzitzit as an example.

items.text: Story of the man saved by tzitzit
items.text_en: Story of the man saved by tzitzit
items.desc_en: A man who was meticulous about tzitzit hired a prostitute for 400 gold coins, but when he came to her, his tzitzit slapped his face, preventing him from sinning. The woman was so impressed that she converted, and the story illustrates the reward for tzitzit in this world.

items.text: Rav Yehuda on a borrowed tallit and a baraita on mezuzah
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda on a borrowed tallit and a baraita on mezuzah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that a borrowed tallit is exempt from tzitzit for 30 days, then obligated. A baraita supports this with a parallel law about mezuzah for a rented house, with an exception for Israel due to settlement.

items.text: Rav Chisda on tefillin not impeding each other
items.text_en: Rav Chisda on tefillin not impeding each other
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda clarifies that the rule that tefillin shel yad does not impede shel rosh applies only when one has both; if one lacks both, he must still perform the one he can. The Gemara explains his initial reasoning and retraction.

items.text: Rav Sheshet and Resh Lakish on positive commandments
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet and Resh Lakish on positive commandments
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet lists the number of positive commandments one violates by neglecting tefillin (8), tzitzit (5), priestly blessing (3), and mezuzah (2). Resh Lakish adds that one who wears tefillin prolongs life.

items.text: Opening verse
items.text_en: Opening verse
items.desc_en: A biblical verse is cited as a preamble.

sub.desc_en: The opening verse from Isaiah is cited as a preamble to the sugya.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the meal-offering and oil do not impede the wine, nor does the wine impede them; similarly, the blood applications on the outer altar do not impede each other.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the meal-offering and oil do not impede the wine, nor does the wine impede them, and the blood applications on the outer altar do not impede each other.

items.text: Gemara: Order of meal-offering and libations
items.text_en: Gemara: Order of meal-offering and libations
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether the meal-offering precedes libations or vice versa, based on verses. The Sages and Rabbi hold different positions, with the dispute limited to offerings brought independently, not with a sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וּמִנְחָתָם וְנִסְכֵּיהֶם' (their meal-offering and their libations) to teach that the meal-offering precedes the libations.
Rabbi cites the verse 'זֶבַח וּנְסָכִים' (sacrifice and libations) to argue that the sacrifice precedes the libations, implying a different order.
The Gemara asks: how does Rabbi reconcile his position with the verse 'וּמִנְחָתָם וְנִסְכֵּיהֶם' that seems to prioritize the meal-offering?
The Gemara explains that Rabbi interprets the verse 'וּמִנְחָתָם וְנִסְכֵּיהֶם' to teach that the meal-offering and libations may be brought at night or even the next day, not to establish order.
The Gemara asks: how do the Sages (רבנן) reconcile their position with the verse 'זֶבַח וּנְסָכִים' that seems to prioritize the sacrifice?
The Gemara explains that the Sages interpret the verse 'זֶבַח וּנְסָכִים' to teach Ze'iri's principle: libations become sanctified only through the slaughter of the sacrifice, not to establish order.
The Gemara objects: Rabbi could also use the verse for Ze'iri's principle, and the Sages could also use it for the night/day teaching, so the dispute remains unresolved.
The Gemara resolves: the Sages derive the order from the verse 'עֹלָה וּמִנְחָה' (burnt-offering and meal-offering), but the Gemara questions whether Rabbi also has this verse.
The Gemara concludes: when offerings come with a sacrifice, all agree that the meal-offering precedes libations based on 'עֹלָה וּמִנְחָה'; the dispute is only about offerings brought independently.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi holds that for offerings brought with a sacrifice, the order follows the eating process, but for independent offerings, libations take precedence because song is recited over them.

items.text: Mishnah restatement
items.text_en: Mishnah restatement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's ruling about blood applications on the outer altar is repeated.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah restates that the blood applications on the outer altar do not impede each other.

items.text: Baraita: One application suffices
items.text_en: Baraita: One application suffices
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from a verse that all offerings placed on the outer altar can be atoned for with a single application.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking for the scriptural source that a single application of blood on the outer altar suffices for atonement.

The baraita cites the verse 'וְדַם זְבָחֶיךָ יִשָּׁפֵךְ עַל מִזְבַּח ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ' (the blood of your offerings shall be poured out on the altar of the Lord your God) as the proof that one application is sufficient.

items.text: Mishnah: Animals do not impede each other
items.text_en: Mishnah: Animals do not impede each other
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that different types of animal offerings do not impede each other; Rabbi Shimon adds a caveat about bringing libations with at least one bull.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that different types of animal offerings (bulls, rams, lambs, goats) do not impede each other.
Rabbi Shimon adds a caveat: if they have many bulls but no libations, they should bring one bull with libations rather than offering all without libations.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the offerings
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which offerings are referred to, concluding they are those of Rosh Chodesh and Shavuot from the book of Numbers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which category of bulls and rams is discussed in the Mishnah, initially suggesting those of the festival of Sukkot, but noting that the Torah explicitly prescribes their libations there.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to the bulls, rams, and lambs of Rosh Chodesh and Shavuot as listed in the book of Numbers (Homesh HaPekudim), where libations are not specified for each individual animal.

items.text: Clarifying which rams are meant and whether they are mutually indispensable
items.text_en: Clarifying which rams are meant and whether they are mutually indispensable
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which rams are referred to in a prior statement, distinguishing between the rams of the Torah portion and those of the festival of Shavuot in Torat Kohanim. It concludes that neither set of rams is indispensable for the other, but the bulls mentioned are indispensable for each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which rams are being discussed, distinguishing between those of the Torah portion and those of the festival of Shavuot in Torat Kohanim.
The Gemara answers that the rams are those of Torat Kohanim, and explains that neither set of rams is indispensable for the other.
The Gemara concludes that the bulls are mutually indispensable, while the rams from both contexts are not.

items.text: The Tanna teaches items separately
items.text_en: The Tanna teaches items separately
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Tanna lists items separately, implying that each is a distinct teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Tanna teaches items separately, implying they are not mutually indispensable.

items.text: Deriving the law of reduced offerings from the verses in Ezekiel
items.text_en: Deriving the law of reduced offerings from the verses in Ezekiel
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the verse in Ezekiel about the new moon offering, deriving that if one cannot find two bulls, he brings one; similarly, if he cannot find seven lambs, he brings six, and so on down to one. The word 'יִהְיוּ' teaches that the rams in Torat Kohanim are indispensable for each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about the new moon offering and asks why the singular 'פַּר' (bull) is used.
The Gemara answers that the singular form teaches that if one cannot find two bulls, he may bring one.
The Gemara asks why the verse specifies six lambs instead of the usual seven, and answers that it teaches if one cannot find seven, he brings six.
The Gemara derives from another verse that one may progressively reduce the number of lambs down to one.
The Gemara resolves that the specification of six lambs teaches that we should seek as many as possible.
The Gemara derives from the word 'יִהְיוּ' that the rams of Torat Kohanim are mutually indispensable.

items.text: The contradiction in Ezekiel's purification offering and the resolution
items.text_en: The contradiction in Ezekiel's purification offering and the resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Ezekiel calls a burnt offering a 'chatat' (sin offering). Rabbi Yochanan says Elijah will resolve this. Rav Ashi and a baraita with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei explain that in Ezra's time they offered miluim (inaugural offerings) as in Moses' time, resolving the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Ezekiel's verse calling a burnt offering a 'chatat' (sin offering) and questions the contradiction.
Rabbi Yochanan says that Elijah the prophet will resolve this contradiction in the future.
Rav Ashi explains that the offering in Ezekiel was a miluim (inaugural offering) like in Moses' time, not a regular sin offering.

sub.text: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Ashi: Rabbi Yehuda says Elijah will resolve it, but Rabbi Yosei says they offered miluim in Ezra's time, and Rabbi Yehuda concedes.

items.text: The prohibition of neveilah and tereifah for priests
items.text_en: The prohibition of neveilah and tereifah for priests
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse specifies that priests may not eat neveilah and tereifah, implying Israelites may. Rabbi Yochanan says Elijah will resolve this. Ravina explains that the verse is necessary to prevent a mistaken inference from the permissibility of melikah for priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse specifies that priests may not eat neveilah and tereifah, implying that Israelites may.
Rabbi Yochanan says that this verse's difficulty will be resolved by Elijah in the future.
Ravina explains that the verse is necessary to prevent a mistaken inference from the permissibility of melikah for priests.

items.text: Interpreting the seven in Ezekiel's verse
items.text_en: Interpreting the seven in Ezekiel's verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the 'seven' refers to seven tribes that sinned, even if not a majority. The word 'חֹדֶשׁ' indicates if they innovated and said fat is permitted, and 'מֵאִישׁ שֹׁגֶה וּמִפֶּתִי' teaches liability only for unwitting action with unawareness of the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'שִׁבְעָה' (seven) in the verse from Ezekiel.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'seven' refers to seven tribes that sinned, even though they were not a majority of the community.
The Gemara interprets 'חֹדֶשׁ' (month) as teaching that liability applies only when they innovated a permission and acted inadvertently.

items.text: Praise for Chanina ben Chizkiyah who reconciled Ezekiel with the Torah
items.text_en: Praise for Chanina ben Chizkiyah who reconciled Ezekiel with the Torah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav praises Chanina ben Chizkiyah, who, to prevent the book of Ezekiel from being hidden because it contradicted the Torah, sat in an upper chamber with 300 jugs of oil and expounded it, reconciling the contradictions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav praises Chanina ben Chizkiya, who reconciled the book of Ezekiel with the Torah by studying it with 300 jugs of oil.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's principle: bring one bull with its libations rather than many without
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's principle: bring one bull with its libations rather than many without
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that if they had many bulls but no libations, they should bring one bull with its libations rather than all without. The baraita elaborates on the verse about the ephah for the bull and ram, and the lamb according to what one can afford.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon begins a statement about many bulls without libations.
Rabbi Shimon questions whether the measure of bulls and rams is the same, based on a baraita.
Rabbi Shimon answers that if they had many bulls without libations, they should bring one bull with its libations rather than all without.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the bull, rams, lambs, and goat do not impede the loaves, nor do the loaves impede them. However, the loaves impede the lambs, but the lambs do not impede the loaves, according to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Shimon ben Nannas argues the opposite: the lambs impede the loaves, but the loaves do not impede the lambs, citing the precedent of the wilderness where lambs were offered without loaves. Rabbi Shimon rules in accordance with ben Nannas but offers a different reason.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the bull, rams, lambs, and goat do not impede the loaves, nor do the loaves impede them.
Rabbi Akiva states that the loaves impede the lambs, but the lambs do not impede the loaves.
Rabbi Shimon ben Nannas argues the opposite: the lambs impede the loaves, but the loaves do not impede the lambs, citing the precedent of the wilderness where lambs were offered without loaves.
Rabbi Shimon rules in accordance with ben Nannas but offers a different reason.
Rabbi Shimon explains that everything stated in the Book of Numbers was offered in the wilderness, while everything stated in Leviticus was not offered until they entered the land.
Rabbi Shimon concludes that lambs may be offered without loaves because the lambs permit themselves, but the loaves cannot be offered without lambs since they have no one to permit them.

items.text: Gemara's Opening Baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's Opening Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'and you shall offer upon the loaves' that the lambs are a duty upon the loaves, but they can be offered even without loaves. Rabbi Tarfon explains that the phrase 'upon the loaves' teaches that the obligation for lambs only came after the obligation for loaves.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse that the lambs are a duty upon the loaves but can be offered even without loaves.
Rabbi Tarfon explains that the phrase 'upon the loaves' teaches that the obligation for lambs only came after the obligation for loaves.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's Distinction and the Gemara's Analysis
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's Distinction and the Gemara's Analysis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva argues that the lambs mentioned in the Torah portion for Shavuot are different from those in the book of Numbers, as the bulls and rams differ. The Gemara questions this, suggesting that perhaps only the bulls and rams are different, but the lambs are the same. It then proves that the order of animals is changed, indicating they are different.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva proposes that the lambs mentioned in the Torah portion for Shavuot (Torat Kohanim) are different from those in the book of Numbers (Chomesh HaPekudim), just as the bulls and rams differ, with the former coming for their own sake and the latter for the sake of the bread.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Akiva's reasoning, suggesting that perhaps only the bulls and rams are different, but the lambs might be the same.
The Gemara answers that since the order of animals is changed (from bull and two rams to two bulls and one ram), it proves that the lambs are also different.

items.text: Hermeneutical Dispute: Gezerah Shavah
items.text_en: Hermeneutical Dispute: Gezerah Shavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning behind Rabbi Akiva and ben Nannas. Rabbi Akiva learns a gezerah shavah from 'yihyu' to 'tihyenah' (from the loaves), while ben Nannas learns from 'yihyu' to 'yihyu' (from the lambs). The Gemara questions why ben Nannas does not learn from 'tihyenah', and answers that one derives 'yihyu' from 'yihyu', not from 'tihyenah'. It then cites a principle from the school of Rabbi Yishmael about similar wording.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of Rabbi Akiva that the loaves prevent the sheep.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'יִהְיוּ' to 'תִּהְיֶינָה', concluding that just as there it refers to loaves, so too here it refers to loaves.
The Gemara explains that Ben Nannas derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'יִהְיוּ' to 'יִהְיוּ', concluding that just as there it refers to sheep, so too here it refers to sheep.
The Gemara objects that Ben Nannas should also learn from 'תִּהְיֶינָה', and answers that one derives 'יִהְיוּ' from 'יִהְיוּ', not from 'תִּהְיֶינָה'.
The Gemara cites a principle from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that when there is a similar term, one derives from it, but when there is no similar term, one may derive from a non-identical term.

The Gemara asks why Rabbi Akiva does not learn from 'יִהְיוּ' to 'יִהְיוּ', and answers that he prefers to derive a matter that is a gift to the priest from another matter that is a gift to the priest, excluding the burnt offerings.

items.text: Alternative Explanation: The Verse 'Kodesh Yihyu'
items.text_en: Alternative Explanation: The Verse 'Kodesh Yihyu'
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: they dispute the interpretation of the verse 'Kodesh yihyu laHashem lakohen'. Rabbi Akiva holds that it refers to something entirely for the priest, i.e., the loaves. Ben Nannas holds it refers to something partly for God and partly for the priest, i.e., the lambs. Rabbi Akiva counters that the verse does not say 'laHashem velakohen', but rather 'laHashem lakohen', as per Rav Huna, meaning God acquired it and gave it to the priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation: the dispute is about interpreting the verse 'קֹדֶשׁ יִהְיוּ לַה׳ לַכֹּהֵן' (they shall be holy to the Lord for the priest). Rabbi Akiva holds that it refers to something entirely for the priest, i.e., the loaves.

Ben Nannas argues that the verse does not say 'קֹדֶשׁ יִהְיוּ לַכֹּהֵן' (they shall be holy for the priest) but rather 'קֹדֶשׁ יִהְיוּ לַה׳ לַכֹּהֵן' (they shall be holy to the Lord for the priest), indicating something partially for God and partially for the priest, i.e., the lambs.

Rabbi Akiva counters that the verse does not say 'לַה׳ וְלַכֹּהֵן' (to the Lord and to the priest) but rather 'לַה׳ לַכֹּהֵן' (to the Lord for the priest), as per Rav Huna, meaning God acquired it and gave it to the priest.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's Statement
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's Statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan begins a statement that 'everyone agrees', but the text cuts off, likely indicating the start of a new discussion that continues on the next page.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan begins a statement that 'everyone agrees', but the text cuts off, indicating the start of a new discussion that continues on the next page.

items.text: Opening statement: definition of זיקה
items.text_en: Opening statement: definition of זיקה
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that once the bread and animal are bound together (הוזקו), they impede each other, and the binding act is slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines זיקה (binding) as the act of slaughter that binds the bread and animal together, such that they impede each other.

items.text: Ulla's question and the Gemara's deliberation
items.text_en: Ulla's question and the Gemara's deliberation
items.desc_en: Ulla asks whether waving also creates a binding. The Gemara attempts to resolve from Rabbi Yochanan's statement, but then questions whether Rabbi Yochanan was certain about slaughter and uncertain about waving, concluding with תיקו.

sub.desc_en: Ulla reports that the rabbis of the West (Eretz Yisrael) asked whether waving (תנופה) creates a binding (זיקה) between the animal and the bread, or not.
The Gemara proposes to resolve the question from Rabbi Yochanan's statement that slaughter creates a binding, implying that waving does not.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan's own position is uncertain: perhaps he was certain about slaughter but uncertain about waving.
The Gemara concludes with תיקו (teiku — the question stands unresolved).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Chanina's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Chanina's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Chanina challenges the idea that waving does not create a binding, citing that the verse 'קדש יהיו לה׳ לכהן' is written after waving, and that Ben Nannas and Rabbi Akiva dispute it. The Gemara responds that the verse refers to something ultimately for the priest, not the timing of the binding.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Chanina challenges Rav Huna bar Yehoshua by noting that the verse 'קדש יהיו לה׳ לכהן' is written after the waving, and that Ben Nannas and Rabbi Akiva dispute its implication.
The Gemara objects: according to your reasoning, the verse is written after waving and not after slaughter, but that does not prove waving creates a binding.
The Gemara resolves that the verse 'קדש יהיו לה׳ לכהן' refers to something ultimately for the priest, not the timing of the binding, and the same applies here.

items.text: Contradiction from the baraita about the thanksgiving offering
items.text_en: Contradiction from the baraita about the thanksgiving offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if slaughter creates a binding, then once slaughtered, the bread should be invalidated if lost or defiled, yet the baraita allows the blood to be sprinkled and the meat eaten. The Gemara resolves that the thanksgiving offering is different because the Torah calls it 'שלמים', and just as peace offerings are brought without bread, so too the thanksgiving offering can be brought without bread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if slaughter creates a binding (זיקה), then once slaughtered, the bread should be invalidated if lost or defiled, yet the baraita allows the blood to be sprinkled and the meat eaten.
The baraita details three cases (bread broken, taken out, or defiled) before and after slaughter, showing that after slaughter the offering proceeds despite the bread's invalidation.
The Gemara objects: if slaughter creates a binding, then once the bread is invalidated, the thanksgiving offering itself should be invalidated.

The Gemara resolves that the thanksgiving offering is different because the Torah calls it 'שלמים' (peace offerings), and just as peace offerings are brought without bread, so too the thanksgiving offering can be brought without bread.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's hypothetical conclusion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's hypothetical conclusion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya states that if waving creates a binding, then if the bread is lost, the offering is invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya states that if waving creates a binding (זיקה), then if the bread is lost, the offering is invalid.

items.text: Question about waving when lambs are lost
items.text_en: Question about waving when lambs are lost
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a case where the lambs are lost after the loaves and lambs were waved. It questions whether a replacement loaf requires waving, especially according to Rabbi Akiva who considers the loaf primary. The issue remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that if the lambs are lost, the bread is also lost, establishing the initial premise.
The Gemara raises a hypothetical: if waving does not create a binding connection, and the bread is lost after waving, does a replacement loaf require waving?
The Gemara clarifies that if the lambs are lost, the replacement bread certainly requires waving; the question is only when the bread itself is lost.
The Gemara specifies that according to Ben Nannas, who holds the lambs are primary, the question does not arise; the question is only according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds the bread is primary.
The Gemara presents the unresolved question: since the bread is primary, does it require waving, or since the lambs are its permitter, does it not? The question stands unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Why two lambs sanctify the loaves but other animals do not
items.text_en: Why two lambs sanctify the loaves but other animals do not
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rava why the two lambs sanctify and impede the loaves, while the seven lambs, bull, and rams do not. Rava answers because they are linked by waving. The Gemara compares to the todah offering and the ram of a nazirite, concluding that only the ram sanctifies the bread, as derived from a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rava: why do the two lambs sanctify the bread and impede it, while the seven lambs, bull, and rams do not sanctify or impede?
Rava answers: because they were bound together through waving.
Abaye objects: but the thanksgiving offering (תודה) was not bound through waving, yet it sanctifies and impedes!
The Gemara answers: it is like the thanksgiving offering — just as the thanksgiving offering is a peace-offering (שלמים), so too here the lambs are peace-offerings.
The Gemara objects: are they comparable? There (in the thanksgiving offering) there are no other sacrifices with it, but here there are other sacrifices — why don't they all sanctify?
The Gemara answers: it is like the ram of a nazirite — just as there, despite other sacrifices, only the peace-offering sanctifies, so too here it is no different.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse that the ram sanctifies the bread, and if slaughtered not for its sake, the bread is not sanctified.

items.text: Two loaves brought alone: waved, form marred, burned
items.text_en: Two loaves brought alone: waved, form marred, burned
items.desc_en: A baraita states that two loaves brought alone are waved, have their form marred, and are burned. The Gemara questions why they are not eaten immediately if for consumption, or burned immediately if for burning. Rabbah explains it is a decree lest lambs become available later and people mistakenly think the loaves can be eaten without lambs.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states: two loaves that come by themselves are waved, their form is marred, and they go out to be burned.
The Gemara asks: what is your position? If they are for eating, let them be eaten; if for burning, let them be burned immediately — why mar their form?
Rabbah answers: they are indeed for eating, but there is a decree lest lambs become available next year and people mistakenly think they can eat the bread without lambs.
Rabbah explains: they do not know that last year there were no lambs; they think the lambs permit the bread now.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda's testimony that loaves are for consumption
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda's testimony that loaves are for consumption
items.desc_en: Rabbah cites a mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda reports Ben Bukhri's testimony about priests who donate, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's response. The Gemara infers that the two loaves are for consumption because they are compared to bikurim, which are eaten.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda reports Ben Bukhri's testimony in Yavneh, and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's response about priests interpreting a verse for themselves.
The verse states that every priest's meal-offering is entirely burnt and not eaten, and the priests question how the omer, two loaves, and showbread can be eaten.
The Gemara asks: what case are these two loaves? If they come with the sacrifice, do not priests donate a thanksgiving offering and eat its bread?
The Gemara concludes: rather, they come by themselves, and the question 'how are they eaten' shows they are for eating.

items.text: Abaye and Rav Yosef's alternative explanations
items.text_en: Abaye and Rav Yosef's alternative explanations
items.desc_en: Abaye argues the loaves come with the sacrifice and are called minchah. Rav Yosef initially says they are for burning but delayed due to Yom Tov, then changes to a decree about future lambs. Abaye questions why they aren't burned after the time passes, and explains 'form marred' refers to the form of their offering.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that the two loaves always come with the sacrifice, and the objection from the תודה (thanksgiving offering) is resolved because the loaves of the תודה are not called 'מנחה' (meal-offering), whereas the two loaves are called 'מנחה' by the verse.
Rav Yosef initially says the loaves are intended for burning, but they are not burned immediately because sacred items are not burned on Yom Tov (a festival day).

Abaye objects that the case is not comparable: the loaves' mitzvah is to be burned, so they should be burned immediately, unlike the bull and goat of Yom Kippur whose burning is not their primary mitzvah.

Rav Yosef revises his answer: the loaves are kept to prevent a decree that people might mistakenly use them with future lambs; Abaye questions why they are not burned after the time passes, and Rav Yosef explains that 'form marred' refers to the form of their offering.

items.text: Rava's conclusion: loaves are for consumption, based on verse
items.text_en: Rava's conclusion: loaves are for consumption, based on verse
items.desc_en: Rava concludes the loaves are for consumption, citing a decree similar to Rabbah's but derived from a verse comparing the loaves to bikurim, which are eaten.

sub.desc_en: Rava says: they are for eating, and the decree is like Rabbah's but not for his reason — rather from a verse.
Rava proves from the verse that just as first fruits (ביכורים) come by themselves and are for eating, so too the two loaves come by themselves and are for eating.

items.text: Opening Tannaic dispute on sanctification of the loaves
items.text_en: Opening Tannaic dispute on sanctification of the loaves
items.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi holds that slaughter sanctifies the loaves, so if slaughter is proper but sprinkling is improper, the loaves are in an intermediate state; Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Simon holds that both slaughter and sprinkling must be proper for sanctification.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the general rule: the lambs of Shavuot sanctify the loaves only through slaughter.
The baraita gives the first case: if both slaughter and sprinkling are performed for their own sake, the loaves are sanctified.
The baraita gives the second case: if both slaughter and sprinkling are not for their own sake, the loaves are not sanctified.
Rabbi holds that when slaughter is proper but sprinkling is improper, the loaves are in an intermediate state — sanctified and not sanctified.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds that the loaves are never sanctified unless both slaughter and sprinkling are performed for their own sake.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the scriptural basis
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the scriptural basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for Rabbi's reasoning, citing a verse that links slaughter to the loaves. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon requires all actions from the verse 'ya'aseh'. The Gemara then refines the interpretation of the verse to support Rabbi's position, and introduces Rabbi Yochanan's principle that the loaves must exist at the time of slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi's position that slaughter alone sanctifies the loaves.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וְאֶת הָאַיִל יַעֲשֶׂה זֶבַח שְׁלָמִים לַה׳ עַל סַל הַמַּצּוֹת' to indicate that slaughter sanctifies the loaves.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon interprets the word 'יַעֲשֶׂה' to require all actions (slaughter and blood throwing) to be performed for the loaves to be sanctified.
The Gemara refines the interpretation: since the verse says 'יַעֲשֶׂה זֶבַח' (make a sacrifice) rather than 'זֶבַח יַעֲשֶׂה', it specifies that the action is done through slaughter alone.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon uses the word 'זֶבַח' for Rabbi Yochanan's principle that the loaves must exist at the time of slaughter.

items.text: Abaye and Rava interpret Rabbi's intermediate status
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava interpret Rabbi's intermediate status
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava dispute the meaning of 'kadosh ve'eino kadosh': Abaye says it is sanctified but not completely, Rava says it is sanctified but not permitted for consumption. The practical difference is whether redemption takes effect. The Gemara then notes that according to Abaye, there is no difference between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon regarding the loaves' status, except for disqualification by being taken outside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'sanctified but not sanctified' means in Rabbi's statement.
Abaye explains that the bread is sanctified but not completely sanctified (קדוש ואינו גמור).
Rava explains that the bread is sanctified but not permitted for consumption (קדוש ואינו ניתר).
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Abaye's and Rava's interpretations.
The Gemara explains that the difference is whether redemption takes effect: according to Abaye it does not, according to Rava it does.
The Gemara notes that according to Rava there is a clear difference between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, but asks what difference exists according to Abaye.
The Gemara answers that according to Abaye, the difference between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon is regarding disqualification by being taken outside (יוצא).

items.text: Inquiry about the loaves' permissibility and a related Tannaic dispute
items.text_en: Inquiry about the loaves' permissibility and a related Tannaic dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba about the loaves' permissibility when slaughter is proper but sprinkling is improper. The Gemara clarifies the question is according to a different Tanna, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva dispute whether the loaves become piggul when the lambs are slaughtered outside their time. Rav Sheshet explains that both Tannaim agree with Rabbi that slaughter sanctifies, but differ on whether sprinkling affects an object that left the Temple courtyard.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba about the permissibility of eating the loaves when the lambs were slaughtered properly but the blood was sprinkled improperly.
The Gemara objects that the question seems irrelevant according to both Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi, as each has a clear position on the matter.

The Gemara explains that the question is according to a different Tanna, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva dispute whether the loaves become piggul when the lambs are slaughtered outside their time after the loaves left the courtyard.
Rav Sheshet states that both Tannaim agree with Rabbi that slaughter sanctifies the loaves.
Rav Sheshet explains that Rabbi Eliezer holds that sprinkling does not affect an object that left the courtyard, while Rabbi Akiva holds that it does, resolving the dispute.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute about the limbs of lesser holy offerings that left the courtyard before blood sprinkling. Rabbi Eliezer holds that they are not subject to me'ilah or liability for piggul, notar, or tumah, while Rabbi Akiva holds that they are.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva regarding the limbs of lesser holy offerings that left the courtyard before blood sprinkling, with Rabbi Eliezer exempting them from me'ilah and liability for piggul, notar, and tumah, and Rabbi Akiva imposing liability.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does sprinkling affect limbs that left?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does sprinkling affect limbs that left?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the principle that piggul sprinkling establishes piggul for bread when the meat left applies also to a sprinkling not for its name, or whether such leniency is only for stringency, not leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the principle that piggul sprinkling establishes piggul for bread when the meat left applies also to a sprinkling not for its name, or whether such leniency is only for stringency, not leniency.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection: Alternative interpretation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection: Alternative interpretation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the premise, suggesting the dispute might be about limbs that left and were then brought back. Rabbi Eliezer follows Rabbi's view that slaughter sanctifies, so they become invalid by leaving; Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon that slaughter does not sanctify, so they are not invalidated.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects that the dispute might not be about limbs that are outside, but rather about limbs that left and were then brought back.

Rav Pappa explains that Rabbi Eliezer follows Rabbi's view that slaughter sanctifies, so the limbs become invalid by leaving; Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon that slaughter does not sanctify, so they are not invalidated.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Difficulty with Rabbi Akiva's position
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Difficulty with Rabbi Akiva's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if Rabbi Akiva held like Rabbi (slaughter sanctifies), his ruling is consistent. But if he held like Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon (slaughter does not sanctify), how could piggul sprinkling sanctify? This is supported by Rav Giddel's statement that piggul sprinkling does not bring about or remove me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi (slaughter sanctifies), his ruling is consistent; the slaughter sanctifies the limbs, and then the piggul sprinkling establishes piggul.
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon (slaughter does not sanctify), how could piggul sprinkling sanctify the limbs?

sub.text: Supporting statement of Rav Giddel citing Rav
sub.text_en: Supporting statement of Rav Giddel citing Rav
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Giddel's statement that piggul sprinkling neither brings about nor removes me'ilah, supporting the objection.

items.text: Explanation of Rav Giddel's statement
items.text_en: Explanation of Rav Giddel's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies: 'Does not bring to me'ilah' refers to limbs of lesser holy offerings; 'does not remove from me'ilah' refers to meat of most holy offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rav Giddel's statement: 'does not bring to me'ilah' refers to limbs of lesser holy offerings, and 'does not remove from me'ilah' refers to meat of most holy offerings.

items.text: Question: Was Rav Giddel refuted?
items.text_en: Question: Was Rav Giddel refuted?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav Giddel's statement was refuted, implying a challenge to its validity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav Giddel's statement was refuted, implying a challenge to its validity.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's inquiry about lost bread and sprinkling not for its name
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's inquiry about lost bread and sprinkling not for its name
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about the lambs of Shavuot whose bread was lost: can one sprinkle their blood not for their name to permit the meat? Rabbi Zeira initially rejects the idea, but after several counterexamples (Pesach before noon, Pesach after its time, Todah), he concedes, though Todah is distinguished because the Torah calls it 'shelamim'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether the lambs of Shavuot whose bread was lost can have their blood sprinkled not for their name to permit the meat.
Rabbi Zeira rejects the idea, asserting there is no case where an offering is unfit for its own name but fit for another name.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects with the counterexample of the Pesach offering before noon, which is unfit for its own name but fit for another name.
Rabbi Zeira refines his rejection: he asks for a case where the offering was initially fit for its own name, then became excluded, and is still unfit for its own name yet fit for another name.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects with the Pesach offering after its time but before noon on other days, which fits the refined description.
Rabbi Zeira further refines: he asks for a case where the offering was slaughtered for its own name, then became excluded, and is still unfit for its own name yet fit for another name.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects with the Todah offering, which fits the refined description.
The Gemara resolves that the Todah is different because the Torah calls it 'שלמים' (peace offerings), so it is not a valid counterexample.

items.text: Baraitha: Slaughtering two lambs on four loaves
items.text_en: Baraitha: Slaughtering two lambs on four loaves
items.desc_en: A Baraitha begins discussing a case where one slaughters two lambs on four loaves, and then pulls two loaves and waves them.

sub.desc_en: The Baraitha opens a case where one slaughters two lambs on four loaves, then pulls two loaves and waves them.

items.text: Question about redeeming inside the courtyard
items.text_en: Question about redeeming inside the courtyard
items.desc_en: The rabbis ask Rav Chisda about a Mishnah that says the remainder is eaten after redemption, noting this contradicts Rabbi's view that slaughter sanctifies. They question where the redemption occurs: outside would disqualify due to 'before the Lord', inside would bring unconsecrated animals into the courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis ask Rav Chisda how the Mishnah's statement that the remainder is eaten after redemption can align with Rabbi's view that slaughter sanctifies, since redemption outside would disqualify due to 'before the Lord' and redemption inside would bring unconsecrated animals into the courtyard.

items.text: Rav Chisda's answer
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda responds that the Mishnah can align with Rabbi's view: redemption occurs inside, and the unconsecrated status arises automatically without intentional entry.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda responds that the Mishnah can align with Rabbi's view: redemption occurs inside, and the unconsecrated status arises automatically without intentional entry.

items.text: Objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Ravina cites a baraita stating that redemption must be outside, which contradicts Rav Chisda's answer. He concludes the Mishnah must follow Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rav Ashi by citing a baraita that redemption must be performed outside the Temple courtyard, contradicting Rav Chisda's earlier answer that redemption could be inside.

Ravina concludes that the Mishnah must follow Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi, because if it followed Rabbi, the animals would have been disqualified as יוצא (taken outside the permitted area).

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava suggests this is a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan, who said that forty loaves from eighty do not become sanctified. Rabbi Zeira clarifies that all agree if one explicitly says 'let forty of eighty be sanctified', they are sanctified; similarly here one says 'let two of four be sanctified'.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava suggests that the case of the four lambs and two loaves constitutes a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan's view that forty loaves from eighty do not become sanctified.

Rabbi Zeira clarifies that all agree that if one explicitly says 'let forty of eighty be sanctified', they are sanctified; similarly here the owner says 'let two of four be sanctified', so the case does not refute Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: The principle 'sin to gain merit'
items.text_en: The principle 'sin to gain merit'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina of Tirata teaches before Rabbi Yochanan: if one slaughters four lambs for two loaves, he should withdraw two and sprinkle their blood not for their sake, otherwise the latter ones are lost. Rabbi Yochanan objects: we do not tell a person to sin to gain merit.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina of Tirata's teaching before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina of Tirata's teaching before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina of Tirata teaches before Rabbi Yochanan that if one slaughters four lambs for two loaves, he should withdraw two and sprinkle their blood not for their sake.
Rabbi Chanina explains that if you do not do this, you will lose the latter lambs.
Rabbi Yochanan objects: we do not tell a person to sin in order to gain merit.

items.text: Distinction between same and different types
items.text_en: Distinction between same and different types
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions from a Mishnah about limbs of a sin-offering mixed with a burnt-offering: Rabbi Eliezer says place them above, the Sages say let them rot. Why not say 'sin to gain merit'? The answer: we say it for sin-offering to gain sin-offering, but not for sin-offering to gain burnt-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where limbs of a sin-offering (חטאת) are mixed with limbs of a burnt-offering (עולה), and Rabbi Eliezer says to place them above, while the Sages say to let them rot, and asks why we do not apply the principle 'stand and sin to gain merit' (עמוד וחטא בשביל שתזכה) to permit offering them.

The Gemara answers that the principle 'stand and sin to gain merit' applies only when the sin and the merit are of the same type (sin-offering to gain sin-offering), but not when they are of different types (sin-offering to gain burnt-offering).

items.text: Distinction between Sabbath and weekday
items.text_en: Distinction between Sabbath and weekday
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions from a baraita about lambs of Shavuot slaughtered not for their sake or at the wrong time: the blood is sprinkled and the meat eaten, but on Shabbat one should not sprinkle. Why not say 'sin to gain merit'? The answer: we say it for Sabbath to gain Sabbath, but not for Sabbath to gain weekday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that one may say 'sin to gain merit' only within the same category, citing a baraita about Shavuot lambs slaughtered improperly where the blood is sprinkled and meat eaten.
The baraita adds that on Shabbat one should not sprinkle the blood, but if sprinkled, the sacrificial portions may be offered in the evening.
The Gemara asks why the baraita prohibits sprinkling on Shabbat, since one could say 'sin to gain merit' by violating Shabbat to enable the offering.
The Gemara answers that the principle 'sin to gain merit' applies only when the gain is in the same category (Shabbat for Shabbat), not when violating Shabbat to gain a weekday offering.

items.text: Distinction between two matters
items.text_en: Distinction between two matters
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions from a Mishnah about a barrel of terumah broken in an upper vat with impure hullin below: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree that if one can save a quarter-log in purity he should. The Gemara begins to cite the continuation, implying the principle does not apply across two different matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that one does not say 'sin to gain merit' across two different matters by citing a Mishnah about a barrel of תרומה (priestly portion) broken above an upper vat with impure חולין (non-sacred produce) below.
The Mishnah states that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree that if one can save a quarter-log of the תרומה in purity he should, implying the principle does not apply across two different matters.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a firstborn animal falls into a pit, it should be left to become impure rather than being deliberately defiled by hand; Rabbi Yehoshua permits deliberate defilement.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a firstborn animal falls into a pit, it should be left to become impure rather than being deliberately defiled by hand; Rabbi Yehoshua permits deliberate defilement.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case is different because the animal is destined for impurity anyway.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case is different because the animal is destined for impurity anyway.

items.text: Rav Yitzchak's baraita on sheep of Atzeret
items.text_en: Rav Yitzchak's baraita on sheep of Atzeret
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak teaches a baraita: sheep of Atzeret slaughtered not according to their requirement are invalid, their form must be marred, and they go to the place of burning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak teaches a baraita that sheep of Atzeret slaughtered not according to their requirement are invalid, their form must be marred, and they go to the place of burning.

items.text: Rav Nachman's analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the one who compares these to a sin-offering teaches they are invalid, while the school of Levi, who derives obligatory peace-offerings from voluntary ones, teaches they are valid. Levi's baraita states that other peace-offerings of a nazirite slaughtered not according to their requirement are valid but do not fulfill the obligation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the Tanna who compares these offerings to a sin-offering (חטאת) rules them invalid.

Rav Nachman contrasts the school of Levi, who derive obligatory peace-offerings (שלמי חובה) from voluntary ones (שלמי נדבה), and thus rule them valid, citing Levi's baraita about other peace-offerings of a nazirite.

items.text: Objection from a baraita on asham and olah
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita on asham and olah
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: an asham of the wrong age is invalid, but olot of nazirite, yoledet, and metzora that were two years old are valid. The general rule: whatever is valid for a voluntary olah is valid for an obligatory olah, and whatever is invalid for a sin-offering is invalid for an asham, except for offerings not offered for their proper sake.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: an asham brought at the wrong age is invalid and must be burned.
The baraita continues: olot of nazirite, yoledet, and metzora that were two years old are valid.

The baraita states a general rule: whatever is valid for a voluntary olah is valid for an obligatory olah, and whatever is invalid for a sin-offering is invalid for an asham, except for offerings not offered for their proper sake.

items.text: Identification of the baraita's author
items.text_en: Identification of the baraita's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that this baraita is from the school of Levi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the baraita in question is from the school of Levi.

items.text: Further challenge and resolution by Rav Shimi bar Ashi
items.text_en: Further challenge and resolution by Rav Shimi bar Ashi
items.desc_en: A baraita of Levi is cited: asham of nazirite and metzora slaughtered not for their sake are valid but do not fulfill the obligation; if slaughtered before their time or at the wrong age, they are invalid. The Gemara questions why we don't derive from peace-offerings, and Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers that we derive something not in its proper form from something not in its proper form, but not from something in its proper form.

sub.desc_en: A baraita of Levi is cited: an asham of a nazirite and an asham of a metzora slaughtered not for their sake are valid but do not fulfill the obligation.
The baraita continues: if these asham offerings were slaughtered before their proper time or at the wrong age, they are invalid.
The Gemara questions why we do not derive the law of asham from peace-offerings, and answers that peace-offerings are derived from peace-offerings, but asham is not derived from peace-offerings.
The Gemara further questions why we do not derive asham from asham, i.e., the asham of nazirite and metzora from the asham of robbery and the asham of misuse, or vice versa.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi resolves: we derive something not in its proper form from something not in its proper form, but not from something in its proper form.

items.text: Counter-challenge from a baraita on yotzei
items.text_en: Counter-challenge from a baraita on yotzei
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Shimi's principle with a baraita that derives the law of yotzei (an animal that left the Temple courtyard) from a bamah, where it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Shimi's principle by citing a baraita that derives the law of יוֹצֵא (an animal that left the Temple courtyard) from a בָּמָה (private altar), where it is valid, implying that a rule can be learned from a case that is not in its proper context.

items.text: Opening exposition: the verse that teaches intention for sacrifices
items.text_en: Opening exposition: the verse that teaches intention for sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that derives from the verse 'This is the law of the burnt-offering' that intention (shem) is required for sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that derives from the verse 'This is the law of the burnt-offering' that intention (shem) is required for sacrifices.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah about mistaken intent
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah about mistaken intent
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah taught that lambs of Atzeret slaughtered as rams are valid but do not fulfill the owners' obligation. Rav disagreed, saying they do fulfill the obligation. Rav Chisda explains that Rav's ruling applies only when the slaughterer thought they were rams but slaughtered them as lambs, but not when they thought they were rams and slaughtered them as rams, because that would be a mistaken uprooting. Rabbah holds that a mistaken uprooting is not considered an uprooting.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah taught before Rav that lambs of Atzeret slaughtered for the sake of rams are valid but do not fulfill the owners' obligation.
Rav disagreed, asserting that the lambs do fulfill the owners' obligation.
Rav Chisda explains that Rav's ruling applies only when the slaughterer thought they were rams but slaughtered them as lambs, since they were actually slaughtered for the sake of lambs.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's distinction and Rabbah's position
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's distinction and Rabbah's position
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda distinguishes that if they thought they were rams and slaughtered them as rams, it is a mistaken uprooting, which Rav considers an uprooting, but Rabbah holds that a mistaken uprooting is not an uprooting.

items.text: Challenge from piggul in the Temple
items.text_en: Challenge from piggul in the Temple
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the principle by citing a baraita about priests who committed piggul in the Temple: if they did so intentionally they are liable, but if unintentionally they are exempt, yet the piggul is still piggul. The Gemara analyzes the case: if the priest knew it was a sin-offering but thought about it as a peace-offering, that is intentional. So it must be that he thought it was a peace-offering and thought about it as a peace-offering, proving that a mistaken uprooting is an uprooting.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges the principle by citing a baraita about priests who committed piggul in the Temple: if intentional they are liable, if unintentional they are exempt, yet the piggul is still piggul.
The Gemara analyzes the case: if the priest knew it was a sin-offering but thought about it as a peace-offering, that is intentional, not unintentional.
The Gemara concludes that the case must be where the priest mistakenly thought it was a peace-offering and thought about it as a peace-offering, proving that a mistaken uprooting is an uprooting.

items.text: Abaye's answer: the case of 'permitted'
items.text_en: Abaye's answer: the case of 'permitted'
items.desc_en: Abaye rejects the proof, explaining that the case is where the priest knew it was a sin-offering but thought about it as a peace-offering, and he said 'permitted' (meaning he thought the sacrifice was permitted for that purpose).

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the case is where the priest knew it was a sin-offering but thought it was permitted to sacrifice it for a different purpose, so the error is not about the identity of the sacrifice but about its permissibility.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Shimon's ruling on meal-offerings
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Shimon's ruling on meal-offerings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges with Rabbi Shimon's ruling that all meal-offerings whose handful was taken not for their name are valid and fulfill the owners' obligation, because the actions of the meal-offering (e.g., baking) reveal its type. The Gemara analyzes: if the priest knew it was a griddle-cake but took the handful as a deep-pan cake, the actions reveal it, so why is it valid? It must be that he thought it was a deep-pan cake, proving that a mistaken uprooting is an uprooting.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges by citing Rabbi Shimon's ruling that all meal-offerings whose handful was taken not for their name are valid and fulfill the owners' obligation, because the actions of the meal-offering reveal its type, unlike animal sacrifices where all actions are uniform.
The Gemara asks: if the priest knew it was a griddle-cake but took the handful as a deep-pan cake, what do the actions prove? He has clearly uprooted the offering!
The Gemara concludes: it must be that he thought it was a deep-pan cake, proving that a mistaken uprooting (עקירה בטעות) is considered an uprooting.

items.text: Abaye's answer: Rava's principle of recognizable intent
items.text_en: Abaye's answer: Rava's principle of recognizable intent
items.desc_en: Abaye again rejects the proof, explaining that the case is where the priest knew it was a griddle-cake but took the handful as a deep-pan cake, and Rava holds that an unrecognizable intent (one that does not manifest in the action) is invalid, but a recognizable intent is valid, so the actions reveal the intent and the offering is valid.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the case is where the priest knew it was a griddle-cake but took the handful as a deep-pan cake, and Rava holds that an unrecognizable intent is invalid but a recognizable intent is valid, so the offering is valid.

items.text: Mishnah: The order of daily and additional offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: The order of daily and additional offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the daily offerings (temidin) do not prevent the additional offerings (musafin), and vice versa, and additional offerings do not prevent each other. If the morning lamb was not offered, it can be offered in the afternoon. Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between cases of duress or error versus intentional neglect. The same applies to the incense and the consecration of the vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the daily offerings (תמידין) do not prevent the additional offerings (מוספין), and vice versa, and additional offerings do not prevent each other; if the morning lamb was not offered, it can be offered in the afternoon.

Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between cases of duress or error (אונסין או שוגגין) and intentional neglect (מזידין), ruling that only in the former may the missed morning lamb be offered in the afternoon.
