items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that communal peace offerings require waving after slaughter with the breast and thigh, while Rabbi says they are waved as they are (whole). Rav Chisda explains the dispute: the Sages derive from individual peace offerings that both the requirement of waving after slaughter and the parts (breast and thigh) apply, while Rabbi derives only the requirement of waving after slaughter but not the parts, so they are waved whole.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the dispute: Rabbi says communal peace offerings require waving after slaughter and are waved whole, while the Sages say they require waving with the breast and thigh.
The gemara asks: what is the basis of their dispute?

Rav Chisda (or Rav Hamnuna) explains that they dispute the hermeneutical principle of 'דון מינה ומינה' (derive from it and apply the same) versus 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה' (derive from it but leave it in its place).

The Sages apply 'דון מינה ומינה' (derive from it and apply the same): from individual peace offerings they derive both the requirement of waving after slaughter and the parts (breast and thigh), so communal peace offerings also require waving with breast and thigh.

Rabbi applies 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה' (derive from it but leave it in its place): from individual peace offerings he derives only the requirement of waving after slaughter, but leaves the parts in their original context, so communal peace offerings are waved whole, as they are in life.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Ravina's dispute on the underlying principle
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Ravina's dispute on the underlying principle
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa holds that all agree the debate is about deriving from the same source (minnah u-minnah), while Ravina holds that all agree it is about establishing the law in its place (minnah v'okei b'atreh). They explain the reasoning of Rabbi and the Rabbis respectively.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that all agree the debate is about deriving from the same source (מִינַּהּ וּמִינַּהּ), and explains Rabbi's reasoning by analogy to the wave-offering of the leper's guilt-offering.

Ravina counters that all agree the debate is about establishing the law in its place (מִינַּהּ וְאוֹקֵי בְאַתְרַהּ), and explains the Rabbis' reasoning that the word 'שַׁלְמֵיהֶם' is a ריבוי (amplification) to include communal peace-offerings.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's list of three types of offerings and their required rites
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's list of three types of offerings and their required rites
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that three types of offerings require three rites each, with two rites common to all and one missing in each: individual peace-offerings require semikhah alive and tenufah slaughtered; communal peace-offerings require tenufah alive and slaughtered; the guilt-offering of a metzora requires semikhah and tenufah alive.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon opens by stating that three types of offerings require three rites each, with two rites common to all and one missing in each, listing the three types: individual peace-offerings, communal peace-offerings, and the guilt-offering of a metzora.

Rabbi Shimon details the specific rites for each offering: individual peace-offerings require semikhah alive and tenufah slaughtered, communal peace-offerings require tenufah alive and slaughtered, and the guilt-offering of a metzora requires semikhah and tenufah alive.

items.text: A fortiori argument for tenufah alive on individual peace-offerings and its exclusion
items.text_en: A fortiori argument for tenufah alive on individual peace-offerings and its exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that individual peace-offerings should require tenufah alive by a fortiori from communal peace-offerings. The Torah excludes this by the words 'you' and 'them' (אַתֶּם, אוֹתָם) to exclude individual peace-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that individual peace-offerings should require tenufah alive by a fortiori from communal peace-offerings.
The Torah excludes individual peace-offerings from tenufah alive by the words 'אַתֶּם' (you) and 'אוֹתָם' (them).

items.text: A fortiori argument for semikhah on communal peace-offerings and Ravina's tradition
items.text_en: A fortiori argument for semikhah on communal peace-offerings and Ravina's tradition
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that communal peace-offerings should require semikhah by a fortiori from individual peace-offerings. Ravina responds with a tradition that there are only two semikhahs in the community (i.e., on the communal sin-offering and guilt-offering, not on peace-offerings).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) that communal peace-offerings should require סמיכה (laying of hands) because individual peace-offerings, which lack תנופה (waving) while alive, require סמיכה, so communal peace-offerings, which have תנופה alive, should certainly require סמיכה.

Ravina responds with a received tradition (גמירי) that there are only two סמיכות (laying of hands) in communal offerings — on the communal sin-offering and guilt-offering — thus excluding communal peace-offerings from the requirement.

items.text: A fortiori argument for tenufah slaughtered on the guilt-offering of a metzora and its exclusion
items.text_en: A fortiori argument for tenufah slaughtered on the guilt-offering of a metzora and its exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the guilt-offering of a metzora should require tenufah slaughtered by a fortiori from individual peace-offerings. The Torah excludes this by the repeated word 'oto' (אֹתוֹ) to exclude the guilt-offering of a metzora.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) that the guilt-offering of a metzora should require tenufah slaughtered, since individual peace-offerings require it even though they lack tenufah alive.
The Torah excludes the guilt-offering of a metzora from tenufah slaughtered by the repeated word 'אֹתוֹ' (oto) written by individual peace-offerings.

items.text: Baraita on waving by proxy for multiple people
items.text_en: Baraita on waving by proxy for multiple people
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that when five people bring one offering, one person waves on behalf of all; for a woman, the priest waves on her behalf; similarly for one who sends his offerings from overseas, the priest waves on his behalf.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that when five people bring one offering, one person waves on behalf of all; for a woman, the priest waves on her behalf; similarly for one who sends his offerings from overseas, the priest waves on his behalf.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between Machavat and Marchevet
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between Machavat and Marchevet
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one vows to bring a minchah in a machavat, they may not bring it in a marchevet, and vice versa. Rabbi Yosei HaGlili distinguishes them by the presence of a cover, while Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel distinguishes by depth and texture of the baked goods.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that one who vows a minchah in a machavat cannot bring it in a marchevet, and vice versa, and presents two opinions distinguishing them: Rabbi Yosei HaGlili says the marchevet has a cover while the machavat does not; Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel says the marchevet is deep with soft products, the machavat is shallow with hard products.

items.text: Gemara's Analysis of Rabbi Yosei's Reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's Analysis of Rabbi Yosei's Reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the basis for Rabbi Yosei's distinction, suggesting etymological derivations from verses and common speech. It then proposes the opposite interpretation, but concludes that the tradition is received from Sinai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Yosei's reasoning, and proposes that the names 'מרחשת' and 'מחבת' derive from verses about heart-whispering and mouth-barking respectively.
The Gemara objects that the opposite derivation is equally plausible, associating 'מחבת' with heart-concealment and 'מרחשת' with lip-whispering.
The Gemara concludes that the distinction is not derived from verses but is a received tradition from Sinai (גְּמָרָא).

items.text: Support for Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel from Verses
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel from Verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses to support Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's definitions: 'marchevet' is deep (עֲמוּקָּה) from the verse 'and all that is made in the marchevet', and 'machavat' is shallow (צָפָה) from the verse 'and upon the machavat'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses to support Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's definitions: 'marchevet' is deep (עֲמוּקָּה) from the verse 'and all that is made in the marchevet', and 'machavat' is shallow (צָפָה) from the verse 'and upon the machavat'.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on Naming
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on Naming
items.desc_en: A baraita records that Beit Shammai says one who vows a 'marchevet' must leave the offering until Elijah comes, uncertain whether the name derives from the vessel or the method. Beit Hillel rules that the name derives from the vessel, citing a specific vessel in the Temple and a verse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Beit Shammai's ruling: one who vows a 'marchevet' must leave the offering until Elijah comes, because they are uncertain about the name's derivation.
The baraita explains Beit Shammai's uncertainty: whether the name 'marchevet' derives from the vessel or from the method of preparation.
Beit Hillel rules that the name derives from the vessel, describing a specific deep vessel in the Temple that resembles a deep 'kalbos' and produces apple-shaped loaves.
Beit Hillel cites the verse 'וכל נעשה במרחשת ועל מחבת' to prove that the names derive from the vessels, not from the methods.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows for Tanur and Minchat Ma'afeh
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows for Tanur and Minchat Ma'afeh
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one vows a minchah baked in a tanur, they may not bring it from a kuppach, re'afim, or Arab pots; Rabbi Yehuda permits kuppach. For a minchat ma'afeh, one may not bring half loaves and half wafers; Rabbi Shimon permits it as one offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who vows a minchah baked in a תנור (oven) may not bring it from a כופח (small oven), רעפים (tiles), or יורות הערביים (Arab pots).
Rabbi Yehuda permits bringing a minchah baked in a כופח (small oven) if one wishes.
The Mishnah rules that one who vows a minchat ma'afeh (baked meal-offering) may not bring half loaves and half wafers.
Rabbi Shimon permits mixing loaves and wafers because they constitute one offering.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation from Repetition of 'Tanur'
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation from Repetition of 'Tanur'
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon interpreting the double mention of 'tanur' in the Torah. Rabbi Yehuda uses it to validate kuppach; Rabbi Shimon requires both baking and consecration in a tanur. The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's consistency and Rava clarifies his intent.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the general rule that 'oven-baked' excludes kuppach, tile-baked, and Arab pot-baked.
Rabbi Yehuda interprets the double mention of 'tanur' to validate kuppach-baked offerings.
Rabbi Shimon interprets the double 'tanur' to require both baking in an oven and consecration in an oven.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon's position seems inconsistent with his ruling that the two loaves and showbread are valid even when baked outside the Temple courtyard.
Rava resolves the objection by clarifying that Rabbi Shimon only requires the consecration to be for the sake of an oven, not that the baking itself occur in an oven.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation for Minchat Ma'afeh
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation for Minchat Ma'afeh
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'When you offer a korban minchah' to teach that it is optional. Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'korban minchah' that one who vows a minchat ma'afeh may not bring half loaves and half wafers, as it is one offering. Rabbi Shimon responds.

sub.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'וְכִי תַּקְרִיב' (when you offer) to teach that the minchah offering is optional (רשות), not obligatory.

Rabbi Yehuda derives from the phrase 'קׇרְבַּן מִנְחָה' (a korban minchah) that one who vows a minchat ma'afeh may not bring half loaves and half wafers, because the singular 'korban' indicates one offering, not two or three.
Rabbi Shimon begins his response to Rabbi Yehuda, objecting to the derivation.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah's inference
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah's inference
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's derivation that one who vows a מנחת מאפה may bring half loaves and half wafers, arguing that the Torah only mentions one korban, not two. It concludes that one may bring either type or a mixture, and the kemitzah is taken from both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's inference, arguing that the Torah only mentions one korban (קרבן), not two, yet it includes both loaves and wafers.
The Gemara concludes that one may bring either loaves or wafers or a mixture, and the kemitzah (קמיצה) is taken from both types, and if the handful contains from one type it suffices for both.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda argues that one who vows a מנחת מאפה may not bring half loaves and half wafers, deriving from the repeated word 'וכל' in the verses that the two types must be distinct and separate.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda opens by asking the source that one who vows a מנחת מאפה (oven-baked meal offering) may not bring half loaves and half wafers, and cites three verses beginning with 'וכל' (and every) as the basis.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's conclusion
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's conclusion
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda resolves by arguing through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) that just as the later 'וכל' verses refer to two distinct types, so too the earlier 'וכל' in the context of מנחת מאפה requires two distinct types, forbidding a mixture.

items.text: Reconciliation of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Reconciliation of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda accepts Rabbi Shimon's view because the repetition of 'בשמן' is like the repetition of 'קרבן', allowing a mixture. Rabbi Shimon argues that without 'בשמן' twice, one might think only a mixture is valid, but the repetition teaches that pure loaves or wafers are also acceptable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda can accept Rabbi Shimon's view, given the apparent contradiction.
Rabbi Yehuda explains that the repetition of 'בשמן' (in oil) is analogous to the repetition of 'קרבן' (offering), allowing a mixture.
Rabbi Shimon argues that without the repetition of 'בשמן', one might think only a mixture is valid, but the repetition teaches that pure loaves or wafers are also acceptable.

items.text: Transition and conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Transition and conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position is identical to his father's, with a practical difference regarding one who already acted. The chapter concludes with 'הדרן עלך כל המנחות'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position is identical to his father's, and notes the practical difference lies in a case where one already acted.
The Gemara resolves that the difference between them is in the case of one who already acted, and then concludes the chapter with the standard closing formula.

items.text: Opening Mishnah of the new chapter: Omer dispute
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah of the new chapter: Omer dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says the Omer is brought from three se'ah on Shabbat and five on a weekday; the Sages say it is always from three. Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim adds details about the number of reapers, baskets, and sickles, with the Sages disagreeing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Yishmael's opinion that the omer (עומר) offering on Shabbat comes from three se'ahs (סאין) and on a weekday from five, while the Sages say it always comes from three.

The Mishnah continues with Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim's opinion that on Shabbat the omer is reaped by one person with one sickle and one basket, while on a weekday by three, and the Sages say it is always done by three.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yishmael's logic: if a choice tenth-ephah comes from five se'ah, it should apply on Shabbat too; if from three, on weekdays. Rava explains that Rabbi Yishmael holds that a choice tenth-ephah comes from five se'ah without extra effort, but on Shabbat it is better to increase one type of labor (sifting) rather than multiple labors.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages hold that a choice issaron (עשרון) comes from three se'ahs, and there is no difference between weekday and Shabbat.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning: if a choice issaron comes only from five, then even on Shabbat it should be from five; if from three, then even on a weekday it should be from three.

Rava answers that Rabbi Yishmael holds that a choice issaron comes from five without extra effort, but from three with effort; on a weekday we bring from five for quality, on Shabbat it is better to increase one type of labor (sifting) rather than many labors.

items.text: Parallel between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
items.text_en: Parallel between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
items.desc_en: Rabbah suggests that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka share the same principle: where possible, one avoids extra effort. The Gemara challenges this, noting that the latter's leniency regarding the Paschal sacrifice might be due to the absence of desecration of sacred objects, unlike the Omer case.

sub.desc_en: Rabba states that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka said the same thing, citing a baraita about the Passover sacrifice on Shabbat where the latter limits skinning to the chest.
The Gemara explains that just as Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka there said we do not exert effort where possible, so too here we do not exert effort where possible.

The Gemara objects: perhaps Rabbi Yishmael's ruling here is only because there is no degradation of sacred objects, but there (in the Passover case) there is degradation of sacred objects, so the parallel may not hold.

items.text: First attempt to align Rabbi Yishmael with the Rabbis
items.text_en: First attempt to align Rabbi Yishmael with the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yishmael might actually agree with the Rabbis, because his leniency only applies when there is a need for Heaven, but here there is no such need and Shabbat must be violated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yishmael might actually agree with the Rabbis, because his leniency only applies when there is a need for Heaven, but here there is no such need and Shabbat must be violated.

items.text: Rabba aligns Rabbi Yishmael with Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim
items.text_en: Rabba aligns Rabbi Yishmael with Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim
items.desc_en: Rabba argues that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim said the same thing: since it is possible to harvest with fewer people, we do not trouble to do more. This is based on a Mishnah where Rabbi Chanina allows harvesting on Shabbat with one person, one sickle, and one basket.

sub.desc_en: Rabba asserts that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim said the same thing, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Chanina permits harvesting on Shabbat with minimal equipment.
The Gemara infers that Rabbi Chanina's reasoning is that since it is possible to do less, we do not trouble to do more, and applies the same logic to Rabbi Yishmael's position.

items.text: Rejection of Rabba's alignment
items.text_en: Rejection of Rabba's alignment
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rabba's proof, suggesting that Rabbi Yishmael's leniency might be due to lack of publicity, while Rabbi Chanina's case involves publicity, so he might agree with the Rabbis. Alternatively, Rabbi Chanina's leniency is because the need of Heaven is fulfilled properly even with one, but here it is not fulfilled properly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yishmael's leniency might be due to lack of publicity, while Rabbi Chanina's case involves publicity, so he might agree with the Rabbis.

Alternatively, the Gemara objects that Rabbi Chanina's leniency is because the need of Heaven is fulfilled properly even with one, but here it is not fulfilled properly, so he might agree with the Rabbis.

items.text: Rav Ashi aligns Rabbi Yishmael with Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rav Ashi aligns Rabbi Yishmael with Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yosei said the same thing: since it is possible to avoid violating Shabbat, we do not trouble. This is based on a Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei says that if the new moon is seen clearly, we do not desecrate Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asserts that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yosei agree, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei rules that if the new moon is clearly seen, Shabbat is not desecrated.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei's principle is that since it is possible to avoid desecrating Shabbat, we do not trouble; the same applies to the omer offering.

items.text: Rejection of Rav Ashi's alignment
items.text_en: Rejection of Rav Ashi's alignment
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rav Ashi's proof, suggesting that Rabbi Yishmael's leniency is because there is no risk of causing future stumbling, while Rabbi Yosei's case involves such risk, so he might agree with the Rabbis. Alternatively, Rabbi Yosei's leniency is because there is no need of Heaven and Shabbat was not given to be violated, but here there is a need of Heaven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Ashi's comparison: Rabbi Yishmael's leniency in the omer case may be because there is no risk of causing future stumbling, but in the new moon case there is such a risk, so he might agree with the Rabbis.

Alternatively, the Gemara objects: Rabbi Yosei's leniency in the new moon case may be because there is no need of Heaven and Shabbat was not given to be violated, but in the omer case there is a need of Heaven, so he might agree with the Rabbis.

items.text: Rabba's ruling on slaughtering two communal sin-offerings
items.text_en: Rabba's ruling on slaughtering two communal sin-offerings
items.desc_en: It was stated: If one slaughtered two communal sin-offerings but only needed one, Rabba (or Rabbi Ami) says he is liable for the second and exempt for the first, even if the first was found to be blemished. This is challenged from another statement of Rabba where he rules differently based on the order of slaughter.

sub.desc_en: It was stated: If one slaughtered two communal sin-offerings but only needed one, Rabba (or Rabbi Ami) rules he is liable for the second and exempt for the first, even if the first was found to be gaunt.

The Gemara challenges: Did Rabba really say this? He elsewhere ruled that if one slaughtered a gaunt animal first and then a choice one, he is exempt, and they tell him to bring the choice one ab initio.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by suggesting either that the blemished animal was the first, or that the statement was actually said by Rabbi Ami, not Rabba.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by suggesting that the blemished animal was slaughtered first, making the later fat one a voluntary offering.
Alternatively, the Gemara resolves that the problematic statement was actually said by Rabbi Ami, not Rabba, thus removing the contradiction.

items.text: Ravina's question about intention vs. action
items.text_en: Ravina's question about intention vs. action
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: If the first offering was found blemished in the intestines, do we follow his intention (to sin) or his action? Rav Ashi compares this to a dispute between Rabba and Rava about a person who spread a net to catch fish but rescued a child, where Rabba follows the action and Rava follows the intention.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if the first offering was found blemished in the intestines, do we follow his intention (to sin) or his action?
Rav Ashi answers that this is the same dispute between Rabba and Rava about a person who spread a net to catch fish but rescued a child.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabba only exempts when he heard the child drowning, implying his mind was on the child, but not when he did not hear.
An alternative version states that Rav Ashi explicitly identified the dispute between Rabba and Rava: Rabba follows the action, Rava follows the intention.

items.text: Rabba's ruling on a sick person and Rava's question
items.text_en: Rabba's ruling on a sick person and Rava's question
items.desc_en: Rabba rules that if a sick person was assessed to need one fig, and ten people each brought one fig simultaneously, they are all exempt, even if he recovered after the first. Rava asks: if he needed two figs, and there are two figs on two stems and three on one stem, which do we bring? The Gemara concludes that we bring three to minimize harvesting.

sub.desc_en: Rabba rules that if a sick person was assessed to need one fig, and ten people each brought one fig simultaneously, they are all exempt, even if he recovered after the first.
Rava asks: if the sick person needed two figs, and there are two figs on two stems and three on one stem, which do we bring — two that are exactly needed, or three to minimize harvesting?
The Gemara concludes that we bring three figs to minimize the amount of harvesting.

items.text: Conclusion of previous sugya
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous sugya
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yishmael's position applies only when reducing consumption also reduces harvesting, but here reducing consumption increases harvesting, so three se'ah are brought.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yishmael's position applies only when reducing consumption also reduces harvesting, but here reducing consumption increases harvesting, so three se'ah are brought.

items.text: Mishnah: Omer from nearby fields
items.text_en: Mishnah: Omer from nearby fields
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the omer should be brought from the nearest field; if not yet ripe, it may be brought from anywhere. It recounts that the omer once came from Gaggot Tzerifin and the two loaves from the valley of Ein Sokher.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the mitzvah of the omer is to bring it from nearby, but if not available, from anywhere, and recounts a story of the omer coming from Gagot Tzerifin and the two loaves from the valley of Ein Sokher.

items.text: Gemara: Reasons for bringing from nearby
items.text_en: Gemara: Reasons for bringing from nearby
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the omer is brought from nearby, offering two answers: because of the verse 'karmel' (soft grain), and because one should not pass over mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the omer is brought from nearby.
One answer: because the verse uses the term 'כרמל' (soft grain), implying it must be from a place where grain is soft and fresh, i.e., nearby.
Another answer: because one should not pass over a mitzvah (i.e., one should bring from the nearest available source).

items.text: Story of the siege and the omer from Gaggot Tzerifin
items.text_en: Story of the siege and the omer from Gaggot Tzerifin
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the Hasmonean civil war: Hyrcanus outside, Aristobulus inside. An elder advised sending a pig instead of the daily sacrifice, causing the land to quake. The Sages then cursed pig-rearing and Greek wisdom, and the omer came from Gaggot Tzerifin.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the Hasmonean siege: Hyrcanus outside, Aristobulus inside, and daily they would lower coins and receive the daily sacrifice.
An elder knowledgeable in Greek wisdom advised the besiegers that as long as the daily sacrifice continues, they cannot be defeated; the next day they sent a pig instead of the sacrifice.
When the pig reached half the wall, it clawed into the wall and the land of Israel quaked for 400 parasangs.
At that hour the Sages cursed pig-rearing and Greek wisdom, and the mishnah records that the omer came from Gaggot Tzerifin and the two loaves from the valley of Ein Socher.

items.text: Finding the location of Gaggot Tzerifin and Ein Sokher
items.text_en: Finding the location of Gaggot Tzerifin and Ein Sokher
items.desc_en: When the omer was needed, they did not know where Gaggot Tzerifin was. A mute man gestured, and Mordechai deduced the name. Similarly for the two loaves, a mute man gestured, and Mordechai found Ein Sokher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that when the time came for the עומר (omer) offering, they did not know where to find it; a deaf-mute came and gestured with one hand toward a roof and one toward a hut.
מרדכי (Mordechai) asked if there is a place called 'גגות צריפין' (Gaggot Tzerifin) or 'צריפין גגות' (Tzerifin Gaggot); they checked and found it.

Similarly, when they needed to bring the שתי הלחם (two loaves), they did not know where to find the wheat; another deaf-mute came and gestured with one hand toward his eye and one toward a door latch.
מרדכי (Mordechai) asked if there is a place called 'עין סוכר' (Ein Sokher) or 'סוכר עין' (Sokher Ayin); they checked and found it.

items.text: Three women bringing offerings
items.text_en: Three women bringing offerings
items.desc_en: Three women brought pairs of birds, each saying a word: 'lizivati', 'liyammati', 'le'onati'. The Sages initially thought they referred to a zavah, the sea, and her time, requiring a sin-offering and burnt-offering. Mordechai suggested they meant 'sikhnah' (danger) in each case, so all were burnt-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces three women who each brought a pair of birds and stated a cryptic phrase: 'lizivati', 'liyammati', 'le'onati'.

The Sages initially interpret each phrase literally — 'zivati' as a actual זבה (zavah), 'yammati' as the sea, 'onati' as her time — concluding each woman owes one חטאת (sin-offering) and one עולה (burnt-offering).
Mordechai objects, suggesting each woman meant she was endangered — by a flow (זוב), at sea (ים), or through her eye (עין) — so all three pairs are burnt-offerings only.
The Sages investigated and confirmed Mordechai's interpretation was correct.

items.text: Petachyah's unique linguistic skill
items.text_en: Petachyah's unique linguistic skill
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Petachyah (identified as Mordechai) was called Petachyah because he could open and expound matters and knew seventy languages. It clarifies that all Sanhedrin members knew seventy languages, but Mordechai's uniqueness was that he could blend languages and expound, as written 'Bilshan'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishnah's identification of Petachyah as Mordechai and explains the name means he opens and expounds matters and knows seventy languages.
The Gemara objects that all Sanhedrin members knew seventy languages, citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Sanhedrin members must know seventy languages to avoid needing a translator.
The Gemara resolves that Mordechai's uniqueness was his ability to blend languages and expound, as written 'Bilshan'.

items.text: Mishnah: Procedure for harvesting the Omer
items.text_en: Mishnah: Procedure for harvesting the Omer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes how the court's agents go out before Yom Tov, bind the sheaves while still attached to the ground, and all nearby towns gather to harvest it with great fanfare. At nightfall, the agent asks about the sun, the sickle, and the basket, and on Shabbat asks about Shabbat, each time receiving affirmative answers, repeating three times, all to counter the Boethusians who denied that the Omer could be cut after Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing how the court's agents prepare the sheaves before Yom Tov and how all nearby towns gather to harvest the Omer with great fanfare.
The Mishnah details the repeated questioning about the sun, the sickle, and the basket, with affirmative responses, to ensure proper timing.
The Mishnah adds that on Shabbat the agent asks about Shabbat and receives permission to cut, with repeated affirmations.
The Mishnah explains that all this repetition is done to counter the Boethusians, who denied that the Omer could be cut after Yom Tov.

items.text: Gemara: Days when fasting and eulogizing are prohibited – the Tamid dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Days when fasting and eulogizing are prohibited – the Tamid dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing days when fasting and eulogizing are prohibited. From Rosh Chodesh Nisan until the eighth, the daily Tamid offering was established, because the Sadducees claimed an individual could donate and bring the Tamid. The Gemara explains the Sadducees' derivation from 'את הכבש האחד' and the Sages' counter-derivation from 'את קרבני לחמי' that all offerings must come from the Temple treasury.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists days when fasting and eulogizing are prohibited, specifying from Rosh Chodesh Nisan until the eighth as the period when the daily Tamid offering was established, prohibiting eulogizing.

The Gemara explains that the Sadducees argued an individual could donate and bring the daily Tamid, deriving this from the verse 'את הכבש האחד תעשה בבקר' (the one lamb you shall offer in the morning).

The Gemara explains that the Sages countered the Sadducees by deriving from the verse 'את קרבני לחמי לאישי תשמרו' (My offering, My food for My fires, you shall guard) that all offerings must come from the Temple treasury (תרומת הלשכה).

items.text: Gemara: The Shavuot dispute with the Boethusians
items.text_en: Gemara: The Shavuot dispute with the Boethusians
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues the baraita: from the eighth of Nisan until the end of the festival, the festival of Shavuot was established, because the Boethusians claimed Shavuot always falls after Shabbat. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai confronted them, calling them fools, and only one old man responded with a weak argument that Moses loved Israel and instituted Shavuot after Shabbat to give them two days of enjoyment. Rabban Yochanan refuted him with the verse about the eleven-day journey from Chorev.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that from the eighth of Nisan until the end of the festival, the festival of Shavuot was established as a day of no mourning, because the Boethusians claimed Shavuot always falls after Shabbat.

sub.text: Story of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai
sub.text_en: Story of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai
sub.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai confronted the Boethusians, called them fools, and refuted an old man's weak argument that Moses loved Israel and instituted Shavuot after Shabbat for two days of enjoyment, by citing the verse about the eleven-day journey from Chorev.

items.text: Opening anecdote: Moses' love for Israel
items.text_en: Opening anecdote: Moses' love for Israel
items.desc_en: A story is told where a heretic questions why Moses delayed Israel in the desert for forty years if he loved them. The rabbi responds sharply, then transitions to the main discussion about the verses of counting.

sub.desc_en: A heretic asks why Moses, if he loved Israel, delayed them in the desert for forty years.
The rabbi rebukes the heretic, asserting that the Torah's discussion is not like idle chatter.

items.text: Reconciling the two verses about counting
items.text_en: Reconciling the two verses about counting
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes two verses: one says 'count fifty days' and another says 'seven complete weeks'. It resolves the contradiction by explaining that one refers to when the festival falls on Shabbat, and the other when it falls during the week.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two verses: one says 'count fifty days' and the other says 'seven complete weeks'.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one verse applies when the festival falls on Shabbat, the other when it falls during the week.

items.text: Mnemonic for the Tannaic opinions
items.text_en: Mnemonic for the Tannaic opinions
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is provided listing the names of the rabbis and their associated actions: Rabbi Eliezer (sofer), Rabbi Yehoshua (moneh), Rabbi Yishmael (me'amer), Rabbi Yehuda (lematah).

sub.desc_en: A mnemonic lists the sages: Rabbi Eliezer (sofer), Rabbi Yehoshua (moneh), Rabbi Yishmael (me'amer), Rabbi Yehuda (lematah).

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion: counting depends on the court
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion: counting depends on the court
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that the verse 'count for yourself' indicates that counting is dependent on the court, which knows how to intercalate. 'The morrow of the Sabbath' means the morrow of the festival, excluding the weekly Sabbath whose counting is known to all.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer says no special counting is needed; counting depends on the court's knowledge of the new moon, and 'the day after Shabbat' means after the festival, excluding Shabbat Bereishit.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion: analogy to the new moon
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion: analogy to the new moon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua argues that just as the new moon is recognizable close to its arrival, so too Shavuot should be recognizable close to its arrival. If Shavuot always fell after the weekly Sabbath, it would not be recognizable from the preceding days.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua argues by analogy: just as the new moon is recognizable close to its arrival, so too Shavuot (עֲצֶרֶת) should be recognizable close to its arrival.
The gemara raises an objection: if Shavuot always fell after the weekly Sabbath, how would it be recognizable from the preceding days?

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's opinion: analogy to the Omer and Two Loaves
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's opinion: analogy to the Omer and Two Loaves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael argues that just as the Omer is brought on Passover, a festival and the beginning of the festival, so too the Two Loaves are brought on Shavuot, a festival and the beginning of the festival.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael argues that just as the Omer is brought at the beginning of Passover (a festival), so too the two loaves are brought at the beginning of Shavuot.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's opinion: gezerah shavah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's opinion: gezerah shavah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira uses a gezerah shavah: 'Sabbath' is stated above (in the Omer) and below (in the Two Loaves). Just as above it is a festival and the beginning of the festival adjacent to it, so too below it is a festival and the beginning of the festival adjacent to it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira uses a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'Shabbat' above and below to argue that Shavuot is a festival at the beginning of a festival period.

items.text: Baraita: individual counting and the meaning of 'morrow of the Sabbath'
items.text_en: Baraita: individual counting and the meaning of 'morrow of the Sabbath'
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that counting is for each individual. It then debates whether 'morrow of the Sabbath' means the morrow of the festival or the weekly Sabbath. Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda argues that if it meant the weekly Sabbath, the count would sometimes be 51, 52, etc., up to 56 days, contradicting the verse 'count fifty days'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by teaching that the verse 'וּסְפַרְתֶּם לָכֶם' (you shall count for yourselves) implies that counting the Omer is an individual obligation for each person.
The baraita poses a question: does 'מִמָּחֳרַת הַשַּׁבָּת' (the morrow of the Sabbath) refer to the morrow of the festival (Passover) or the morrow of the weekly Sabbath (שבת בראשית)?

Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda answers that 'מִמָּחֳרַת הַשַּׁבָּת' means the morrow of the festival, because if it meant the weekly Sabbath, the count would sometimes be 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, or 56 days, contradicting the verse 'תִּסְפְּרוּ חֲמִשִּׁים יוֹם' (you shall count fifty days).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's alternative argument
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's alternative argument
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira states that no further proof is needed, implying that his previous gezerah shavah is sufficient.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says no special counting is needed (the verse itself suffices).

items.text: Opening Tannaitic dispute on the counting of the Omer
items.text_en: Opening Tannaitic dispute on the counting of the Omer
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a Tanna who derives from the verse "תִּסְפׇּר לָךְ" that the counting of the Omer is dependent on the court, excluding the counting of the days of the week which is done by every individual.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma derives from the verse 'תִּסְפׇּר לָךְ' that the counting of the Omer is dependent on the court, excluding the counting of the days of the week which is done by every individual.

items.text: Rabbi Yose's interpretation of 'Shabbat'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose's interpretation of 'Shabbat'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose argues that 'מִמָּחֳרַת הַשַּׁבָּת' refers to the day after Yom Tov, not Shabbat Bereishit, using a kal vachomer and a gezerah shavah from the word 'Shabbat' used above.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose asserts that 'מִמָּחֳרַת הַשַּׁבָּת' (the day after the Sabbath) refers to the day after Yom Tov, and raises the alternative possibility that it might mean the day after Shabbat Bereishit.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yose's interpretation, noting that the verse does not specify 'the Sabbath within Passover', so one must determine which Sabbath is meant.

Rabbi Yose adds a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): the word 'שַׁבָּת' (Sabbath) used below (in the Omer verse) and above (in the context of the festival) both refer to a festival and the beginning of a festival.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's resolution of a contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's resolution of a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar resolves a contradiction between two verses about eating matzah: one says six days, the other seven. He explains that matzah from the new grain can be eaten for six days, but not seven.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar resolves the contradiction between the verses 'שֵׁשֶׁת יָמִים תֹּאכַל מַצּוֹת' and 'שִׁבְעַת יָמִים מַצּוֹת תֹּאכֵלוּ' by explaining that matzah from the new grain may be eaten for six days but not seven.

items.text: Derivation of the order of harvesting, counting, and bringing the Omer
items.text_en: Derivation of the order of harvesting, counting, and bringing the Omer
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that the Omer must be harvested, counted, and brought in a specific sequence: harvesting and counting can be at night, but the bringing must be during the day, and the counting must begin in the evening to have seven complete weeks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possible inference from the verse: perhaps one may harvest and bring the Omer, and count whenever he wishes.
The verse 'מֵהָחֵל חֶרְמֵשׁ' teaches that harvesting and counting must be linked, but this still leaves the bringing unconstrained.
The verse 'מִיּוֹם הֲבִיאֲכֶם' teaches that the bringing must also be tied to the counting, establishing a sequence.
The Gemara asks: perhaps all three actions—harvesting, counting, and bringing—must be done during the day?
The verse 'שֶׁבַע שַׁבָּתוֹת תְּמִימֹת' teaches that counting must begin in the evening to achieve seven complete weeks, so counting is at night.
The Gemara asks: perhaps harvesting and bringing can also be done at night?
The verse 'מִיּוֹם הֲבִיאֲכֶם' teaches that the bringing must be during the day, while harvesting and counting are at night.

items.text: Rava's analysis of the Tannaitic opinions
items.text_en: Rava's analysis of the Tannaitic opinions
items.desc_en: Rava states that all the earlier Tannaim have refutations except for the last two, Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira. The Gemara then examines each opinion, finding potential flaws in Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Yose, while confirming that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira are unrefuted.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that all the earlier Tannaim have refutations except for the last two, Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, in both the first and second Mishnah.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's opinion might be explained by Abaye's principle that one must count both days and weeks.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion might refer to the last day of the festival rather than the first.

sub.text: Gemara's confirmation of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.text_en: Gemara's confirmation of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.desc_en: The Gemara confirms that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira have no refutation.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda's opinion might mean fifty days excluding the six days of counting.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's opinion might refer to the last day of the festival rather than the first.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yose also saw a refutation, and that is why he said 'and furthermore' in his statement.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on counting days and weeks
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on counting days and weeks
items.desc_en: Abaye states that it is a mitzvah to count both the days and the weeks of the Omer. The Gemara notes that the Rabbis of the house of Rav Ashi counted both, while Ameimar counted only days, considering the counting of weeks as merely a remembrance of the Temple.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that it is a mitzvah (מצוה) to count both the days and the weeks of the Omer.

sub.text: Practice of the Rabbis of the house of Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Practice of the Rabbis of the house of Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: The Rabbis of the house of Rav Ashi practiced counting both days and weeks, supporting Abaye's ruling.
Ameimar counted only days, not weeks, contradicting Abaye's ruling.
Ameimar explains that counting weeks is merely a remembrance of the Temple (זכר למקדש), not a full obligation.

items.text: Mishnah: The process of preparing the Omer offering
items.text_en: Mishnah: The process of preparing the Omer offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for preparing the Omer: it is harvested, brought to the Temple courtyard, parched (according to Rabbi Meir) or beaten with reeds (according to the Sages), placed in a perforated tube, spread out, ground, and sifted. The remainder is redeemed and eaten, with a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages regarding its liability for challah and tithes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the initial steps of the Omer preparation: harvesting, bringing to the Temple courtyard, and parching with fire according to Rabbi Meir.
The Sages disagree with Rabbi Meir, stating that the grain is beaten with reeds and stalks to prevent crushing.
The Mishnah continues: the grain is placed in a perforated tube for even roasting, then spread in the courtyard for the wind to blow over it.
The Mishnah describes grinding, sifting through thirteen sieves, redeeming the remainder, and its exemption from tithes.
Rabbi Akiva disputes the exemption, ruling that the remainder is liable for both חלה (dough offering) and מעשרות (tithes).

items.text: Gemara: Source for parching the Omer
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for parching the Omer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraitha that derives from the verse 'אָבִיב קָלוּי בָּאֵשׁ' that the Omer must be parched, supporting Rabbi Meir's view, while the Sages disagree.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'אָבִיב קָלוּי בָּאֵשׁ' to teach that the Omer must be parched, supporting Rabbi Meir's view, while the Sages disagree.

items.text: Interpretation of 'ur' and 'kali'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'ur' and 'kali'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that 'ur' does not mean roasted but rather a different thing, and describes the perforated pipe used for roasting to ensure the fire reaches all parts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that 'אור' (ur) does not mean roasted but rather a different thing, and describes the perforated pipe used for roasting to ensure the fire reaches all parts.

items.text: Clarifying 'aviv kaluy' and 'geres'
items.text_en: Clarifying 'aviv kaluy' and 'geres'
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an ambiguity whether 'aviv kaluy' or 'geres kaluy' is intended, concluding that 'ba'esh' separates the subject.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an ambiguity whether the phrase 'aviv kaluy' or 'geres kaluy' is intended.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'ba'esh' separates the subject, indicating that 'aviv kaluy' is the correct reading.

items.text: Exegesis of 'karmel'
items.text_en: Exegesis of 'karmel'
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets 'karmel' as 'rakh u'mal' (tender and full), citing verses and a teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that it means 'kar maleh' (full heap).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by interpreting 'karmel' (כרמל) as 'rakh u'mal' (tender and full).
The Gemara cites three verses (from Kings, Proverbs, and Job) to support the interpretation of 'karmel' as tender and full.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that 'karmel' means 'kar maleh' (a full heap), providing an alternative exegesis.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's ruling on hallah and tithes
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's ruling on hallah and tithes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva obligates the omer grain in hallah and tithes, and Rav Kahana reports his reasoning that the drying process of consecrated grain does not exempt it.

sub.desc_en: The stam reports that Rabbi Akiva obligates the omer grain in hallah and tithes, and Rav Kahana explains Rabbi Akiva's reasoning: the drying process of consecrated grain (מֵירוּחַ הֶקְדֵּשׁ) does not exempt it from these obligations.

items.text: Challenge from the surplus omer
items.text_en: Challenge from the surplus omer
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishet challenges Rabbi Akiva's position from a baraita about the surplus omer, which is obligated in hallah but exempt from tithes, implying that consecration drying does exempt. The Gemara questions the counterargument.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet challenges Rabbi Akiva's position by citing a baraita about the surplus omer, which is obligated in hallah but exempt from tithes, implying that consecration drying does exempt.
The Gemara questions the counterargument: if consecration drying does not exempt, why did the sages offer a different proof? The very same issue is at stake.

items.text: Resolution by Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Resolution by Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana bar Tachlifa cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva obligates because the money was given only for their needs, not because drying doesn't exempt. Rabbi Yochanan affirms this as a well-established tradition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana bar Tachlifa objects to Rav Kahana bar Matitya by citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva obligates the remainder in חלה (ḥalla) and מעשרות (tithes) because the Temple money was given only for the needs of the offering, implying that consecrated grain would otherwise be exempt.

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the dispute by stating that it is a settled tradition in Rabbi Akiva's mouth that the Temple money was given only for the needs of the offering, so Rabbi Akiva's ruling is limited to that case and does not imply that smoothing consecrated grain generally fails to exempt from tithes.

items.text: Rava's clarification
items.text_en: Rava's clarification
items.desc_en: Rava states that it is obvious that the drying process of consecrated grain exempts, and even Rabbi Akiva only obligates there because the money was given for their needs, but generally drying exempts.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves that it is obvious that the drying process of consecrated grain exempts from tithes, and even Rabbi Akiva only obligates in the specific case where the money was given for their needs, but generally drying exempts.

items.text: Dispute about drying by a gentile
items.text_en: Dispute about drying by a gentile
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the issue of drying by a gentile is a tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, who allow terumah from various sources, and Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon, who restrict certain combinations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute about drying by a gentile as a tannaitic issue, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda permit terumah from various sources.
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon restrict the combinations for terumah, prohibiting certain cross-sources.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about the effect of consecration (hekdesh) on dough: if consecrated before kneading (gilgul) and then redeemed, it is liable; if consecrated after kneading, it is liable; but if consecrated before kneading and the treasurer kneads it, then it is redeemed, it is exempt because at the time of obligation it was exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah establishing that consecration (הקדש) after kneading (גלגול) exempts dough from חלה (the priestly portion), with specific cases of timing and redemption.

items.text: Rava's question about a non-Jew's kneading
items.text_en: Rava's question about a non-Jew's kneading
items.desc_en: Rava asks: does kneading by a non-Jew (gilgul goy) exempt the dough from challah? He cites a baraita: a convert who had dough before conversion is exempt, but if after conversion, liable; if uncertain, liable.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether kneading by a non-Jew (גילגול גוי) exempts the dough from the obligation of challah.
Rava cites a baraita about a convert's dough: if kneaded before conversion it is exempt, if after conversion it is liable, and if uncertain it is liable.

items.text: First interpretation: the baraita is unanimous
items.text_en: First interpretation: the baraita is unanimous
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the baraita reflects all opinions, even Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda who obligate in the case of a non-Jew's kneading elsewhere, but here they exempt. The reason is that the verse 'your dough' (עֲרִסֹתֵיכֶם) appears twice: one for your dough, and one to exclude non-Jews and consecrated dough. The earlier case (of a non-Jew's kneading) is derived from a different verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita about a non-Jew's kneading.
The Gemara answers that the baraita reflects all opinions, including Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda who obligate elsewhere but exempt here.

The Gemara explains that the earlier case of a non-Jew's kneading is derived from the double mention of 'דְּגָנְךָ' (your grain), which creates a מיעוט אחר מיעוט (a double exclusion that includes) even a non-Jew.
The Gemara resolves that here the verse 'עֲרִסֹתֵיכֶם' (your dough) appears twice: one for your dough, and one to exclude non-Jews and consecrated dough.

items.text: Alternative interpretation: the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation: the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: perhaps the baraita is taught by Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon, who exempt, but Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda learn a gezerah shavah from 'first' (רֵאשִׁית) to obligate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative interpretation: the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon who exempt, but Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda learn a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'first' (רֵאשִׁית) to obligate.

items.text: Rava's resolution and ruling
items.text_en: Rava's resolution and ruling
items.desc_en: Rava expresses a wish to see the answer in a dream, then concludes: one who says that a non-Jew's mere airing (meiruach) exempts, holds that kneading by a non-Jew exempts; one who says that a non-Jew's airing does not exempt, holds that kneading by a non-Jew does not exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rava expresses a wish to see the answer in a dream, then concludes that the ruling on a non-Jew's kneading (גלגול הגוי) follows the ruling on a non-Jew's mere airing (מירוח הגוי).

items.text: Objections from baraitot
items.text_en: Objections from baraitot
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Ravina object to Rava from baraitot: a non-Jew who separates challah or terumah is informed he is exempt, and his challah may be eaten by non-priests, but his terumah is forbidden. This implies that the tanna holds that a non-Jew's airing does not exempt, but his kneading does exempt. The Gemara notes the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects to Rava by citing a baraita: a non-Jew who separates פטר חמור (firstborn donkey) and חלה (challah) is informed he is exempt; his challah may be eaten by non-priests, and the donkey is shorn and worked.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that the tanna holds that a non-Jew's airing (מֵירוּחַ) does not exempt, but his kneading (גִּלְגּוּל) does exempt, contradicting Rava's position.

Ravina objects further with another baraita: a non-Jew's challah in the Land and his תרומה (priestly portion) outside the Land are exempt, but his תרומה in the Land is forbidden and imparts דמע (mixture prohibition).

sub.text: Gemara's inference from the second baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's inference from the second baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara again infers that this tanna holds that a non-Jew's airing does not exempt, but his kneading does exempt, reinforcing the contradiction to Rava.
The Gemara resolves that the prohibition on a non-Jew's תרומה is only מדרבנן (rabbinic), enacted as a גזירה (decree) to prevent abuse by wealthy owners (בעלי כיסים).

items.text: Resolution: the exemption is rabbinic
items.text_en: Resolution: the exemption is rabbinic
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: the exemption of a non-Jew's kneading is rabbinic (mid'rabbanan), a decree due to those who have money (ba'alei kisim).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the exemption of a non-Jew's kneading is rabbinic (mid'rabbanan), a decree due to those who have money (ba'alei kisim).

items.text: Gemara's challenge to the previous sugya
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to the previous sugya
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the leniency allowing a sick person to eat less than five quarters of flour applies also to terumah, suggesting that one could circumvent the prohibition by feeding it to an animal or bringing it in through roofs. It concludes that the public nature of the act makes it shameful, unlike the private case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the leniency for a sick person to eat less than five quarters of flour applies also to terumah, suggesting one could circumvent the prohibition by baking a small amount.
The Gemara proposes that for terumah one could use Rabbi Oshaya's method of bringing grain in its chaff to exempt it from tithes, or bring it through roofs and courtyards to avoid liability.

The Gemara resolves that in a public setting (like the marketplace) it is shameful to circumvent the law, but in private (like a sick person's home) it is not shameful, so the leniency applies only privately.

items.text: Mishnah: The procedure for the tenth of an ephah and the market after the Omer
items.text_en: Mishnah: The procedure for the tenth of an ephah and the market after the Omer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the process for the tenth of an ephah offering, and then records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about whether the practice of selling roasted grain in the Jerusalem market after the Omer was against or with the approval of the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for the tenth of an ephah offering: oil and frankincense are placed, pouring, mixing, waving, presenting, kemitzah (taking a handful), burning, and the remainder is eaten by the priests.
Rabbi Meir states that after the Omer was offered, the Jerusalem market was found full of roasted grain, but this was done against the Sages' will.
Rabbi Yehuda disputes Rabbi Meir, asserting that the practice of selling roasted grain in the market was done with the Sages' approval.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's positions
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda does not forbid selling roasted grain lest one eat from it before the Omer, and cites a contradiction from a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda requires checking for leaven multiple times, implying he is stringent. Rabba resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between new grain (chadash) and leaven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda does not forbid selling roasted grain (קלי) before the Omer, lest one eat from it prematurely.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda requires checking for leaven multiple times, implying he is stringent about potential violations.
Rabba resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between new grain (חדש) and leaven (חמץ), explaining that the concern for premature eating differs between the two.

items.text: Abaye's challenge from Beit HaSh'lachin
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge from Beit HaSh'lachin
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the earlier resolution that harvesting is permitted only through cutting (kituf), asking about grinding and sifting. The Gemara answers that grinding is done with a hand-mill and sifting with a sieve. Abaye then raises a new difficulty from Beit HaSh'lachin (irrigated fields) where harvesting is permitted even without cutting, as per the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that since harvesting is permitted only through picking by hand (קיטוף), one will remember the prohibition and not eat.
Abaye challenges: the explanation works for harvesting, but what about grinding and sifting, which are done in a typical manner?
The Gemara answers: grinding is done with a hand-mill and sifting on top of the sieve, both atypical, so there is no concern.
Abaye raises a new difficulty from Beit HaSh'lachin (irrigated fields), where the Mishnah permits typical harvesting, so the earlier answer fails.

items.text: Abaye's new distinction: chadash is separate, chametz is not
items.text_en: Abaye's new distinction: chadash is separate, chametz is not
items.desc_en: Abaye offers a new resolution: regarding new grain (chadash), one separates from it, but regarding chametz, one does not separate from it, thus resolving the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Abaye offers a new resolution: regarding new grain (chadash), one separates from it, but regarding chametz, one does not separate from it, thus resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava objects that Abaye's resolution only addresses Rabbi Yehuda's contradiction but not that of the Rabbis. Rava then resolves both: for Rabbi Yehuda, the earlier resolution stands; for the Rabbis, since the person himself seeks to burn the chametz, would he eat from it?

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that Abaye's resolution only addresses Rabbi Yehuda's contradiction but not that of the Rabbis.
Rava resolves both contradictions: for Rabbi Yehuda, the earlier resolution stands; for the Rabbis, since the person himself seeks to burn the chametz, would he eat from it?

items.text: Rav Ashi's rejected answer
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's rejected answer
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi suggests that the Mishnah teaches 'roasted flour' (kemach kali), implying that only roasted grain is permitted, not raw. The Gemara rejects this, raising difficulties from the period before roasting and from Beit HaSh'lachin, concluding that Rav Ashi's answer is invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proposes that the contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's positions is resolved because the Mishnah teaches 'roasted flour' (קמח קלי), implying only roasted grain is permitted, not raw grain.
The Gemara objects that Rav Ashi's statement is an error, because while it works for the period after roasting, it fails to explain the period before roasting when the grain is still edible.

The Gemara further rejects Rav Ashi's answer by raising the difficulty from Beit HaSh'lachin (irrigated fields) where typical harvesting is permitted, concluding that Rav Ashi's statement is indeed an error.

items.text: Mishnah: Omer permits new grain; Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment
items.text_en: Mishnah: Omer permits new grain; Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that once the Omer is offered, new grain is permitted immediately; those far away are permitted from midday onward. After the Temple's destruction, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that the entire waving day is forbidden. Rabbi Yehuda comments that the Torah itself forbids it until 'the essence of the day,' and explains why distant people are permitted from midday.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: once the Omer is offered, new grain is permitted immediately; those far away are permitted from midday onward. After the Temple's destruction, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that the entire waving day is forbidden.
Rabbi Yehuda questions the Mishnah's ruling, arguing that the Torah itself forbids new grain until 'the essence of the day,' so why are distant people permitted from midday?
Rabbi Yehuda answers his own question: distant people are permitted from midday because they know that the court is not indolent in sacrificing the Omer, so by midday it has certainly been offered.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel: Omer permits when Temple stands, sunrise when not
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel: Omer permits when Temple stands, sunrise when not
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel both state that when the Temple stands, the Omer permits new grain; when the Temple is not standing, sunrise permits it. They derive this from two verses: 'until the day you bring' and 'until the essence of this day,' applying each to a different scenario.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel both state that when the Temple stands, the Omer permits new grain; when the Temple is not standing, sunrise permits it.
The gemara asks for the reasoning behind this distinction and notes that two verses are written, raising the question of how they apply.
The gemara resolves the two verses: one applies when the Temple stands, the other when the Temple is not standing.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish: Sunrise always permits; Omer is only a mitzvah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish: Sunrise always permits; Omer is only a mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish both say that even when the Temple stands, sunrise permits new grain. They explain that the verse 'until you bring' is merely a mitzvah (to bring the Omer), not a condition for permission. They further clarify that the Omer permits in the country, and the two loaves permit in the Temple, but all are only for the mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish state that even when the Temple stands, sunrise permits new grain.
The Gemara objects by citing the verse 'עַד הֲבִיאֲכֶם' (until you bring), which seems to require the Omer offering.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's answer
sub.desc_en: They answer that the verse is only for the mitzvah (commandment) of bringing the Omer, not a condition for permission.
The Gemara objects from the Mishnah that once the Omer is offered, new grain is permitted immediately, implying the Omer is the permitting factor.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's answer
sub.desc_en: They again answer that this is only for the mitzvah (commandment) of bringing the Omer, not a condition for permission.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from the Mishnah's continuation
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from the Mishnah's continuation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects further from the Mishnah that the Omer permits in the country and the two loaves permit in the Temple, implying they are the permitting factors.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's resolution
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's resolution
sub.desc_en: They resolve that all these are only for the mitzvah (commandment), not a condition for permission.

items.text: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment and the Gemara's question
items.text_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment and the Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after the Temple's destruction, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that the entire day of waving (the Omer) is forbidden. The Gemara questions the reason, suggesting that people might mistakenly think that since they could eat after dawn in Temple times, they can do so now, not realizing that the Omer itself permits the new grain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after the Temple's destruction, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that the entire day of waving (the Omer) is forbidden.

The Gemara asks the reason for the enactment, suggesting that people might mistakenly think that since they could eat after dawn in Temple times, they can do so now, not realizing that the Omer itself permits the new grain.
The Gemara objects that if the enactment is merely a מצוה (commandment), why would one institute a decree for that reason?

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation: following Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation: following Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment follows Rabbi Yehuda's view that the prohibition is from the Torah, based on the verse 'until the selfsame day' meaning the entire day is included.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment follows Rabbi Yehuda's view that the prohibition is from the Torah, based on the verse 'עַד עֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה' (until the selfsame day), interpreted as 'עַד עִיצּוּמוֹ שֶׁל יוֹם' (until the very essence of the day), and holds that 'עַד' (until) includes the day itself.

items.text: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda actually disagrees with Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, as a Mishnah shows Rabbi Yehuda stating the prohibition is from the Torah, implying Rabban Yochanan's enactment was rabbinic. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda misunderstood; Rabban Yochanan's enactment was indeed Torah-based, and the term 'enacted' refers to his teaching and establishing the law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda states the prohibition is from the Torah, implying Rabban Yochanan's enactment was rabbinic.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda misunderstood; Rabban Yochanan's enactment was indeed Torah-based, and the term 'enacted' refers to his teaching and establishing the law.

items.text: Practices of later Amoraim regarding new grain outside Israel
items.text_en: Practices of later Amoraim regarding new grain outside Israel
items.desc_en: The Gemara records different practices: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua ate new grain on the night of the 16th (the 17th by night), considering the prohibition of new grain outside Israel as rabbinic and not worrying about doubt. The Rabbis of Rav Ashi's house ate on the morning of the 17th, considering it Torah law. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment was rabbinic and did not apply to doubt. Ravina reports his father followed Rabbi Yehuda and worried about doubt, eating only on the night of the 18th.

sub.desc_en: Reports that Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua ate new grain on the night of the 16th (the 17th by night), considering the prohibition of new grain outside Israel as rabbinic and not worrying about doubt.
Reports that the Rabbis of Rav Ashi's house ate on the morning of the 17th, considering the prohibition of new grain outside Israel as Torah law.
Explains that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment was rabbinic and did not apply to doubt, resolving the difference in practice.
Ravina reports that his father followed Rabbi Yehuda and worried about doubt, eating only on the night of the 18th.

items.text: Mishnah: The Omer and Two Loaves permit new grain
items.text_en: Mishnah: The Omer and Two Loaves permit new grain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Omer permits new grain in the countryside, and the Two Loaves permit it in the Temple. Offerings brought before the Omer are invalid, but before the Two Loaves they are valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Omer permits new grain in the countryside, the Two Loaves permit it in the Temple, and offerings brought before the Omer are invalid but before the Two Loaves are valid.

items.text: Rabbi Tarfon's question and Yehuda ben Nechemya's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Tarfon's question and Yehuda ben Nechemya's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon asks why offerings before the Omer are invalid but before the Two Loaves are valid. Yehuda ben Nechemya answers that before the Omer, new grain was not permitted at all for commoners, but before the Two Loaves, it was already permitted for commoners. Rabbi Tarfon's face shone, but Rabbi Akiva rebuked Yehuda, predicting his early death, which came true.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon asks why offerings before the Omer are invalid but before the Two Loaves are valid.
Yehuda ben Nechemya answers that before the Omer, new grain was not permitted at all for commoners, but before the Two Loaves, it was already permitted for commoners.
Rabbi Tarfon's face shone, but Rabbi Akiva rebuked Yehuda, predicting his early death, which came true.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's inference: libations and first fruits before the Omer
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's inference: libations and first fruits before the Omer
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak infers from Yehuda ben Nechemya's reasoning that libations and first fruits brought before the Omer are valid, as they were never prohibited at all. The Gemara clarifies that this is obvious, but the teaching is that even more so here, since they were never forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak infers from Yehuda ben Nechemya's reasoning that libations and first fruits brought before the Omer are valid, and the Gemara notes this is obvious.
The Gemara clarifies that the teaching is necessary to counter a possible objection, and concludes that here, since libations and first fruits were never prohibited at all, they are certainly valid.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's query: Do the Two Loaves permit out of order?
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's query: Do the Two Loaves permit out of order?
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the Two Loaves permit new grain if brought out of their proper order, e.g., if the Omer was planted between the Omer and the Two Loaves. Rabba attempts to answer from a baraita about the Omer, but the Gemara shows that if the Two Loaves permit out of order, one could find a case where the Omer is brought from grain that took root before the Two Loaves, and the Two Loaves from grain that took root before the current Omer, but the Gemara cuts off with 'Do you think?'

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the Two Loaves (שתי הלחם) permit new grain if brought out of their proper order, e.g., if grain was planted between the Omer and the Two Loaves.

sub.text: Rabba's attempted answer from a baraita
sub.text_en: Rabba's attempted answer from a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabba attempts to answer from a baraita about the Omer, citing Rabbi Eliezer's argument that the Omer must be barley based on a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'aviv' (אביב).

Rabbi Akiva offers a different proof that the Omer is barley, based on the principle that the community brings its obligation from wheat (for the Two Loaves) and barley (for the Omer), and that if the Omer were wheat, the Two Loaves would not be called 'first fruits' (ביכורים).

The Gemara objects that if the Two Loaves permit out of order, one could find a case where the Omer is brought from grain that took root before the Two Loaves, and the Two Loaves from grain that took root before the current Omer, undermining Rabbi Akiva's proof.
The Gemara cuts off the objection with 'Do you think?' (מי סברת), implying the scenario is impossible and rejecting the premise.

items.text: Clarification of the previous discussion
items.text_en: Clarification of the previous discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the previous discussion about first fruits (ביכורים) referred to fruit, not to the altar, since the altar consumes fruit from the current year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the previous discussion referred to first fruits (ביכורים) as fruit or as an altar offering, and clarifies that it refers to fruit, since the altar consumes fruit from the current year.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's inquiry about the two loaves and the stage of growth
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's inquiry about the two loaves and the stage of growth
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the two loaves (שתי הלחם) permit the new grain at the stage of flowering (הנצה) or at the stage of budding (חנטה). He clarifies that the question is about the flowering and budding of the leaf, not the fruit, and whether these are comparable to rooting. The inquiry remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the two loaves (שתי הלחם) permit new grain at the stage of flowering (הנצה) or budding (חנטה), and the gemara clarifies that the question cannot refer to the fruit's stages since rooting already permits.
