The baraita further derives from the verse that all meal offerings require pouring, but the oven-baked mincha is excluded by the phrase 'עָלֶיהָ שָׁמֶן'.
The Gemara questions whether the exclusion from pouring applies only to loaves but not to wafers.
The Gemara answers that the word 'הִיא' in the verse excludes wafers as well.
The Gemara asks what the biblical derivation is for the exclusion of wafers.
The Gemara suggests an alternative interpretation: perhaps the word 'הִיא' serves to exclude the priests' meal offering from the requirement of pouring.

items.text: Rabbah's opening statement
items.text_en: Rabbah's opening statement
items.desc_en: Rabbah identifies the meal offering of baked goods as requiring two exclusions from the general law of breaking.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah identifies the baked meal offering (מנחת מאפה) as the case requiring two exclusions from the general law of breaking.

items.text: Mishnah: Folding and breaking of meal offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Folding and breaking of meal offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an Israelite's meal offering is folded one into two and two into four and then separated; a priest's offering is folded but not separated; the anointed priest's offering is not folded at all. Rabbi Shimon adds that priestly and anointed priest offerings have no breaking because they have no handful taking, and all are broken into olive-sized pieces.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that an Israelite's meal offering is folded one into two and two into four and then separated.
The Mishnah continues that a priest's meal offering is folded but not separated.
The Mishnah states that the anointed priest's meal offering is not folded at all.
Rabbi Shimon adds that priestly and anointed priest offerings have no breaking because they have no handful taking.
The Mishnah concludes that all meal offerings are broken into olive-sized pieces.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of the folding and breaking laws
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of the folding and breaking laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verses 'פָּתוֹת' and 'פִּתִּים' and 'אֹתָהּ' that the offering is broken into pieces but not crumbs. It then clarifies that the Mishnah's statement that the anointed priest's offering is not folded means it is not folded into four, but it is folded into two.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verses 'פָּתוֹת' and 'פִּתִּים' and 'אֹתָהּ' that the offering is broken into pieces but not crumbs.
The Gemara questions the baraita's statement that the anointed priest's offering is folded, since the Mishnah says it is not folded at all.
Rabbah resolves that the Mishnah means it is not folded into four, but it is folded into two.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's statement and Rav Yosef's ruling on blessing for a dish with crumbs
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's statement and Rav Yosef's ruling on blessing for a dish with crumbs
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that a dish (חֲבִיצָא) containing olive-sized crumbs requires the blessing 'הַמּוֹצִיא לֶחֶם מִן הָאָרֶץ', but if it lacks olive-sized crumbs, the blessing is 'בּוֹרֵא מִינֵי מְזוֹנוֹת'. He supports this from a baraita about the blessing for meal offerings and the Mishnah that all are broken into olive-sized pieces.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that meal offerings of priests and the anointed priest have no breaking into pieces.
Rav Yosef rules that a dish (חֲבִיצָא) with olive-sized crumbs requires the blessing 'הַמּוֹצִיא לֶחֶם מִן הָאָרֶץ', but without such crumbs, the blessing is 'בּוֹרֵא מִינֵי מְזוֹנוֹת'.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's proof from a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's proof from a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks for the source of his ruling and cites a baraita about the blessing recited when standing to offer meal offerings in Jerusalem.

sub.text: Baraita citation: blessing for eating meal offerings
sub.text_en: Baraita citation: blessing for eating meal offerings
sub.desc_en: The baraita states that when taking the meal offerings to eat, one recites the blessing 'הַמּוֹצִיא לֶחֶם מִן הָאָרֶץ'.

sub.text: Mishnah citation: all are broken into olive-sized pieces
sub.text_en: Mishnah citation: all are broken into olive-sized pieces
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites the Mishnah that all meal offerings are broken into olive-sized pieces, supporting that olive-sized crumbs trigger the bread blessing.

items.text: Abaye's objection from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: according to the school of Rabbi Yishmael, who says the offering is crumbled until returned to flour, would one not recite 'הַמּוֹצִיא'? A baraita shows that if one gathers an olive-sized amount from such crumbs, it is liable for karet if leavened, and one fulfills the obligation with it on Passover, implying it is still bread.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects: according to the school of Rabbi Yishmael, who says the offering is crumbled until returned to flour, would one not recite 'הַמּוֹצִיא' (the blessing over bread)?
Abaye cites a baraita: if one gathers an olive-sized amount from such crumbs, it is liable for karet if leavened, and one fulfills the obligation with it on Passover, implying it is still bread.

items.text: Resolution: The case is of kneaded crumbs or from a large loaf
items.text_en: Resolution: The case is of kneaded crumbs or from a large loaf
items.desc_en: The Gemara first suggests the case is where the crumbs were kneaded together, but then objects that the baraita says 'אֲכָלוֹ' (ate it) rather than 'אֲכָלָן' (ate them). It then resolves that the case is where the crumbs came from a large loaf, so they retain the status of bread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the case in the baraita is where the crumbs were kneaded together into a loaf.
The Gemara objects that if the crumbs were kneaded, the baraita should have said 'אֲכָלוֹ' (ate it) in the singular, not 'אֲכָלָן' (ate them) in the plural.
The Gemara resolves that the case is where the crumbs came from a large loaf, so they retain the status of bread and are referred to in the plural.

items.text: Rav Sheshet and Rava's final ruling on crumbs
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet and Rava's final ruling on crumbs
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet rules that even crumbs without an olive-sized amount require 'הַמּוֹצִיא', and Rava adds that this applies only if the crumbs still have the appearance of bread (תּוֹרִיתָא דְּנַהְמָא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the final ruling is regarding the blessing on crumbs.
Rav Sheshet rules that even crumbs without an olive-sized amount require the blessing 'הַמּוֹצִיא'.
Rava qualifies that Rav Sheshet's ruling applies only if the crumbs still have the appearance of bread (תּוֹרִיתָא דְּנַהְמָא).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all meal offerings require three hundred kneadings and five hundred beatings, with the kneading and beating done on the wheat (or dough according to Rabbi Yosei). It then discusses the number of loaves for various offerings: all meal offerings come as ten loaves, except for the showbread and the High Priest's griddle cakes which come as twelve (Rabbi Yehuda), while Rabbi Meir says all come as twelve except for the loaves of thanksgiving and the Nazirite's offering which come as ten.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all meal offerings require three hundred kneadings and five hundred beatings, with the kneading and beating done on the wheat (or dough according to Rabbi Yosei), and then lists the number of loaves for various offerings.

items.text: Gemara's question on the ratio of kneading to beating
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the ratio of kneading to beating
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught that for each kneading there are two beatings, and for two kneadings three beatings. Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the counting of 'one' and 'two' refers to the combined action or separate actions, and the question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches the ratio of kneading to beating: one kneading requires two beatings, two kneadings require three beatings.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the counting of 'one' and 'two' refers to the combined action of bringing and taking or to separate actions.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Clarifying Rabbi Yosei's position on kneading and beating
items.text_en: Clarifying Rabbi Yosei's position on kneading and beating
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether Rabbi Yosei means that kneading and beating are done on the dough exclusively, or also on the dough (in addition to wheat). A baraita is cited to resolve the issue: Rabbi Yosei says kneading and beating are done on the dough.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yosei means kneading and beating are done exclusively on the dough, or also on the dough in addition to wheat.
A baraita is cited to resolve the question, stating that Rabbi Yosei explicitly says kneading and beating are done on the dough.

items.text: Source for twelve loaves of showbread and High Priest's griddle cakes
items.text_en: Source for twelve loaves of showbread and High Priest's griddle cakes
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the twelve loaves of showbread are explicitly written in the Torah. For the High Priest's griddle cakes, the number twelve is derived through a verbal analogy (gezeirah shavah) of 'chukah' from showbread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the twelve loaves of showbread are explicitly written in the Torah.
The Gemara derives the number twelve for the High Priest's griddle cakes through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'חוקה' from showbread.

items.text: Debate on deriving ten loaves for all meal offerings
items.text_en: Debate on deriving ten loaves for all meal offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for all meal offerings coming as ten loaves. It proposes deriving from the loaves of thanksgiving, but an objection is raised to derive from showbread (twelve). The Gemara compares the attributes of each source, noting that thanksgiving loaves share more commonalities with standard meal offerings (individual, voluntary, oil, invalidated, not on Shabbat, not in impurity). A further attempt to derive from the High Priest's griddle cakes is rejected because the commonalities are fewer, and the principle that a commoner learns from a commoner is preferred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that all meal offerings come as ten loaves.
The Gemara proposes deriving the ten loaves from the loaves of the thanksgiving offering.
An objection is raised: why not derive from the showbread, which has twelve loaves?

The Gemara argues that the thanksgiving loaves are a better source because they share more commonalities with standard meal offerings: individual, voluntary, oil, invalidated, not on Shabbat, not in impurity.
A counter-objection argues that showbread has other commonalities: sanctity, frankincense, matzah, and bone.
The Gemara rejects the counter-objection, noting that the commonalities of the thanksgiving loaves are more numerous.

The Gemara raises an alternative: if a matter learned by a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) can then teach by a בנין אב (building from a precedent), why not derive from the High Priest's griddle cakes (twelve loaves)?
The Gemara answers that the thanksgiving loaves are still preferable because they share the attributes of a commoner who donates halves, invalidation by piggul, and not on Shabbat or in impurity.
A counter-objection argues that the High Priest's griddle cakes have more commonalities: an עישרון (tenth-ephah), a sacred vessel, frankincense, matzah, bone, presentation, and fire-offering.
The Gemara resolves the debate by stating that a commoner (standard meal offering) prefers to learn from a commoner (thanksgiving offering) rather than from the High Priest.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's reasoning for twelve loaves
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's reasoning for twelve loaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes Rabbi Meir's opinion that all meal offerings come as twelve loaves. If he holds that something learned through a verbal analogy can then teach through a building of a father (binyan av), he derives from the High Priest's griddle cakes (more commonalities). If not, he derives from showbread, preferring sacred from sacred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what reasoning underlies Rabbi Meir's opinion that all meal offerings come as twelve loaves.

The Gemara suggests that if Rabbi Meir holds that something learned through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) can then teach through a בנין אב (building of a father), he derives the twelve-loaf requirement from the High Priest's griddle cakes, since those have more commonalities.

The Gemara suggests that if Rabbi Meir holds that something learned through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) cannot teach through a בנין אב (building of a father), he derives from showbread, preferring to learn sacred from sacred.

items.text: Source for ten loaves of thanksgiving and Nazirite offerings
items.text_en: Source for ten loaves of thanksgiving and Nazirite offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the ten loaves of thanksgiving are explicitly written in the Torah. For the Nazirite offering, it is derived from the verse 'his peace offerings' which includes the peace offerings of a Nazirite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the ten loaves of thanksgiving are explicitly written in the Torah.
The Gemara cites Mar's teaching that the verse 'his peace offerings' includes the peace offerings of a Nazirite, deriving the ten loaves for the Nazirite offering.

items.text: Discussion on baking thanksgiving loaves into four loaves
items.text_en: Discussion on baking thanksgiving loaves into four loaves
items.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Kisna said in the name of Shmuel that if one baked the loaves of thanksgiving into four loaves (instead of forty), he has fulfilled his obligation. The Gemara objects that forty loaves are required for the mitzvah, and also that one must separate terumah from them, which requires taking from each type, and the Torah says 'one' meaning not broken pieces. The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita stating that all meal offerings are valid if the measure of their loaves is increased or decreased, except for showbread, High Priest's griddle cakes, and loaves of thanksgiving and Nazirite.

sub.text: Rav Tovi bar Kisna in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Tovi bar Kisna in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Kisna reports Shmuel's ruling that if one baked the loaves of thanksgiving into four loaves (instead of forty), he has fulfilled his obligation.
The Gemara objects that forty loaves are required for the mitzvah, so baking only four seems insufficient.

The Gemara further objects that one must separate תרומה (priestly portion) from the loaves, and the Torah requires taking from each type with whole loaves, not broken pieces, which would be impossible if only four loaves are baked.

The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita stating that all meal offerings are valid if the measure of their loaves is increased or decreased, except for showbread, High Priest's griddle cakes, and loaves of thanksgiving and Nazirite.

items.text: Baraita on varying measures for meal offerings
items.text_en: Baraita on varying measures for meal offerings
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that all meal offerings are valid if their measure of loaves is increased or decreased, except for the showbread and the loaves of the High Priest; some add the loaves of the thanksgiving offering and the Nazirite's offering.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that all meal offerings are valid if their loaf measure is increased or decreased, except for showbread and High Priest's loaves, with some adding thanksgiving and Nazirite loaves.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on baking a meal offering as one loaf
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on baking a meal offering as one loaf
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one baked a meal offering of the oven as a single loaf, it is valid, based on the singular form 'מַצָּת' in the verse. Rav Pappa objects, citing the case of the thanksgiving loaves where the plural 'מַצּוֹת' is written, yet Samuel ruled that baking them as four loaves is valid; the Gemara notes that this is a dispute.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one baked a meal offering of the oven as a single loaf, it is valid.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Huna's reasoning is based on the singular form 'מַצָּת' (matzah) in the verse, implying a single loaf.
Rav Pappa objects: if the reason is the singular 'מַצָּת', then where the plural 'מַצּוֹת' is written, would it be invalid?

sub.text: Rav Pappa's supporting evidence from thanksgiving loaves
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's supporting evidence from thanksgiving loaves
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites the case of thanksgiving loaves where the plural 'מַצּוֹת' is written, yet Samuel ruled that baking them as four loaves is valid, contradicting Rav Huna's inference.
The Gemara resolves that the case of thanksgiving loaves is a dispute (between Rav Huna and Samuel), so Rav Huna's ruling stands within his own position.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on measures for the omer, two loaves, and showbread
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on measures for the omer, two loaves, and showbread
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the omer comes from one tenth of an ephah from three se'ahs, the two loaves from two tenths from three se'ahs, and the showbread from twenty-four tenths from twenty-four se'ahs. The Gemara explains the reasoning: the omer, being from new grain and barley, requires a selection from three se'ahs; the two loaves, from wheat and new grain, require two tenths from three se'ahs; the showbread, from wheat and old grain, requires a selection from one se'ah per tenth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the required measures for the omer (one tenth from three se'ahs), the two loaves (two tenths from three se'ahs), and the showbread (twenty-four tenths from twenty-four se'ahs).
The Gemara asks for the rationale behind the Mishnah's measures.

The Gemara explains that the omer, being from new grain and barley, requires a selection from three se'ahs to obtain a choice tenth; the two loaves, from new wheat, also require three se'ahs for two choice tenths.
The Gemara explains that the showbread, from wheat and old grain, yields a choice tenth from each se'ah, thus requiring one se'ah per tenth.

items.text: Baraita on increasing or decreasing the measure of tenths
items.text_en: Baraita on increasing or decreasing the measure of tenths
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that for all meal offerings, if one increased or decreased the measure of tenths, they are invalid; but if one increased or decreased the measure of se'ahs (the volume from which the flour is taken), they are valid.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that for all meal offerings, if one increased or decreased the measure of tenths they are invalid, but if one increased or decreased the measure of se'ahs they are valid.

items.text: Mishnah and baraita on sifting procedures for meal offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah and baraita on sifting procedures for meal offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the omer was sifted through thirteen sieves, the two loaves through twelve, and the showbread through eleven. Rabbi Shimon says there was no fixed number; rather, one would bring fine flour sifted as needed. A baraita adds that there were thirteen sieves in the Temple, one above the other, with the top catching bran and the bottom catching fine flour.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the different sifting standards for the omer, the two loaves, and the showbread, and Rabbi Shimon says there was no fixed number; fine flour was sifted as needed.
A baraita adds that there were thirteen sieves in the Temple, one above the other, with the top catching bran and the bottom catching fine flour.

items.text: Derivation of the requirement for sifted flour from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of the requirement for sifted flour from the verse
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'סֹלֶת וְאָפִיתָ אֹתָהּ' that the flour must be sifted; from 'וְלָקַחְתָּ' that even wheat may be taken; and from 'אֹתָהּ' that this applies only to the showbread, not other offerings, due to financial consideration. Rabbi Elazar explains that the Torah is concerned for the money of Israel, citing a verse about watering the congregation and their cattle.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'סֹלֶת וְאָפִיתָ אֹתָהּ' (fine flour and you shall bake it) to teach that the showbread is acquired as sifted fine flour.
The baraita asks: from where is it derived that even wheat kernels may be purchased? It answers: from the verse 'וְלָקַחְתָּ' (and you shall take), implying any form of taking.

The baraita asks: one might think that other meal offerings may also be purchased as kernels; it answers: the verse says 'אֹתָהּ' (it), limiting this leniency to the showbread alone, due to sparing (financial consideration).
רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) asks: what is the meaning of 'because of the sparing'? He answers: the Torah spared the money of the Jewish people.

The Gemara asks: where is this principle alluded to? It answers: from the verse 'וְהִשְׁקִיתָ אֶת הָעֵדָה וְאֶת בְּעִירָם' (and you shall give drink to the congregation and their cattle), showing concern for even the livestock.
The Gemara concludes the chapter with the formula 'הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ אֵלּוּ מְנָחוֹת נִקְמָצוֹת' (we return to you, 'These meal offerings are taken by handful'), marking the end of the chapter.

items.text: Mishnah on the measure of the thanksgiving offering
items.text_en: Mishnah on the measure of the thanksgiving offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the thanksgiving offering came from five Jerusalem se'ahs, which are six desert se'ahs, i.e., two ephahs (each ephah being three se'ahs), totaling twenty tenths: ten for the leavened bread and ten for the matzah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measure of flour for the thanksgiving offering: five Jerusalem se'ahs (six desert se'ahs), i.e., two ephahs, totaling twenty tenths, divided equally between leavened and unleavened loaves.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Measurements for the thanksgiving offering
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Measurements for the thanksgiving offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the thanksgiving offering requires ten Jerusalem se'ah: five for leavened bread and five for matzah. The matzah consists of three types—hallot, rekikin, and rebukhah—resulting in three and one-third issaron per type, with three loaves per issaron. In Jerusalem measure, this amounts to thirty kav, fifteen for leavened and fifteen for matzah, with each type receiving five kav and two loaves per kav.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measurements for the thanksgiving offering: ten se'ah in Jerusalem measure, divided equally between leavened and matzah bread, with the matzah comprising three types each receiving five kav and two loaves per kav.

items.text: Gemara: Deriving the ephah from the bat
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving the ephah from the bat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The thanksgiving offering comes with five Jerusalem se'ah—from where do we know this? Rav Chisda answers from the verse "the ephah and the bat shall be of one measure" (Ezekiel 45:11), teaching that just as a bat is three se'ah, so too an ephah is three se'ah. The Gemara then questions how we know the bat itself is three se'ah, rejecting a proof from the verse about the chomer and instead citing a different verse that explicitly states ten baths make a chomer, establishing the bat's volume.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that the thanksgiving offering comes with five Jerusalem se'ah?
Rav Chisda cites a verse equating the ephah and the bath, deriving that just as a bath is three se'ah, so too an ephah is three se'ah.
The Gemara asks: from where do we know the bath itself is three se'ah, rejecting a possible derivation from the chomer because the chomer's size is unknown.
The Gemara cites a verse that explicitly states ten baths equal one chomer, establishing the bath as three se'ah.

items.text: Shmuel's principle: No more than one-sixth addition
items.text_en: Shmuel's principle: No more than one-sixth addition
items.desc_en: Shmuel states a general rule: one may not add more than one-sixth to measures, nor more than one-sixth to coinage, and a merchant may not profit more than one-sixth.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states a general rule: one may not add more than one-sixth to measures, nor more than one-sixth to coinage, and a merchant may not profit more than one-sixth.

items.text: Gemara: Exploring the reason for Shmuel's rule
items.text_en: Gemara: Exploring the reason for Shmuel's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the rationale behind Shmuel's rule. It first suggests it is to prevent loss to the seller, but then objects that if so, even one-sixth should be prohibited. It then suggests it is due to the law of overreaching (ona'ah), but Rava's statement that any deviation in measures requires return undermines this. Finally, it suggests it is for the benefit of the merchant, but the Gemara questions why profit is allowed at all. The discussion concludes without a definitive answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind Shmuel's rule, and first suggests it is to prevent loss to the seller (אפקועי תרעא), but objects that if so, even one-sixth should be prohibited.
The Gemara suggests the rule is due to the law of overreaching (אונאה), but Rava's statement that any deviation in measures requires return undermines this.

The Gemara suggests the rule is for the benefit of the merchant (תגרא), but questions why profit is allowed at all, concluding that the merchant would not be called a merchant if he only buys and sells without profit.

items.text: Rav Chisda: Shmuel's rule derived from a verse
items.text_en: Rav Chisda: Shmuel's rule derived from a verse
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that Shmuel found a scriptural basis for his rule in the verse about the shekel and the maneh (Ezekiel 45:12). From the fact that the verse lists twenty, twenty-five, and fifteen shekels totaling sixty, but a maneh is 240, the Gemara learns three things: the sacred maneh was double, one may add to measures but not more than one-sixth, and the one-sixth is added externally (i.e., the addition is calculated from the original measure).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda introduces that Shmuel derived his rule from a verse, citing Ezekiel 45:12 which lists shekels totaling sixty, though a maneh is 240.
The Gemara infers three lessons from the verse: the sacred maneh was double, one may add up to one-sixth to measures, and the one-sixth is added externally (from the original measure).

items.text: Ravina: Support from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Ravina: Support from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Ravina notes that the Mishnah itself supports Shmuel's rule, as it states that the thanksgiving offering comes with five Jerusalem se'ah, which are six desert se'ah—an addition of one-sixth.

sub.desc_en: Ravina notes that the Mishnah itself supports this, as it states that the thanksgiving offering comes with five Jerusalem se'ah which are six desert se'ah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that from each type of thanksgiving loaf the priest takes one-tenth as terumah, citing the verse, and explains the derivation: 'one' means not a broken piece, 'from every offering' means all offerings are equal, and the rest is eaten by the owners.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that from each type of thanksgiving loaf the priest takes one-tenth as תרומה (priestly portion), citing the verse and explaining the derivation: 'אחד' (one) means not a broken piece, 'מכל קרבן' (from every offering) means all offerings are equal, and the rest is eaten by the owners.

items.text: Gemara's derivation of the one-tenth measure for terumah
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation of the one-tenth measure for terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the one-tenth measure for the terumah of the thanksgiving loaves via a gezeirah shavah from terumat ma'aser, rejecting a possible derivation from bikurim and from terumat ma'aser's being eaten anywhere.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse and notes that the measure of the terumah is not specified.
The Gemara proposes a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from תרומת מעשר (tithe of the tithe) to derive the one-tenth measure.
An alternative derivation from ביכורים (first fruits) is considered, which would yield no fixed measure.
The Gemara rejects the bikurim derivation because bikurim is followed by terumah, unlike the terumah of the thanksgiving loaves.
An alternative objection argues that the derivation should be from a terumah eaten in a holy place, excluding תרומת מעשר (tithe of the tithe) which is eaten anywhere.
The Gemara resolves the derivation by citing the shared phrase 'ממנו תרומה' (from it a terumah) to establish a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) with תרומת מעשר (tithe of the tithe).

items.text: Derivation of the number of tenth-ephahs for the loaves
items.text_en: Derivation of the number of tenth-ephahs for the loaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that each loaf of the thanksgiving offering requires one-tenth of an ephah, using a gezeirah shavah from the two loaves, rejecting a derivation from the showbread, and concluding that the total is twenty tenth-ephahs: ten for the leavened loaves and ten for the matzah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that while the amount of the priestly portion (תרומה) is known to be one-tenth, the amount of flour per loaf (חלה) is unknown.

The Gemara proposes a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'לחם' (bread) used in the thanksgiving offering and in the two loaves (שתי הלחם), concluding that each loaf requires one-tenth of an ephah.
The Gemara raises an alternative: perhaps the analogy should be to the showbread (לחם הפנים), which requires two tenth-ephahs per loaf.
The Gemara resolves that the analogy to the two loaves is preferable because both are offerings that come with leaven (חמץ) together with the sacrifice, unlike the showbread.

The Gemara raises another alternative: perhaps the analogy should be based on offerings that come from both the Land and outside, from new and old grain, unlike the two loaves which come only from new grain and from the Land.

The Gemara concludes with a scriptural derivation: the extra word 'תָּבִיאוּ' (you shall bring) in the verse about the two loaves teaches that any bread brought from elsewhere is like the two loaves, establishing one-tenth per loaf.
The Gemara objects: if the analogy is to the two loaves, why not require two tenth-ephahs per loaf, as in the two loaves?
The Gemara resolves that the word 'תִּהְיֶינָה' (they shall be) limits the analogy, teaching that each loaf gets one-tenth, not two.
The Gemara asks: we have learned ten tenth-ephahs for the leavened loaves, but from where do we derive ten for the matzah loaves?
The Gemara answers that the verse 'עַל חַלֹּת לֶחֶם חָמֵץ' (upon the leavened bread loaves) implies that the matzah loaves are brought corresponding to the leavened ones.
The Gemara concludes: corresponding to the leavened loaves, bring matzah, resulting in a total of twenty tenth-ephahs for the thanksgiving loaves — ten for leavened and ten for matzah.

items.text: Derivation of the number of loaves per tenth-ephah
items.text_en: Derivation of the number of loaves per tenth-ephah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the ten matzah loaves are made from three types (each with its own tenth-ephah), resulting in three and a third tenth-ephahs per type and three loaves per tenth-ephah, totaling forty loaves; the priest takes four and the rest are eaten by the owners.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the ten matzah loaves could all be from one type.

The Gemara answers by citing the verse listing three types of matzah, deriving that each type gets a tenth-ephah, yielding three loaves per tenth-ephah, totaling forty loaves, with four given to the priest and the rest eaten by the owners.

items.text: Clarifications and objections regarding the derivations
items.text_en: Clarifications and objections regarding the derivations
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'from the connected' in the baraita, citing Rav Chisda's explanation that it refers to not cutting the meat before removing the sacrificial parts. It then addresses why the gezeirah shavah is from terumat ma'aser and not from terumat Midyan or challah, providing reasons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's interpretation of 'from the connected' by citing a similar verse about removing fat, asking what 'connected' could mean there.
Rav Chisda explains that 'from the connected' means one must not cut the meat before removing the sacrificial parts.
Mar reiterates the gezeirah shavah (גזירה שווה) between the terumah of the todah and terumat ma'aser.
The Gemara objects that one could derive from terumat Midyan instead, and rejects it because that terumah is not perpetual.
The Gemara objects that one could derive from challah, and the Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael rejects it because the phrase 'from it a terumah to the Lord' is absent there.

items.text: Rava's query about the status of the terumah of the thanksgiving loaves
items.text_en: Rava's query about the status of the terumah of the thanksgiving loaves
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether the terumah of the thanksgiving loaves is subject to the death penalty and the added fifth, and whether it imparts tum'ah to other produce. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether the terumah of the thanksgiving loaves is subject to the death penalty and the added fifth for a non-priest who eats it intentionally.

The Gemara articulates the two sides of Rava's doubt: since the terumah of the loaves is juxtaposed to terumah ma'aser, it might be like it, or perhaps the verse's phrase 'בּוֹ וַחֲמִשִּׁיתוֹ' (on it and its fifth) excludes this case.
Rava further asks whether this terumah imparts tum'ah to other produce (מדמעת), and the Gemara leaves both questions unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Query about the derivation from 'tihyenah'
items.text_en: Query about the derivation from 'tihyenah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the derivation from the word 'tihyenah' is, which was used earlier to limit the number of tenth-ephahs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not derive from the תרומה of חלה (dough)? The school of Rabbi Yishmael answers: we derive from something that says 'ממנו תרומה לה׳', excluding חלה which does not say that.

items.text: Gemara's question on the number of tenth-ephahs for the leavened bread
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the number of tenth-ephahs for the leavened bread
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi notes that the verse says 'tihyena' (they shall be), implying ten loaves. Rava explains that the verse speaks in terms of tenth-ephahs, establishing that ten tenth-ephahs are used for the leavened bread.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi notes the verse says 'תִּהְיֶינָה' (they shall be) and questions whether this implies ten loaves (קפיזי).
Rava answers that the verse speaks in terms of עשרונות (tenth-ephahs), not loaves, establishing ten tenth-ephahs for the leavened bread.

items.text: Deriving ten tenth-ephahs for matzah and the hekesh debate
items.text_en: Deriving ten tenth-ephahs for matzah and the hekesh debate
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives ten tenth-ephahs for matzah from the hekesh (analogy) to leavened bread. It then questions whether a hekesh can teach another hekesh, and resolves that for those who reject such a hekesh, the word 'tavi'u' (you shall bring) serves as a ribbui (amplification).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have derived ten tenth-ephahs for leavened bread; from where do we derive ten for matzah? It answers with a hekesh (analogy) from the verse 'עַל חַלּוֹת לֶחֶם חָמֵץ' — bring matzah corresponding to leavened bread.

The Gemara objects: can a matter learned through a hekesh (analogy) then teach another hekesh? It answers that this is a case of 'הֵימֶנּוּ וְדָבָר אַחֵר' (deriving from it to something else), and such a derivation is not a valid hekesh.

The Gemara resolves: this works for the one who says such a hekesh is invalid; but for the one who says it is valid, the word 'תָּבִיאוּ' (you shall bring) serves as a ribbui (amplification) to include the ten tenth-ephahs for matzah.

items.text: Mishnah: The milu'im and Nazirite offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: The milu'im and Nazirite offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the milu'im (consecration offerings) come like the matzah of the todah (thanksgiving offering) – with challot, rekikin, and rebukha. The Nazirite offering comes with two types (challot and rekikin) but without rebukha, totaling ten Jerusalemite kavim, which are six tenth-ephahs and a remainder.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the milu'im (consecration offerings) come like the matzah of the todah (thanksgiving offering) – with challot, rekikin, and rebukha, and the Nazirite offering comes with two types but without rebukha, totaling ten Jerusalemite kavim.

items.text: Gemara: Source for rebukha in the milu'im
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for rebukha in the milu'im
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites a verse from the milu'im to prove rebukha is included. Rav Avya objects, suggesting the 'shemen' refers to oil, not rebukha. Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda resolves this by deriving rebukha from the hekesh of the anointing day to the inauguration day of the high priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that rebukha is included in the milu'im) derived?

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites a verse from the milu'im (Leviticus 8:26) listing חַלַּת מַצָּה, חַלַּת לֶחֶם שֶׁמֶן, and רָקִיק, and argues that 'שֶׁמֶן' (oil) refers to rebukha.
Rav Avya objects: perhaps 'שֶׁמֶן' simply means oil (the anointing oil), not rebukha.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda citing Rabbi Tavla
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda citing Rabbi Tavla
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda resolves the issue by deriving rebukha from a הֶקֵּשׁ (verbal analogy) between the anointing day (הִמָּשְׁחוֹ) and the inauguration day (חִינּוּכוֹ) of the high priest, as taught by Rabbi Tavla.

items.text: Number of tenth-ephahs for the high priest's offerings
items.text_en: Number of tenth-ephahs for the high priest's offerings
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says a high priest approaching service needs two tenth-ephahs – one for his anointing and one for his inauguration. Mar bar Rav Ashi says three. They do not disagree: one refers to a priest who served as a common priest, the other to one who did not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that a high priest approaching service requires two tenth-ephahs: one for his anointing and one for his inauguration.
Mar bar Rav Ashi counters that the high priest requires three tenth-ephahs.
The Gemara resolves that they do not disagree: Rav Chisda refers to a priest who served as a common priest, while Mar bar Rav Ashi refers to one who did not.
The mishnah states that the nazirite's offering comes with two parts, like the matza of the thanks offering.

items.text: Source for the Nazirite's offering excluding rebukha
items.text_en: Source for the Nazirite's offering excluding rebukha
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that 'shelamav' (his peace-offerings) includes the Nazirite's peace-offerings for ten kavim and a quarter-log of oil. One might think all items mentioned in the context are included, but 'matzot' teaches otherwise. Rav Pappa explains that 'matzot' excludes rebukha, which is not called 'matzot'. The school of Rabbi Yishmael uses a klal u'frat (general and specific) to limit the offerings to challot and rekikin only.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that 'שְׁלָמָיו' (his peace-offerings) includes the Nazirite's peace-offerings, requiring ten Jerusalem kavim and a quarter-log of oil.
The baraita raises the possibility that all items mentioned in the context might be included, but then states that 'מַצּוֹת' (unleavened bread) teaches otherwise.
Rav Pappa explains that 'מַצּוֹת' excludes rebukha, which is not called 'מַצּוֹת' (unleavened bread).

The school of Rabbi Yishmael uses a כלל ופרט (general and specific) principle: 'מַצּוֹת' is the general, 'חַלּוֹת וּרְקִיקִין' (loaves and wafers) are the specific, so only those are included, excluding other items like rebukha.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one slaughters the todah offering inside the Temple and its bread outside the wall, the bread is not sanctified. It also rules that if the bread has not formed a crust in the oven, even if all but one loaf has formed a crust, the bread is not sanctified.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with two rulings: slaughtering the todah inside and its bread outside the wall does not sanctify the bread; if the bread has not formed a crust in the oven, even if all but one loaf has formed a crust, the bread is not sanctified.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the meaning of 'outside the wall'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the meaning of 'outside the wall'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's phrase 'outside the wall'. Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to outside the wall of Beit Pagei, while Reish Lakish says it refers to outside the wall of the Temple courtyard. They argue whether the bread is sanctified if slaughtered in the courtyard but outside Beit Pagei. The Gemara notes that they had a similar dispute elsewhere regarding the Paschal lamb, and explains why both disputes are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'outside the wall'.
Rabbi Yochanan says it means outside the wall of Beit Pagei, while Reish Lakish says it means outside the wall of the Temple courtyard.
Reish Lakish explains that the verse requires the bread to be 'upon' the sacrifice in close proximity, so only within the courtyard sanctifies.
Rabbi Yochanan says that outside the courtyard still sanctifies, and the proximity requirement is not needed.
The Gemara objects that they already disputed a similar point elsewhere.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah about slaughtering the Paschal lamb with leaven, where Reish Lakish requires the owner to be in the courtyard, while Rabbi Yochanan does not.
The Gemara explains that both disputes are necessary, as each one teaches a unique aspect not covered by the other.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's opinion, stating that if one slaughters the todah inside and its bread outside the wall of Beit Pagei, the bread is not sanctified.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan: slaughtering the todah inside and its bread outside the wall of Beit Pagei does not sanctify the bread.

items.text: Source for the requirement of crust formation
items.text_en: Source for the requirement of crust formation
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verse that the bread is not sanctified unless its faces have formed a crust in the oven, and that the bread is sanctified only through the slaughter of the animal. It also learns that if slaughtered not for its own sake, the bread is not sanctified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the rule that the bread must have formed a crust in the oven.

The baraita derives from the verse 'עַל חַלּוֹת לֶחֶם חָמֵץ יַקְרִיב קׇרְבָּנוֹ עַל זֶבַח' that the bread is sanctified only if its faces have formed a crust in the oven, only through the slaughter of the animal, and if slaughtered not for its own sake the bread is not sanctified.

items.text: Discussion on the definition of 'matzah na' and its application to todah bread
items.text_en: Discussion on the definition of 'matzah na' and its application to todah bread
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses what constitutes 'matzah na' (soft matzah) and applies it to the bread of the todah. Rava states that the same principle applies to todah bread, and the Gemara clarifies that the verse 'one' teaches that one may not take a broken piece, but this is not considered broken.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one fulfills the obligation with matzah that is 'na' (half-baked), and Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines 'na' as matzah that can be broken without threads stretching from it.
Rava states that the same definition applies to the bread of the todah, since both are called 'bread' in the verse.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is necessary lest one think that 'one' loaf means it must be whole, but the half-baked bread is like broken, so the baraita teaches that it is valid.

items.text: Dispute about a todah slaughtered for eighty loaves
items.text_en: Dispute about a todah slaughtered for eighty loaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan regarding a todah slaughtered for eighty loaves: Chizkiyah says forty out of eighty are sanctified, while Rabbi Yochanan says they are not. Rabbi Zeira explains that they agree if specified, but disagree in an unspecified case. Abaye and Rav Pappa offer different explanations for the dispute, involving intent and the sanctifying power of service vessels and the knife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: if one slaughters the todah for eighty loaves, Chizkiya says forty out of eighty are sanctified, while Rabbi Yochanan says forty out of eighty are not sanctified.

Rabbi Zeira explains that all agree if he explicitly said 'let forty be sanctified from the eighty' they are sanctified; the dispute is when he said nothing, one holds he intends responsibility, the other holds he intends a large offering.
Abaye says all agree he intends responsibility, but they dispute whether sacred vessels sanctify without knowledge.
Rav Pappa says all agree sacred vessels sanctify without knowledge, but they dispute whether a knife sanctifies like a sacred vessel.
An alternative version: Rav Pappa says all agree sacred vessels sanctify only with knowledge, but they dispute whether a knife is more powerful than a sacred vessel.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases where bread is or is not sanctified
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases where bread is or is not sanctified
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if the todah is slaughtered outside its time or place, the bread is sanctified; if found to be a tereifah, it is not. Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages dispute a blemished animal. Slaughtering not for its own sake, as well as for the ram of inauguration and the two lambs of Shavuot, does not sanctify the bread.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by ruling that if the thanks-offering is slaughtered outside its time or place, the bread is sanctified; but if found to be a tereifah, the bread is not sanctified.
The Mishnah records that if the animal is found to be blemished, Rabbi Eliezer rules the bread is sanctified.
The Mishnah records that the Sages dispute Rabbi Eliezer and rule the bread is not sanctified.
The Mishnah concludes that slaughtering the thanks-offering not for its own sake, as well as for the ram of inauguration and the two lambs of Shavuot, does not sanctify the bread.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Mishnah's author and the principle
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Mishnah's author and the principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Meir, citing a baraita that states a general rule: if the disqualification occurs before slaughter, the bread is not sanctified; if after slaughter, it is sanctified. Examples are given.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion is expressed in the Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir.
A baraita is cited stating the general principle: if the disqualification precedes slaughter, the bread is not sanctified; if after slaughter, it is sanctified, with examples.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on blemished animal
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on blemished animal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer holds that an animal slaughtered and found to be blemished is consecrated, while Rabbi Yehoshua says it is not consecrated. This is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer holds that an animal slaughtered and found to be blemished is consecrated, while Rabbi Yehoshua says it is not consecrated, as stated by Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's clarification of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's clarification of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree that a tereifah is not consecrated, and that an animal slaughtered outside its proper time is consecrated, and that a blemished animal is not consecrated. They only disagree about an animal slaughtered outside its proper place.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda redefines the dispute: they agree that a terefah does not consecrate and that a blemished animal does not consecrate, but disagree only on an animal slaughtered outside its proper place.

items.text: Arguments from analogy: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Arguments from analogy: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues by analogy from outside its proper time to outside its proper place, while Rabbi Yehoshua argues by analogy from a blemished animal to outside its proper place.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues by analogy: just as an animal slaughtered outside its proper time is consecrated, so too one slaughtered outside its proper place is consecrated.
Rabbi Yehoshua counters by analogy: just as a blemished animal does not consecrate, so too one slaughtered outside its proper place does not consecrate.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's challenge and proposal
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's challenge and proposal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer challenges Rabbi Yehoshua's analogy, stating that he compared it to outside its proper time while Rabbi Yehoshua compared it to a blemished animal. He proposes to judge it based on which analogy is more fitting.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer challenges: I analogized to outside its time, you to a blemish; let us see which analogy is more fitting.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua's detailed arguments
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua's detailed arguments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that a disqualification of thought (מחשבה) should be derived from another disqualification of thought, not from a physical disqualification. Rabbi Yehoshua argues that a disqualification without כרת should be derived from another without כרת, and that outside its proper time (which involves כרת) should not be a proof. He also suggests deriving it from שלא לשמו, which is a disqualification of thought without כרת.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that a disqualification of thought (מחשבה) should be derived from another disqualification of thought, not from a physical disqualification.

Rabbi Yehoshua argues that a disqualification without כרת (karet) should be derived from another without כרת, and that outside its proper time (which involves כרת) should not be a proof; he also suggests deriving it from שלא לשמו (not for its own sake), which is a disqualification of thought without כרת.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's silence
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's silence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer is silent, indicating he accepts Rabbi Yehoshua's argument.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer falls silent, conceding the argument.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Meir's position
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Meir's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Meir distinguishes between a tereifah (disqualified before slaughter) and a blemished animal (disqualified after slaughter). It explains that this follows Rabbi Akiva's view that if such offerings ascended the altar, they do not descend, but Rabbi Yehoshua limits this to physical disqualifications, not to consecrating bread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir distinguishes between a tereifah (disqualified before slaughter) and a blemished animal (disqualified after slaughter).

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Akiva's view that if such offerings ascended the altar, they do not descend, but Rabbi Yehoshua limits this to physical disqualifications, not to consecrating bread.

items.text: Dispute between Rava and Rabbah on ascending
items.text_en: Dispute between Rava and Rabbah on ascending
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case of a sin-offering slaughtered outside its proper time or place. Rava says it descends (following Rabbi Yehoshua), while Rabbah says it does not descend (following Rabbi Eliezer). Rabbah later retracts in light of Rabbi Eliezer's retraction, but some say he did not retract because the analogy to שלא לשמו would still prevent descent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a dispute: for a sin-offering slaughtered outside its proper time, if it ascended it does not descend; for one slaughtered outside its proper place, Rava says it descends and Rabbah says it does not descend.

The Gemara explains that Rava follows Rabbi Yehoshua (who compares outside the place to a blemish, so it descends), while Rabbah follows Rabbi Eliezer (who compares outside the place to outside the time, so it does not descend).
The Gemara reports that Rabbah retracted his opinion in favor of Rava, because Rabbi Eliezer retracted in favor of Rabbi Yehoshua.

An alternative version objects: even though Rabbi Eliezer retracted, Rabbah did not retract, because in the case of the loaves Rabbi Eliezer conceded due to the analogy to שלא לשמו (not for its sake), but here, if one deduces from שלא לשמו, the rule would be that if it ascended it does not descend.

items.text: Rabbi Pappa's comment on the Mishnah's choice of example
items.text_en: Rabbi Pappa's comment on the Mishnah's choice of example
items.desc_en: Rabbi Pappa explains why the Mishnah (in the previous chapter) mentions a ram of a Nazirite rather than the ram of consecration, stating that the Tanna chose the more common case.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Pappa questions why the Tanna of our Mishnah omits the common case of the Nazirite's ram and instead teaches the ram of consecration.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna of our Mishnah taught the primary matter, i.e., the first offering brought with loaves.

items.text: Mishnah: Libations consecrated in a vessel
items.text_en: Mishnah: Libations consecrated in a vessel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if libations were consecrated in a vessel and the accompanying animal was found to be invalid, if there is another animal, they are offered with it; otherwise, they are invalidated by being left overnight.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: libations that were consecrated in a vessel and the sacrifice was found invalid — if there is another sacrifice, they are offered with it; if not, they are invalidated by overnight stay.

items.text: Gemara: Ze'iri's principle and analysis of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Ze'iri's principle and analysis of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Ze'iri states that libations are only consecrated through the slaughter of the animal, based on the verse 'זבח ונסכים'. The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case, suggesting the animal was invalidated during slaughter, but resolves that it was invalidated during sprinkling. It then discusses whether this follows Rabbi's view that two permitting factors can substitute for each other, or Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's view in a case where the blood was received in a cup and spilled.

sub.desc_en: Ze'iri states that libations (נסכים) are only consecrated through the slaughter of the animal, citing the verse 'זבח ונסכים' (sacrifice and libations).
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's case of a disqualified animal refers to disqualification during slaughter.
The Gemara answers that the disqualification occurred during the sprinkling (זריקה), not during slaughter.
The Gemara asks whose view this follows, suggesting it aligns with Rabbi's principle that two permitting factors (דברים המתירין) can substitute for each other.

The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, the case involves receiving the blood in a cup that was spilled, so the libations were already consecrated before the disqualification.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds like his father, Rabbi Shimon, that anything standing to be sprinkled is considered as if already sprinkled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds like his father Rabbi Shimon, that anything standing to be sprinkled is considered as if already sprinkled.

items.text: Conditional stipulation for libations
items.text_en: Conditional stipulation for libations
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how libations can be used for another sacrifice if they were designated for a specific one. Rabbi Yannai answers that the court stipulates conditionally: if needed, they are used; if not, they go to another sacrifice. The Gemara objects that oil is part of the meal offering itself, and questions why they are not redeemed for non-sacred use, but a decree prevents that due to potential misunderstanding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how libations designated for one sacrifice can be used for another, citing Rav Chisda's ruling that oil designated for one meal offering is invalid for another.
Rabbi Yannai answers that the court stipulates conditionally: if the libations are needed for the original sacrifice they are used, otherwise they go to another sacrifice.
The Gemara objects that the same conditional stipulation should apply to oil, but notes that oil is an integral part of the meal offering itself.
The Gemara questions why the libations are not redeemed for non-sacred use, and answers that a decree prevents this due to potential misunderstanding.
The Gemara resolves that the decree also applies here, lest people mistakenly think libations designated for one sacrifice are valid for another.

items.text: Matitya ben Yehuda's condition
items.text_en: Matitya ben Yehuda's condition
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Matitya ben Yehuda that the ruling applies only when the sacrifice is already slaughtered at that time. If not, the libations become invalid due to being left overnight. The Gemara clarifies that the baraita itself implies this distinction.

sub.desc_en: Matitya ben Yehuda teaches that the ruling applies only when the sacrifice is already slaughtered at that time.
The Gemara asks: if there is no sacrifice slaughtered at that time, are the libations invalidated by being left overnight?
The Gemara objects: the baraita's latter clause should have explicitly distinguished this case rather than just saying 'if not, they are invalidated by being left overnight'.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita indeed means: when there is no sacrifice slaughtered, the libations are considered as if invalidated by being left overnight and are invalid.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and conditional stipulation
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and conditional stipulation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar accepts the principle of conditional stipulation by the court, citing a dispute about tamid offerings that were not needed. The Gemara distinguishes because there the animals can be redeemed through pasturing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar accepts the principle of לב בית דין מתנה עליהם (the court's conditional stipulation).

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Amram citing Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Amram citing Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a tradition about tamid offerings that were not needed, where Rabbi Shimon holds they cannot be redeemed while still unblemished, suggesting he rejects the court's conditional stipulation.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing the tamid case, because there the animals have a remedy through pasturing (they can be redeemed after becoming blemished).

items.text: Mishnah: Offspring of a todah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Offspring of a todah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that the offspring, substitute, or replacement of a todah offering does not require bread, as the verse specifies 'upon the sacrifice of the todah'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that the offspring, substitute, or replacement of a todah offering does not require bread, as the verse specifies 'upon the sacrifice of the todah'.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara expounds the verses to show that if a todah was lost and replaced, either may be offered with bread, but the second does not require bread. It also derives that offspring, substitutes, and replacements may be offered but do not require bread.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking what the verse 'תּוֹדָה יַקְרִיב' (he shall offer a todah) includes, and derives that if one set aside a todah and it was lost, then replaced, and both are now available, either may be offered with its bread, as the verse 'הַתּוֹדָה יַקְרִיב' (the todah he shall offer) teaches.

The baraita then clarifies that the second todah does not require its own bread, derived from 'יַקְרִיבֶנּוּ' (he shall offer it) – one, not two; then it includes offspring, substitutes, and replacements for offering via 'אִם עַל תּוֹדָה', yet excludes them from requiring bread via 'וְהִקְרִיב עַל זֶבַח הַתּוֹדָה' (he shall offer upon the todah sacrifice).

items.text: Rav Chanina's distinction and Rav Amram's question
items.text_en: Rav Chanina's distinction and Rav Amram's question
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah's ruling applies only after atonement, but before atonement they require bread. Rav Amram questions this, asking whether it refers to replacements of a todah of obligation, since the Mishnah already covers both cases.

sub.text: Rav Chanina in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Chanina in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah's ruling applies only after atonement (לאחר כפרה), but before atonement (לפני כפרה) the replacements require bread.

Rav Amram questions which case Rav Chanina's distinction refers to, arguing that whether it is before or after atonement, the Mishnah already covers both scenarios for replacements of a todah of obligation.

items.text: Gemara's initial analysis of Rabbi Yochanan's distinctions
items.text_en: Gemara's initial analysis of Rabbi Yochanan's distinctions
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a substitute for a voluntary todah requires bread both before and after atonement, while the offspring of a voluntary todah never requires bread, and the offspring of an obligatory todah requires bread only before atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by analyzing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: a substitute for a voluntary todah (תודה) requires bread both before and after atonement, because it is considered an increase in todah offerings.
The Gemara continues: the offspring of a voluntary todah never requires bread, as it is a leftover of the todah; the offspring of an obligatory todah requires bread only before atonement, not after.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's principle
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds the principle that a person achieves atonement through the improvement of the consecrated animal, and Abaye similarly holds this view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yochanan's statement teaches us.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds the principle that a person achieves atonement through the improvement of the consecrated animal, and Abaye similarly holds this view.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explicit statement
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explicit statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef reports Rabbi Yochanan's explicit ruling, repeating the same distinctions between substitute and offspring of voluntary and obligatory todah.

sub.text: Stam's citation of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Stam's citation of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The gemara cites an explicit statement by Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, repeating the same distinctions between substitute and offspring of voluntary and obligatory todah.

items.text: Shmuel's general rule
items.text_en: Shmuel's general rule
items.desc_en: Shmuel states a general principle: whatever would cause a chatat to die (if lost and found after atonement) makes a todah not require bread, and whatever would cause a chatat to graze (if lost and found before atonement) makes a todah require bread.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states a general rule linking the fate of a chatat (death or grazing) to whether a todah requires bread.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about todah and chatat
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about todah and chatat
items.desc_en: Rav Amram raises an objection from a baraita that discusses a case where a todah was lost and replaced, and then the original was found: only one requires bread, and the second does not. The Gemara contrasts this with a similar case for chatat, where the second animal grazes according to the Sages, but dies according to Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram raises an objection from a baraita about a todah that was lost and replaced, showing that only one requires bread, not two.
The Gemara contrasts the todah case with a similar chatat case, where the second animal grazes according to the Sages but dies according to Rabbi.

items.text: Resolution of Shmuel's position
items.text_en: Resolution of Shmuel's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to align Shmuel's rule with the baraita, first suggesting he follows Rabbi (who says a lost chatat dies), but then noting that Rabbi has no case of a grazing chatat. It then suggests Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon (who says five chatat die), but Rabbi Shimon has no grazing chatat at all. The Gemara concludes that Shmuel's statement is a single point: to reject Rabbi Yochanan's principle that a person achieves atonement through improvement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Shmuel holds like Rabbi, who rules that a lost chatat found after a replacement was offered dies.
The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi, where do we find a case of a grazing chatat, and answers via Rabbi Oshaya's case of two chatat set aside for backup.
The Gemara objects that in the todah case of Rabbi Oshaya's scenario, the todah would not require bread, so it suggests Shmuel holds like Rabbi Shimon, who lists five chatat that die.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon has no concept of a grazing chatat at all, so the parallel fails.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement is a single point: to reject Rabbi Yochanan's principle that a person achieves atonement through improvement (שבח הקדש).

items.text: Rabbi Abba's ruling on lost bread or todah
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's ruling on lost bread or todah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rules that if the bread of a todah is lost, one brings other bread, but if the todah itself is lost, one does not bring another todah, because bread comes on account of the todah, not vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rules that if the bread of a todah is lost, one brings other bread, but if the todah itself is lost, one does not bring another todah, because bread comes on account of the todah, not vice versa.

items.text: Rava's statement on money for todah
items.text_en: Rava's statement on money for todah
items.desc_en: Rava begins a statement about setting aside money for a todah, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins a statement about setting aside money for a todah, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Bread of todah that was lost and found
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Bread of todah that was lost and found
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the bread of a todah was lost and then found, it can be used for other todah bread, but not for a new todah itself. The Gemara begins to explore the reason.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that leftover bread from a todah can be used for other todah bread but not to bring a new todah itself.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Kahana's proof
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Kahana's proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the bread cannot be used for a new todah. It suggests Rav Kahana's teaching that todah bread is called 'todah' in Scripture, implying that the bread itself is considered the offering, so it cannot be reused for another todah. The Gemara then notes that the reverse is also true: the animal is not called 'bread'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the Mishnah's distinction.

The Gemara proposes Rav Kahana's teaching that todah bread is called 'todah' but the animal itself is not called 'bread', and then rejects this as insufficient because it would imply the opposite ruling.
The Gemara concludes that since the bread is called 'todah' but the animal is not called 'bread', the bread cannot be reused for another todah.

items.text: Rava's case of three todahs and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rava's case of three todahs and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rava presents a case where one set aside a todah, it was lost, and he set aside two more, then all three were found. The ruling depends on which one was used for atonement: the second never requires bread, while the first or third may. Abaye argues that all are interchangeable, so none require bread.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules on the status of bread for multiple todah animals that were lost and found, with Abaye adding that all are considered interchangeable.
Abaye objects that all three todahs are interchangeable, so none require bread regardless of which one was used for atonement.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's parallel to sin-offerings and the meaning of 'and similarly'
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's parallel to sin-offerings and the meaning of 'and similarly'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira applies the same logic to sin-offerings: if one set aside three sin-offerings and one was used for atonement, the second must die, the third grazes. Abaye again says all are interchangeable. The Gemara explains that 'and similarly' teaches that even though one might think the todah case is different because one can be 'increasing todahs', for sin-offerings one cannot increase, so the ruling is still applied.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira opens a parallel case: for sin-offerings (חטאות), if one set aside three and one was used for atonement, the second must die and the third grazes.
Abaye objects that all three sin-offerings are interchangeable, so if atonement was achieved with any one, the other two must die.

The Gemara explains that 'and similarly' (וכן) teaches that even though one might think the todah case is different because one can be 'increasing todahs' (מרבה בתודות), for sin-offerings one cannot increase, so the ruling is still applied.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Chiyya: Todah mixed with its substitute
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Chiyya: Todah mixed with its substitute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches that if a todah became mixed with its substitute (temurah) and one died, the remaining animal has no remedy. The Gemara analyzes the case: if the person said 'upon me' (obligation), he could bring another animal and bread with a condition. The baraita must be referring to a case where he said 'this is' (designation), leaving no solution.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches that if a todah became mixed with its substitute and one died, the remaining animal has no remedy, because bringing bread risks it being a substitute, and not bringing bread risks it being a todah.
The Gemara questions the circumstances: if the person said 'עלי' (upon me), he could bring another animal and bread with a conditional stipulation, designating the extra animal as a guarantee.
The Gemara answers that the baraita is necessary only when he said 'הרי זו' (this is), designating a specific animal, which leaves no remedy.
The Gemara provides a mnemonic for the upcoming series of challenges and topics related to the baraita.

items.text: Debate before Rabbi: Proposed solutions and rejections
items.text_en: Debate before Rabbi: Proposed solutions and rejections
items.desc_en: Students proposed to Rabbi: bring bread and condition that if the animal is the todah, it is its bread, otherwise it is non-sacred. Rabbi rejected because non-sacred items cannot enter the Temple courtyard. Another proposal: bring another animal and bread, condition that if the mixed animal is the substitute, the new animal is the todah, otherwise it is a peace-offering. Rabbi rejected because it reduces the eating time of peace-offerings. Levi proposed making the extra animal a 'surplus of todah', but Rabbi dismissed him as foolish.

sub.desc_en: Students propose to Rabbi: bring bread and condition that if the extant animal is the todah, it is its bread, otherwise it goes out to non-sacred status.
Rabbi rejects the proposal because non-sacred items cannot enter the Temple courtyard.
Students propose: bring another animal and bread, condition that if the mixed animal is the substitute, the new animal is the todah with its bread, otherwise the new animal is a peace-offering.
Rabbi rejects because it reduces the eating time of peace-offerings (two days vs. one day for todah).
Levi proposes: bring another animal and bread, condition that if the mixed animal is the substitute, the new animal is the todah with its bread, otherwise the new animal is a surplus of todah.
Rabbi dismisses Levi's proposal as foolish, saying he seems to have no brain in his skull.

items.text: Opening question
items.text_en: Opening question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Do we separate (bread) initially for leftovers? This introduces the problem of uncertainty regarding which animal is the todah and which is the temurah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one may separate bread initially for leftovers, challenging the mishnah's procedure for an uncertain todah and temurah.

items.text: First proposal: conditional declaration
items.text_en: First proposal: conditional declaration
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta suggests bringing an animal and bread, and making a conditional statement to cover both possibilities. Rav Nachman rejects this, noting that the animal would be carrying forty loaves on its shoulder, which is invalid.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta's proposal
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta's proposal
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta proposes bringing an animal and bread with a conditional declaration to cover both the possibility that the animal is a substitute and that it is the original thanks-offering.
Rav Nachman rejects the proposal, arguing that the animal would be carrying forty loaves on its shoulder, which is invalid.

items.text: Second proposal: using Rabbi Yochanan's principle
items.text_en: Second proposal: using Rabbi Yochanan's principle
items.desc_en: Abaye and the Rabbis propose using Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the area outside the Temple courtyard wall is sacred, by placing the bread there. The Gemara objects that the bread requires waving (tenufah) before God, which cannot be done outside, and bringing it inside would introduce non-sacred items into the courtyard.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and the Rabbis propose using Rabbi Yochanan's principle that the area outside the Temple courtyard wall is sacred, by placing the bread there and designating it conditionally.
The Gemara objects that the bread requires waving (tenufah) before God, which cannot be done outside the courtyard, and bringing it inside would introduce non-sacred items into the courtyard.

items.text: Third proposal: using Chizkiyah's principle
items.text_en: Third proposal: using Chizkiyah's principle
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi suggests using Chizkiyah's principle that forty loaves can be consecrated out of eighty, by bringing an animal and eighty loaves. The Gemara rejects this because it would reduce the consumption of the forty loaves (by the priests).

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's proposal
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's proposal
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi proposes using Chizkiyah's principle that forty loaves can be consecrated out of eighty, by bringing an animal and eighty loaves with a conditional declaration.
The Gemara rejects the proposal because it would reduce the consumption of the forty loaves by the priests.

items.text: Fourth proposal: using a pregnant animal
items.text_en: Fourth proposal: using a pregnant animal
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi suggests using Rabbi Yochanan's ruling about a pregnant sin-offering, by bringing a pregnant animal and waiting for it to give birth. Rav Kahana rejects this, questioning whether Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies when the leftover is not actually left over, suggesting instead that the reason is atonement through the value of the offering.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proposes using Rabbi Yochanan's ruling about a pregnant sin-offering: bring a pregnant animal, wait for it to give birth, and designate the offspring as the todah offering, with the original animal as temurah.

Rav Kahana objects that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling may only apply when the leftover is not actually left over, and the true reason is that a person gains atonement through the value of the consecrated item.

items.text: Fifth proposal: vowing a todah
items.text_en: Fifth proposal: vowing a todah
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Rav Huna suggests bringing an animal with a vow ("upon me") and another animal with bread, to cover the uncertainty. Ravina rejects this, citing the verse that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.

sub.text: Rav Dimi bar Rav Huna's proposal
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi bar Rav Huna's proposal
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Rav Huna proposes bringing an animal with a vow ("upon me") and another animal with bread, to cover the uncertainty of which animal is the todah and which is the temurah.
Ravina rejects the proposal, citing the verse that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay, arguing that one should not initiate a vow in the first place.

items.text: Mishnah: basic rule for todah
items.text_en: Mishnah: basic rule for todah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'upon me a todah' must bring the animal and its bread from non-sacred funds.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states: one who says 'I pledge a todah' brings the animal and its bread from non-sacred property.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
