items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases of a person who vows a todah offering, specifying that the animal or its bread comes from chullin or ma'aser sheni. It rules that if the animal is from ma'aser sheni and the bread from chullin, he brings both from chullin; if both are from ma'aser sheni, he brings them from ma'aser sheni money, not from ma'aser sheni wheat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases of a person who vows a todah offering, specifying that the animal or its bread comes from chullin or ma'aser sheni, and rules that if the animal is from ma'aser sheni and the bread from chullin, he brings both from chullin; if both are from ma'aser sheni, he brings them from ma'aser sheni money, not from ma'aser sheni wheat.

items.text: Rav Huna's principle
items.text_en: Rav Huna's principle
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that if one says 'I vow the bread of a todah,' he must bring a todah and its bread, because everyone knows that bread cannot be offered without a todah, so he meant the todah as well.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that one who vows 'the bread of a todah' must bring a todah and its bread, because he intended the todah and merely mentioned its bread.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution on the Mishnah's first case
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution on the Mishnah's first case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that if one says 'todah from ma'aser and its bread from chullin,' he brings both from chullin, arguing that since he specified the bread from chullin, he should bring the animal from chullin as well. It answers that saying 'todah from ma'aser' is like saying 'I vow bread to exempt so-and-so's todah,' which is invalid. The Gemara then challenges this logic with the reverse case and resolves that bread can exempt a todah, but a todah cannot exempt bread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that if one says 'todah from ma'aser and its bread from chullin,' he brings both from chullin, arguing that since he specified the bread from chullin, he should bring the animal from chullin as well.
The Gemara answers that saying 'todah from ma'aser' is like saying 'I vow bread to exempt so-and-so's todah,' which is invalid, so the specification is disregarded.

The Gemara challenges that by the same logic, the reverse case (todah from chullin and bread from ma'aser) should also be invalid, as it would be like saying 'I vow a todah to exempt so-and-so's bread.'
The Gemara resolves that bread can exempt a todah, but a todah cannot exempt bread, so the two cases are not parallel.

items.text: Baraita on coercion to bring bread with todah
items.text_en: Baraita on coercion to bring bread with todah
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one says 'I vow a todah without bread' or 'a sacrifice without libations,' the court forces him to bring the todah with its bread and the sacrifice with its libations. The Gemara infers that this applies only if he explicitly said 'todah,' but if he did not, he is not forced. It then explains that the baraita mentions 'todah' because it parallels 'sacrifice without libations,' which cannot be stated as 'libations without sacrifice.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that teaches: one who vows a todah without bread or a sacrifice without libations is forced by the court to bring the todah with its bread and the sacrifice with its libations.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that only if he explicitly said 'todah' is he forced, but if he did not say 'todah,' he is not forced.

The Gemara explains that the same rule applies even if he did not say 'todah,' but the baraita mentions 'todah' because it parallels 'sacrifice without libations,' which cannot be stated as 'libations without sacrifice.'

items.text: Debate between Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan on the baraita
items.text_en: Debate between Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan on the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the court forces him, since his vow includes a condition (nedar u'fitcho imo). Chizkiyah answers that the baraita follows Beit Shammai, who hold 'tifos lashon harishon' (grasp the first expression). Rabbi Yochanan says it could even be Beit Hillel, if he later says he would not have vowed that way. The Gemara then notes that a later baraita supports Chizkiyah, and Rabbi Yochanan concedes it is Beit Shammai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the court forces him, since his vow includes a condition (נדר ופתחו עמו) that should nullify it.
Chizkiyah answers that the baraita follows Beit Shammai, who hold 'תפוס לשון ראשון' (grasp the first expression), citing a Mishnah about a nazirite vow.
Rabbi Yochanan says the baraita could even follow Beit Hillel, if the person later says he would not have vowed that way, and 'forcing' means he wants to retract.
A baraita is cited that supports Chizkiyah, describing a case where the person says he would not have vowed that way and is forced to bring the full offering.
The Gemara notes that the baraita is consistent with Chizkiyah but difficult for Rabbi Yochanan, and Rabbi Yochanan concedes it is indeed Beit Shammai.

items.text: Interpretation of 'Shamor ve'Shamata'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Shamor ve'Shamata'
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava debate the meaning of the verse 'Shamor ve'Shamata' cited in the baraita. Abaye says 'Shamor' means bring the todah, 've'Shamata' means bring its bread. Rava says 'Shamor' means bring the todah and its bread, and 've'Shamata' means do not be accustomed to act this way.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'שְׁמֹר וְשָׁמַעְתָּ' (Shamor ve'Shamata) in the baraita means.
Abaye explains: 'שְׁמֹר' means bring the todah, and 'וְשָׁמַעְתָּ' means bring its bread.
Rava explains: 'שְׁמֹר' means bring the todah and its bread together, and 'וְשָׁמַעְתָּ' means do not be accustomed to act this way (i.e., do not make such a vow).

items.text: Discussion on bringing todah from ma'aser sheni money
items.text_en: Discussion on bringing todah from ma'aser sheni money
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's ruling that one brings the todah from ma'aser sheni money, not from ma'aser sheni wheat. Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda say that if he wants, he may bring, but if not, he need not. They also say that the prohibition applies only to ma'aser sheni wheat, but wheat purchased with ma'aser sheni money is permitted. Rabbi Yirmiyah and Rabbi Zeira debate this, with Rabbi Zeira arguing that even wheat purchased with ma'aser sheni money is forbidden, deriving from the laws of shelamim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one brings the todah and its bread from ma'aser sheni, asking whether it is obligatory or optional.
Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda answer that bringing the todah from ma'aser sheni is optional: if he wants, he brings; if not, he need not.
Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda clarify that the prohibition applies only to ma'aser sheni wheat itself, but wheat purchased with ma'aser sheni money is permitted.
Rabbi Yirmiyah, sitting before Rabbi Zeira, repeats the lenient ruling that wheat purchased with ma'aser sheni money is permitted.
Rabbi Zeira objects, stating that even wheat purchased with ma'aser sheni money is forbidden, and he offers to explain both his own reasoning and Rabbi Yirmiyah's.
Rabbi Zeira begins his explanation by noting that the law of todah is derived from shelamim, implying a stricter application.

items.text: Gemara's inference: todah cannot come from second-tithe money
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: todah cannot come from second-tithe money
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the comparison of shelamim to ma'aser that just as shelamim are not themselves ma'aser, so too the todah offering cannot be brought from wheat purchased with second-tithe money. It then clarifies the reasoning: the comparison is to exclude items that are themselves a type of ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'שם' between shelamim and ma'aser that just as shelamim are not themselves ma'aser, so too the todah offering cannot be brought from wheat purchased with second-tithe money.
The Gemara clarifies the reasoning: the comparison is to exclude items that are themselves a type of ma'aser (מין מעשר), such as wheat bought with second-tithe money.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's ruling: designating second-tithe money for shelamim does not acquire
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's ruling: designating second-tithe money for shelamim does not acquire
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami states that one who designates second-tithe money for peace offerings does not acquire them, because the sanctity of peace offerings is not strong enough to override the sanctity of second tithe.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami rules that one who designates second-tithe money for peace offerings does not acquire them, because the sanctity of peace offerings is not strong enough to override the sanctity of second tithe.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and Rav's resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and Rav's resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita about purchasing an animal for peace offerings, which implies that the animal is acquired for peace offerings. Rav resolves that the baraita means the hide does not become unconsecrated, and Rabbah explains it is like buying an ox for plowing.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita: one who purchases an animal for peace offerings does not cause the hide to become unconsecrated, implying that the animal is acquired for peace offerings.
Rav resolves that the baraita means the hide does not become unconsecrated, and Rabbah explains it is like buying an ox for plowing — the animal is not consecrated.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar, framed by Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar, framed by Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says one who designates second-tithe money for shelamim acquires them, while Rabbi Elazar says not. This is explained in the context of Rabbi Yehuda (who holds second tithe is owner's property) and Rabbi Meir (who holds it is sacred property). The dispute is only according to Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says one who designates second-tithe money for shelamim acquires them, while Rabbi Elazar says not.
The Gemara explains that the dispute is only according to Rabbi Meir, who holds second tithe is sacred property; according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds it is owner's property, all agree one acquires.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about adding two fifths, and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about adding two fifths, and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who designates second-tithe money for shelamim, when redeeming it, adds two fifths—one for hekdesh and one for ma'aser. The Gemara resolves that this baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda's view, not the general dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states one who designates second-tithe money for shelamim adds two fifths when redeeming them, one for hekdesh and one for ma'aser.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita is not a universal view but follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, thus not contradicting the earlier dispute.

items.text: Mishnah: Obligatory offerings must come from chullin
items.text_en: Mishnah: Obligatory offerings must come from chullin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one who vows a todah or shelamim must bring it from unconsecrated funds, derived from a hekesh to the paschal offering. The verse 'You shall sacrifice the Passover... sheep and cattle' teaches that all obligatory offerings from sheep or cattle must come from chullin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking the source for the rule that one who vows a todah must bring it from unconsecrated funds, and derives it via a hekesh (analogy) to the paschal offering.
The Mishnah concludes that one who vows a todah or shelamim, since they are obligatory, must bring them only from unconsecrated funds, and their libations likewise.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation for the paschal offering itself, and dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation for the paschal offering itself, and dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know the paschal offering itself must come from chullin. Rabbi Eliezer derives it from a gezerah shavah between the Passover in Egypt and later generations. Rabbi Akiva objects that one cannot derive a possible case from an impossible one, but Rabbi Eliezer insists it is a strong proof. Rabbi Akiva then offers an alternative derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the paschal offering itself must come from chullin?
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer derives from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the Passover in Egypt and later generations that the paschal offering must come from chullin.
Rabbi Akiva objects: Can one derive a possible case (later generations) from an impossible one (Egypt, where there was no maaser)?
Rabbi Eliezer rejects the objection, insisting that despite the impossibility, it is a strong proof and we learn from it.
Rabbi Akiva offers an alternative derivation, noting that the Passover in Egypt did not require blood placement on the altar or burning of sacrificial portions (אימורין), implying a different basis.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's objection to Rabbi Eliezer's analogy
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's objection to Rabbi Eliezer's analogy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva challenges Rabbi Eliezer's comparison of the Paschal lamb of later generations to the Passover of Egypt, arguing that the latter does not require blood and sacrificial portions on the altar, unlike the former.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva objects to Rabbi Eliezer's analogy by arguing that the Paschal lamb of later generations (פסח דורות) requires blood and sacrificial portions on the altar, unlike the Passover of Egypt.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's response with a verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's response with a verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer responds by citing the verse 'And you shall perform this service in this month' to argue that all services of that month should be like the Passover of Egypt.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer responds by citing the verse 'וְעָבַדְתָּ אֶת הָעֲבֹדָה הַזֹּאת בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה' (And you shall perform this service in this month) to argue that all services of that month should be like the Passover of Egypt.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Akiva's position
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Akiva's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Akiva's consistency: if he holds that one cannot derive a possible case from an impossible one, he should stand by his view; but if he retracted, the Passover of the wilderness would prove the point.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Akiva's consistency: if he holds that one cannot derive a possible case from an impossible one, he should stand by his view.
The Gemara suggests that if Rabbi Akiva retracted, the Passover of the wilderness would prove the point.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's argument within Rabbi Eliezer's framework
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's argument within Rabbi Eliezer's framework
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva argues according to Rabbi Eliezer's own logic: even if one can derive a possible case from an impossible one, the Passover of Egypt lacks blood and portions on the altar, so the later generations' Passover should not require them. Rabbi Eliezer responds with the verse 'And you shall perform'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Akiva argues within Rabbi Eliezer's own framework: since the Passover of Egypt lacks blood and portions on the altar, the later generations' Passover should not require them.
Rabbi Eliezer responds by citing the verse 'וְעָבַדְתָּ' (And you shall perform) to counter Rabbi Akiva's argument.

items.text: Gemara's question and explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's response
items.text_en: Gemara's question and explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Eliezer did not simply cite the Passover of the wilderness as a proof. It explains that Rabbi Eliezer was speaking within Rabbi Akiva's framework: for himself, the wilderness Passover would prove the point, but for Rabbi Akiva who does not derive possible from impossible, the verse 'And you shall perform' is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Eliezer did not simply cite the Passover of the wilderness as a proof against Rabbi Akiva's objection.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer was speaking within Rabbi Akiva's framework: for himself, the wilderness Passover would prove the point, but for Rabbi Akiva who does not derive possible from impossible, the verse 'וְעָבַדְתָּ' (and you shall perform) is needed.

items.text: Discussion on responding to a hekesh
items.text_en: Discussion on responding to a hekesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the objection is not raised now. Rav Sheshet says this teaches that one does not respond to a hekesh. In the academy it was said: Can something learned by a hekesh then teach by a hekesh? It was stated as a general principle: the entire Passover is one matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the objection is not raised now, given the current context.
Rav Sheshet answers that this teaches that one does not respond to a hekesh (analogy).
In the academy it was asked: Can something learned by a hekesh then teach by a hekesh?
It was stated as a general principle: the entire Passover is one matter, so the hekesh is not applied recursively.

items.text: Source for the Paschal lamb coming from non-sacred animals
items.text_en: Source for the Paschal lamb coming from non-sacred animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Akiva derives that the Paschal lamb must come from non-sacred animals. It cites a teaching of Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Eliezer from the verse 'This is the law of the burnt offering, the meal offering, the sin offering, the guilt offering, the inauguration offerings, and the peace offering'. It then begins to expound the verse: 'burnt offering' teaches that all require a vessel, and 'meal offering' teaches that all are eaten only by male priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Akiva derives that the Paschal lamb must come from non-sacred animals.

The Gemara cites a teaching of Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Eliezer from the verse 'This is the law of the burnt offering, the meal offering, the sin offering, the guilt offering, the inauguration offerings, and the peace offering'.

The Gemara expounds that 'burnt offering' teaches that all offerings require a vessel, and questions whether this refers to a sprinkling basin, noting that communal peace offerings also have such a vessel.
The Gemara resolves that the vessel is a knife, and derives that a burnt offering requires a knife from the binding of Isaac.
The Gemara expounds that 'meal offering' teaches that all offerings are eaten only by male priests, and begins to question whether this applies to sin and guilt offerings.

items.text: Derivation of communal peace-offerings from a verse
items.text_en: Derivation of communal peace-offerings from a verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the law that communal peace-offerings are eaten only by male priests is derived from a verse or from a general principle. It suggests that it comes from the verse 'in the most holy place you shall eat it'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse about communal peace-offerings is written explicitly, not derived from a general principle.
The Gemara explains that the verse 'בְּקֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים תֹּאכְלֶנּוּ' teaches that communal peace-offerings are eaten only by male priests.

items.text: Dispute among Tannaim
items.text_en: Dispute among Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that there is a dispute among Tannaim: some derive this law from one source, others from another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute among Tannaim is about the source for the law, with some deriving it from one verse and others from another.

items.text: Derivations from chatat, asham, miluim, shelamim, and minchah
items.text_en: Derivations from chatat, asham, miluim, shelamim, and minchah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives various laws for all offerings from specific offerings: chatat teaches that offerings sanctify through absorption; asham teaches that a fetus and placenta are not sanctified; miluim teaches that leftover offerings are burned but not living animals; shelamim teaches that offerings can become piggul; and minchah also teaches sanctification through absorption. The Gemara explains why both chatat and minchah are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from chatat that all offerings sanctify through absorption.
The Gemara derives from asham that a fetus and placenta are not sanctified, based on the principle that offspring of consecrated animals are sanctified only by their own existence.
The Gemara derives from miluim that leftover offerings are burned but living animals are not burned.
The Gemara derives from shelamim that offerings can become piggul (invalidated by improper intent).

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: A baraita taught in the name of Rabbi Akiva derives from minchah that all offerings sanctify through absorption.
The Gemara explains why both chatat and minchah are needed: each teaches sanctification through absorption in a case where the other might not apply.

items.text: Derivation of laws from chatat: from chullin, by day, with right hand
items.text_en: Derivation of laws from chatat: from chullin, by day, with right hand
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that all offerings must be brought from non-sacred property, by day, and with the right hand, based on the chatat. It then provides sources for these laws regarding the chatat itself: from the verse 'his own' for chullin, from 'on the day of his command' for daytime, and from a principle of Rava bar bar Chanah for the right hand.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the sin offering that all offerings must be brought from non-sacred property, by day, and with the right hand.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive these laws for the sin offering itself?
Rav Chisda answers that the sin offering must come from non-sacred property, derived from the verse 'which is his' — from his own, not from tithe money.
The Gemara questions the need to derive the daytime requirement from the sin offering, since it is already derived from the phrase 'on the day of His commanding'.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita cited the daytime principle from the sin offering for no reason, merely as a citation.
The Gemara questions the need to derive the right-hand requirement from the sin offering, since it is already derived from the statement of Rabbah bar bar Chanah.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah says in the name of Reish Lakish that wherever 'finger' and 'priesthood' are mentioned, the rite is performed only with the right hand.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita cited the right-hand principle from the sin offering for no reason, since it is actually derived from Rabbah bar bar Chanah's statement.

items.text: Derivation from asham: bones are permitted; Rabbi Akiva's source
items.text_en: Derivation from asham: bones are permitted; Rabbi Akiva's source
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the bones of all offerings are permitted, based on the asham. It then begins to cite Rabbi Akiva's teaching from a baraitha regarding the verse 'and you shall slaughter the Passover'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the guilt offering (אשם) that just as its bones are permitted, so too the bones of all offerings are permitted.
The Gemara begins to cite Rabbi Akiva's teaching regarding the verse 'וְזָבַחְתָּ פֶּסַח' (And you shall slaughter the Passover).

items.text: Gemara's question on the use of the leftover Passover
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the use of the leftover Passover
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is done with the leftover Passover offering, and cites Rav Nachman's derivation that it is brought as a peace offering, based on the verse 'And you shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God, flock and herd.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is done with the leftover Passover offering, and cites Rav Nachman's derivation that it is brought as a peace offering, based on the verse 'And you shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God, flock and herd.'

items.text: Alternative derivation from the father of Shmuel
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from the father of Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the same law is derived from the father of Shmuel, who interprets the verse 'If his offering is from the flock for a peace offering' to mean that something from the flock is for a peace offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the derivation of the leftover Passover sacrifice as a peace offering comes from this source.

The Gemara answers that it derives from the father of Shmuel, who interprets the verse 'If his offering is from the flock for a peace offering' to mean that something from the flock is for a peace offering.

items.text: Further derivation from the verses about the lamb and goat
items.text_en: Further derivation from the verses about the lamb and goat
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for multiple derivations and cites a baraita that expounds the verses 'lamb' and 'if a lamb' to include the Passover for the tail, and a Passover that has passed its year, and peace offerings that come due to Passover, requiring all the rites of peace offerings. The verse 'if a goat' teaches that a goat does not require the tail.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the derivation from the verses about the lamb and goat is needed, since the same law could be derived from another source.
A baraita is cited, expounding the word 'כֶּבֶשׂ' (lamb) to include the Passover offering for the requirement of the tail (אַלְיָה).

The baraita continues, expounding 'אִם כֶּבֶשׂ' (if a lamb) to include a Passover that has passed its year and peace offerings that come due to Passover, requiring all the rites of peace offerings: semikhah (סמיכה), libations (נסכים), and waving of the breast and thigh (תנופת חזה ושוק).
The baraita concludes, expounding 'וְאִם עֵז' (if a goat) to teach that a goat does not require the tail (אַלְיָה).

items.text: Explanation of the three verses for different cases
items.text_en: Explanation of the three verses for different cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that three verses are needed: one for a Passover that passed its time and its year, one for one that passed its time but not its year, and one for one that did not pass its time nor its year. Each case is necessary because one might think it is not brought as a peace offering due to its potential for another Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that three verses are written: one for a Passover that passed its time and its year, one for one that passed its time but not its year, and one for one that did not pass its time nor its year.

The Gemara explains that the first case is necessary because one might think that only a Passover that is entirely rejected (passed both time and year) is brought as a peace offering, but not one that passed its time but not its year, which could still be used for the second Passover.

The Gemara explains that the third case is also necessary: one might think that only a Passover rejected from the first Passover is brought as a peace offering, but not one that is still fit for the first Passover itself.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the phrase 'We have returned to you, the thanksgiving offering was brought.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formulaic phrase 'We have returned to you, the thanksgiving offering was brought.'

items.text: Mishnah: All offerings come from anywhere, except Omer and Two Loaves
items.text_en: Mishnah: All offerings come from anywhere, except Omer and Two Loaves
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all communal and individual offerings may come from inside or outside the Land, from new or old grain, except for the Omer and the Two Loaves, which must come from new grain and from within the Land. All offerings must come from the choicest quality, and the best places for flour are specified.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all communal and individual offerings may come from inside or outside the Land, from new or old grain, except for the Omer and the Two Loaves, which must come from new grain and from within the Land.
The Mishnah adds that all offerings must come from the choicest quality, specifying the best places for flour and noting that all lands are fit but these were the preferred sources.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about the Omer and Two Loaves from old grain
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about the Omer and Two Loaves from old grain
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with a baraita that says the Omer and Two Loaves from old grain are valid, though they lack a mitzvah. It then derives from verses that the Omer must be from new grain, and the Two Loaves must be from within the Land, but can be from old grain. The Gemara resolves a contradiction in the verses and cites Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Akiva who hold that the Two Loaves from old grain are valid, and the word 'new' teaches that all meal offerings must be from new grain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with a baraita that says the Omer and Two Loaves from old grain are valid, though they lack a mitzvah.
The Gemara derives from the verse 'תַּקְרִיב אֵת מִנְחַת בִּכּוּרֶיךָ' that the Omer can come even from old grain stored in the loft.

sub.text: Gemara's derivation for the Two Loaves
sub.text_en: Gemara's derivation for the Two Loaves
sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'מִמּוֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם תָּבִיאּוּ' that the Two Loaves must come from within the Land but can be from old grain.
The Gemara questions the derivation from 'תָּבִיאּוּ', and resolves that the plural form teaches both that the loaves come from within the Land and that they can be from old grain.
The Gemara objects that the word 'רֵאשִׁית' (first) in the verse teaches that using new grain is a mitzvah, not an absolute requirement.

The Gemara cites Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Akiva who hold that the Two Loaves from old grain are valid, and the word 'חֲדָשָׁה' (new) teaches that all meal offerings must be from new grain, and they only dispute regarding new grain.

items.text: The omer from outside the Land
items.text_en: The omer from outside the Land
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier dispute about the omer and two loaves applies only to produce from outside the Land; all agree that from the Land they are brought. It then cites Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the omer may come from outside the Land, interpreting 'when you come to the Land' as a time condition, not a location requirement, and that new grain outside the Land is biblically prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute about the omer and two loaves applies only to produce from outside the Land; from the Land they are brought, from outside they are not.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holds that the omer may come from outside the Land, interpreting 'when you come to the Land' as a time condition, not a location requirement.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holds that new grain outside the Land is biblically prohibited, and since it is biblical, they may also bring the omer as an offering.

items.text: Guards of seventh-year aftergrowths and the requirement of fresh barley
items.text_en: Guards of seventh-year aftergrowths and the requirement of fresh barley
items.desc_en: A mishnah states that guards of aftergrowths in the seventh year receive their wages from the chamber funds. Rami bar Chama challenges Rav Chisda: the verse says 'for eating' not 'for burning', implying that produce designated for the omer should not be burned if it becomes unfit. Rav Chisda responds that the verse 'for your generations' requires the omer to be brought even from such produce. Rami bar Chama then objects that the omer requires fresh ('carmel') barley, which is unavailable from old produce.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that guards of aftergrowths in the seventh year receive their wages from the chamber funds.
Rami bar Chama challenges Rav Chisda by citing the verse 'for eating' not 'for burning', implying produce designated for the omer should not be burned if it becomes unfit.
Rav Chisda responds that the verse 'for your generations' requires the omer to be brought even from such produce, so it cannot be nullified.
Rami bar Chama objects that he never said it should be nullified; rather, the omer requires fresh ('carmel') barley, which is unavailable from old produce.
The gemara resolves that even if one brings fresh barley that has dried, the verse 'carmel takriv' requires fresh barley at the time of offering, which is unavailable.

items.text: Two interpretations of the omer's source
items.text_en: Two interpretations of the omer's source
items.desc_en: It was stated: Rabbi Yochanan says the omer must be from fresh barley based on 'carmel takriv', while Rabbi Elazar says it must be from the beginning of the harvest based on 'reishit ketzircha'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar regarding the biblical source for the omer's requirement to come from fresh barley.
Rabbi Yochanan derives the omer's requirement from the verse 'כרמל תקריב' (you shall offer fresh grain), indicating it must be from fresh barley.
Rabbi Elazar derives the omer's requirement from the verse 'ראשית קצירך' (the beginning of your harvest), meaning it must come from the start of the harvest, not the end.

items.text: The omer must be from barley: tannaitic debate
items.text_en: The omer must be from barley: tannaitic debate
items.desc_en: Rabbah raises a question about the omer's grain type. Rabbi Eliezer uses a verbal analogy from 'aviv' in Egypt to prove it is barley. Rabbi Akiva argues that since the community brings its obligation from both wheat and barley (via the two loaves and the omer), if the omer were from wheat, the community would never bring an obligation from barley. An alternative explanation: if the omer were from wheat, the two loaves would not be 'first fruits', which is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah raises a question about the omer offering, asking whether it comes from barley or wheat.
Rabbi Eliezer uses a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'aviv' in Egypt to prove the omer is barley.
Rabbi Akiva argues that since the community brings its obligation from both wheat (two loaves) and barley (omer), if the omer were wheat, the community would never bring an obligation from barley.
The Gemara offers an alternative refutation: if the omer were from wheat, the two loaves would not be 'first fruits' (ביכורים), which is a conclusive refutation.

items.text: Beginning of the laws of first fruits
items.text_en: Beginning of the laws of first fruits
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new topic: first fruits are only brought from the seven species, and not...

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that first fruits (ביכורים) are only brought from the seven species.

items.text: Ulla's ruling on mountain dates and valley fruits
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling on mountain dates and valley fruits
items.desc_en: Ulla states that if one brings dates from mountains or fruits from valleys for bikurim, they are not sanctified.

sub.desc_en: Ulla rules that dates from mountains or fruits from valleys brought as bikurim are not sanctified.

items.text: Baraita on bikurim precedence and inclusion
items.text_en: Baraita on bikurim precedence and inclusion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Abba cites a baraita that derives from verses that bikurim must be the first of all offerings, and includes wheat, barley, and produce from various places like roof, ruin, planter, and ship.

sub.desc_en: Rabba sits and teaches a certain tradition about bikurim.
Rabbi Acha bar Abba objects to Rabba by citing a baraita that derives from verses that bikurim must be the first of all offerings.

sub.text: Baraita's derivation for wheat and barley
sub.text_en: Baraita's derivation for wheat and barley
sub.desc_en: The baraita derives that the new offering includes both wheat and barley through a verbal repetition of 'חֲדָשָׁה'.
The baraita derives that the new offering precedes bikurim, and includes barley harvest through a verse.
The baraita includes produce that grew on its own from the word 'בַּשָּׂדֶה'.

sub.text: Baraita's inclusion of roof, ruin, planter, and ship
sub.text_en: Baraita's inclusion of roof, ruin, planter, and ship
sub.desc_en: The baraita includes produce from roof, ruin, planter, and ship from the verse 'בִּכּוּרֵי כׇּל אֲשֶׁר בְּאַרְצָם'.

sub.text: Baraita's derivation for precedence over libations and tree fruit
sub.text_en: Baraita's derivation for precedence over libations and tree fruit
sub.desc_en: The baraita derives that bikurim precedes libations and tree fruit through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'מַעֲשֶׂיךָ'.

items.text: Gemara's analysis and resolution of the baraita's contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis and resolution of the baraita's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita mentions roof, ruin, planter, and ship, and questions whether this refers to bikurim or menachot. Rav Ada bar Ahava objects that if it were menachot, they are eaten only by priests. Rav Mesharshiya resolves with two verses: one for bikurim, one for menachot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita lists roof, ruin, planter, and ship, and concludes that the latter part of the verse refers to menachot.
Rav Ada bar Ahava objects that if the verse refers to menachot, they are eaten only by priests, contradicting the verse's implication that any pure person may eat.
Rav Mesharshiya resolves the contradiction by explaining that one verse applies to bikurim and the other to menachot.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says the entire baraita refers to menachot, and the end of the verse refers to loaves of thanksgiving.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by asserting that the entire baraita deals with menachot (meal-offerings), and the end of the verse refers to the loaves of the thanksgiving offering.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on Ulla's ruling
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on Ulla's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Ulla that bringing such produce does not sanctify, while Reish Lakish argues it does, treating it like a blemish in sacrifices. Rabbi Elazar explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning from the verse 'meireishit' and 'me'artzekha'. Reish Lakish uses 'aretz' for a gezerah shavah about the land's praise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one brought such produce it does not sanctify, while Reish Lakish rules that it does sanctify, treating it like a blemish in sacrifices.
The Gemara asks: Reish Lakish's reasoning is clear, but what is Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning?

Rabbi Elazar reports that Rabbi Yochanan saw in a dream a superior explanation: the verse says 'מֵרֵאשִׁית' (from the first) — not all first, and 'מֵאַרְצְךָ' (from your land) — not all your land, excluding produce from roofs, ruins, etc.
The Gemara asks: How does Reish Lakish interpret the word 'אַרְצְךָ' (your land)?

The Gemara answers that Reish Lakish uses the word for a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) taught by Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi: just as 'אֶרֶץ' elsewhere refers to the land's praise, so too here it requires produce that is a praise of the land.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan could counter: the verse says 'מֵאֶרֶץ' (from the land), not 'אֶרֶץ' (the land), so the verbal analogy is not applicable.
The Gemara concludes that Reish Lakish does not derive a distinction between 'אֶרֶץ' and 'מֵאָרֶץ', so he applies the verbal analogy.

items.text: Reconciliation of conflicting baraitot on roof, ruin, planter, ship
items.text_en: Reconciliation of conflicting baraitot on roof, ruin, planter, ship
items.desc_en: Two baraitot conflict: one says one brings and recites, the other says brings but does not recite. The Gemara resolves each case: roof of a cave vs. roof of a house, worked vs. unworked ruin, perforated vs. unperforated planter, wooden vs. earthen ship.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that produce grown on a roof, in a ruin, in a planter, or on a ship is brought and the declaration is recited.
The Gemara cites a second baraita that contradicts the first: one brings but does not recite the declaration.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding the roof: one baraita refers to a cave roof (considered attached to the ground), the other to a house roof (not attached).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding the ruin: one baraita refers to a worked ruin (fit for cultivation), the other to an unworked ruin.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding the planter: one baraita refers to a perforated planter (connected to the ground), the other to an unperforated planter.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding the ship: one baraita refers to a wooden ship (considered attached to the ground), the other to an earthen ship (not attached).

items.text: Resolving Rav Yochanan's difficulty — a tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Resolving Rav Yochanan's difficulty — a tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction by citing a baraita where rabbis debate whether produce from a roof or ruin is brought and the recitation is said, while produce from a pot or ship is not brought at all. It then recounts a parable of Yochana and Mamre arguing with Moses about bringing straw to a city full of straw, to which Moses replies with a proverb about taking local produce.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: forbidden field types and the procedure for preparing a field
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: forbidden field types and the procedure for preparing a field
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not bring grain from dunghills, irrigated fields, or tree-planted fields, but if brought it is valid. It then describes how to prepare a field: plow it the first year, sow it seventy days before Passover in the second year, and it yields abundant flour. The procedure for the treasurer to check for dust or weevils is given.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry on the sequence of plowing and sowing
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry on the sequence of plowing and sowing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrasing: does it mean plowing the first year and also plowing the second year before sowing, or plowing the first year and sowing the second without plowing? It brings a baraita of Rabbi Yosei that describes plowing the first year, then plowing again in the second year, and sowing seventy days before Passover to get thin stalks and long ears.

items.text: Detailed procedures and a tannaitic proof
items.text_en: Detailed procedures and a tannaitic proof
items.desc_en: The baraita details the full process from harvesting to bringing to the treasurer, who checks for dust. Per Rabbi Natan, the treasurer oils his hand to collect all dust. The Gemara notes that the baraita explicitly says 'plows again', confirming the second plowing. It then questions whether the Mishnah itself omits the word 'again'.

items.text: Reconciling the baraita with the Mishnah
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita with the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita uses the term 'shoneh' (repeats) while the Mishnah uses a different term. It resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a field that has been worked (avudah) and one that has not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita uses the term 'שונה' (repeats) while the Mishnah uses a different term, implying a contradiction.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a field that has been worked (עבוד) and one that has not.

items.text: The practice of plowing half and sowing half
items.text_en: The practice of plowing half and sowing half
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita describing the practice of plowing half a field and sowing the other half, and then switching. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Omer is brought from fields where the sun rises and sets. Abba Shaul and a story about Rav Chilkiyah bar Tovi illustrate this practice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the practice is and cites a baraita describing plowing half and sowing half.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Omer is brought only from fields where the sun rises and sets.
Abba Shaul supports this by describing the Omer field in the valley of Beit Miklah, which was sun-exposed and plowed half and sown half.

sub.text: Story about Rav Chilkiyah bar Tovi
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Chilkiyah bar Tovi
sub.desc_en: A story about Rav Chilkiyah bar Tovi illustrates the practice of plowing half and sowing half, yielding double produce.

items.text: Wheat infested with worms
items.text_en: Wheat infested with worms
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the wheat became infested, it is invalid. The Gemara cites a baraita that if most of the wheat is infested, it is invalid. Rabbi Yirmeyah raises a question about whether the majority is measured by the wheat or by the se'ah, and it remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the wheat became infested with worms, it is invalid for the meal offering.
A baraita is cited, teaching that if most of the fine flour or most of the wheat is infested, it is invalid.
Rabbi Yirmeyah raises an unresolved question: is the majority measured by the number of individual wheat kernels or by the volume of a se'ah?
The Gemara concludes that the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Lashes for consecrating infested wheat
items.text_en: Lashes for consecrating infested wheat
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether one who consecrates infested wheat is liable for lashes due to the prohibition of a blemished offering. The question is whether the wheat is considered blemished or if the prohibition applies only to animals. It remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether one who consecrates infested wheat is liable for lashes because it is considered a blemished offering.
The gemara raises the alternative that the prohibition of a blemished offering applies only to animals, not to wheat, leaving the question unresolved.

items.text: Wood infested with worms
items.text_en: Wood infested with worms
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any wood found with a worm is invalid for the altar. Shmuel distinguishes between moist wood, where the worm invalidates, and dry wood, where one can scrape it off and it remains valid. Rava asks the same question about lashes for consecrating such wood, and it remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any wood found with a worm is invalid for the altar.
Shmuel distinguishes between moist wood, where the worm invalidates, and dry wood, where one can scrape it off and it remains valid.
Rava asks whether one who consecrates such worm-infested wood is liable for lashes due to the prohibition of a בעל מום (blemished offering).
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: The Mishnah on oil and its sources
items.text_en: The Mishnah on oil and its sources
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Tekoa is the primary source for oil, and Abba Shaul adds Regev in Transjordan. It lists restrictions on bringing oil from certain types of fields or processed olives, with some invalidating and others being valid if brought.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that Tekoa is the primary source for oil, and Abba Shaul adds Regev in Transjordan, then lists restrictions on bringing oil from certain types of fields or processed olives.
The Mishnah adds Abba Shaul's opinion that Regev is second to Tekoa, and lists invalid sources for oil, concluding that if brought from those sources it is invalid.

items.text: The story of the oil merchant and the people of Ludkiya
items.text_en: The story of the oil merchant and the people of Ludkiya
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Tekoa is associated with wisdom, citing Rabbi Yochanan. It then tells a lengthy story about a man from Ludkiya who was sent to buy oil, and a generous farmer who provided him with vast quantities of oil, fulfilling the verse about dipping one's foot in oil.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse specifies that Yoav sent to Tekoa for a wise woman.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that because the people of Tekoa are accustomed to olive oil, wisdom is found among them.
A baraita interprets the verse 'and he dips his foot in oil' as referring to the tribe of Asher, which produces oil like a spring.
The story begins: the people of Ludkiya needed oil and appointed an agent to buy oil worth one hundred myriad.
The agent is directed from Jerusalem to Tyre to Gush Halav, and finally to a certain farmer working under his olive trees.
The agent asks for oil worth one hundred myriad, and the farmer asks him to wait until he finishes his work.
After finishing, the farmer walks behind the agent, who suspects he is being mocked.
At the farmer's home, his maid brings hot water and then a golden cup of oil, fulfilling the verse about dipping one's foot in oil.
After eating, the farmer measures out one hundred myriad of oil and offers to accompany the agent to collect payment for an additional eighteen myriad.
The farmer measures an additional eighteen myriad of oil and hires every available animal in the land to transport it.
Upon arrival, the agent redirects praise to the farmer, fulfilling the verse about one who becomes rich yet remains generous.

items.text: Beginning of a new discussion on oil restrictions
items.text_en: Beginning of a new discussion on oil restrictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to analyze the Mishnah's statement about not bringing oil from Beit HaZevallim, citing a baraita that seems to contradict it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's prohibition on bringing oil from Beit HaZevallim by citing a baraita that seems to permit bringing oil from anpakton (a type of pressed olive product).

items.text: Reconciling a contradiction about bringing invalid oil
items.text_en: Reconciling a contradiction about bringing invalid oil
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves a contradiction between two baraitot: one says if one brought oil from soaked olives it is invalid, another says it is valid. He attributes the lenient view to Rabbi Chiyya, who would sprinkle such oil, and the strict view to Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi, who would dip in it, with a mnemonic about the rich pinching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one baraita rules that oil from soaked olives is invalid (פסול), while another baraita rules it is valid (כשר), because it is merely residue (שרף).

Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing the lenient view to Rabbi Chiyya, who would sprinkle such oil, and the strict view to Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi, who would dip in it, with a mnemonic about the rich pinching.

items.text: Definition of 'shemen hamor'
items.text_en: Definition of 'shemen hamor'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the meaning of 'shemen hamor' from the Book of Esther. Rav Huna bar Chiyya says it is stacte, while Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says it is olive oil that has not reached a third of its growth. A baraita supports Rabbi Yirmeya's view, citing Rabbi Yehuda that it is oil that removes hair and softens the skin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'shemen hamor' refers to.
Rav Huna bar Chiyya identifies it as stacte (a resin).
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba identifies it as olive oil from olives that have not reached a third of their growth.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yirmeya's view, citing Rabbi Yehuda that 'anpikinon' is olive oil from olives that have not reached a third, used to remove hair and soften skin.

items.text: Oil from soaked olives and a question about consecration
items.text_en: Oil from soaked olives and a question about consecration
items.desc_en: A baraita states that oil from soaked, boiled, or steeped olives, or from sediment or foul-smelling oil, is invalid for the menorah. Rabba then asks whether one who consecrates such oil is liable for offering a blemished animal, concluding with teiku (undecided).

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that oil from soaked, boiled, steeped olives, sediment, or foul-smelling oil is invalid for the menorah.
Rabba asks whether one who consecrates such invalid oil is liable for offering a blemished animal, or if the law of blemish applies only to animals.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Mishnah: The three olives and their three oils
items.text_en: Mishnah: The three olives and their three oils
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes three types of olives, each yielding three grades of oil. For the first olive, the process involves crushing at the top of the olive, pressing in a basket (Rabbi Yehuda says around the basket), then pressing with a beam (Rabbi Yehuda says with stones), and finally grinding and pressing again. The first oil is for the menorah, the rest for meal offerings. The same pattern applies to the second and third olives, with variations in the initial processing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that there are three types of olives, each yielding three grades of oil.
The Mishnah describes the process for the first olive: picking at the top, crushing, and placing in a basket; Rabbi Yehuda says to place around the basket, and this is the first grade.
The Mishnah states that one then presses with a beam; Rabbi Yehuda says with stones, and this is the second grade.
The Mishnah states that one then grinds and presses again, and this is the third grade.
The Mishnah rules that the first grade is for the menorah, and the rest for meal offerings.
The Mishnah describes the process for the second olive: picking from the rooftop, crushing, and placing in a basket; Rabbi Yehuda says around the basket, and this is the first grade.
The Mishnah states that one then presses with a beam; Rabbi Yehuda says with stones, and this is the second grade.
The Mishnah states that one then grinds and presses again, and this is the third grade.
The Mishnah rules that the first grade is for the menorah, and the rest for meal offerings.

The Mishnah describes the process for the third olive: packing in the press house until it softens, drying on the roof, crushing, and placing in a basket; Rabbi Yehuda says around the basket, and this is the first grade.
The Mishnah states that one then presses with a beam; Rabbi Yehuda says with stones, and this is the second grade.
The Mishnah states that one then grinds and presses again, and this is the third grade.
The Mishnah rules that the first grade is for the menorah, and the rest for meal offerings.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's language and a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's language and a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah says 'megargero' (crush) or 'megalgelo' (roll). A baraita is brought that uses 'megalgelo' and details the process for the first, second, and third olives, including Rabbi Yehuda's alternative methods. The Gemara then notes a contradiction within the baraita regarding Rabbi Yehuda's view and resolves it by saying the tanna agrees with him on one point and disagrees on another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma about the correct reading of the Mishnah: is it 'megargero' (crush) or 'megalgelo' (roll)?
The Gemara brings a baraita that uses 'megalgelo' and describes the process for the first olive harvest, resolving the dilemma in favor of 'megalgelo'.
The baraita continues detailing the second and third grades of oil from the first harvest, and notes the same process applies to the second harvest.
The baraita describes the special processing for the third olive harvest, including softening in a vat and drying on the roof, to produce the first grade oil.
The baraita concludes the third harvest process with the second and third grades of oil, reiterating that the first grade is for the Candelabrum and the rest for meal offerings.
Rabbi Yehuda presents his alternative methods: crushing in a mortar instead of grinding, pressing with stones instead of a beam, and placing olives on the basket walls instead of the bottom.
The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: the crushing method aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, but placing olives inside the basket aligns with the Rabbis.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the tanna of the baraita agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on one point (crushing) but disagrees on another (placement in the basket).

items.text: Mishnah: Grades of oil and the derivation for meal offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Grades of oil and the derivation for meal offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah ranks the oils: the first of the first is highest, the second of the first equals the first of the second, etc., down to the third of the third which is lowest. It then argues that meal offerings should logically require pure olive oil like the menorah, but a verse limits 'zach' (pure) to the menorah, excluding meal offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: the first grade of the first olive is the highest quality; the third grade of the third olive is the lowest; intermediate grades are equivalent.

The Mishnah presents a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if the menorah, which is not for eating, requires pure olive oil, then meal-offerings, which are for eating, should also require pure oil — but the verse limits 'זך כתית' (pure pressed oil) to the menorah, not to meal-offerings.
The Mishnah resolves the argument by citing the verse 'זך כתית למאור' (pure pressed oil for light), which limits the requirement of pure oil to the menorah and excludes meal offerings.

items.text: Clarification of 'equal' regarding oil for menorah and meal-offerings
items.text_en: Clarification of 'equal' regarding oil for menorah and meal-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that the first oil is for the menorah and the rest for meal-offerings, asking how they can be equal. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'equal' means they are equal in that both are valid for meal-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can say the oils are 'equal' when the first is designated for the menorah and the rest for meal-offerings.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'equal' means both oils are equally valid for use in meal-offerings.

items.text: Interpretation of 'zach' and 'kattit' and the reason for the menorah's oil
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'zach' and 'kattit' and the reason for the menorah's oil
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that 'zach' means pure and 'kattit' means crushed. The Gemara questions whether such oil could be invalid for meal-offerings, but a verse shows it is valid. The phrase 'for the light' indicates a concern for financial loss, as Rabbi Elazar explains that the Torah is frugal with Israel's money.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa defines 'zach' as pure and 'kattit' as crushed, with Rabbi Yehuda emphasizing the latter.
The Gemara questions whether such oil could be invalid for meal-offerings, and answers with a verse showing it is valid.
The Gemara explains that the phrase 'for the light' indicates a concern for financial loss, not a requirement for the oil's quality.
Rabbi Elazar resolves the question by stating that the Torah is frugal with Israel's money, explaining the concern for loss.

items.text: Proofs that the menorah is not for light but for testimony
items.text_en: Proofs that the menorah is not for light but for testimony
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani interprets 'to you' as meaning God does not need the light. Rabbi Zerika quotes Rabbi Elazar that neither the table nor the menorah are for God's needs. A baraisa on the windows of the Temple shows they were designed to let light in, indicating God does not need the menorah's light.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani interprets the verse 'אֵלֶיךָ' (to you) to mean that God does not need the light of the menorah.
Rabbi Zerika quotes Rabbi Elazar that the placement of the table in the north and the menorah in the south shows God needs neither food nor light.
A baraita explains that the Temple's windows were narrow inside and wide outside, indicating God does not need the menorah's light.

items.text: The menorah as testimony to the Divine Presence
items.text_en: The menorah as testimony to the Divine Presence
items.desc_en: The verse 'outside the curtain of the testimony' indicates the menorah is testimony to all the world that the Shekhina rests in Israel. The Gemara rejects the possibility that the light is needed, noting that Israel was guided by God's light in the desert. Rava explains that the western lamp, which was lit from the others and where the lighting ended, serves as this testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the verse 'outside the curtain of the testimony' teaches that the menorah is testimony to all the world that the Divine Presence rests in Israel.
The Gemara raises the objection that perhaps the menorah is needed for light, but then rejects this by noting that Israel walked by God's light in the desert for forty years.
The Gemara concludes that the menorah is testimony to all humanity that the Divine Presence rests in Israel.
Rava explains that the testimony is the western lamp, which was given oil equal to the others, was used to kindle the other lamps, and was where the lighting concluded, demonstrating a miracle.

items.text: Mishnah: Sources and handling of wine for libations
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sources and handling of wine for libations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah specifies the preferred locations for wine: Kedorim and Atulin are first, then Beit Rimah and Beit Lavan in the hill country, and Kfar Signa in the valley. It lists disqualifications: wine from fertilized or irrigated fields, or from between them, is valid if brought; aged wine is disputed between Rabbi and the Sages; sweet, smoked, or boiled wine is invalid; wine from trellised vines is not brought, only from ground vines and cultivated vineyards. It also details storage in small jars, not filling them to the top for aroma, and not bringing wine from the mouth of the jar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the preferred wine sources: Kedorim and Atulin as first choice, then Beit Rimah and Beit Lavan in the hill country, and Kfar Signa in the valley, with all lands being valid but these being the preferred sources.

The Mishnah lists disqualifications: wine from fertilized or irrigated fields, or from between them, is valid if brought; aged wine is disputed between Rabbi and the Sages; sweet, smoked, or boiled wine is invalid; wine from trellised vines is not brought, only from ground vines and cultivated vineyards.
The Mishnah details storage in small jars, not filling them to the top for aroma.
The Mishnah states that one does not bring wine from the mouth of the jar, because of the reason that follows (the text is cut off at the end of the daf).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Wine libation rules and inspection
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Wine libation rules and inspection
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that wine for libations is not brought from sweet, boiled, or smoked grapes, nor from old wine according to Rabbi, but the Sages permit old wine. It also describes the inspection method using a reed and gypsum.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that wine for libations is not brought from the sediment or dregs, but from the middle third.
The Mishnah describes the inspection method: the treasurer sits with a reed, throws gypsum, and taps the reed.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda rules that wine with sediment is invalid, citing the verse requiring perfection for offerings.

items.text: Gemara's question on sweet wine and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question on sweet wine and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a contradiction: the Mishnah says sweet wine is invalid, but the earlier clause says helistyon (a sweet wine) is valid. Ravina resolves by saying to roll and repeat, while Rav Ashi distinguishes between sweet from sun (not repulsive) and sweet from fruit (repulsive).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the contradiction: the Mishnah says sweet, boiled, or smoked wine is invalid, yet the first clause says helistyon wine is valid if brought.
Ravina resolves the contradiction by saying the Mishnah should be combined and taught as a single unit.
Rav Ashi distinguishes: sun-heated wine is not repulsive, but fruit-heated wine is repulsive and thus invalid.

items.text: Dispute on old wine: Rabbi vs. Sages
items.text_en: Dispute on old wine: Rabbi vs. Sages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records that Rabbi prohibits old wine, while the Sages permit it. Hezekiah explains Rabbi's reasoning from a verse comparing wine to a lamb in its first year. The Gemara objects that a two-year-old lamb is invalid, so wine should be too, but a baraita says two-year-old wine is valid if brought. Rava gives a different reason: the verse 'Do not look at wine when it is red' implies it should be fresh.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi prohibits old wine for libations, while the Sages permit it.
Chizkiya asks for Rabbi's reasoning and cites the verse 'for the lamb, wine' to suggest a comparison.
The Gemara objects: if the analogy extends to a two-year-old lamb being invalid, then two-year-old wine should also be invalid, but a baraita says it is valid after the fact.
Rava provides Rabbi's true reasoning: the verse 'Do not look at wine when it is red' implies that only fresh red wine is suitable.

items.text: Laws of wine from vines and storage
items.text_en: Laws of wine from vines and storage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states wine is not brought from vines trained on trellises. A baraita explains these are vineyards worked twice a year. Rav Yosef's practice is cited. The Mishnah also says wine is not stored in large jars but in specific types, and jars are placed one by one.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that wine is not brought from vines trained on trellises, and that jars are not stored in pairs but one by one.
A baraita explains that the prohibited vines are those worked twice a year.
A story is cited about Rav Yosef's practice with a vineyard that produced wine of double strength.
A baraita specifies that wine is stored in specific types of jars: large, Ludian, and medium.

items.text: Inspection method and speech's effect on wine
items.text_en: Inspection method and speech's effect on wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the inspection: the treasurer throws gypsum and taps with a reed. A baraita clarifies the order. The Gemara asks why not just speak, and supports Rabbi Yochanan's statement that speech is good for spices but bad for wine.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the inspection procedure: the treasurer sits with a reed and taps it.
A baraita adds that the treasurer taps the reed after throwing the gypsum of dregs.
The Gemara questions why the treasurer does not simply speak, and cites Rabbi Yochanan's principle.
Rabbi Yochanan teaches that speech is beneficial for spices but harmful for wine.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's ruling and question on consecration
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's ruling and question on consecration
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says wine with sediment is invalid. Rabbi Yochanan asks if one who consecrates such wine is liable for a blemished offering, left unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks whether one who consecrates wine with sediment is liable for offering a blemished sacrifice, and the question remains unresolved.
Rabbi Yochanan asks whether one who consecrates such invalid wine is liable for offering a blemished sacrifice.
The Gemara considers two possibilities: since the wine is invalid, it is like a blemished offering; or the concept of blemish applies only to animals.
The question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Sources of animals for offerings and a homiletic digression
items.text_en: Sources of animals for offerings and a homiletic digression
items.desc_en: A baraita lists the origins of various offerings: rams from Moab, lambs from Hebron, calves from Sharon, doves from Har Hamelech. Rabbi Yehuda requires lambs as high as they are wide, supported by a verse. The Gemara then digresses into a homily about the watchmen on Jerusalem's walls and their recitation of Psalms.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists the optimal sources for offerings: rams from Moab, lambs from Hebron, calves from Sharon, and doves from Har Hamelech.
רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) states that one should bring lambs whose height equals their width.

רבא בר רב שילא (Rava bar Rav Sheila) explains the reason of רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) by citing the verse 'יִרְעֶה מִקְנְךָ בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא כַּר נִרְחָב' (your cattle shall graze in wide pastures), interpreting 'כַּר' as lamb and 'נִרְחָב' as wide.
The Gemara shifts to a homiletic digression, quoting the verse about watchmen on Jerusalem's walls and asking what they say.
רבא בר רב שילא (Rava bar Rav Sheila) answers that the watchmen recite the verse 'אַתָּה תָקוּם תְּרַחֵם צִיּוֹן' (You will arise and have compassion upon Zion).
רב נחמן בר יצחק (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) offers an alternative answer: the watchmen recite the verse 'בּוֹנֵה יְרוּשָׁלַיִם ה׳' (The Lord builds up Jerusalem).
The Gemara asks what the watchmen said initially, when the Temple still stood.

רבא בר רב שילא (Rava bar Rav Sheila) answers that initially they recited the verse 'כִּי בָחַר ה׳ בְּצִיּוֹן אִוָּהּ לְמוֹשָׁב לוֹ' (For the Lord has chosen Zion; He has desired it for His habitation).
The Gemara concludes the chapter with the formulaic phrase 'הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ כׇּל קׇרְבְּנוֹת הַצִּיבּוּר' (We return to you, all communal offerings).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on dry measures in the Temple
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on dry measures in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes two dry measures: a tenth-ephah and a half-tenth-ephah, with Rabbi Meir adding a second tenth-ephah. The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir derives from a verse that there were two tenth-ephah measures, one heaped and one leveled.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that there were two dry measures in the Temple: a tenth-ephah and a half-tenth-ephah, and Rabbi Meir adds a second tenth-ephah.
The Mishnah explains that the tenth-ephah measure was used for all meal offerings, measuring each tenth separately rather than using a larger vessel for bulls or rams.
The Mishnah explains that the half-tenth-ephah measure was used for the High Priest's griddle-cake offering, half in the morning and half in the afternoon.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir derives from the verse 'עִשָּׂרוֹן עִשָּׂרוֹן' (a tenth, a tenth) that there were two tenth-ephah measures in the Temple: one heaped and one leveled.
The baraita concludes that the heaped tenth-ephah measure was used for all meal offerings.

items.text: Dispute over the half-issaron and its derivation
items.text_en: Dispute over the half-issaron and its derivation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a leveled issaron was used for the High Priest's griddle cakes. The Sages argue there was only one issaron, deriving the half-issaron from the repetition of 'issaron'. Rabbi Meir derives it from the vav in 've'issaron', while the Sages do not expound the vav. The Sages derive the prohibition of measuring with larger measures from a dotted vav, which Rabbi Meir does not expound.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a leveled issaron was used for the High Priest's griddle cakes.
The Sages argue there was only one issaron, deriving the half-issaron from the repetition of 'issaron'.
Rabbi Meir derives the half-issaron from the vav in 've'issaron', while the Sages do not expound the vav.

sub.text: Rabbi Meir's explanation of the verse
sub.text_en: Rabbi Meir's explanation of the verse
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir explains that the verse 've'issaron echad lakeves ha'echad' teaches not to measure with larger measures for the bull or ram.
The Sages derive the prohibition of measuring with larger measures from a dotted vav, which Rabbi Meir does not expound.

items.text: Clarification of 'measuring' the half-issaron
items.text_en: Clarification of 'measuring' the half-issaron
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the half-issaron could be used for measuring, since the High Priest's griddle cakes did not come in halves; rather, a full issaron was brought and halved. Rav Sheshet explains that 'measuring' actually means 'dividing'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose the half-issaron served, and answers that it was used for measuring the High Priest's griddle cakes.
The Gemara objects: the High Priest's griddle cakes did not come in halves; rather, a full issaron was brought and then halved.
Rav Sheshet resolves that 'measuring' in the Mishnah actually means 'dividing'.

items.text: Inquiry: Was the half-issaron heaped or leveled?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Was the half-issaron heaped or leveled?
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether Rabbi Meir's half-issaron was heaped or leveled. Rav Chisda responds that since Rabbi Meir holds the issaron was leveled, the half-issaron was also leveled; and from Rabbi Meir's view, the Sages' issaron is also inferred to be leveled.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether Rabbi Meir's half-issaron was heaped (גָּדוּשׁ) or leveled (מָחוּק).
The Gemara interjects: why not ask the same question about the Sages' full issaron? It replies that the Sages' own issaron is itself in doubt.
Rav Chisda responds: from Rabbi Meir's view we learn about Rabbi Meir, and from Rabbi Meir we learn about the Sages.
Rav Chisda explains: since Rabbi Meir holds the issaron was leveled, the half-issaron was also leveled; and from Rabbi Meir's leveled view, the Sages' issaron is likewise inferred to be leveled.

items.text: Inquiry: Dividing the griddle cakes by hand or vessel
items.text_en: Inquiry: Dividing the griddle cakes by hand or vessel
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether the High Priest's griddle cakes were divided into loaves by hand or with a vessel. The Gemara concludes it was by hand, as using a vessel would be improper since the cakes are associated with a curse.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether the High Priest's griddle cakes were divided into loaves by hand or with a vessel.
The Gemara asserts it is obvious that division was by hand, because using a vessel would require inserting lumps of dough.
The Gemara objects: why not insert lumps of dough into a vessel?
The Gemara resolves that since the griddle cakes are associated with a curse (קללה), using a vessel would be improper (לאו אורח ארעא).

items.text: Inquiry: Does the Table sanctify the showbread's loaves?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Does the Table sanctify the showbread's loaves?
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether the Table sanctifies the loaves of showbread with its height. Rav Chisda initially says it does not, but Rabbi Yochanan's statement about the Table sanctifying a certain height above it leads to a resolution: the Table sanctifies to disqualify but not to permit offering.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether the Table sanctifies the handfuls of flour (קמצים) with its height, similar to how it sanctifies the showbread.
Rav Chisda initially answers that the Table does not sanctify the handfuls.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the Table sanctifies a certain height above it, implying it does sanctify.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: the Table does not sanctify the handfuls to permit offering (ליקרב), but it does sanctify them to disqualify (ליפסל).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the seven liquid measures
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the seven liquid measures
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists seven liquid measures in the Temple: hin, half-hin, third-hin, quarter-hin, log, half-log, and quarter-log. Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok describes markings on the hin for different offerings. Rabbi Shimon says there was no hin, but a measure of a log and a half for the High Priest's meal-offering. The Gemara cites a baraita with the same dispute among Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the seven liquid measures in the Temple: hin, half-hin, third-hin, quarter-hin, log, half-log, and quarter-log.
רבי אליעזר בר רבי צדוק (Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok) says there were markings on the hin vessel indicating the amounts for the bull, ram, and lamb.
רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon) says there was no hin vessel; instead, a measure of a log and a half was used for the High Priest's meal-offering, half in the morning and half in the afternoon.

The Gemara cites a baraita that records the same dispute: Rabbi Yehuda lists the measures in ascending order, Rabbi Meir in descending order, and Rabbi Shimon again denies the existence of a hin vessel.

items.text: Debate about the log and a half measure
items.text_en: Debate about the log and a half measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what measure was used for the High Priest's log and a half. The Sages suggest a half-log measure could be used, but Rabbi Meir argues that a half-log and a log would not suffice, and a quarter-log could be used instead, concluding that each measure serves only its specific purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what measure could replace the log and a half, and explains that an extra measure of a log and a half existed for the High Priest's חביתים (loaf-offerings).
The Sages respond that a half-log measure was there, and one could estimate using the half-log.
Rabbi Meir objects that even according to the Sages, a half-log and a log would not work; a quarter-log could be used, but the rule in the Temple is that each vessel serves only its own measure.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's statement
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok states that there were graduated measures in the hin, introducing an alternative view.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok states that there were graduated measures in the hin, introducing an alternative view.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda concerns whether measure remnants were sanctified. One opinion holds they were sanctified, so the quarter-log was given to Moses; the other holds they were not, so the hin was given and remnants were excluded.
