sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the opinions of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda regarding the measurement system.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the dispute concerns whether measure remnants (בירוצי מדות) were sanctified.

sub.text: Gemara's elaboration of the first opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's elaboration of the first opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the opinion that measures were filled from bottom to top, the remnants were sanctified, so the quarter-log was given to Moses and the remnants entered the vessel.

sub.text: Gemara's elaboration of the second opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's elaboration of the second opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the opinion that measures were filled from top to bottom, the remnants were not sanctified, so the hin was given to Moses and the remnants exited.

items.text: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that all agree remnants could be either sanctified or not; the real dispute is about 'full measures'—whether they must not be lacking or also not exceeding. One opinion requires no excess, the other allows excess as still called 'full'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces an alternative explanation: all agree that remnants (בירוצי מדות) may or may not be sanctified, but the real dispute is about the interpretation of 'full measures' (מלאים).

sub.text: Abaye's explanation of the first opinion
sub.text_en: Abaye's explanation of the first opinion
sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the opinion measuring from top to bottom holds that 'full measures' (מלאים) means neither lacking nor exceeding.

sub.text: Abaye's explanation of the second opinion
sub.text_en: Abaye's explanation of the second opinion
sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the opinion measuring from bottom to top holds that 'full measures' (מלאים) means not lacking, but excess is still called 'full'.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's view on the hin
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's view on the hin
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses Rabbi Shimon's statement that there was no hin measure. The Rabbis argue that Moses made a hin for anointing oil, but Rabbi Shimon holds it was only temporary and then hidden, while the Rabbis say it remained.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Shimon's position that there was no hin measure, and notes that he argued well against the Rabbis.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis hold there was a hin because Moses made one for the anointing oil, as the verse says 'ושמן זית הין' (and olive oil, a hin).
Mar holds that since the hin was not needed for future generations, it was made only temporarily and then hidden.
The other side (the Rabbis) holds that since the hin existed, it remained in use.

items.text: Clarification of the seven liquid measures
items.text_en: Clarification of the seven liquid measures
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the necessity of bringing a substitute measure, citing a tradition of seven liquid measures. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's view is reconciled by interpreting 'seven measures' as seven measurements, not vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the necessity of bringing a substitute measure, asking why a replacement is needed at all.
Ravina answers that just as there is a tradition of two supports in the community, so too there is a tradition that seven liquid measures were in the Temple, necessitating a replacement.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, who says there were changes in the hin, seems to contradict the tradition of seven measures.
The Gemara first answers that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok simply does not hold of the seven-measure tradition.
Alternatively, the Gemara resolves that 'seven measures' means seven measurements, not seven distinct vessels, reconciling Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's view.

items.text: Mishnah: Uses of the quarter-log and half-log
items.text_en: Mishnah: Uses of the quarter-log and half-log
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the uses of the quarter-log (for the leper's water and nazirite's oil) and half-log (for the sotah's water and thanksgiving offering's oil). The log measures all meal offerings, with a dispute about a sixty-issaron offering. The Gemara begins questioning the quarter-log's use.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks what the quarter-log measure was used for, answering: a quarter-log of water for the leper and a quarter-log of oil for the nazirite.
The Mishnah asks what the half-log measure was used for, answering: a half-log of water for the sotah and a half-log of oil for the thanksgiving offering.
The Mishnah states that the log measure was used for all meal offerings.

The Mishnah rules that even a meal offering of sixty issarons receives sixty logs, but Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov argues it only gets its single log, citing the verse 'for a meal offering and a log of oil'.
The Mishnah lists the oil measures for offerings: six logs for a bull, four for a ram, and three for a lamb.
The Mishnah lists the oil measure for the menorah: three and a half logs total, a half-log per lamp.
The Gemara reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was troubled: why was the quarter-log measure created? If for the leper's water, it could be measured with the half-log.

items.text: Gemara's question about the half-log measure
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the half-log measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a half-log measure was anointed, since it is used for the sotah (where the water is already sanctified) and for the todah (where the bread is sanctified by the slaughter of the offering).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a half-log measure was anointed, since it is used for the sotah (where the water is already sanctified) and for the todah (where the bread is sanctified by the slaughter of the offering).

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya's answer: for the High Priest's loaves
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya's answer: for the High Priest's loaves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya answers that the half-log measure was used to measure a quarter-log of oil for each loaf of the High Priest's griddle-cakes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya answers that the half-log measure was used to measure oil for the High Priest's loaves, a quarter-log per loaf, and he cites a verse criticizing those who question God's wisdom.

items.text: Rabbi's question and Rabbi Shimon's answer about the half-log
items.text_en: Rabbi's question and Rabbi Shimon's answer about the half-log
items.desc_en: Rabbi questions the purpose of the half-log measure, and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi answers that it was used to distribute half a log of oil to each lamp of the menorah. Rabbi approves.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi questions the purpose of the half-log measure, rejecting that it was for the sotah (suspected adulteress) or the todah (thanksgiving offering), since those are sanctified by their respective rituals.
Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi answers that the half-log was used to distribute half a log of oil to each lamp of the menorah, and Rabbi approves.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a lamp that went out
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a lamp that went out
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports in the name of Rabbi that if a lamp goes out, the oil and wick are considered removed. The procedure is to trim it, add oil, and relight it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports in the name of Rabbi (Judah the Prince) the procedure for a lamp that went out: remove the soot, add oil, and relight it.

items.text: Rabbi Zerika's inquiry and Rabbi Yirmeya's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Zerika's inquiry and Rabbi Yirmeya's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika asks whether the oil added to the lamp should be the original measure or the amount that was missing. Rabbi Yirmeya answers that it is the original measure, because otherwise one would not know how much was missing, and it would multiply the measures.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika asks whether, when adding oil to the lamp, one should add the original measure or only the amount that was missing.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that it is the original measure, because otherwise one would not know how much was missing and it would multiply the measures.

items.text: Supporting tradition and alternative attribution
items.text_en: Supporting tradition and alternative attribution
items.desc_en: A supporting tradition is cited, with Rabbi Avahu or Rabbi Abba reporting that Rabbi Yochanan or Rabbi Chanina said in the name of Rabbi that the oil is added in the original measure.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites a verse of praise applied to Rabbi Yirmeya's correct reasoning.
An alternative tradition is cited: Rabbi Avahu or Rabbi Abba report in the name of Rabbi Yochanan or Rabbi Chanina that Rabbi ruled the oil is added in the original measure.

items.text: Rav Huna's explanation: a removable lamp
items.text_en: Rav Huna's explanation: a removable lamp
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav Sheshet that the lamp in the Temple was removable (of parts), because otherwise it could not be trimmed since the menorah was made from a single talent.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rav Sheshet that the lamp in the Temple was made of removable parts.
The Gemara explains Rav Sheshet's reasoning: since the menorah was made from a single talent (כִּכָּר) and was hammered (מִקְשָׁה), it could not be trimmed unless it was of removable parts.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita that describes removing the lamps, placing them in a tent, and wiping them with a sponge. The Gemara resolves that Rav Sheshet follows the opinion of the Sages who say the lamp was never moved from its place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that describes removing the lamps, placing them in a tent, wiping them with a sponge, and then re-oiling and lighting them, implying the lamp was moved.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Sheshet follows the opinion of the Sages who say the lamp was never moved from its place.

items.text: Clarification and identification of the Sages
items.text_en: Clarification and identification of the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Sages' statement means the lamp never moved, and identifies them as Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, who describes a gold plate on the lamp that could be pressed to allow trimming and oiling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the statement 'they never moved it' implies that if they wanted to move it, they could.
The Gemara resolves that the correct reading is 'it never moved from its place,' meaning it was fixed.
The Gemara identifies the anonymous Sages as Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, who describes a gold plate on the lamp that could be pressed to allow trimming and oiling.

items.text: Dispute about the menorah's construction from a talent
items.text_en: Dispute about the menorah's construction from a talent
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Nechemya and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha about whether the menorah's lamps, tongs, and snuffers were made from the same talent of gold as the menorah itself, with scriptural derivations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Nechemya and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha about whether the menorah's lamps, tongs, and snuffers were made from the same talent of gold as the menorah itself.
The Gemara asks: on what scriptural basis do they disagree?

Rabbi Nechemya derives from the verse 'כִּכָּר זָהָב טָהוֹר יַעֲשֶׂה אֹתָהּ' (a talent of pure gold he shall make it) that the menorah itself comes from the talent, and from 'אֶת כׇּל הַכֵּלִים הָאֵלֶּה' (all these vessels) he includes the lamps, but excludes the tongs and snuffers via the restrictive word 'אֹתָהּ' (it).
The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction within Rabbi Nechemya's own statements, and resolves that there are two different Tannaic traditions attributed to him.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha holds that only the menorah itself comes from the talent, while the lamps, tongs, and snuffers are not from the talent; he interprets 'אֶת כׇּל הַכֵּלִים הָאֵלֶּה' (all these vessels) as referring to vessels made of gold, not necessarily from the same talent.

The Gemara supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha by citing the verse that explicitly states the tongs and snuffers are made of pure gold, and explains that the verse was necessary because one might have thought that since the lamp tips become blackened, the Torah would economize on Israel's money and allow them to be made of cheaper material.

items.text: Introduction to the half-log for the todah
items.text_en: Introduction to the half-log for the todah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the verse teaches that the oil for the todah is a half-log, not a full log like other minchot.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's derivation of the half-log
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's derivation of the half-log
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva derives the half-log from the double mention of 'bashemen' in the verse, interpreting it as a limitation. The Gemara questions this and offers a revised version of his argument.

items.text: Distribution of the half-log among the three types
items.text_en: Distribution of the half-log among the three types
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the half-log is divided: half for the challot and rekinim, and half for the revicha, based on an extra 'bashemen' in the revicha.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's rejection and halachic tradition
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's rejection and halachic tradition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya rejects Rabbi Akiva's derivation, asserting that the half-log for the todah, the quarter-log for the nazir, and the eleven days between niddot are halachot from Sinai. The Gemara adds that he measured with a log.

items.text: Debate on the log for the minchah of a poor metzora
items.text_en: Debate on the log for the minchah of a poor metzora
items.desc_en: The Sages derive from the verse that each isaron requires a log of oil, while Rabbi Nechemya and Rabbi Eliezer argue that even sixty esronim require only one log. The Gemara discusses the scriptural sources and the reasoning behind each position.

items.text: Libation measures for bulls, rams, and lambs, and the menorah
items.text_en: Libation measures for bulls, rams, and lambs, and the menorah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the libation measures: six logs for a bull, four for a ram, three for a lamb, from the verse. It also discusses the half-log for each menorah lamp, with a debate on whether the measure was derived from above or below.

items.text: Mishnah: mixing libations
items.text_en: Mishnah: mixing libations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that libations of bulls may be mixed with those of rams, and those of rams with those of lambs, and individual with communal libations.

items.text: Conclusion of previous sugya: Asham nedavah and the baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous sugya: Asham nedavah and the baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that there is no such thing as a free-will asham, and cites a baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan's view that an asham metzora slaughtered not for its sake becomes an olah requiring libations and another asham.

items.text: Mishnah: Measures in the Temple and the dispute over their surplus
items.text_en: Mishnah: Measures in the Temple and the dispute over their surplus
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all dry measures in the Temple were heaped except the High Priest's, which was heaped inward. For liquid measures, the surplus is sacred; for dry measures, it is unconsecrated. Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei dispute the reason.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's author and Rav Chisda's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's author and Rav Chisda's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah's first clause, suggesting it fits neither Rabbi Meir nor the Sages. Rav Chisda resolves that it is Rabbi Meir, interpreting 'all measures' as 'all measurements' (not just the vessels).

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yosei on the sanctity of measures
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yosei on the sanctity of measures
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: Tanna Kamma holds liquid measures were anointed inside and out, dry only inside; Rabbi Akiva holds dry were not anointed at all; Rabbi Yosei holds both were anointed inside only, but liquid's surplus is sacred because it is 'pulled' from the vessel, while dry is not.

items.text: Rav Dimi and Ravina: Do Temple vessels sanctify unintentionally?
items.text_en: Rav Dimi and Ravina: Do Temple vessels sanctify unintentionally?
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi cites Rav that this shows Temple vessels sanctify even without intent. Ravina disagrees, saying they only sanctify with intent, but a decree prevents people from thinking surplus can be taken out to unconsecrated use.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's objection and resolution: Inside vs. outside
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's objection and resolution: Inside vs. outside
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects from a case of showbread where vessels do not sanctify without intent. The Gemara resolves that inside the Temple, not everyone knows, so a decree is needed; outside, everyone knows, so no decree is needed.

items.text: Dispute over 'surplus libations' and the beginning of a new topic
items.text_en: Dispute over 'surplus libations' and the beginning of a new topic
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about surplus libations going to the altar maintenance, and disputes its meaning: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef says it refers to measure surpluses; Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to a case where one undertook to supply flour at a certain price and it dropped.

items.text: Dispute about leftover flour for libations
items.text_en: Dispute about leftover flour for libations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one undertook to supply flour from four se'ah and it stood at three, or from three and it stood at four, he supplies from four because the hand of the consecrated is on the upper side. Two baraitot are cited: one supporting Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef, which discusses using leftover flour for other offerings or as a 'summer' offering for the altar; the other supporting Rabbi Yochanan, which reiterates the Mishnah's rule and connects it to the principle of 'the hand of the consecrated is on the upper side' and the leftover libations for the summer altar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that if one undertook to supply flour from three se'ah and it stood at four, he supplies from four, because the hand of consecrated property is on the upper side.
The Gemara announces that two baraitot are cited, one supporting Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef and one supporting Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef
sub.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef
sub.desc_en: The baraita explains that leftover flour from these measures is used for another offering if available, otherwise it becomes invalid by being left overnight, or it is used as a 'summer' offering for the altar, which is an עולה (burnt offering) whose meat is for God and hides for the priests.

The baraita reiterates the Mishnah's rule that the supplier provides from four se'ah in both cases, because the hand of consecrated property is on the upper side, and identifies this as the source for the rule that leftover libations go to the summer altar.

items.text: Mishnah: Offerings requiring libations
items.text_en: Mishnah: Offerings requiring libations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all communal and individual offerings require libations, except for the firstborn, tithe, Passover, sin-offering, and guilt-offering. However, the sin-offering and guilt-offering of a leper do require libations.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all communal and individual offerings require libations, except for the firstborn, tithe, Passover, sin-offering, and guilt-offering, but the sin-offering and guilt-offering of a leper do require libations.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of libation requirements from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of libation requirements from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'And you shall make an offering by fire to the Lord' that only offerings that come as a vow or freewill offering require libations, excluding the firstborn, tithe, Passover, sin-offering, and guilt-offering. It further includes festival offerings like burnt-offerings of appearance and peace-offerings of the festival, but excludes goats of sin-offerings that come as a duty on the festival, using the verse 'And when you make a young bull' to teach that only offerings that come as a vow or freewill offering require libations.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'And you shall make an offering by fire to the Lord' and derives that only burnt-offerings, peace-offerings, and thank-offerings require libations, excluding meal-offerings.

The baraita considers whether firstborn, tithe, Passover, sin-offering, and guilt-offering might be included, then excludes them using the verse 'to fulfill a vow or a freewill offering' — only offerings that come as a vow or freewill offering require libations.

The baraita considers excluding festival burnt-offerings of appearance and peace-offerings of the festival, but includes them using the verse 'or in your appointed times' — all that comes in your appointed times requires libations.

The baraita considers including goats of sin-offerings that come as a duty on the festival, but excludes them using the verse 'And when you make a young bull' — just as a young bull is unique in coming as a vow or freewill offering, so too only offerings that come as a vow or freewill offering require libations.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan about bird offerings
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan about bird offerings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiya derives from the verse 'from the cattle or from the flock' that bird offerings do not require libations. Rabbi Yonatan argues that this is unnecessary because the word 'zebach' (sacrifice) excludes birds, and the verse comes to teach that one may bring either one or two animals for a vow. The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yonatan needs this verse, given his principle that a verse must explicitly say 'together' to require both, and concludes that it is necessary to counter a possible assumption.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiya derives from the verse that bird offerings do not require libations, since the verse specifies 'from the cattle or from the flock'.
Rabbi Yonatan objects that the verse is unnecessary because the word 'zebach' (sacrifice) already excludes birds.
Rabbi Yonatan explains that the verse comes to teach that one may bring either one or two animals for a vow, not that both are required.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yonatan needs this verse at all, given his principle that a verse must explicitly say 'together' to require both.
The Gemara resolves that the verse is necessary to counter a possible assumption that one might otherwise derive.

items.text: Derivation of libations for animal offerings from the juxtaposition of 'from the cattle' and 'from the flock'
items.text_en: Derivation of libations for animal offerings from the juxtaposition of 'from the cattle' and 'from the flock'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'if from the flock' implies that libations are required for each type of animal separately, even without the word 'together'. Rabbi Yoshiyah's view is challenged, and the necessity of the verse is explained to counter a potential assumption that unspecified offerings could be brought from both types with a single libation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the verse 'from the flock' is treated as if it also said 'together', implying separate libations for each type.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yoshiyah's view that even without 'together' it is as if written, asking why a verse is needed at all.
The Gemara answers by citing the verses that explicitly separate cattle and flock offerings.
The Gemara resolves that the verse is necessary to counter a potential assumption that unspecified offerings could be brought from both types with a single libation.

items.text: Derivation that the todah requires libations despite its bread
items.text_en: Derivation that the todah requires libations despite its bread
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the todah, which is a peace offering, needs a special verse to teach that it requires libations, since it is a 'zebach'. The answer is that one might have thought that because it has bread, it does not require libations, but the verse 'or zebach' teaches otherwise. A comparison with the ram of a nazirite, which also has bread but requires libations, is addressed.

sub.desc_en: Mar introduces the question: from where is it derived that the todah requires libations?
The Gemara objects: is the todah not a zebach (peace offering) that would automatically require libations?
The Gemara explains that the verse is necessary because one might have thought that since the todah has bread, it does not require libations, but the verse teaches otherwise.

items.text: Exegesis of 'olah' to exclude certain offerings from libations
items.text_en: Exegesis of 'olah' to exclude certain offerings from libations
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Torah wrote 'olah' explicitly. Without it, a general principle (klal ufrat uchlal) would include only offerings that do not come for sin, excluding chatat and asham but including bekhor, ma'aser, and pesach. The word 'olah' teaches that only offerings that are not obligatory and standing (i.e., not already obligated) require libations, thereby including certain cases like offspring of consecrated animals, temurah, and offerings that were disqualified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah needed to write the word 'עולה' (burnt offering) explicitly, since the verse 'לפלא נדר או לנדבה' (to express a vow or a freewill offering) might have sufficed.

The Gemara explains that without 'עולה', a hermeneutical principle of כלל ופרט וכלל (general, specific, and general) would have limited libations to offerings that do not come for sin, excluding חטאת (sin offering) and אשם (guilt offering) but including בכור (firstborn), מעשר (tithe), and פסח (paschal lamb); the word 'עולה' teaches that only offerings that are not obligatory and standing require libations.

Now that 'עולה' is written, the Gemara applies the כלל ופרט (general and specific) principle to include only offerings that are not already obligatory, thereby bringing in ולדות קדשים (offspring of consecrated animals), תמורה (substitution), and offerings that were disqualified or slaughtered not for their proper name.

items.text: The word 'or' in 'to fulfill a vow or a freewill offering' teaches separate libations for each
items.text_en: The word 'or' in 'to fulfill a vow or a freewill offering' teaches separate libations for each
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word 'or' (אוֹ) in the verse 'to fulfill a vow or a freewill offering' is necessary to teach that even if one brings only a vow or only a freewill offering, libations are required. Without it, one might think libations are only required when bringing both together.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that the word 'אוֹ' (or) is used for a different derivation, why is the phrase 'לְפַלֵּא נֶדֶר אוֹ לִנְדָבָה' (to fulfill a vow or a freewill offering) needed?
The Gemara answers: it is necessary to separate them, teaching that even if one brings only a vow or only a freewill offering, libations are required.

items.text: The word 'or' according to Rabbi Yonatan teaches separate libations for each type
items.text_en: The word 'or' according to Rabbi Yonatan teaches separate libations for each type
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yonatan, who does not require the word 'or' for the previous derivation, the word 'or' is needed to teach that when one brings both a vow and a freewill offering, each requires its own libation, not a single libation for both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: This derivation of the word 'or' works for Rabbi Yoshiya, but for Rabbi Yonatan, what purpose does the word 'or' serve?
The Gemara answers: The word 'or' teaches that even when one brings both a vow and a freewill offering, each requires its own libation, not a single libation for both.

items.text: The phrase 'or in your appointed times' teaches separate libations for mixed vow and freewill offerings
items.text_en: The phrase 'or in your appointed times' teaches separate libations for mixed vow and freewill offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the phrase 'or in your appointed times' is necessary to teach that even if one brings an olah as a vow and a shelamim as a freewill offering (or vice versa), each requires its own libation, and not a single libation for both, since they are considered separate categories.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the phrase 'or in your appointed times' is needed.

The Gemara answers that the phrase teaches that even if one brings an olah as a vow and a shelamim as a freewill offering (or vice versa), each requires its own libation, not a single libation for both.

items.text: The verse 'when you make a young bull as an olah or a zebach' teaches separate libations for two olot or two shelamim of different types
items.text_en: The verse 'when you make a young bull as an olah or a zebach' teaches separate libations for two olot or two shelamim of different types
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that this verse is needed to teach that if one brings two olot, one as a vow and one as a freewill offering, or two shelamim in the same manner, each requires its own libation, and not a single libation for both, despite being the same type of offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'when you make a young bull as an olah or a zebach' is needed.

The Gemara explains that the verse is necessary to teach that even when bringing two olot or two shelamim of different types (one as a vow and one as a freewill offering), each requires its own libation, and not a single libation for both.

items.text: The phrase 'to fulfill a vow or shelamim' teaches separate libations for multiple offerings of the same type
items.text_en: The phrase 'to fulfill a vow or shelamim' teaches separate libations for multiple offerings of the same type
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that this phrase is necessary to teach that even if one brings two olot as a vow and two olot as a freewill offering, or two shelamim as a vow and two shelamim as a freewill offering, each requires its own libation, and not a single libation for all, since the vow and freewill offering are distinct categories.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse includes the phrase 'to fulfill a vow or shelamim'.

The Gemara answers that without this phrase, one might think that if one brings two olot as a vow and two olot as a freewill offering, or two shelamim as a vow and two shelamim as a freewill offering, a single libation would suffice; the phrase teaches that each requires its own libation.

items.text: Rabbi Yoshiyah's derivation from 'from the cattle or from the flock' and 'thus you shall do for each one'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yoshiyah's derivation from 'from the cattle or from the flock' and 'thus you shall do for each one'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yoshiyah, the phrase 'from the cattle or from the flock' teaches that even within the same species, each animal requires its own libation, and the phrase 'thus you shall do for each one' teaches that even if brought at once, each requires its own libation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yoshiyah, why is the phrase 'from the cattle or from the flock' needed?

The Gemara explains that without the word 'or', one might think that separate libations are needed only for two different species, but for one species a single libation suffices; the verse teaches that each animal requires its own libation.
The Gemara further explains that the phrase 'thus you shall do for each one' teaches that even if the animals are consecrated at the same time, each requires its own libation, not just one for all.

items.text: Derivation that the chatat and asham of a metzora require libations
items.text_en: Derivation that the chatat and asham of a metzora require libations
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'and three tenths of fine flour as a meal offering' that the meal offering mentioned is the one that accompanies a sacrifice. From the verse 'and wine for the libation, a fourth of a hin, you shall make upon the olah or for the zebach for each lamb', it is derived that 'olah' refers to the olah of a metzora, 'zebach' to his chatat, and 'or for the zebach' to his asham. The Gemara then questions why both 'zebach' and 'or for the zebach' are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived — that the sin offering and guilt offering of a leper require libations?
The baraita explains that the verse 'and three tenths of fine flour for a meal offering' speaks of a meal offering that accompanies an animal sacrifice, not an independent meal offering.
The baraita clarifies that the verse 'and the priest shall offer the burnt offering and the meal offering' proves that the meal offering accompanies the sacrifice.

The baraita derives from the verse 'and wine for the libation... upon the burnt offering or for the sacrifice' that 'burnt offering' refers to the leper's burnt offering, 'sacrifice' to his sin offering, and 'or for the sacrifice' to his guilt offering.
The Gemara questions: Why not derive both the sin offering and the guilt offering from the single word 'sacrifice' without needing the word 'or'?

items.text: Initial derivation for chatat and asham of a leper
items.text_en: Initial derivation for chatat and asham of a leper
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a teaching that the word "zavach" includes both a chatat and an asham. It then qualifies that this applies only when both are of equal status, but when the asham is for qualification and the chatat for atonement, two separate verses are needed.

sub.desc_en: Mar cites a teaching that the word 'זבח' (sacrifice) includes both a chatat and an asham.
The Gemara qualifies that this applies only when both are of equal status, but when the asham is for qualification and the chatat for atonement, two separate verses are needed.

items.text: Rejecting the identification with the nazirite's offerings
items.text_en: Rejecting the identification with the nazirite's offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that "zavach" refers to the leper's chatat, and asks if it could instead refer to the nazirite's chatat and asham. It rejects this by citing a baraita that the verse "u'minchatam v'niskam" speaks only of olah and shelamim, and the ram that emerges from the general category teaches that all offerings brought as a vow or freewill offering require libations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that 'zavach' refers to the leper's chatat, and asks if it could instead refer to the nazirite's chatat and asham.

The Gemara rejects this by citing a baraita that the verse 'u'minchatam v'niskam' speaks only of olah and shelamim, and the ram that emerges from the general category teaches that all offerings brought as a vow or freewill offering require libations.

items.text: Derivation for the leper's olah
items.text_en: Derivation for the leper's olah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that "olah" refers to the leper's olah, and asks if it could refer to the olah of a woman after childbirth. Abaye answers that the olah of a woman after childbirth is derived from the end of the verse, citing Rabbi Nathan's teaching that "lakeves" refers to that olah, and that the principle is that the secondary element cannot be more stringent than the primary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that 'עֹלָה' (olah) refers to the leper's olah, and then questions whether it could instead refer to the olah of a woman after childbirth.
Abaye answers that the olah of a woman after childbirth is derived from the end of the verse, not from the word 'עֹלָה'.

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Nathan teaches that 'לַכֶּבֶשׂ' (for the lamb) refers to the olah of a woman after childbirth, and 'הָאֶחָד' (the one) refers to the eleventh animal of the tithe which is offered as a peace-offering.
The Gemara concludes that the principle is that the secondary element (the olah of a woman after childbirth) cannot be more stringent than the primary (the leper's olah), so the derivation stands.

items.text: Rava's identification and the need for three expansions
items.text_en: Rava's identification and the need for three expansions
items.desc_en: Rava states that the thing requiring three expansions is the leper. The Gemara then asks why the verse says "la'ayil" and Rav Sheshet answers that it includes Aaron's ram. The Gemara objects that this is already derived from "b'mo'adeichem", but explains that one might have thought it applies only to communal offerings, not individual ones. It then compares this to the olah of a woman after childbirth, and explains that the verse teaches that even a fixed-time offering requires libations.

sub.desc_en: Rava identifies the thing requiring three expansions as the leper.
The Gemara asks why the verse includes the word 'la'ayil' (for the ram).
Rav Sheshet answers that it includes Aaron's ram (the ram of the consecration offering).
The Gemara objects that Aaron's ram is already derived from the verse 'b'mo'adeichem' (in your appointed times).
The Gemara explains that one might have thought the verse applies only to communal offerings, not individual ones, so the word 'la'ayil' is needed to include Aaron's individual ram.
The Gemara asks why this case is different from the olah of a woman after childbirth, which is also an individual offering.

The Gemara resolves that one might have thought the rule applies only to offerings without a fixed time, but for a fixed-time offering like Aaron's ram, one might exclude it; therefore the verse teaches that even a fixed-time offering requires libations.

items.text: The inclusion of the palgas
items.text_en: The inclusion of the palgas
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse says "o la'ayil" and answers that it includes the palgas (a ram in its second year). It notes that this works according to Rabbi Yochanan, who says it is a distinct entity, but for Bar Pada, who says it is a doubtful case, a verse is not needed to include a doubt. The Gemara concludes that this is indeed a difficulty for Bar Pada.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse includes the phrase 'or to the ram' and answers that it includes the palgas (a ram in its second year).
The Gemara notes that this works according to Rabbi Yochanan, who considers the palgas a distinct entity, but for Bar Pada, who considers it a doubtful case, a verse is not needed to include a doubt.
The Gemara concludes that this is indeed a difficulty for Bar Pada.

items.text: Derivations from the verse about libations for different animals
items.text_en: Derivations from the verse about libations for different animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara expounds the verse "kakah ye'aseh lashor ha'echad..." to teach that there is no distinction between the libations of a bull and a calf, between a two-year-old and a three-year-old animal, between a lamb and a ewe, and between a kid and a goat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins expounding the verse: 'Thus shall be done for the one bull or for the one ram or for the lamb in the sheep or in the goats.' 'For the one bull' — what does it teach? Since we find that the verse distinguishes between the libations of a ram and those of a lamb, we might distinguish between the libations of a bull and those of a calf. The verse teaches 'for the one bull'.

items.text: Rav Pappa's statement
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says that Rava tested them (the students) on this matter.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports that Rava tested them (the students) on this matter.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Laws of Semikhah on Communal and Individual Offerings
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Laws of Semikhah on Communal and Individual Offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that most communal offerings do not require semikhah, except for the bull brought for all commandments and the scapegoat; Rabbi Shimon adds the goat for idolatry. Individual offerings require semikhah except for the firstborn, tithe, and Passover. The heir may perform semikhah, bring libations, and effect exchange.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a question about the libations of a ewe and answers it by citing a baraita about a goat serving for all sheep offerings except rams.
The Mishnah states that most communal offerings do not require semikhah, except for the bull brought for all commandments and the scapegoat; Rabbi Shimon adds the goat for idolatry.
The Mishnah states that all individual offerings require semikhah except for the firstborn, tithe, and Passover.
The Mishnah concludes that the heir may perform semikhah, bring libations, and effect exchange.

items.text: Baraita: Dispute Between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon on Semikhah for Goats of Idolatry
items.text_en: Baraita: Dispute Between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon on Semikhah for Goats of Idolatry
items.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Shimon includes the goats of idolatry as requiring semikhah, while Rabbi Yehudah excludes them and instead includes the scapegoat.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that records the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda regarding which communal offerings require semikhah.
Rabbi Yehudah counters that the goats of idolatry do not require semikhah, and instead he includes the scapegoat as requiring semikhah.

items.text: Gemara's Question and Ravina's Answer: Two Semikhahs in the Community
items.text_en: Gemara's Question and Ravina's Answer: Two Semikhahs in the Community
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita must include the scapegoat. Ravina explains that there is a tradition of two semikhahs in the community. Rabbi Shimon argues that semikhah is only performed by the owners, and here Aaron and his sons perform it; Rabbi Yehudah responds that they also achieve atonement through it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita must include the scapegoat, implying it is redundant.
Ravina explains that there is a tradition of two semikhahs in the community, so the scapegoat is needed as one of them.
Rabbi Shimon objects that semikhah is only performed by the owners, yet here Aaron and his sons perform it on the scapegoat.
Rabbi Yehudah responds that Aaron and his sons also achieve atonement through the scapegoat, so they are considered its owners.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeyah: The Dispute Reflects Their Positions on Atonement
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah: The Dispute Reflects Their Positions on Atonement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah states that the dispute follows their respective views. A baraita explains that Rabbi Yehudah holds that all groups (priests, Levites, Israelites) are atoned for by the scapegoat, while Rabbi Shimon holds that the bull atones for priests and the scapegoat for Israelites. The Gemara clarifies that for Rabbi Shimon, each atones for its own group.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah states that the dispute between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon follows their respective positions on atonement.
A baraita is cited, interpreting verses to show that Rabbi Yehudah holds that all groups (priests, Levites, Israelites) are atoned for by the scapegoat.
The baraita continues with Rabbi Shimon's position that the bull atones for priests and the scapegoat for Israelites, each for its own category of sin.
The Gemara clarifies that for Rabbi Shimon, although all groups are included in atonement, each offering atones for its own group.

items.text: Detailed Explanation of the Dispute: Atonement for Temple Impurity and Other Sins
items.text_en: Detailed Explanation of the Dispute: Atonement for Temple Impurity and Other Sins
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates: For Rabbi Yehudah, Israelites are atoned by the blood of the inner goat for Temple impurity, and priests by the bull of Aaron; for other sins, both are atoned by the scapegoat's confession. For Rabbi Shimon, priests are atoned by the bull's confession. A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yehudah, Israelites are atoned by the blood of the inner goat for Temple impurity, priests by Aaron's bull, and both are atoned by the scapegoat's confession for other sins.
A baraita is cited that distinguishes between Israelites and priests regarding atonement for Temple impurity, in accordance with Rabbi Yehudah's view.
The baraita continues with Rabbi Shimon's view that the bull's blood atones for priests regarding Temple impurity, and the bull's confession atones for priests regarding other sins.

items.text: Baraita on Semikhah for the Bull and Goats of Idolatry, and a Contradiction Resolved
items.text_en: Baraita on Semikhah for the Bull and Goats of Idolatry, and a Contradiction Resolved
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the bull requires semikhah by the elders, but the goats of idolatry do not, according to Rabbi Yehudah. Rabbi Shimon says the bull requires semikhah by elders, but the goats require semikhah by Aaron. A contradiction is raised from another baraita, which is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse requiring the elders to perform semikhah (סמיכה, laying of hands) on the bull, and reports that Rabbi Yehudah rules that the bull requires semikhah but the goats for idolatry do not.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon's position in the baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's position in the baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon disagrees and rules that the bull requires semikhah by the elders, but the goats of idolatry do not require semikhah by elders, rather by Aaron.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita, which apparently states that the living goat requires semikhah, implying a conflict with Rabbi Yehudah's ruling.

items.text: Opening statement: Scapegoats of idolatry require semikhah by elders, not Aharon
items.text_en: Opening statement: Scapegoats of idolatry require semikhah by elders, not Aharon
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that the scapegoats of idolatry do not require semikhah by Aharon, but by the elders.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution of the mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution of the mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges the previous interpretation of the mishnah, citing Rabbi Shimon's view that semikhah must be performed by the owners. The Gemara then reinterprets the mishnah: according to Rabbi Yehudah, the scapegoats require no semikhah; according to Rabbi Shimon, they require semikhah but not by Aharon, only by elders. Rabbi Shimon explains to Rabbi Yehudah that the scapegoats require semikhah, and the exclusion from Aharon is derived from the word 'the living'.

items.text: Question: Why does Rabbi Yehudah need a verse?
items.text_en: Question: Why does Rabbi Yehudah need a verse?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehudah needs a verse to exclude the scapegoats from semikhah, given Ravina's tradition that there are only two communal semikhah offerings.

items.text: Source for Rabbi Shimon: scapegoats require semikhah
items.text_en: Source for Rabbi Shimon: scapegoats require semikhah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Rabbi Shimon derives that the scapegoats require semikhah. It cites a baraita: Rabbi Yehudah derives from 'and he shall lay his hand on the head of the goat' to include the goat of Nachshon; Rabbi Shimon derives it to include the scapegoats of idolatry, as he holds that any sin-offering whose blood enters the inner sanctum requires semikhah.

items.text: Clarification and objection: Why the phrase 'he used to say'?
items.text_en: Clarification and objection: Why the phrase 'he used to say'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita uses the phrase 'he used to say' and explains it as a mere marker. It then objects: why not say the goat that is done inside (Yom Kippur) is included? The Gemara answers that it is analogous to the prince's goat, which atones for a known transgression of a positive commandment.

items.text: Ravina's tradition and the need for both halakhah and verse
items.text_en: Ravina's tradition and the need for both halakhah and verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why verses are needed if Ravina says there are only two communal semikhah offerings. It answers that both halakhah and verses are necessary: the halakhah prevents a kal vachomer argument from communal peace-offerings, and the verse identifies which offerings (analogous to the prince's goat).

items.text: Baraita: All individual offerings require semikhah except firstborn, tithe, and paschal lamb
items.text_en: Baraita: All individual offerings require semikhah except firstborn, tithe, and paschal lamb
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that all individual offerings require semikhah except the firstborn, tithe, and paschal lamb, each excluded by the word 'his offering'. The Gemara notes that a kal vachomer could be refuted, so these are mere supports (asmakhta).

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial derivation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah writes 'his offering' three times, deriving that an heir may perform semikhah, and that a non-Jew's offering and a friend's offering are excluded.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Chananya and Rava
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Chananya and Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Chananya teaches before Rava that an heir does not perform semikhah or temurah, but the Mishnah states the opposite. Rava suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that an heir does not perform semikhah or temurah.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's and the Rabbis' reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's and the Rabbis' reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'his offering' that an heir does not perform temurah, and learns the end of consecration (semikhah) from the beginning (temurah). The Rabbis derive from 'he shall substitute' that an heir may perform temurah, and learn the beginning from the end.

items.text: The Rabbis' use of 'his offering' and Rabbi Yehuda's alternative
items.text_en: The Rabbis' use of 'his offering' and Rabbi Yehuda's alternative
items.desc_en: The Rabbis use the three instances of 'his offering' to exclude a non-Jew, a friend, and to include all owners for semikhah. Rabbi Yehuda lacks the inclusion for semikhah, but derives it from two verses, using one to exclude the father's offering.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's use of 'he shall substitute' and the Rabbis' alternative
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's use of 'he shall substitute' and the Rabbis' alternative
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda uses the verse 'he shall substitute' to include a woman in temurah, while the Rabbis derive this from the word 'and if'. Rabbi Yehuda does not expound the word 'and if'.

items.text: Mishnah: Who may perform semikhah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who may perform semikhah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who may perform semikhah (everyone except a deaf-mute, imbecile, minor, blind person, non-Jew, slave, agent, and woman), and describes the procedure: two hands on the head, immediately followed by slaughter.

items.text: Gemara: Why is a blind person excluded?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why is a blind person excluded?
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the exclusion of a deaf-mute, imbecile, minor, and non-Jew, then asks why a blind person is excluded. Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi debate whether it is derived from the elders of the congregation or from the olat re'iyah (festival burnt-offering).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Stringencies of Semikhah vs. Tenufah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Stringencies of Semikhah vs. Tenufah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that semikhah is more stringent than tenufah in that one person can wave for all partners but cannot lay hands for all, while tenufah applies to both individual and communal offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that semikhah is more stringent than tenufah in that one person can wave for all partners but cannot lay hands for all.
The Gemara cites a baraita taught before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba that derives semikhah for obligation offerings from the verse 'וַיַּקְרֵב אֶת הָעֹלָה וַיַּעֲשֶׂהָ כַּמִּשְׁפָּט'.
The Gemara asks which persons cannot perform semikhah, citing a baraita that excludes a slave, an agent, and a woman from the verse 'יָדוֹ'.
The Gemara explains that each exclusion is necessary: a slave is not a mitzvah-doer, an agent is a mitzvah-doer but not like his own body, and a wife is like his body but still excluded.
The Gemara questions how semikhah can atone when atonement is only through blood, citing a baraita that juxtaposes 'וְסָמַךְ' and 'וְנִרְצָה'.
The Gemara resolves that if one performs semikhah as a leftover mitzvah, Scripture considers it as if he did not atone but still atoned.
A baraita applies the same logic to tenufah, stating that if performed as a leftover mitzvah, it is credited as if he atoned.
The Gemara asks where the hand must be placed, citing a baraita that excludes the neck, back, and chest from the verse 'יָדוֹ עַל הָרֹאשׁ'.

The Gemara explains that each exclusion is necessary: the neck is not adjacent to the head, the back is adjacent but not included in tenufah, and the chest is included in tenufah but still excluded from semikhah.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the hand may be placed on the sides of the head, and a baraita from Abba Bira in Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that it must be on the head, not the sides.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether a cloth interposes between the hand and the animal, and a baraita answers that nothing may interpose between him and the sacrifice.
The Gemara asks the source for requiring two hands, and Resh Lakish derives from 'וְסָמַךְ אַהֲרֹן אֶת שְׁתֵּי יָדָו' that wherever 'יָדוֹ' is written, it implies two hands unless specified 'אַחַת'.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar and Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar and Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar taught Resh Lakish's tradition without attribution, causing Resh Lakish to object by citing many instances of 'יָדָיו' in Scripture, but later they reconcile by clarifying that 'יָדָיו' refers to semikhah of an animal, not human.
The Gemara clarifies that in the place where semikhah is performed, slaughter follows immediately, establishing the sequence of semikhah then slaughter.
The Mishnah concludes that tenufah is more stringent because it applies to both individual and communal offerings, while semikhah only applies to individual offerings of obligation.

items.text: Gemara's Sixth Question: The Sequence of Semikhah and Slaughter
items.text_en: Gemara's Sixth Question: The Sequence of Semikhah and Slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that in the place where semikhah is performed, slaughter follows immediately, as stated: 'בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁסּוֹמְכִין שׁוֹחֲטִין, תֵּכֶף לִסְמִיכָה שְׁחִיטָה'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that semikhah is more stringent than tenufah in that one person can wave for all partners but cannot lay hands for all.
The Gemara cites a baraita taught before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba that derives semikhah for obligation offerings from the verse 'וַיַּקְרֵב אֶת הָעֹלָה וַיַּעֲשֶׂהָ כַּמִּשְׁפָּט'.
The Gemara asks which persons cannot perform semikhah, citing a baraita that excludes a slave, an agent, and a woman from the verse 'יָדוֹ'.
The Gemara explains that each exclusion is necessary: a slave is not a mitzvah-doer, an agent is a mitzvah-doer but not like his own body, and a wife is like his body but still excluded.
The Gemara questions how semikhah can atone when atonement is only through blood, citing a baraita that juxtaposes 'וְסָמַךְ' and 'וְנִרְצָה'.
The Gemara resolves that if one performs semikhah as a leftover mitzvah, Scripture considers it as if he did not atone but still atoned.
A baraita applies the same logic to tenufah, stating that if performed as a leftover mitzvah, it is credited as if he atoned.
The Gemara asks where the hand must be placed, citing a baraita that excludes the neck, back, and chest from the verse 'יָדוֹ עַל הָרֹאשׁ'.

The Gemara explains that each exclusion is necessary: the neck is not adjacent to the head, the back is adjacent but not included in tenufah, and the chest is included in tenufah but still excluded from semikhah.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the hand may be placed on the sides of the head, and a baraita from Abba Bira in Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that it must be on the head, not the sides.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether a cloth interposes between the hand and the animal, and a baraita answers that nothing may interpose between him and the sacrifice.
The Gemara asks the source for requiring two hands, and Resh Lakish derives from 'וְסָמַךְ אַהֲרֹן אֶת שְׁתֵּי יָדָו' that wherever 'יָדוֹ' is written, it implies two hands unless specified 'אַחַת'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Semikhah applies to all owners except partners
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Semikhah applies to all owners except partners
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that semikhah applies to all who bring an offering, including partners, unlike tenufah (wave offering) which does not apply to partners.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that semikhah applies to all who bring an offering, including partners, unlike tenufah which does not apply to partners.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation that partners perform semikhah
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation that partners perform semikhah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that uses the word 'קָרְבָּנוֹ' to include all owners for semikhah, rejecting a kal vachomer that would exclude partners. It then considers whether tenufah could be derived for partners via kal vachomer, but rejects it because tenufah cannot be performed jointly without interruption.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse 'קָרְבָּנוֹ' to include all owners for semikhah (סמיכה).
The Gemara raises a possible kal vachomer (קל וחומר) that would exclude partners from semikhah, since tenufah (תנופה) which is derived from slaughtered animals is excluded for partners.
The Gemara rejects the kal vachomer by invoking the verse 'קָרְבָּנוֹ' to include all owners for semikhah.
The Gemara asks whether tenufah could be derived for partners via a kal vachomer from semikhah.
The Gemara rejects the derivation because tenufah cannot be performed jointly without interruption, as the Torah requires a single act of waving (תנופה) not multiple wavings (תנופות).

items.text: Gemara: Semikhah on slaughtered animals?
items.text_en: Gemara: Semikhah on slaughtered animals?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether semikhah applies to slaughtered animals, citing a Mishnah where the High Priest performs semikhah on limbs after slaughter. Abaye explains that this is only due to the honor of the High Priest, not a general rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether semikhah applies to slaughtered animals, citing a Mishnah about the High Priest's actions.
The Mishnah describes the High Priest performing semikhah on limbs after slaughter, implying semikhah applies to slaughtered animals.
Abaye resolves that the semikhah in the Mishnah is only due to the honor of the High Priest, not a general rule.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the phrase 'הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ שְׁתֵּי מִדּוֹת' (We return to you, Two Measures).

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes the chapter with the formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you, chapter 'Two Measures').

items.text: New Mishnah: Preparation of showbread and two loaves
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Preparation of showbread and two loaves
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the two loaves are kneaded and baked one at a time, while the showbread is kneaded one at a time but baked two at a time, and molds are used to prevent spoilage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the two loaves (שתי הלחם) are kneaded and baked one at a time, while the showbread (לחם הפנים) is kneaded one at a time but baked two at a time, and both are made in molds.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural sources for kneading and baking
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural sources for kneading and baking
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that showbread is kneaded one at a time, and that the two loaves follow suit. It also derives that showbread is baked two at a time, while the two loaves are baked one at a time, using the word 'אוֹתָם' to exclude the two loaves from the two-at-a-time rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's rules about kneading and baking showbread and the two loaves, and cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'שְׁנֵי עֶשְׂרֹנִים יִהְיֶה הַחַלָּה הָאֶחָת' that showbread is kneaded one at a time.

The baraita continues, deriving from the word 'יִהְיֶה' that the two loaves are also kneaded one at a time, and from 'וְשַׂמְתָּ אוֹתָם' that showbread is baked two at a time, but the word 'אוֹתָם' excludes the two loaves from this rule.

The Gemara resolves a potential redundancy: since the verse could have said 'וְשַׂמְתָּם' but instead says 'וְשַׂמְתָּ אוֹתָם', the extra word teaches two things — both the baking in pairs and the exclusion of the two loaves.

items.text: Baraita: Three molds for showbread
items.text_en: Baraita: Three molds for showbread
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that there are three molds for the showbread: one for the dough, one in the oven, and one for removal to prevent spoilage. The dough is not returned to the first mold after baking because it expands.

sub.desc_en: The baraita explains the three molds used for the showbread: one for the dough, one in the oven, and one for removal to prevent spoilage; it notes that after baking the bread expands and cannot be returned to the first mold.
The baraita details the three molds: one for the dough, one in the oven, and one for removal to prevent spoilage.
The gemara asks why the bread is not returned to the first mold after baking.
The gemara answers that once baked, the bread expands and no longer fits the original mold.

items.text: Transition to next sugya: How is showbread made?
items.text_en: Transition to next sugya: How is showbread made?
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new discussion: how the showbread is actually prepared.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a discussion about how the showbread is made.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rabbi Chanina vs Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rabbi Chanina vs Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina says the bread arrangement is like a broken box (protzah); Rabbi Yochanan says it is like a rocking ship (rokdet). The Gemara begins by clarifying how the loaves (bazikhin) sit in each model.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that the bread arrangement is like a broken box (תיבה פרוצה).
Rabbi Yochanan states that the bread arrangement is like a rocking ship (ספינה רוקדת).

items.text: Gemara's first question: seating the loaves
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: seating the loaves
items.desc_en: For the broken-box view, loaves sit inside the box; for the rocking-ship view, the loaves must be placed on a raised platform (makom) to avoid falling. The Gemara asks how the loaves sit in the rocking-ship model.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the broken-box model, the loaves (בזיכין) sit flat, but according to the rocking-ship model, how do they sit?
The Gemara answers: the ship has a recessed place (מקום) made for the loaves to sit.

items.text: Second question: seating the kanim (supports)
items.text_en: Second question: seating the kanim (supports)
items.desc_en: For the broken-box view, the kanim (supports) sit inside the box; for the rocking-ship view, the kanim must be attached via a mursha (a type of joint). The Gemara asks how the kanim sit in the rocking-ship model.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the broken-box model, the reeds (קנים) sit flat, but according to the rocking-ship model, how do they sit?
The Gemara answers: the ship has a socket (מורשא) made for the reeds.

items.text: Third question: how the sanifin (supports) support the bread
items.text_en: Third question: how the sanifin (supports) support the bread
items.desc_en: For the broken-box view, the sanifin (supports) lean against the bread; for the rocking-ship view, the sanifin must be curved (agil) to support the bread. The Gemara asks how the sanifin support the bread in the rocking-ship model.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the broken-box model, the supports (סניפין) lean against the bread, but according to the rocking-ship model, how do they lean?
The Gemara answers: the supports are curved (מעגל) to fit the ship's shape.

items.text: Fourth question: why sanifin are needed at all
items.text_en: Fourth question: why sanifin are needed at all
items.desc_en: For the rocking-ship view, sanifin are needed to prevent the bread from falling; for the broken-box view, the bread is already contained, so why need sanifin? The Gemara answers: due to the weight of the bread (yukra d'lechem), the sanifin prevent the box from collapsing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the rocking-ship model, supports are needed, but according to the broken-box model, why are supports needed?
The Gemara answers: because of the bread's weight, it would tilt (תלח) without supports.

items.text: Fifth question: placement of sanifin on the Table vs on the ground
items.text_en: Fifth question: placement of sanifin on the Table vs on the ground
items.desc_en: For the rocking-ship view, sanifin are placed on the Table; for the broken-box view, they are placed on the ground. Rabbi Abba bar Memel clarifies: for the rocking-ship view, sanifin are on the Table; for the broken-box view, they are on the ground.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the rocking-ship model, supports are placed on the table, but according to the broken-box model, where are they placed?
The Gemara suggests: perhaps they are placed on the ground.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel confirms: according to the rocking-ship view, supports are on the table; according to the broken-box view, supports are on the ground.

items.text: Final resolution: Rabbi Yehuda's statement aligns with the rocking-ship view
items.text_en: Final resolution: Rabbi Yehuda's statement aligns with the rocking-ship view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says: the bread supports the sanifin and the sanifin support the bread. This matches the rocking-ship model where the bread and supports are interdependent, not the broken-box model where the bread is self-contained.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: with which view does Rabbi Yehuda's statement that the bread and supports mutually support each other align?
The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yehuda's statement aligns with the view that the arrangement is like a rocking ship.

items.text: Supporting baraita for the shape of the showbread
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for the shape of the showbread
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited describing the showbread as resembling a ship tossed on the sea, supporting the view that it was shaped like a boat. This is contrasted with a previous description of its appearance as a square tablet.

items.text: Dispute over showbread invalidation during journeys
items.text_en: Dispute over showbread invalidation during journeys
items.desc_en: An inquiry is raised whether the showbread is invalidated during the journeys of the camp. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagree: one says it is invalidated, the other says it is not.

items.text: First set of proofs from verses
items.text_en: First set of proofs from verses
items.desc_en: The one who says it is invalidated cites the verse 'as they encamp, so shall they journey' – just as during encampment it is invalidated by leaving its place, so during travel it is invalidated. The one who says it is not invalidated cites the verse 'and the continual bread shall be upon it'.

items.text: Refutation and resolution by Rav Dimi
items.text_en: Refutation and resolution by Rav Dimi
items.desc_en: Each side challenges the other's verse. Rav Dimi resolves that the dispute is only when the bread has been removed from the table; when it is still arranged, all agree it is not invalidated.

items.text: Alternative proof and resolution with additional verses
items.text_en: Alternative proof and resolution with additional verses
items.desc_en: The one who says it is invalidated again cites 'as they encamp, so shall they journey'. The other side cites 'and the Tent of Meeting journeyed' – even when it travels, it is still the Tent of Meeting. The Gemara explains that the latter verse refers to the standards, and the former is derived from 'the camp of the Levites within the camps'.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about invalidation during journeys
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about invalidation during journeys
items.desc_en: A baraita states that during the dismantling of the camp, sacred items are invalidated by leaving their place, and zavim and lepers are sent outside. The Gemara questions whether this includes the showbread, and then challenges the logic of the distinction.

items.text: Final resolution by Ravin
items.text_en: Final resolution by Ravin
items.desc_en: Ravin reports that the two opinions are not actually in dispute: one refers to when the bread is arranged, the other to when it has been removed, and they do not disagree.

items.text: Abaye's inference about nighttime journeys
items.text_en: Abaye's inference about nighttime journeys
items.desc_en: Abaye infers from the discussion that there is dismantling of the camp at night, otherwise the showbread would be invalidated by staying overnight rather than by leaving its place. The Gemara supports this with the verse 'to go day and night'.

items.text: Contradiction regarding the curtains and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding the curtains and resolution
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: when the curtains are rolled, zavim and lepers are permitted to enter. Rav Ashi resolves that one view follows Rabbi Eliezer, the other follows the Rabbis, as taught in a baraita.

items.text: Introduction to the Mishnah's dispute
items.text_en: Introduction to the Mishnah's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagree in the Gemara itself, and it proves this from the Mishnah's phrasing where Rabbi Shimon says one should always say that the two loaves and the showbread are valid in the Temple courtyard and valid in Beit Pagei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagree in the Gemara itself, based on the Mishnah's phrasing.

The Gemara proves its observation from the Mishnah's wording, where Rabbi Shimon says one should always say that the two loaves and the showbread are valid in the Temple courtyard and valid in Beit Pagei.

items.text: Mishnah: Labors for the High Priest's griddle-cakes and general rules for meal offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Labors for the High Priest's griddle-cakes and general rules for meal offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the kneading, arranging, and baking of the High Priest's griddle-cakes are done inside and override Shabbat, but grinding and sifting do not. Rabbi Akiva gives a general rule: any labor that can be done before Shabbat does not override Shabbat, but one that cannot does. It then discusses the dimensions of the two loaves and the showbread, the table, and the arrangement of the showbread, including the opinions of Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Meir, and Abba Shaul, as well as the details of the supports and the poles.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that the kneading, arranging, and baking of the High Priest's griddle-cakes are done inside and override Shabbat, but grinding and sifting do not.
Rabbi Akiva states a general rule: any labor that can be done before Shabbat does not override Shabbat, but one that cannot does.
The Mishnah states that all meal offerings involve a vessel service inside but not outside.
The Mishnah specifies the dimensions of the two loaves and the showbread.
Rabbi Yehuda gives a mnemonic to avoid confusion about the dimensions.
Ben Zoma derives from the verse that the showbread must have 'faces' (sides).
The Mishnah states the dimensions of the table and the showbread.
Rabbi Yehuda explains how the showbread is placed on the table, with a fold of one and a half handbreadths on each side.
Rabbi Meir gives different dimensions for the table and showbread, with a two-handbreadth fold on each side and a two-handbreadth gap in the middle for air to circulate.
Abba Shaul states that two bowls of frankincense were placed there for the showbread.
The Sages object to Abba Shaul, citing a verse that seems to place the frankincense on the arrangement, not on the table.
Abba Shaul responds by citing another verse that uses similar language to support his interpretation.
The Mishnah describes the four golden supports and the twenty-eight rods used for the showbread.
The Mishnah states that arranging and removing the rods does not override Shabbat; instead, one does it before Shabbat.
The Mishnah concludes with a general rule that all vessels in the Temple were placed lengthwise along the length of the building.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation that all meal offerings require a vessel inside
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation that all meal offerings require a vessel inside
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the source for the Mishnah's statement that all meal offerings have the act of a vessel inside. Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) answers with a verse from Ezekiel, comparing the meal offering to the guilt offering and sin offering, which require a vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's statement that all meal offerings require the act of a vessel inside.
The Gemara asks Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) for the source of this rule.
Rabbi answers by citing a verse from Ezekiel (46:20) that mentions baking the meal offering in the same context as the guilt offering and sin offering.
The Gemara concludes by applying a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה): just as the guilt offering and sin offering require a vessel, so too the meal offering requires a vessel.

items.text: Gemara: Discussion of the table's sanctification and the showbread's placement
items.text_en: Gemara: Discussion of the table's sanctification and the showbread's placement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan calculates how many handbreadths the table sanctifies above it according to the opinions of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir. The Gemara then addresses objections about the poles and the supports, explaining that the poles are recessed, the supports are inside the bread, and the horns are folded inward, so the bread rests on them without affecting the table's sanctification.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dimensions of the table: its length is ten handbreadths and its width is five.

Rabbi Yochanan calculates that according to the opinion that folds two and a half handbreadths, the table sanctifies fifteen handbreadths above it, and according to the opinion that folds two handbreadths, it sanctifies twelve handbreadths above it.
The Gemara objects: But what about the rods (קנים) that support the bread? The Gemara answers that the rods are recessed (שַׁקּוֹעֵי מְשַׁקַּע לְהוּ) into the table.
The Gemara asks why the rods are recessed, and answers that it is to prevent the bread from molding (אִיעַפּוֹשֵׁי לֶחֶם), and that the bread is slightly raised above the rods.
The Gemara objects: But what about that slight gap? The answer is that since it is less than a handbreadth (טֶפַח), it is not considered significant.

The Gemara objects about the bowls (בזיכין) and the horns (קרנות), and resolves that the bowls sit inside the bread, the horns are folded inward, and the bread rests on them, so they do not affect the table's sanctification.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about the Table's border
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about the Table's border
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a contradiction regarding the Table's border (מסגרת). It explains that according to the opinion that the border was below, the Table had a frame; according to the opinion that it was above, the frame served as a partition, and the bread sat within the Table.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the verse mentions the Table's border (מסגרת), but the earlier description of the Table's construction seems to omit it.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing two opinions: one holds the border was below (so the Table had a frame), the other holds it was above (so the frame served as a partition and the bread sat within the Table).

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's statement and the Sages' response
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's statement and the Sages' response
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei says there were no supports (סניפין), but the border of the Table held the bread. The Sages responded that the border was below.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei states that there were no supports (סניפין), but the border of the Table held the bread.
The Sages respond to Rabbi Yosei that the border was below, not above.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on purity of an overturned table
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on purity of an overturned table
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules: According to the opinion that the border was below, an overturned table (טבלא המתהפכת) is impure. According to the opinion that the border was above, its purity status is unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that according to the opinion that the border was below, an overturned table (טבלא המתהפכת) is impure.
Rabbi Yochanan states that according to the opinion that the border was above, the purity status of an overturned table remains unresolved.

items.text: Questioning the Table's susceptibility to impurity
items.text_en: Questioning the Table's susceptibility to impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Table can be susceptible to impurity, as it is a wooden vessel made for resting (כלי עץ העשוי לנחת), which normally does not receive impurity. The reason is that it must be similar to a sack (שק), which is movable when full and empty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Table can be susceptible to impurity, since it is a wooden vessel made for resting (כלי עץ העשוי לנחת), which normally does not receive impurity.
The Gemara answers that the Table must be similar to a sack (שק), which is movable when full and empty, and the Table is also movable when full and empty.

items.text: Resolving the Table's movability and the miracle of the showbread
