items.text_en: Resolving the Table's movability and the miracle of the showbread
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Table is movable when full and empty, as per Resh Lakish's interpretation of the verse 'upon the pure Table' (על השלחן הטהור), implying it was sometimes impure. It was lifted for the pilgrims to see the showbread, and a miracle occurred: the bread remained hot when removed, as taught by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Table is movable when full and empty, citing Resh Lakish's interpretation of the verse 'upon the pure Table' (על השלחן הטהור), which implies it was sometimes impure.
The Gemara explains that the Table was lifted for pilgrims to see the showbread, demonstrating their belovedness before God.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that a great miracle occurred with the showbread: its removal was as hot as its placement, as per the verse 'to place hot bread on the day it was taken' (לשום לחם חם ביום הלקחו).

items.text: Addressing the issue of plating (ציפוי) and its permanence
items.text_en: Addressing the issue of plating (ציפוי) and its permanence
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a mishnah about a table plated with marble: if space for cups remains, it is impure; otherwise not. It then considers whether the plating is permanent or not, referencing Resh Lakish's inquiry to Rabbi Yochanan on this matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a mishnah: a table plated with marble that retains space for cups is impure, implying that plating (ציפוי) affects impurity status.
The Gemara clarifies that the mishnah's ruling applies only when space is left (שייר), not when the plating covers everything.
The Gemara considers distinguishing between permanent and temporary plating, citing Resh Lakish's inquiry to Rabbi Yochanan on this very issue.

items.text: The Table's golden overlay and the verse 'the Table is wood'
items.text_en: The Table's golden overlay and the verse 'the Table is wood'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Table's golden overlay is nullified by the wood, given that wooden vessels are not susceptible to impurity. It distinguishes between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding nullification of important vessels, and resolves that the Table is different because the Torah calls it 'wood' (Ezekiel 41:22).

items.text: The Table as atonement in the absence of the Temple
items.text_en: The Table as atonement in the absence of the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse begins with the altar and ends with the Table. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar explain that when the Temple stood, the altar atoned for a person; now that the Temple is destroyed, a person's table atones for him.

items.text: Derivation of the four golden supports and accessories
items.text_en: Derivation of the four golden supports and accessories
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states there were four golden supports. Rav Ketina derives them from the verse 'And you shall make its bowls, its spoons, its supports, and its covers' (Exodus 25:29), explaining each term: bowls are molds, spoons are frankincense bowls, supports are the golden supports, and covers are the tubes that protect the bread.

items.text: Rava's objection and retraction regarding Shabbat
items.text_en: Rava's objection and retraction regarding Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rava objects that if the arrangement of tubes is Torah-mandated, it should override Shabbat, but the Mishnah says it does not. He retracts, citing Rabbi Akiva's principle that any work possible before Shabbat does not override it, and since the bread does not become stale in that short time, it can be done beforehand.

items.text: Procedure for removing and replacing tubes on Shabbat eve
items.text_en: Procedure for removing and replacing tubes on Shabbat eve
items.desc_en: A baraita describes how to handle the tubes on Shabbat eve: one removes them and places them lengthwise on the Table, then after Shabbat lifts each loaf and inserts tubes underneath. The top loaf needs only two tubes, the bottom loaf none, as it rests directly on the Table.

items.text: Dispute about cubit measures in the Temple
items.text_en: Dispute about cubit measures in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: Rabbi Meir says all Temple cubits were medium (six handbreadths) except for the golden altar, horn, surround, and base; Rabbi Yehuda says the building cubit was six handbreadths and the vessel cubit five. Rabbi Yochanan states both derive from the same verse (Ezekiel 43:13).

items.text: Opening verse interpretation
items.text_en: Opening verse interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita that interprets each phrase in Ezekiel's description of the altar (Ezekiel 43:13-14) as referring to specific parts of the altar: the base, the surrounding ledge, the horns, and the golden altar.

sub.desc_en: The baraita interprets Ezekiel's description of the altar, identifying each phrase with a specific part: the base (יסוד), the surrounding ledge (סובב), the horns (קרנות), and the golden altar (מזבח הזהב).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Judah on the cubit measure
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Judah on the cubit measure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir holds that 'this' (the altar's cubit) was of five handbreadths, implying all other vessel cubits were of six. Rabbi Judah holds that all vessel cubits should be like this one, i.e., of five handbreadths.

sub.text: Stam's report of Rabbi Judah's position
sub.text_en: Stam's report of Rabbi Judah's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Judah holds that all vessel cubits should be like this one, i.e., of five handbreadths.

items.text: Initial assumption about the height and the cubit measure
items.text_en: Initial assumption about the height and the cubit measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that from the base to the surrounding ledge in height was measured with a five-handbreadth cubit, and interprets the verse accordingly. It calculates the total height of the altar as ten cubits: six of five handbreadths and four of six handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that the height from the base (יסוד) to the surrounding ledge (סובב) was measured with a five-handbreadth cubit.
The Gemara calculates the total height of the altar as ten cubits: six cubits of five handbreadths each and four cubits of six handbreadths each.

items.text: Calculation of the altar's halved dimensions and the red line
items.text_en: Calculation of the altar's halved dimensions and the red line
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the area of the altar (54 cubits), its half (27), and the distance from the horns to the surrounding ledge (24), finding a discrepancy of three. It cites the mishnah about the red line that girdles the altar at its midpoint to separate upper and lower blood applications.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for half the altar's area and calculates it as 27 cubits.
The Gemara asks the distance from the horns to the surrounding ledge and calculates it as 24 cubits.
The Gemara asks how much the distance from horns to ledge falls short of half the altar, finding a deficit of three cubits.
The Gemara cites the mishnah that a red line girdles the altar at its midpoint to separate upper and lower blood applications.

items.text: Challenge from the bird-offering baraita
items.text_en: Challenge from the bird-offering baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about the bird burnt offering: the priest ascends the ramp, turns to the surrounding ledge, approaches the southeast horn, pinches the head opposite the nape, separates, and squeezes the blood on the altar wall. If done below his feet even one cubit, it is valid. This challenges the previous calculation because it would place the upper blood application below two handbreadths from the top.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about the bird burnt offering: the priest ascends the ramp, turns to the surrounding ledge, approaches the southeast horn, pinches the head opposite the nape, separates, and squeezes the blood on the altar wall. If done below his feet even one cubit, it is valid.
The Gemara objects: according to the previous calculation, this would place the upper blood application below two handbreadths from the top, contradicting the baraita's validity.

items.text: Alternative interpretation: all cubits are recesses
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation: all cubits are recesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the verse: 'the bosom of the cubit' means a recess, 'a cubit in breadth' means a recess, 'its border to its lip round about' means a recess. This changes the dimensions of the altar.

items.text: Recalculation and challenge from the Mishnah of the altar's dimensions
items.text_en: Recalculation and challenge from the Mishnah of the altar's dimensions
items.desc_en: With the new interpretation, the altar is now 60 cubits, its half 30, the distance from horns to surrounding ledge 24, leaving a discrepancy of six. The baraita about the bird offering now fits. However, the Gemara asks how this can be reconciled with the Mishnah that describes the altar as 32 by 32 cubits, with the base reducing it to 30 by 30. The Gemara notes that 30 by 30 actually means 30 by 30 plus two handbreadths (since the cubit is 5 handbreadths and the remaining part is a fraction).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recalculates the altar's height as 60 cubits, its half as 30, the distance from horns to surrounding ledge as 24, leaving a discrepancy of 6, and notes that the baraita about the bird offering fits.
The Gemara asks how this can be reconciled with the Mishnah that describes the altar as 32 by 32 cubits, with the base reducing it to 30 by 30.
The Gemara resolves that 30 by 30 actually means 30 by 30 plus two handbreadths, since the cubit is 5 handbreadths and the remaining part is a fraction.

items.text: Further dimensions and the place of the horns
items.text_en: Further dimensions and the place of the horns
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues to analyze the Mishnah: the surrounding ledge makes it 28 by 28 cubits, plus four handbreadths. But if the horns do not occupy a full cubit, the area of the horns would be 26 by 26. The Gemara corrects: it should be 27, but the Mishnah was imprecise. This imprecision is acceptable because the Torah itself in describing the altar (Ariel) at 12 by 12 implies a central area of 12 cubits in each direction, which might also be imprecise.

items.text: The place for the priests' walk and the arrangement
items.text_en: The place for the priests' walk and the arrangement
items.desc_en: A cubit on each side for the priests' walking leaves 24 by 24 for the arrangement. The Gemara notes that it should be 25, indicating the Mishnah was imprecise again.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: The place for the priests' walk is a cubit from here and a cubit from there. Result: 24 by 24 for the arrangement area. That would be 25! (i.e., 25 cubits, not 24).

items.text: Resolving the imprecision and the potential space problem in the Temple courtyard
items.text_en: Resolving the imprecision and the potential space problem in the Temple courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that perhaps the six handbreadths from the original five-handbreadth cubits cause the courtyard to be too spacious. It cites the Mishnah of the courtyard's dimensions: 187 by 135 cubits. Using the new interpretation avoids this problem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possible objection: if we say the verse 'והאריאל' (the altar hearth) is imprecise, the verse itself specifies that the hearth is twelve cubits by twelve cubits, measured from the center.
The Gemara objects: if we bring the six cubits from the original five-handbreadth cubits, the courtyard (עזרה) would become too spacious.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's dimensions of the courtyard (עזרה): 187 cubits long by 135 cubits wide, with specific allocations for the Israelite area, priestly area, altar, and Temple.

items.text: Final resolution of the verse interpretation
items.text_en: Final resolution of the verse interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that 'the bosom of the cubit' refers to height, 'a cubit in breadth' to a recess, and 'its border to its lip round about' to the horns. This resolves the challenges.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: But 'the bosom of the cubit' – in height, 'a cubit in breadth' – a recess, 'its border to its lip round about' –

items.text: Dimensions of the altar and the validity of offering below the feet
items.text_en: Dimensions of the altar and the validity of offering below the feet
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the height of the altar and its half, then notes that if the offering was placed even one cubit below the feet, it is valid, citing a mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that it is no different here and no different there, introducing the discussion.
The Gemara calculates the altar's height (58 cubits), its half (29), and the distance from the horns to the surrounding ledge (23 cubits).
The Gemara notes that the half-altar is six cubits short, and cites the mishnah that if the offering was placed even one cubit below the feet, it is valid.

items.text: Proof from the verse about the altar's dimensions
items.text_en: Proof from the verse about the altar's dimensions
items.desc_en: The Gemara deduces from the verse 'חֵיק הָאַמָּה' and 'אַמָּה רֹחַב' that the altar's dimensions are as calculated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deduces from the verse 'חֵיק הָאַמָּה' and 'אַמָּה רֹחַב' that the altar's dimensions are as calculated.

items.text: The standard cubit and the Shushan cubits
items.text_en: The standard cubit and the Shushan cubits
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states the standard cubit is six handbreadths, supported by Rabbi Yosei bar Avin from the table's dimensions. The Gemara then discusses the two cubits in Shushan the capital, one larger and one smaller, used for different purposes to prevent misuse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the standard cubit's size, and Rabbi Yochanan answers it is six handbreadths.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin supports Rabbi Yochanan's statement by citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir gives the table's dimensions as 12 by 6 handbreadths, implying a 6-handbreadth cubit.
The Gemara infers that there must be a larger cubit, and confirms this by citing a Mishnah about two cubits in Shushan the capital.

The Mishnah describes the two cubits: one on the northeast corner exceeds Moses' cubit by half a finger, and the one on the southeast corner exceeds that by another half finger, totaling one finger larger than Moses' cubit.
The Gemara asks why one cubit is larger and one smaller, and answers that craftsmen take materials with the small cubit and return with the large one to prevent misuse of sacred property.
The Gemara asks why two cubits are needed, and answers that one is for silver and gold and the other for building.

items.text: The reason for the Shushan fortress image on the eastern gate
items.text_en: The reason for the Shushan fortress image on the eastern gate
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the image of Shushan the capital was on the eastern gate. Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi offer two reasons: to remind of the origin of the exiles, and to instill fear of the kingdom. Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yochanan support the latter with verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about the image of Shushan the capital on the eastern gate and asks for the reason.

sub.text: Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi offer two reasons: one says to remind the exiles of their origin, and the other says to instill fear of the kingdom.
Rabbi Yannai supports the second reason with a verse from Exodus showing that even Moses showed deference to Pharaoh.
Rabbi Yochanan supports the second reason with a verse from Kings showing Elijah running before King Ahab out of fear of the kingdom.

items.text: Interpretation of 'וְעָלֵהוּ לִתְרוּפָה'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'וְעָלֵהוּ לִתְרוּפָה'
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi debate whether the leaf is for healing the mouth above or below. Chizkiyah and bar Kappara offer alternative interpretations: healing the mute or healing the barren.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse 'וְעָלֵהוּ לִתְרוּפָה' (and its leaf for healing) and introduces the debate between Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi.
One of them (Rav Chisda) says the leaf is to heal the mouth above (i.e., the mouth of the mute).
The other (Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi) says the leaf is to heal the mouth below (i.e., the womb of the barren).
Chizkiyah says the leaf is to heal the mouth of the mute (i.e., restore speech).
Bar Kappara says the leaf is to heal the mouth of the barren (i.e., enable conception).

items.text: The arrangement of the showbread: deriving the correct number of loaves and rows
items.text_en: The arrangement of the showbread: deriving the correct number of loaves and rows
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma derives from the verses that there must be two rows of six loaves each. Rabbi argues that if one places two rows of seven, the top loaf is considered non-existent, based on his interpretation of 'עַל' as adjacent. Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna explain Rabbi's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The baraita begins by stating that if the verse had only said 'שתים עשרה חלות' and 'שתים מערכות' without specifying 'שש', one might have thought to arrange one row of four and one of eight, so the verse specifies 'שש'.
The baraita continues: if the verse had said 'שתים מערכות שש המערכת' without specifying 'שתים עשרה', one might have thought three rows of six, so the verse specifies 'שתים עשרה'.

The baraita concludes: if the verse had said 'שתים עשרה חלות' and 'מערכות' without specifying 'שתים' and 'שש', one might have thought three rows of four, so the verse specifies 'שתים' and 'שש'; without all three verses we would not have learned the correct arrangement.

The baraita concludes: the proper arrangement is two rows of six each; if one placed a row of four and a row of eight he has not fulfilled the obligation; if one placed two rows of seven, Rabbi says we consider the top loaf as if it does not exist.

Rav Chisda (or Rav Hamnuna) explains that Rabbi follows his own principle that 'עַל' means 'adjacent to' (not directly on top), as derived from a baraita where Rabbi interprets 'ונתת על המערכת לבנה זכה' as 'עַל' meaning adjacent, proven from the verse 'וסכות על הארן את הפרוכת'.

items.text: Placement of the Ark and its poles
items.text_en: Placement of the Ark and its poles
items.desc_en: The baraita states that all Temple vessels were placed lengthwise along the house, except the Ark which was placed widthwise. The Gemara clarifies that the poles were arranged accordingly. It then derives from verses that the poles protruded through the curtain but did not tear it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that all Temple vessels were placed lengthwise along the house, except the Ark which was placed widthwise, and its poles were arranged accordingly.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means by 'so it was placed, and so its poles were placed,' and clarifies that the phrase explains the arrangement of the poles.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from verses that the poles protruded through the curtain but did not tear it, leaving the exact arrangement unresolved.

items.text: Opening: description of the cherubim's posture on the Ark-cover
items.text_en: Opening: description of the cherubim's posture on the Ark-cover
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes the cherubim on the Ark-cover, whose wings were folded and whose bodies were positioned like a woman's breasts, with a prooftext from Song of Songs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes the cherubim on the Ark-cover as pressing and protruding through the curtain, resembling a woman's breasts, citing Song of Songs 1:13.

items.text: Discussion: placement of the staves of the Ark
items.text_en: Discussion: placement of the staves of the Ark
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the staves were positioned along the width or length of the Ark. Rabbi Yehuda argues based on spatial constraints, and the Gemara derives from verses that four bearers carried the Ark.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the proof that the staves of the Ark were placed along its width, suggesting they might have been along its length.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that two men cannot fit in a space of one and a half cubits, implying the staves were along the width.
The Gemara derives from the verse that the Ark was carried by four bearers, supporting the spatial argument.

items.text: Baraita: Solomon's ten tables and their arrangement
items.text_en: Baraita: Solomon's ten tables and their arrangement
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that Solomon made ten tables, five on the right and five on the left of the mishkan. The Gemara clarifies that these are not to the right and left of the entrance, but rather to the right and left of Moses' original table in the center.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that Solomon made ten tables, placing five on the right and five on the left of the Temple.
The Gemara objects that if the tables were to the right and left of the entrance, one table would be in the south, contradicting the Torah's command to place the table on the north side.
The Gemara resolves that Moses' original table was in the center, with five tables to its right and five to its left.

items.text: Baraita: Solomon's ten menorahs and their arrangement
items.text_en: Baraita: Solomon's ten menorahs and their arrangement
items.desc_en: Similarly, a baraita teaches that Solomon made ten menorahs, five on the right and five on the left. The Gemara again rejects the idea that these are to the right and left of the entrance, and concludes they flank Moses' original menorah in the center.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Solomon made ten menorahs, five on the right and five on the left, citing the verse.
The Gemara objects that if the menorahs were placed to the right and left of the entrance, a menorah would be in the north, contradicting the verse that places the menorah opposite the table.
The Gemara resolves that Moses' original menorah was in the center, with five menorahs to its right and five to its left.

items.text: Contradiction resolved: placement from half vs. third the house
items.text_en: Contradiction resolved: placement from half vs. third the house
items.desc_en: Two apparently conflicting traditions about the placement of the tables/menorahs are reconciled by noting that one counts the Holy of Holies as part of the Temple, while the other does not.

sub.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one says the tables/menorahs were placed from half the house inward, the other says from a third of the house inward.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one Tanna counts the Holy of Holies as part of the Temple (so the placement starts from half the total length), while the other does not (so it starts from a third).

items.text: Dispute: orientation of the tables – east-west vs. north-south
items.text_en: Dispute: orientation of the tables – east-west vs. north-south
items.desc_en: Rabbi holds that the tables were arranged east-west, deriving from the menorah which itself faces east-west, based on the verse about the western lamp. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon holds north-south, deriving from the Ark. The Gemara defends each position by distinguishing between inside and outside vessels.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the dispute: Rabbi holds the tables were placed east-west, Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon holds north-south.

The Gemara explains Rabbi's reasoning: he derives the table's orientation from the menorah, which itself faces east-west based on the verse about the western lamp being 'before the Lord', implying the others are not.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: he derives from the Ark which was north-south, and rejects Rabbi's derivation because one cannot derive the law of an outer vessel (table) from an inner vessel (Ark).

sub.text: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why doesn't Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon derive from the menorah? He answers that the menorah itself was placed north-south.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution of the verse about the western lamp
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the verse about the western lamp
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the verse about the western lamp: the lamps were angled toward the middle lamp, as taught in a baraita, and Rabbi Nathan adds that this shows the middle lamp is superior.

items.text: Practical challenges to Rabbi Elazar's north-south position
items.text_en: Practical challenges to Rabbi Elazar's north-south position
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises spatial problems: if the tables were north-south, how could ten tables fit in twenty cubits, how would priests enter, and where would Moses' table go? It then reframes the question by noting that there were two storeys (terraces) of tables.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted for Rabbi who says the tables were east-west, ten tables fit in twenty cubits; but for Rabbi Elazar who says north-south, how could ten tables fit in twenty cubits?
The Gemara raises additional spatial problems: how would priests enter, and where would Moses' table be placed?
The Gemara objects: even according to Rabbi who says east-west, where would Moses' table be placed?
The Gemara resolves: do you think there was only one storey? There were two storeys (terraces) of tables.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the Table's placement
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the Table's placement
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction about the Table's position: according to the view that the Table was placed north-south, it works out; according to the view that it was east-west, the calculation shows the Table would extend into the south, but the Gemara answers that Moses' Table was not aligned with the others but was set back like a student before his teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins by noting that according to the view that the Table was placed north-south, the calculation works out fine.
The Gemara raises a difficulty: according to the view that the Table was placed east-west, the calculation shows that the Table would extend half a cubit into the south.
The Gemara answers that Moses' Table was not aligned with the others but was set back like a student before his teacher, thus avoiding the southern extension.

items.text: Debate about Solomon's tables and the Menorot
items.text_en: Debate about Solomon's tables and the Menorot
items.desc_en: A Tosefta states that Solomon made ten tables and ten menorot, but only Moses' were used. Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua argues all were used, citing verses. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda explains that only Moses' table was used for the showbread, but the other tables were for temporary placement of the bread upon entry and exit, based on the principle of ascending in holiness.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta states that Solomon made ten tables and ten menorot, but only Moses' were used for the showbread and lighting, citing verses.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua argues that all tables and menorot were used, citing verses that mention 'the tables' and 'the menorot' in plural.

Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda explains that only Moses' table was used for the showbread, but the other tables in the Temple were for temporary placement of the bread upon entry and exit, based on the principle of ascending in holiness (מעלין בקודש).

items.text: Proofs for the principle of ascending in holiness
items.text_en: Proofs for the principle of ascending in holiness
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the rule that one may only ascend in holiness, not descend. Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) derives it from the construction of the Mishkan, where Moses raised the components. Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov derives the principle of ascending from the incident of the fire-pans, which were elevated from service vessels to the altar itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the principle that one may not descend in holiness?
Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) answers that the source is the verse describing Moses erecting the Mishkan, implying ascending in holiness.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the principle that one may ascend in holiness?
Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov answers that the source is the verse about the fire-pans of the sinners, which were elevated from service vessels to the altar itself.

items.text: Respect for a Torah scholar who forgot his learning
items.text_en: Respect for a Torah scholar who forgot his learning
items.desc_en: From the verse about the broken tablets being placed in the Ark, Rav Yosef teaches that a Torah scholar who forgot his learning due to circumstances beyond his control should not be treated disrespectfully. Reish Lakish adds that sometimes one who forgets is like one who never learned, but the Gemara's discussion continues.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef teaches from the verse about the broken tablets being placed in the Ark that a Torah scholar who forgot his learning due to circumstances beyond his control should not be treated disrespectfully.
The Gemara inserts a mnemonic sign (סִימָן) listing three keywords — 'בִּיטֵּל' (nullified), 'סָרַח' (sinned), 'וְשָׁכַח' (forgot) — to aid memory of the upcoming discussion.
Reish Lakish begins a statement (cut off in the source) that sometimes one who forgets his learning is treated differently.

items.text: The value of breaking the tablets
items.text_en: The value of breaking the tablets
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a teaching that the breaking of the tablets (by Moses) is itself the foundation of Torah, as God praised Moses for breaking them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that the suspension of Torah study (Moses breaking the Tablets) is itself its foundation, citing the verse and God's praise.

items.text: Do not publicly shame a Torah scholar who sinned
items.text_en: Do not publicly shame a Torah scholar who sinned
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish teaches that a Torah scholar who sinned should not be publicly shamed, as derived from the verse about stumbling like a prophet at night.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish teaches that a Torah scholar who sinned should not be publicly shamed, citing the verse about stumbling like a prophet at night.

items.text: The prohibition against forgetting Torah
items.text_en: The prohibition against forgetting Torah
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that forgetting Torah violates a negative commandment, citing the verse 'Guard yourself... lest you forget.' Ravina and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak debate the number of negative commandments involved, and the Gemara limits the prohibition to intentional forgetting.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that forgetting Torah violates a negative commandment, citing the verse 'הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ וּשְׁמֹר נַפְשְׁךָ מְאֹד פֶּן תִּשְׁכַּח' and supporting it with Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Ila'a's principle that 'הִשָּׁמֶר', 'פֶּן', and 'אַל' always indicate a negative commandment.
Ravina argues that 'הִשָּׁמֶר' and 'פֶן' constitute two separate negative commandments.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak counters that there are three negative commandments, counting 'שְׁמֹר' as an additional one.
The Gemara limits the prohibition to intentional forgetting, excluding cases of coercion or when one's learning was overpowered, citing the verses 'וּפֶן יָסוּרוּ מִלְּבָבְךָ' and 'רַק'.

items.text: The reward for guarding Torah
items.text_en: The reward for guarding Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar teach that Torah was given in forty days and the soul is formed in forty days; one who guards Torah has his soul guarded. The school of Rabbi Yishmael offers a parable of a bird to illustrate the severity of losing one's soul.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar teach that Torah was given in forty days and the soul is formed in forty days, so one who guards Torah has his soul guarded, and one who does not guard Torah has his soul unguarded.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael offers a parable of a bird to illustrate the severity of losing one's soul if one fails to guard Torah.

items.text: Mishnah: The showbread tables and the procedure
items.text_en: Mishnah: The showbread tables and the procedure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the two tables in the Temple: one of marble for placing the showbread upon entry, and one of gold for its removal. It details the procedure for the priests, including the placement, removal, and distribution of the showbread, and special rules for Yom Kippur and Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the two tables in the Temple hall: one of marble for placing the showbread upon entry, and one of gold for its removal.
The Mishnah states the principle that one elevates in holiness and does not lower, and notes the inner gold table always holds the showbread.
The Mishnah details the procedure: four priests enter, two carrying the two rows of bread and two carrying the two bowls of frankincense, while four others precede them to remove the old ones.

The Mishnah describes the positioning: those entering stand in the north facing south, those removing stand in the south facing north, and they pull and place with handbreadth opposite handbreadth, as the verse says 'before Me always'.
Rabbi Yose says that even if one group takes and the other places, that too fulfills the requirement of 'always'.
The Mishnah concludes: they exit and place the bread on the gold table in the hall, burn the frankincense bowls, and the loaves are distributed to the priests.

The Mishnah adds special rules: if Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, the loaves are distributed in the evening; if it falls on Friday, the Yom Kippur goat is eaten in the evening, and the Babylonians eat it raw because their disposition is pleasant.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yose's interpretation of 'before Me always'
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yose's interpretation of 'before Me always'
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Yose's view that even if the old showbread was removed in the morning and the new one placed in the evening, it is valid; 'before Me always' means the table should never be without bread.

sub.desc_en: Opening (Gemara): A baraita: Rabbi Yose says: Even if he removed the old in the morning and arranged the new in the evening — nothing wrong; but how do I fulfill 'before Me always'? That the table should not stay overnight without bread.

items.text: The obligation to study Torah day and night
items.text_en: The obligation to study Torah day and night
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami learns from Rabbi Yose that even studying one chapter morning and evening fulfills 'this Torah shall not depart from your mouth.' Rabbi Yochanan says even reciting Shema morning and evening suffices, but this should not be said to ignoramuses; Rava says it is a mitzvah to say it. Ben Dama asks about studying Greek wisdom, and Rabbi Yishmael responds with a verse. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says the verse is a blessing, not an obligation, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael says Torah should not be a burden.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi learns from Rabbi Yose that even studying one chapter morning and evening fulfills the verse 'this Torah shall not depart from your mouth'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says even reciting Shema morning and evening fulfills the verse, but this should not be said to ignoramuses; Rava says it is a mitzvah to say it.
Ben Dama asks Rabbi Yishmael whether one who has studied all Torah may study Greek wisdom, and Rabbi Yishmael responds with a verse implying it is forbidden.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says the verse is a blessing for Joshua, not an obligation, citing Joshua's devotion.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that Torah should not be a burden, but one is not permitted to exempt oneself from it.

items.text: God's measure is unlike human measure
items.text_en: God's measure is unlike human measure
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah explains a verse to show that God entices people from death to life, unlike humans who entice from life to death, with a description of Gehinnom's narrow opening.

sub.desc_en: Answer: Chizkiya says: What is the meaning of the verse 'and also He enticed you from the mouth of distress a wide thing not constrained under it'? Come and see that God's attribute is not like flesh and blood's attribute. Flesh and blood: a person entices his friend from paths of life to paths of death; but the Holy One entices a person from paths of death to paths of life, as the verse 'and He enticed you from the mouth of distress' — from Gehinnom, whose mouth is narrow, whose smoke is gathered.

items.text: Opening exposition on the showbread's preparation
items.text_en: Opening exposition on the showbread's preparation
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets verses from Isaiah to counter potential doubts about the showbread: that its narrow opening implies a narrow interior, that it was not prepared for the king, that it lacks wood, and that its reward is only the ashes. Each doubt is refuted with a scriptural proof.

items.text: Identification of the Babylonians as Alexandrians
items.text_en: Identification of the Babylonians as Alexandrians
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that those referred to as Babylonians are actually Alexandrians, called Babylonians out of hatred. A baraita supports this with Rabbi Yosei saying the same, and Rabbi Yehudah praises him for putting his mind at ease.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of arranging showbread and frankincense at improper times
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of arranging showbread and frankincense at improper times
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three scenarios: arranging the bread on Shabbat and the frankincense after Shabbat, arranging both on Shabbat and offering the frankincense after Shabbat, and arranging both after Shabbat and offering the frankincense on Shabbat. In each case the offering is invalid, and the solution is to leave it for the next Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: Background on the daily offering and the rule of immersion
items.text_en: Gemara: Background on the daily offering and the rule of immersion
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about the officer checking for dawn for the daily offering, and explains that once a lunar eclipse was mistaken for dawn, leading to an improper slaughter. It then states the rule that anyone who defecates requires immersion, and anyone who urinates requires sanctification of hands and feet.

items.text: Baraita: Nighttime offerings and the principle of vessels sanctifying out of time
items.text_en: Baraita: Nighttime offerings and the principle of vessels sanctifying out of time
items.desc_en: The father of Rabbi Avin teaches that a bird offering pinched at night or a meal-offering scooped at night must be taken to the burning place. The Gemara questions why a meal-offering cannot be remedied by returning the scoop, and the father of Rabbi Avin answers that sacred vessels sanctify even out of their designated time.

items.text: Objection from a baraita on daytime offerings
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita on daytime offerings
items.desc_en: A baraita states that anything offered by day is sanctified by day, and by night is sanctified by night, implying that nighttime does not sanctify for offering but does sanctify for invalidation. This challenges the idea that vessels sanctify out of time.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges the principle by citing the Mishnah where arranging bread and frankincense after Shabbat and offering on Shabbat is invalid, and if vessels sanctify out of time, they should be sanctified and invalidated. Rabbah resolves that the father of Rabbi Avin holds that night is not lacking time, but days are lacking time, so the Mishnah's case involves days.

items.text: Conclusion fragment
items.text_en: Conclusion fragment
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a concluding statement with 'סוֹף סוֹף' (ultimately), but the text is cut off, leaving the argument incomplete.

items.text: Gemara's question on the timing of sanctification and disqualification
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the timing of sanctification and disqualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the showbread becomes sanctified and disqualified at sunset on the eve of the Sabbath. Rava answers that it is only if he removed the old bread first. Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi adds that even if he did not remove it first, since the arrangement was not done properly, it is as if a monkey arranged it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the showbread becomes sanctified and disqualified at sunset on the eve of the Sabbath.
Rava answers that the showbread becomes sanctified and disqualified only if he removed the old bread first.

sub.text: Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi's alternative answer
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi's alternative answer
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi adds that even if he did not remove the old bread first, since the arrangement was not done properly, it is as if a monkey arranged it.

items.text: Mishnah: The minimum and maximum days for eating the two loaves and showbread
items.text_en: Mishnah: The minimum and maximum days for eating the two loaves and showbread
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the two loaves are eaten no fewer than two days and no more than three, depending on when the festival falls relative to the Sabbath. The showbread is eaten no fewer than nine days and no more than eleven, with specific cases for when a festival occurs before the Sabbath. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that the showbread overrides a festival but not a fast day.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the minimum and maximum days for eating the two loaves, with examples based on the festival's timing relative to the Sabbath.
The Mishnah states the minimum and maximum days for eating the showbread, with examples based on the festival's timing relative to the Sabbath.
The Mishnah adds that for the two days of Rosh Hashanah, the showbread is eaten on the eleventh day, and it does not override the Sabbath or a festival.

sub.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Shimon ben HaSgan
sub.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Shimon ben HaSgan
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, citing Rabbi Shimon ben HaSgan, adds that the showbread overrides a festival but not a fast day.

items.text: Gemara: Proof that voluntary offerings are not offered on a festival
items.text_en: Gemara: Proof that voluntary offerings are not offered on a festival
items.desc_en: Ravina argues that according to the one who says voluntary offerings are not brought on a festival, it is not merely a rabbinic decree but a Torah law. He proves this from the two loaves, which are an obligation of the day and cannot be delayed, yet the Mishnah states they do not override the Sabbath or festival.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asserts that according to the opinion that voluntary offerings are not brought on a festival, this is not merely a rabbinic decree but a Torah-level prohibition.
Ravina proves his point from the two loaves, which are an obligation of the day and cannot be delayed, yet the Mishnah states they do not override the Sabbath or festival.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter on the two loaves with the standard formula 'We have returned to you, chapter of the two loaves.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula signaling that the discussion of the chapter on the two loaves is complete.

items.text: Mishnah: Redemption of offerings that became impure
items.text_en: Mishnah: Redemption of offerings that became impure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that meal-offerings and libations that became impure before being sanctified in a vessel may be redeemed; after sanctification in a vessel, they cannot be redeemed. Birds, wood, frankincense, and service vessels have no redemption once impure, since redemption is only stated for animals.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that meal-offerings and libations that became impure before being sanctified in a vessel may be redeemed.
The Mishnah continues that after sanctification in a vessel, they cannot be redeemed.
The Mishnah states that birds, wood, frankincense, and service vessels have no redemption once impure.
The Mishnah concludes with the reason: redemption is only stated for animals.

items.text: Gemara: Shmuel's ruling on redeeming pure offerings and the distinction from blemished animals
items.text_en: Gemara: Shmuel's ruling on redeeming pure offerings and the distinction from blemished animals
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that even pure offerings can be redeemed before sanctification in a vessel, as they have sanctity of monetary value. The Gemara explains why the Mishnah mentions impurity, and then addresses a potential comparison to a blemished animal, which is called 'impure' and can be redeemed even with sanctity of the body. The Gemara concludes that the comparison is rejected.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that even pure offerings can be redeemed before sanctification in a vessel, because they have sanctity of monetary value (קְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים), which is redeemable.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'impure' if the rule applies even to pure offerings.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah mentions impurity only for parallelism with the latter clause, where even impure offerings cannot be redeemed after sanctification in a vessel.
The Gemara objects that after sanctification in a vessel, offerings have sanctity of the body (קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף), which obviously cannot be redeemed.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's mention of impurity was necessary to reject a potential comparison to a blemished animal, which is called 'impure' and can be redeemed even with sanctity of the body, but the Torah's term 'impure' for a blemish is not analogous to actual impurity.

items.text: Derivation that 'impure' refers to blemished animals
items.text_en: Derivation that 'impure' refers to blemished animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that the term 'impure' in the verse refers to blemished animals that have been redeemed, not to actually impure animals. It clarifies that only animals with a permanent blemish are redeemable, excluding those with a temporary blemish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Since we find no redemption for Temple vessels, where is the term 'impure' applied to a blemished animal?
A baraita is cited: The verse 'If any impure animal' speaks of blemished animals that are redeemed.
The Gemara objects: Perhaps the verse refers to an actually impure animal, but another verse already addresses that.
The Gemara resolves: The verse must refer to blemished animals that are redeemed.
The Gemara excludes animals with a temporary blemish from redemption, since they are fit for sacrifice later.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Manoach's objection: pure items cannot be redeemed
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach's objection: pure items cannot be redeemed
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach challenges the idea that pure items can be redeemed, using the example of birds, wood, frankincense, and service vessels that became impure. He argues that since these items are inherently pure (e.g., wood and frankincense are not food, and vessels can be purified in a mikveh), they cannot be redeemed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach objects that birds, wood, frankincense, and service vessels that became impure have no redemption because the Torah only mentions redemption for animals.
The gemara explains that birds have inherent sanctity, but wood, frankincense, and vessels are pure items that cannot be redeemed, implying that pure items in general cannot be redeemed.

The gemara elaborates that even though these items became impure, they are considered like pure items because wood and frankincense are not inherently food, and service vessels can be purified in a mikveh.

items.text: Alternative explanation: rarity prevents redemption
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: rarity prevents redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests an alternative: pure items are indeed redeemable, but these specific items (wood, frankincense, service vessels) are not redeemed because they are rare. It explains that wood with worms is invalid for the altar, and frankincense and vessels are uncommon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous reasoning and proposes instead that pure items are redeemable, but these specific items (wood, frankincense, vessels) are not redeemed because they are rare.
The Gemara objects that wood is common, but answers that wood with worms is invalid for the altar, so suitable wood is also rare.

items.text: Rav Pappa's report and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's report and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports that Samuel would have retracted his view if he had heard a baraita about consecrated animals that cannot be redeemed because they are pure. The Gemara concludes that the reason is rarity: blemishes that disqualify animals are common, so blemished animals are not rare and thus not redeemable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports that Samuel would have retracted his view if he had heard a baraita about consecrated animals that cannot be redeemed because they are pure.
The Gemara rejects Rav Pappa's report, stating that Samuel actually heard the baraita but did not retract.
The Gemara explains that the reason pure consecrated animals cannot be redeemed is rarity, as established in the earlier discussion.
The Gemara applies the same reasoning to blemished animals: since disqualifying blemishes are common, blemished animals are not rare and thus not redeemable.

items.text: Rav Kahana and Rabbi Oshaya's ruling: only impure items are redeemed
items.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rabbi Oshaya's ruling: only impure items are redeemed
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rabbi Oshaya state definitively that impure items are redeemed, but pure items are not. Rabbi Elazar adds an exception: the tenth of an ephah of a sin-offering, which is not redeemed because the Torah says 'from his sin-offering' and 'upon his sin-offering'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana states that impure items (טְמֵאִין) are redeemed (נִפְדִּין), but pure items (טְהוֹרִין) are not redeemed.
Rabbi Oshaya agrees with Rav Kahana's ruling, stating the same distinction between impure and pure items.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Oshaya's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Oshaya's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports that Rabbi Oshaya said even pure items are redeemed.

Rabbi Elazar adds an exception: the tenth of an ephah of a sin-offering (עֲשִׂירִית הָאֵיפָה שֶׁל מִנְחַת חוֹטֵא) is not redeemed, because the Torah says 'from his sin-offering' (מֵחַטָּאתוֹ) and 'upon his sin-offering' (עַל חַטָּאתוֹ).

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya's tradition about piggul in a meal-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya's tradition about piggul in a meal-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya reports a tradition that according to Rabbi Shimon, piggul in a meal-offering does not impart food impurity, as taught in a mishnah about orlah and diverse species in a vineyard.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya opens by stating that he heard a tradition regarding piggul in a meal-offering according to Rabbi Shimon.

sub.text: Rabbi Oshaya's citation of a mishnah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya's citation of a mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya reports that according to Rabbi Shimon, piggul in a meal-offering does not impart food impurity, as taught in a mishnah about orlah and diverse species in a vineyard.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about impurity of certain items
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about impurity of certain items
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that are susceptible to food impurity, including a stoned ox, a heifer whose neck is broken, etc. Rabbi Shimon disagrees, except for meat in milk, which he agrees is susceptible because it had a time of fitness.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'from all food that is eaten' that only food which can be fed to others is called food.

items.text: Gemara: Challenge from piggul in a meal-offering and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Challenge from piggul in a meal-offering and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that piggul in a meal-offering is also food that cannot be fed to others, yet Rabbi Shimon holds it is susceptible. It answers that meat in milk is different because it is permitted for benefit, and additionally it had a time of fitness.

items.text: Gemara: Objection from a baraita about notar and piggul
items.text_en: Gemara: Objection from a baraita about notar and piggul
items.desc_en: A baraita states that notar after sprinkling is susceptible to food impurity, but piggul in kodshei kodashim and kodashim kalim is not, while piggul in a meal-offering is. This seems to contradict Rabbi Shimon's principle.

items.text: Gemara: Resolution based on time of fitness and redemption
items.text_en: Gemara: Resolution based on time of fitness and redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the distinction is whether the offering had a time of fitness. For piggul in a meal-offering that was sanctified while attached to the ground, it never had a time of fitness. The Gemara discusses whether it could be redeemed, citing Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Shimon's principle that something standing to be redeemed is considered as redeemed.

items.text: Gemara: Further challenge and resolution regarding notar before sprinkling
items.text_en: Gemara: Further challenge and resolution regarding notar before sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that notar before sprinkling is not susceptible even though it could be sprinkled, and resolves that the case is where there was no time left in the day to sprinkle. It then reinterprets the baraita to refer to before and after the offering became fit for sprinkling, and notes that piggul in kodashim is a case where there is a mitzvah to sprinkle.

items.text: Gemara's question on piggul in sprinkling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on piggul in sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that piggul does not impart food impurity refers to piggul in the sprinkling, and answers that it refers to piggul in the slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that piggul does not impart food impurity refers to piggul in the sprinkling, and answers that it refers to piggul in the slaughter.

items.text: Inference about piggul in sprinkling
items.text_en: Inference about piggul in sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if piggul occurred in the sprinkling, the sacrifice would indeed be susceptible to food impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if piggul occurred in the sprinkling, would the sacrifice be susceptible to food impurity?

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the Mishnah's formulation
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the Mishnah's formulation
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah should have distinguished within its own case of a meal-offering, and explains that it needed to teach that even piggul in the kemitzah (which is like slaughter) still imparts impurity because it had a moment of fitness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah should have distinguished within its own case of a meal-offering, rather than teaching a separate case.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah needed to teach the case of piggul in the kemitzah (which is like slaughter) to show that even such piggul imparts impurity because the offering had a moment of fitness.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that he stated the halakhah before Rav Nachman, explaining that even if piggul occurred in the sprinkling, the sacrifice is still considered food because one could have redeemed it and then sprinkled.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that he stated the halakhah before Rav Nachman, explaining that even if piggul occurred in the sprinkling, the sacrifice is still considered food.
Rav Ashi explains that one could have redeemed the sacrifice and then sprinkled, so the food status applies; but if one could have sprinkled only after the fact, we do not say so.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yehoshua on me'ilah
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yehoshua on me'ilah
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating a general rule: any offering that had a time of permission for the priests is not subject to me'ilah, while one that never had such a time is subject to me'ilah. Examples include an offering that was left overnight, became impure, or was taken out.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites a baraita of Rabbi Yehoshua stating a general rule: any offering that had a time of permission for the priests is not subject to me'ilah, while one that never had such a time is subject to me'ilah, with examples of each category.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita to Rav Ashi's view
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita to Rav Ashi's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Ashi: the baraita says an offering that was left overnight (literally) is not subject to me'ilah, even though it could have been sprinkled. The Gemara deflects by interpreting 'left overnight' as 'fit to be left overnight'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Ashi: the baraita explicitly says 'left overnight' (לָנָה מַמָּשׁ), and even though the blood could have been sprinkled, it rules no me'ilah applies.
The Gemara deflects by interpreting 'left overnight' in the baraita as 'fit to be left overnight' (רְאוּיָה לָלִין), not actual overnight stay.

items.text: Further objection and textual correction
items.text_en: Further objection and textual correction
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if 'left overnight' means 'fit to be left overnight', the baraita's wording should be 'any that has a time of permission' rather than 'had'. It implies a textual correction is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if 'left overnight' means actual left overnight (לינה ממש), the baraita's wording should be 'any that has a time of permission' (כל שיש לה שעת היתר) rather than 'had' (שהיתה), implying a textual correction is needed.

items.text: Rav Ashi's distinction between me'ilah and tum'ah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's distinction between me'ilah and tum'ah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing me'ilah from tum'ah: me'ilah depends on sanctity, which once removed cannot return; tum'ah depends on food status, which can be restored if the blood could still be sprinkled.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between מעילה (misappropriation) and טומאה (ritual impurity): מעילה depends on sanctity, which once removed cannot return, while טומאה depends on food status, which can be restored if the blood could still be sprinkled.

items.text: Beginning of a new challenge from a baraita on a conditional guilt-offering
items.text_en: Beginning of a new challenge from a baraita on a conditional guilt-offering
items.desc_en: A new baraita is introduced about one who brings a conditional guilt-offering and then learns he did not sin; Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute whether it may go out to pasture.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about one who brings a conditional guilt-offering (אשם תלוי) and later learns he did not sin; Rabbi Meir rules it goes out to pasture.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of a sin-offering whose owner dies or is forgiven
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of a sin-offering whose owner dies or is forgiven
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a sin-offering's owner dies or is forgiven after the animal is designated, after slaughter, or after blood is sprinkled. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei offer differing opinions on whether the offering can still be brought or if the blood should be sprinkled.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma rules that if a sin-offering's owner dies or is forgiven before slaughter, the animal must graze until blemished, be sold, and its proceeds fall to the Temple treasury as a free-will offering.
Rabbi Eliezer argues that the offering should be brought, because if it does not atone for this sin, it will atone for another sin.
The Mishnah states that if the owner's death or forgiveness was discovered after slaughter, the blood must be poured out and the meat burned.
The Mishnah rules that if the blood was already sprinkled, the meat may be eaten.
Rabbi Yosei adds that even if the blood is still in the cup (not yet sprinkled), it should be sprinkled and the meat eaten.

items.text: Gemara: Explaining Rabbi Yosei's opinion
items.text_en: Gemara: Explaining Rabbi Yosei's opinion
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Yosei follows Rabbi Shimon's principle that anything standing to be sprinkled is considered as already sprinkled. The Gemara then offers an alternative explanation from the West in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: that service vessels sanctify invalid offerings to be brought.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Yosei's opinion follows Rabbi Shimon's principle that anything standing to be sprinkled is considered as already sprinkled.

sub.text: Alternative explanation from the West in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Alternative explanation from the West in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation from the West in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: that service vessels sanctify invalid offerings to be brought לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Gemara: Rav Ashi's challenge and Rav Kahana's answer
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Ashi's challenge and Rav Kahana's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges Rav Kahana: if standing to be sprinkled is considered as sprinkled, then standing to be burned should also be considered as burned, yet leftover offerings and the red heifer still contract food impurity. Rav Kahana answers that the sanctity of the Temple renders them susceptible to impurity.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's challenge to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges Rav Kahana: if Rabbi Shimon holds that anything standing to be sprinkled is considered as already sprinkled, then by extension anything standing to be burned should be considered as already burned, so why do leftover offerings (נותר) and the red heifer (פרה) contract food impurity — they should be mere ash.
Rav Kahana answers that the sanctity of the Temple (חיבת הקודש) renders them susceptible to impurity, overriding the principle of 'standing to be burned'.

items.text: Gemara: Ravina's question and resolution with Resh Lakish's query
items.text_en: Gemara: Ravina's question and resolution with Resh Lakish's query
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether the sanctity of the Temple also makes these items count as first or second degree impurity. The Gemara notes that this is the same as Resh Lakish's question about the dry flour of meal-offerings, and distinguishes between biblical and rabbinic impurity.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether the sanctity of the Temple (חיבת הקודש) that renders the items fit for impurity also makes them count as first or second degree impurity (טומאה) for the purpose of counting degrees.

sub.text: Gemara's identification with Resh Lakish's query
sub.text_en: Gemara's identification with Resh Lakish's query
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this is the same question that Resh Lakish asked about the dry flour of meal-offerings (צריד של מנחות) — whether one counts first and second degree impurity from it.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution distinguishing biblical and rabbinic impurity
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution distinguishing biblical and rabbinic impurity
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Resh Lakish's question was about biblical impurity (דאורייתא), while Ravina's question is about rabbinic impurity (דרבנן), thus distinguishing the two cases.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows for meal-offerings in wrong vessels or wrong number of vessels
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows for meal-offerings in wrong vessels or wrong number of vessels
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details cases where one vows to bring a meal-offering in a specific vessel (מחבת or מרחשת) or in a specific number of vessels, but brings it differently. If it is a general vow, the offering is brought but the vow is not fulfilled; if it is a designated offering, it is invalid. The Mishnah also discusses cases where the court instructs the person to fulfill the vow correctly.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens: If one vows to bring a meal-offering in a frying pan (מחבת) but brings it in a stew pot (מרחשת), or vice versa, what he brought is brought but he hasn't fulfilled his obligation.

items.text: Gemara: The necessity of both Mishnah cases
items.text_en: Gemara: The necessity of both Mishnah cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to teach both the case of different vessels and the case of different numbers of vessels, as each case might have been thought to have a different ruling without the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes: And it is necessary (to have both cases).
The Gemara opens by stating that both Mishnah cases (vessel type and vessel count) are necessary.
The Gemara explains that without the second case, one might think that when the vessel type is the same but the count differs, the vow is fulfilled.
The Gemara explains that without the first case, one might think that when the vessel count is the same but the type differs, the vow is fulfilled.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita and Abaye's explanation on sanctification
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita and Abaye's explanation on sanctification
items.desc_en: A Baraita records Rabbi Shimon's opinion that one does fulfill the vow even with the wrong vessel. The Gemara questions how the offering can be valid if service vessels did not sanctify it, and Abaye answers that they did sanctify it for invalidation but not for offering. Abaye then notes that the Mishnah only taught the case of different vessels, not different numbers.

sub.desc_en: A Baraita states: What he brought, he brought, but he hasn't fulfilled his vow. Rabbi Shimon says: He also has fulfilled his vow.
The Baraita records Tanna Kamma's ruling that one does not fulfill the vow when bringing in a different vessel, and Rabbi Shimon's dissenting opinion that he does fulfill the vow.
The Gemara questions how the offering can be valid if the service vessels did not sanctify it, citing a baraita that service vessels sanctify offerings.
Abaye answers that the vessels sanctified the offering for invalidation (if it is unfit, it becomes invalid) but not for offering (to be brought on the altar).
Abaye notes that the Mishnah only taught the case of different vessels, not different numbers of vessels.

items.text: Clarification of the earlier ruling on changing the animal
items.text_en: Clarification of the earlier ruling on changing the animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier ruling about changing a designated animal applies only when the change was made at the time of the vow, not at the time of designation, based on the verse "as you vowed" and not "as you designated." This is supported by a statement from Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier ruling applies only when the change was made at the time of the vow, not at the time of designation.
The Gemara cites the verse 'as you vowed' to support that only matters specified at the time of the vow are essential.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Acha bar Chanina and Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Acha bar Chanina and Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement is cited to support the distinction between the time of the vow and the time of designation.

items.text: Mishnah: Invalid specifications in a meal-offering vow
items.text_en: Mishnah: Invalid specifications in a meal-offering vow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one vows a meal-offering with invalid specifications (e.g., barley instead of wheat, coarse flour instead of fine flour, without oil and frankincense, or a half-tenth or one and a half tenths), he must bring a valid offering. Rabbi Shimon exempts him for an improper quantity because he did not donate in the manner of donors.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one vows a meal-offering with invalid specifications (barley, coarse flour, or without oil and frankincense), he must bring a valid offering.
The Mishnah rules that for improper quantities (half-tenth or one and a half tenths), one must bring a valid measure; Rabbi Shimon exempts him because he did not donate in the manner of donors.

items.text: Gemara's first question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's first question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah requires a valid offering, since the vow includes its own opening for nullification (the invalid specification), implying the vow should be void.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah requires a valid offering, since the vow includes its own opening for nullification (the invalid specification), implying the vow should be void.

items.text: First answer: Hezekiah and Rabbi Yochanan's explanations
items.text_en: First answer: Hezekiah and Rabbi Yochanan's explanations
items.desc_en: Hezekiah explains the Mishnah follows Beit Shammai's principle of "תפוס לשון ראשון" (grasp the first expression). Rabbi Yochanan says even Beit Hillel would agree if the speaker said "Had I known one cannot vow that way, I would not have vowed that way but rather this way."

sub.desc_en: Hezekiah answers that the Mishnah follows Beit Shammai's principle of תְּפוֹס לָשׁוֹן רִאשׁוֹן (grasp the first expression), citing a baraita about a nazirite vow.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that even Beit Hillel would agree if the speaker said 'Had I known one cannot vow that way, I would not have vowed that way but rather this way.'

items.text: Hezekiah's limitation and retraction
items.text_en: Hezekiah's limitation and retraction
items.desc_en: Hezekiah initially limits the Mishnah to barley (a valid grain) but not lentils (invalid). The Gemara notes this aligns with Beit Shammai, but questions why lentils would differ. Rava explains Hezekiah retracted because the Mishnah specifically taught "barley" instead of "lentils," implying the speaker erred only with barley, not lentils.

sub.desc_en: Hezekiah limits the Mishnah's ruling to one who says 'a meal-offering of barley' (a valid grain), but not 'of lentils' (an invalid item).
The Gemara questions why Hezekiah's position, which aligns with Beit Shammai's principle of 'תפוס לשון ראשון' (grasp the first expression), would distinguish between barley and lentils.
The Gemara concludes that Hezekiah retracted his original limitation.
The Gemara asks why Hezekiah retracted, and Rava answers that the Mishnah's wording (teaching 'barley' rather than 'lentils') implies the speaker only errs with barley, not lentils.
Rava explains that the Mishnah's choice to teach 'barley' rather than 'lentils' shows the speaker is mistaken only about barley (a valid grain), not about lentils (an invalid item).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's broader view and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's broader view and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds the Mishnah applies even to lentils. The Gemara questions this since Beit Hillel's reasoning is error, and one would not err with lentils. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan was responding to Hezekiah's reasoning: Hezekiah retracted because the Mishnah didn't mention lentils, but Rabbi Yochanan argues the Mishnah used a "not necessary" style—even lentils, where one might think the speaker retracted, the principle of "תפוס לשון ראשון" applies.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the Mishnah's rule applies even to lentils.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's view: since he follows Beit Hillel, whose reasoning is error, one would not err with lentils.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan was responding to Hezekiah's reasoning: even where one might think the speaker retracted, the principle of תְּפוֹס לָשׁוֹן רִאשׁוֹן (grasp the first expression) applies.

items.text: Ze'iri's ruling and the Gemara's challenge
items.text_en: Ze'iri's ruling and the Gemara's challenge
items.desc_en: Ze'iri states that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when one says 'minchah' (meal-offering) explicitly. Rava challenges Rav Nachman by citing cases where one says 'flour' or 'without oil and frankincense' or 'half an isaron', and the Mishnah requires a full measure. The Gemara resolves that in all these cases, the person said 'minchah' implicitly. The discussion concludes with a case where one says 'a minchah of half an isaron and an isaron', leading to a requirement of two isaron.

sub.desc_en: Ze'iri states that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when one explicitly says 'minchah' (meal-offering), but not otherwise.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman by citing the Mishnah's case of 'flour' (קמח) where one must bring fine flour, implying the person did not say 'minchah'.
The Gemara answers that in the 'flour' case, the person actually said 'minchah' implicitly.
Rava challenges with the Mishnah's case of 'without oil and frankincense' where one must bring them, implying no 'minchah' was said.
The Gemara again answers that the person said 'minchah' implicitly.
Rava challenges with the Mishnah's case of 'half an isaron' where one must bring a full isaron, implying no 'minchah' was said.
The Gemara answers that the person said 'minchah' implicitly in this case as well.

The Gemara objects: if the person said 'minchah' in the 'half an isaron' case, then the Mishnah's ruling that 'one and a half isaron' requires two isaron is problematic, because saying 'half an isaron' after 'minchah' is meaningless.

The Gemara resolves that the case is where one says 'a minchah of half an isaron and an isaron', so the 'minchah' obligates one isaron, 'half an isaron' is meaningless, and then 'an isaron' adds another isaron, requiring two total.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's exemption explained
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's exemption explained
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Shimon's ruling (that one who vows improperly is exempt) follows Rabbi Yosei's view that a person can retract his words even at the end of his statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if so, why does Rabbi Shimon exempt one who vowed improperly?
Rava answers that Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Yosei's view that a person can retract his words even at the end of his statement.

items.text: Mishnah: Sixty isaron in one vessel, sixty-one in two
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sixty isaron in one vessel, sixty-one in two
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may donate a meal-offering of sixty isaron and bring it in one vessel, but if one says 'sixty-one', he brings sixty in one vessel and one in another, as the community brings sixty-one on the first festival day of Sukkot that falls on Shabbat. Rabbi Shimon argues that up to sixty can be mixed, but sixty-one cannot, comparing it to the measure of a mikveh (forty se'ah) where a minuscule amount prevents immersion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule: one may donate a meal-offering of sixty isaron and bring it in one vessel, but if one says 'sixty-one', he brings sixty in one vessel and one in another, because the community brings sixty-one on the first festival day of Sukkot that falls on Shabbat.
The Mishnah adds the principle that it is sufficient for an individual to be one less than the community.
Rabbi Shimon objects that the community's offerings are for bulls and sheep which cannot be mixed, so the analogy fails; he argues that up to sixty isaron can be mixed, but sixty-one cannot.

The Sages respond that sixty can be mixed but sixty-one cannot, and Rabbi Shimon replies that all measures of the Sages are like this: with forty se'ah one can immerse, but with forty se'ah minus a kortov one cannot immerse.

items.text: Gemara: Source for the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: A question is asked before Rabbi Yehuda bar Il'ai: from where do we derive that one who says 'sixty-one' brings sixty in one vessel and one in another? He answers by citing the community's practice. Rabbi Shimon objects that the community's offerings are of different types (bulls and rams) that cannot be mixed, and instead derives from the verse 'every meal-offering mixed with oil and dry' that one must bring an offering that can be mixed. The Sages challenge him with the same mikveh analogy.

sub.desc_en: A question is asked before Rabbi Yehuda bar Il'ai: from where do we derive that one who says 'sixty-one' brings sixty in one vessel and one in another?
Rabbi Yehuda bar Il'ai answers by citing the community's practice on the first day of Yom Tov that falls on Shabbat, where they bring sixty-one, and the individual reduces by one.
Rabbi Shimon objects that the community's offerings are of different types (bulls and rams) with different consistencies and times, so they cannot be mixed together.
The Sages challenge Rabbi Shimon to provide his own source, and he derives from the verse 'every meal-offering mixed with oil and dry' that one must bring an offering that can be mixed.
The Sages challenge Rabbi Shimon with the mikveh analogy: just as forty se'ah minus a kortov cannot immerse, so too sixty-one cannot be mixed, but sixty can.

items.text: Analogies and the principle of mixture
items.text_en: Analogies and the principle of mixture
items.desc_en: The Gemara adds other examples of precise measures (egg-sized for food impurity, three-by-three handbreadths for midras impurity) to support the principle. Rabbi Zeira then clarifies that if an item is inherently suitable for mixing, lack of mixing does not invalidate it, but if it is not suitable, mixing is essential.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites examples of precise measures (egg-sized for food impurity, three-by-three handbreadths for midras impurity) to support the principle that a fixed measure is essential.
The Gemara questions why lack of mixing matters, citing the Mishnah that if one did not mix the oil into the flour, the offering is still valid.
Rabbi Zeira resolves that if an item is inherently suitable for mixing, lack of mixing does not invalidate it, but if it is not suitable, mixing is essential.

items.text: Digression: Blood of a mule and a story about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
