items.text_en: Digression: Blood of a mule and a story about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Bivi quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about a mule of Rabbi's household that died, and the Sages estimated its blood to be a quarter-log. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna challenges this with a testimony that blood of neveilot is pure, citing a story where people waded in blood up to their knees without objection. Rabbi Zerika asks why the Sage was silent, and he explains with a verse about relying on uncertain provisions.

sub.text: Rabbi Bivi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Bivi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Bivi reports in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi a story about a mule of the Patriarch's household that died, and the Sages estimated its blood to be a quarter-log.

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna objects by citing a testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira that blood of neveilot (carcasses) is pure, and a story where pilgrims waded in blood up to their knees without any objection.
Rabbi Zerika asks Rabbi Bivi why he remained silent and did not respond to the objection.

sub.text: Rabbi Bivi's answer citing Rabbi Chanin
sub.text_en: Rabbi Bivi's answer citing Rabbi Chanin
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Bivi explains that he could not respond because, as Rabbi Chanin taught, relying on uncertain provisions (like the mule's blood) is forbidden, citing verses about one who buys grain from year to year or from week to week.

items.text: Opening anecdote about Rabbi Yehuda and the Nasi's household
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about Rabbi Yehuda and the Nasi's household
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Yehuda was a teacher in the Nasi's household and taught according to his own tradition, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda lists six leniencies of Beit Shammai and stringencies of Beit Hillel, including the case of blood of neveilot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with an anecdote about a man leaning on a column, and Rav Yosef explains that Rabbi Yehuda was a teacher in the Nasi's household and taught according to his own tradition.

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda lists six leniencies of Beit Shammai and stringencies of Beit Hillel, including the case of blood of neveilot, and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda adds a qualification about the measure of a quarter-log.

items.text: Mishnah: Permitted and prohibited numbers of log offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Permitted and prohibited numbers of log offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not donate a single log, two, or five, but may donate three, four, six, and any number above six.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not donate a single log, two, or five, but may donate three, four, six, and any number above six.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is there a fixed measure for libations?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is there a fixed measure for libations?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether libations have a fixed measure (kava) or not. It explains the practical difference: if one brings five logs, if there is no fixed measure, he can offer four (for a ram) and the fifth is a donation; if there is a fixed measure, he cannot offer them until he completes the required amount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether libations have a fixed measure (קבע) or not.

The Gemara explains the practical difference: if one brings five logs, with no fixed measure he can offer four for a ram and the fifth as a donation; with a fixed measure, he cannot offer until completing the required amount.

items.text: Abaye's attempted proof from the six shofarot for nedavah
items.text_en: Abaye's attempted proof from the six shofarot for nedavah
items.desc_en: Abaye tries to prove that there is no fixed measure from the Mishnah that six logs go to nedavah, corresponding to leftover offerings. If libations had a fixed measure, there should be a seventh shofar for leftover libations. The Gemara deflects: those shofarot are for communal donations, and libations are common and can be combined from different people.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites the Mishnah that six shofarot (trumpets) are designated for nedavah (voluntary offerings), corresponding to leftover sin-offerings, guilt-offerings, etc., and argues that if libations had a fixed measure, there should be a seventh shofar for leftover libations.
The Gemara objects: if libations had no fixed measure, why not establish a seventh shofar for leftover libations?
The Gemara deflects: those shofarot are for communal donations, and libations are common and can be combined from different people, so no separate shofar is needed.

items.text: Rava's proof from the verse about libations
items.text_en: Rava's proof from the verse about libations
items.desc_en: Rava brings a baraita that teaches one may donate libations, and from the verse one can add but not subtract. The Gemara analyzes what 'add' means: if it means four or six, those are already valid for ram or bull; rather it must mean five, proving there is no fixed measure.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita that from the verse 'אזרח' one learns that libations may be donated, with a minimum of three logs, and from 'יהיה' one may add, while from 'ככה' one may not subtract.
The Gemara asks what 'add' means: if it means four or six logs, those are already valid for a ram or bull, so why single out three?
The Gemara concludes that 'add' must mean five logs, proving that there is no fixed measure (אין קבע לנסכים).

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: our Mishnah explicitly says one may not donate five, comparing it to two which is entirely invalid. The Gemara responds that the cases are different: the Mishnah's prohibition of five is a separate issue from the question of fixed measure.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the Mishnah explicitly teaches that five is not donated, comparing it to two which is entirely invalid, implying that five too is entirely invalid.
The Gemara responds that the cases are different: each stands on its own, so the Mishnah's prohibition of five does not contradict the possibility of donating five as a voluntary libation.

items.text: Abaye's concluding analysis
items.text_en: Abaye's concluding analysis
items.desc_en: Abaye concludes that if there is no fixed measure, the matter is clear; if there is a fixed measure, he is certain up to ten, but eleven is questionable.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the uncertainty: if there is no fixed measure for libations (אֵין קֶבַע לִנְסָכִים), the matter is clear; if there is a fixed measure (יֵשׁ קֶבַע לִנְסָכִים), he is certain up to ten, but eleven is questionable.

items.text: Unresolved query about partnership intent
items.text_en: Unresolved query about partnership intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: when two people say they will bring an offering, do they intend to bring two bulls (each for one person) and only sacrifice when both are ready, or do they intend to bring two rams and one lamb? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute on donating wine vs. oil
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute on donating wine vs. oil
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one may donate wine but not oil, according to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Tarfon argues that oil may also be donated, drawing an analogy from wine which comes both as an obligation and as a donation. Rabbi Akiva rebuts that wine is offered independently with its obligation, unlike oil.

items.text: Mishnah: Partnership and types of offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Partnership and types of offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: two people may not donate a single tenth (of flour) together, but they may donate a burnt offering or peace offering together, and even a single bird.

items.text: Rava's deduction: one may donate a meal-offering of libations daily
items.text_en: Rava's deduction: one may donate a meal-offering of libations daily
items.desc_en: Rava learns from both opinions that one may donate a minchat nesachim (meal-offering of libations) any day. The Gemara clarifies that this is not obvious: one might think only the five specified meal-offerings are permitted, but Rava teaches that those restrictions apply only to unspecified vows, whereas if one specifies, it is allowed.

items.text: Reason for no partnership in minchah: the word 'nefesh'
items.text_en: Reason for no partnership in minchah: the word 'nefesh'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why two people cannot donate a single tenth. It rejects the idea that it is derived from the singular verb 'takriv' (you shall offer), since the same applies to burnt offerings. Rather, the reason is the verse 'nefesh' (soul) written regarding the minchah, implying individual offering. A baraita supports this: Rabbi says all offerings may be brought in partnership except the minchah, as it says 'nefesh'.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's homilies on the minchah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's homilies on the minchah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains why the minchah is singled out with 'nefesh': God considers the poor person who brings a minchah as if they offered their very soul. He also explains why five types of frying are specified for the minchah, using a parable of a king who asks his poor friend to prepare five fried dishes so he can enjoy them.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the standard concluding formula: 'We have returned from you, the chapter of Menachot and Nesachim.'

items.text: Mishnah: Vows of tenths and unspecified minchah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows of tenths and unspecified minchah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details cases: if one vows 'a tenth' they bring one; 'tenths' they bring two; if they specified but forgot, they bring sixty tenths. For 'a minchah' they bring any type; Rabbi Yehuda says they bring the fine flour minchah. For 'minchah' or 'type of minchah' they bring one; 'minchot' or 'type of minchot' they bring two; if they forgot which, they bring all five. If they specified a minchah of tenths but forgot the number, they bring sixty tenths; Rabbi says they bring minchot from one to sixty tenths.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah's rulings
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the obviousness of some rulings, then identifies the Tanna of the case of 'I specified but don't know what' as not Rabbi (according to Chizkiyah), but Rabbi Yochanan says it could even be Rabbi, if the person specified tenths but did not designate a vessel, so they bring sixty tenths in sixty vessels.

items.text: Reason for choosing a specific minchah and a question on burnt offerings
items.text_en: Reason for choosing a specific minchah and a question on burnt offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when one says 'I pledge a minchah' they bring any type because the Torah opened with that type. It then questions: if so, when one says 'I pledge a burnt offering' should they bring a bull because the Torah opened with that?

items.text: Opening Mishnah interpretation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when one vows an olah, he brings a lamb because the Torah first mentions the lamb from the flock; similarly, for a bird offering, he brings doves because they are mentioned first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when one vows an olah, he brings a lamb because the Torah first mentions the lamb from the flock; similarly, for a bird offering, he brings doves because they are mentioned first.

items.text: Clarifying the unique minchah
items.text_en: Clarifying the unique minchah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement about a unique minchah, explaining that it refers to a minchah without a modifier, and that the phrase "opened with" is merely a mnemonic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that one who vows an עולה (burnt offering) brings a lamb, and notes that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says a dove or pigeon, and Rabbi Yehuda does not disagree.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's 'unique minchah' refers to a מנחה (meal offering) without a modifier (i.e., no additional name).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah says 'since the verse opened with it first,' and resolves that the phrase 'opened with' is merely identifying which minchah is unique.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah simply refers to the מנחת הסולת (fine flour offering) and the phrase is merely a mnemonic.

items.text: Rav Pappa's query on "minei minchah"
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's query on "minei minchah"
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether the phrase "minei minchah" means two types of minchah or one minchah from a type, and the Gemara presents two possibilities.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks about the meaning of the phrase 'מיני מנחה' (types of minchah).
The Gemara suggests that since he said 'מיני' (types), he means two, and 'מנחה' is a general term for all מנחות (meal-offerings).
Alternatively, the Gemara suggests that since he said 'מנחה' (a minchah), he means one minchah, and 'מיני מנחה' means 'from the types of minchah, one minchah upon me'.

items.text: Attempted resolution from a baraita
items.text_en: Attempted resolution from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to resolve Rav Pappa's query from a baraita, but the baraita's wording is ambiguous and the Gemara rejects the proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita to resolve Rav Pappa's query: the phrase 'minchah' or 'min minchah' requires one offering, implying 'minei minchah' requires two.
The Gemara objects by reading the baraita's end: 'menachot' or 'min menachot' requires two, which would imply 'minei minchah' requires one, making the baraita inconclusive.
The Gemara cites another baraita: 'min menachot alai' requires two offerings of one type, implying 'miminei minchah' requires only one.
The Gemara rejects the proof, suggesting that 'minei minchah' might mean two offerings of two different types, not one.

items.text: Another baraita and Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Another baraita and Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita that seems to resolve the query, but suggests it follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a minchah can have two types, while the Rabbis require two separate minchot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a full baraita that distinguishes between 'מין מנחות' (type of meal offerings) and 'מיני מנחות' (types of meal offerings), implying that 'מיני מנחה' (types of a meal offering) requires only one offering.

The Gemara rejects the proof, suggesting the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, who allows a single meal offering with two types (loaves and wafers), so 'מיני מנחה' means one offering containing two types.
The Gemara notes that according to the Rabbis, who forbid mixing types in one offering, one who says 'מיני מנחה' must bring two separate meal offerings of different types.

items.text: Dispute about an unspecified vow
items.text_en: Dispute about an unspecified vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the case of one who vowed but forgot what he vowed, and debates whether the Tanna is Rabbi Shimon or Rabbi Yehuda, with Abaye arguing that even Rabbi Shimon would require bringing all five types because he holds that one brings and stipulates.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who specified a meal offering but forgot what he specified must bring all five types; the Gemara asks who is the Tanna of this ruling.

רבי ירמיה (Rabbi Yirmeya) answers that the mishnah is not in accordance with the opinion of רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon), because according to רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon) one could bring a single meal offering with half loaves and half wafers, reducing the number of required offerings.

The Gemara objects that even if the Tanna holds like רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda), who says all meal offerings come as ten items, there would be uncertainty requiring fourteen different meal offerings, not just five.

אביי (Abaye) resolves the issue by arguing that even according to רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon), one can bring all five types and stipulate, as we have heard that רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon) holds that one brings an offering and stipulates, citing a baraita about a leper's uncertain guilt offering.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Conditional guilt-offering for a possible metzora
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Conditional guilt-offering for a possible metzora
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes a case where a person brings a guilt-offering and a log of oil for a possible metzora, stipulating that if he is a metzora it is his asham and log, and if not, the asham becomes a voluntary peace-offering. This asham requires slaughter in the north, application to the thumbs, semikhah, libations, and breast-and-thigh waving, and is eaten by male priests for one day and night.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a conditional guilt-offering for a possible metzora, detailing its requirements and consumption.

items.text: Gemara's comment: Even though the master distinguishes in slaughter of sacrifices
items.text_en: Gemara's comment: Even though the master distinguishes in slaughter of sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that even though the master (presumably Rabbi Shimon) distinguishes in the context of slaughter of sacrifices, here he might still allow the conditional offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that even though the master (Rabbi Shimon) distinguishes in the context of slaughter of sacrifices, here he might still allow the conditional offering.

items.text: Gemara's objection: Rabbi Shimon's view is only for rectifying the person
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: Rabbi Shimon's view is only for rectifying the person
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon's leniency applies only when done initially to rectify the person, but in general, if done it is valid, but initially it is not permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon's leniency applies only when done initially to rectify the person, but in general, if done it is valid, but initially it is not permitted.

items.text: Distinction: Peace-offerings reduce consumption, but minchot are different
items.text_en: Distinction: Peace-offerings reduce consumption, but minchot are different
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that this applies to peace-offerings, which reduce their consumption and become disqualified, but with minchot, even initially it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the distinction: the rule that one may not bring a peace-offering לכתחילה (a-priori) applies only to peace-offerings, which reduce their consumption and become disqualified, but with מנחות (meal-offerings), even לכתחילה (a-priori) it is permitted.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question to Abaye: Rabbi Shimon's mixed minchah
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question to Abaye: Rabbi Shimon's mixed minchah
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: Rabbi Shimon says one may bring half loaves and half wafers, but this involves bringing one issaron from two issaron and one log from two logs, which seems problematic.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: Rabbi Shimon says one may bring half loaves and half wafers, but this involves bringing one issaron from two issaron and one log from two logs, which seems problematic.

items.text: Abaye's response: Rabbi Shimon holds that one who brings such is yatza
items.text_en: Abaye's response: Rabbi Shimon holds that one who brings such is yatza
items.desc_en: Abaye responds that we have heard Rabbi Shimon say that if one brought one issaron from two issaron and one log from two logs, he has fulfilled his obligation.

sub.desc_en: Abaye responds that Rabbi Shimon explicitly holds that if one brought one issaron from two issaron and one log from two logs, he has fulfilled his obligation (יצא).

items.text: Gemara's question: How does he perform the kemitzah?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: How does he perform the kemitzah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one performs the kemitzah in such a mixed minchah. The person must stipulate: if these are loaves alone and wafers alone, then the kemitzah from loaves is for loaves and from wafers for wafers; if half wafers and half loaves, then the kemitzah from loaves is for the half-loaves-half-wafers mixture, and similarly for wafers. But one must take one kemitzah from the loaves, which is problematic because the mixture requires a single kemitzah from each type.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one performs the kemitzah (taking a handful) in this mixed minchah, given the need to stipulate for each possible composition.

items.text: Gemara's question on mixing חלות and רקקין
items.text_en: Gemara's question on mixing חלות and רקקין
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a ruling about one who vowed a meal-offering of חלות and רקקין but is uncertain which, citing Rabbi Shimon's view that if he took a handful from one for both he is exempt. It then addresses the issue of leftover oil, explaining that if he said half חלות and half רקקין the oil returns to the חלות, but if all רקקין the oil is eaten by priests, in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda.

items.text: Rav Kahana's question about מנחת נסכים and the list of uncertainties
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's question about מנחת נסכים and the list of uncertainties
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav Ashi about the possibility of uncertainty regarding a מנחת נסכים, citing Rava that one can donate such an offering daily. The Gemara then lists a series of distinctions that are not subject to uncertainty: whether it comes for an individual or community, for itself or with a sacrifice, requires frankincense or not, comes with one or three logs, or requires kemitzah.

items.text: Baraita on one who vowed an unspecified meal-offering of עשרונים
items.text_en: Baraita on one who vowed an unspecified meal-offering of עשרונים
items.desc_en: A baraita presents cases of one who vowed a meal-offering of עשרונים but is uncertain about the details. The Sages rule he brings a single offering of sixty עשרונים, while Rabbi says he brings offerings from one to sixty עשרונים, totaling 1,830. A second case adds more uncertainty, with the Sages requiring five offerings of sixty each (300), and Rabbi requiring five sets from one to sixty (9,150).

items.text: Rav Chisda and Rava's explanations of the dispute
items.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rava's explanations of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains the dispute between the Sages and Rabbi as whether it is permitted to bring non-sacred items into the Temple courtyard: Rabbi holds it is forbidden, the Sages permit it. Rava argues that all agree it is forbidden, but they dispute whether one may mix obligatory and voluntary offerings: the Sages permit it, Rabbi forbids it.

items.text: Abaye's objection to Rava and the Gemara's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rava and the Gemara's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rava's explanation: if mixing is permitted, one would need two handfuls, but the kohen might take from the obligatory for the voluntary and vice versa. The Gemara suggests relying on the kohen's intention, but then questions how to burn the offerings: if the voluntary is burned first, the obligatory might lack its remnants; if the obligatory first, the voluntary is problematic.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps the entire mixture is considered a vow-offering, and any part of it offered for the fire would violate the prohibition of 'בל תקטירו' (not to burn leaven or honey).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps the entire mixture is considered a vow-offering, and any part offered for the fire would violate the prohibition of 'בל תקטירו' (not to burn leaven or honey).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's answer: offered as wood
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's answer: offered as wood
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi answers that the mixture is offered for the sake of wood, following Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that one may offer wood for the altar even if not for the sake of a pleasing aroma.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi answers that the mixture is offered for the sake of wood, citing Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that one may offer wood for the altar even if not for the sake of a pleasing aroma.

items.text: Rav Acha's challenge and Rav Ashi's response
items.text_en: Rav Acha's challenge and Rav Ashi's response
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava challenges Rav Ashi: perhaps everyone agrees that mixing a vow with a freewill offering is permitted, and the dispute is only about Rabbi Eliezer's opinion. Rav Ashi responds that if Rabbi held that mixing is permitted and rejected Rabbi Eliezer, he could bring sixty tenths in one vessel and one in another, touch them, and take a handful.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava challenges Rav Ashi: perhaps everyone agrees that mixing a vow with a freewill offering is permitted, and the dispute is only about whether Rabbi accepts Rabbi Eliezer's opinion.
Rav Ashi responds that if Rabbi held that mixing is permitted and rejected Rabbi Eliezer, he could bring sixty tenths in one vessel and one in another, touch them, and take a handful.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation: dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation: dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rava argues that everyone agrees mixing is permitted and accepts Rabbi Eliezer's opinion; the dispute is between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis regarding the amount of oil for a meal-offering. The Rabbis require sixty logs for sixty tenths, while Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says only one log, leading to uncertainty whether it is one or two offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that everyone agrees mixing is permitted and accepts Rabbi Eliezer's opinion; the dispute is between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis.
The Mishnah is cited: a meal-offering of sixty tenths requires sixty logs of oil, but Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says it needs only one log, based on the verse.
The Rabbis hold that each tenth requires its own log, totaling sixty logs.
Rabbi holds like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, creating uncertainty whether the sixty tenths are one offering needing one log or two offerings needing two logs.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation: dispute about 'small and brought large'
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation: dispute about 'small and brought large'
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the dispute is about whether one who vowed a small offering and brought a large one fulfills his vow. The Rabbis say he does, Rabbi says he does not. The Gemara notes that this was already debated elsewhere, but both cases are necessary to avoid mistaken inferences.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi is about whether one who vowed a small offering and brought a large one fulfills his vow.
The Gemara objects that this dispute was already debated elsewhere, citing a Mishnah where the same positions appear.
The Gemara resolves that both cases are necessary to avoid mistaken inferences: in the first case, the Rabbis might concede to Rabbi, and in the second, Rabbi might concede to the Rabbis.

items.text: Mishnah: minimum measures for donated items
items.text_en: Mishnah: minimum measures for donated items
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists minimum amounts for vows of wood (two logs), frankincense (a handful), gold (a dinar), silver (a dinar), copper (a ma'ah), and the rule for one who forgot what he vowed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists minimum measures for vows of wood, frankincense, gold, silver, copper, and the rule for one who forgot what he vowed.

items.text: Gemara on wood: source and Rabbi's opinion
items.text_en: Gemara on wood: source and Rabbi's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one may donate wood, with a minimum of two logs, and Rabbi says wood requires salt and presentation. Rava adds that according to Rabbi, wood requires a handful, and Rav Papa says wood requires other wood.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the word 'קרבן' (offering) includes wood donations, with a minimum of two logs, citing a verse.
Rabbi states that wood is a full-fledged offering (קרבן) requiring salt and presentation (הגשה).
Rava adds that according to Rabbi, wood requires a handful (קמיצה).
Rav Papa adds that according to Rabbi, wood requires other wood (for the fire).

items.text: Source for frankincense and further discussion
items.text_en: Source for frankincense and further discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the minimum of a handful for frankincense from a verse, and discusses a baraita about one who vows 'to the altar' bringing frankincense. It questions whether there are other items, noting that a burnt-offering has its hide for priests, and a bird burnt-offering has its crop and feathers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that frankincense (לבונה) requires at least a handful (קומץ), and answers by citing a verse that equates frankincense to the handful of the meal-offering.
A baraita teaches that one who vows 'to the altar' brings frankincense, and if unspecified, brings from every item offered on the altar.

The Gemara objects that there are other items offered on the altar, such as a burnt-offering (עולה), but notes that its hide goes to the priests, and a bird burnt-offering has its crop and feathers, implying they are not entirely consumed.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Minimum for bird offerings
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Minimum for bird offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows a bird offering must bring the crop and feathers, but the Gemara questions why other components like libations are not included.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the minimum for a bird offering is the crop and feathers.

items.text: Gemara's clarification on libations and meal-offering
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on libations and meal-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that libations go to the drains, and the meal-offering of libations is not considered a separate vow because the priests eat part of it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what about libations (נסכים) — they go to the drains, so how can one vow them?
The Gemara answers: the meal-offering of libations (מנחת נסכים) is not entirely lost because the priests eat part of it, so the vow is not in vain.

items.text: Minimum for gold and silver donations
items.text_en: Minimum for gold and silver donations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states minimums for gold (a dinar) and silver (a dinar). The Gemara questions whether these could be for libations or small coins, and Rabbi Elazar and Rav Pappa (or Rav Sheishet) explain that the donor specified 'coin' and that small gold or silver coins are not commonly used.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the minimum gold donation is a gold dinar.
The Gemara questions whether the gold might be for libations (נסכים).
Rabbi Elazar answers that the donor specified 'coin' (מטבע), excluding libations.
The Gemara questions whether the gold might be small coins (פריטי).
Rav Pappa answers that people do not make small gold coins, so the minimum is a dinar.
The Mishnah states the minimum silver donation is a silver dinar.
The Gemara questions whether the silver might be for libations.
Rabbi Elazar answers that the donor specified 'coin', excluding libations.
The Gemara questions whether the silver might be small coins.
Rav Sheishet answers that in a place where small silver coins are not used, the minimum is a dinar.

items.text: Minimum for copper and iron donations
items.text_en: Minimum for copper and iron donations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states a minimum for copper (a ma'ah). Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says a small copper hook, and Abaye explains its use. For iron, the Tanna Kamma says a 'kolyah oreiv' (a raven's hook), and Rav Yosef specifies its size as an amah by an amah; an alternative version reverses the explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the minimum copper donation is a ma'ah of silver.
A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion that the minimum is a small copper hook.
Abaye explains the hook's use: for poking wicks and wiping lamps.
A baraita cites Acherim's opinion that the minimum iron donation is a raven's hook.
Rav Yosef specifies the hook's size as one amah by one amah.
An alternative version reverses the explanation, stating the minimum is an amah by an amah.
Rav Yosef explains that the amah-sized piece is used for a raven's hook.

items.text: Mishnah: Minimum for wine and oil, and unspecified vow
items.text_en: Mishnah: Minimum for wine and oil, and unspecified vow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows wine must bring at least three log, and oil at least one log (Rabbi says three log). If one specified a vow but forgot what, they bring the largest amount offered on a festival day.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the minimum amounts for wine (three log) and oil (one log, or three log according to Rabbi).
The Mishnah rules that one who specified a vow but forgot what must bring the largest offering brought on a festival day.

items.text: Gemara: Source for wine and oil, and dispute between Rabbi and Rabbis
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for wine and oil, and dispute between Rabbi and Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the minimum for wine from the verse 'ezrach'. For oil, the Rabbis learn from a 'dayo' argument from the meal-offering (one log), while Rabbi learns from 'korban' that oil is donated like libations (three log). Rav Pappa initially suggests Rabbi learns from the meal-offering with a different hermeneutic, but Rav Huna bar Rav Natan objects with a baraisa showing Rabbi derives from 'korban'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'ezrach' indicates that wine is donated, with a minimum of three log.
The baraita derives from 'yihyeh' that one may add, and from 'kakhah' that one may not reduce.
The Gemara asks: on what basis do the Rabbis and Rabbi dispute the minimum for oil?

The Rabbis explain before Rav Pappa that the dispute is between the hermeneutic principles of 'דון מינה ומינה' (derive from the source and apply its measure) and 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה' (derive from the source but apply the measure of its own context).
The Rabbis hold 'דון מינה ומינה': just as a meal-offering is donated, so oil is donated, and just as a meal-offering requires one log, so oil requires one log.
Rabbi holds 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה': just as a meal-offering is donated, so oil is donated, but the measure is set by its own context of libations, which require three log.
Rav Pappa objects: if Rabbi derived oil from the meal-offering, everyone would agree on 'דון מינה ומינה'; rather, Rabbi derives from 'ezrach' (the verse for wine).

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan's rejection
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan's rejection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan rejects Rav Pappa's suggestion, citing a baraita that Rabbi derives oil from 'קרבן' (korban) with a minimum of three log, and Rav Pappa concedes: 'if it is taught, it is taught'.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of 'like a great day'
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of 'like a great day'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that 'like a great day' refers to the first day of Sukkot that falls on Shabbat, when the largest number of offerings are brought.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that 'like a great day' refers to the first day of Sukkot that falls on Shabbat, when the largest number of offerings are brought.

items.text: Mishnah: Minimum for unspecified animal offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Minimum for unspecified animal offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows an unspecified burnt-offering brings a lamb (Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says a dove or pigeon). If one specified from cattle but forgot, they bring a bull and calf; if from animals, they bring all types; if unspecified, they bring the largest.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the default rule: one who vows an unspecified burnt-offering brings a lamb.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya offers an alternative: the vow can be fulfilled with a dove or pigeon.
The Mishnah rules that if one specified from cattle but forgot, they bring a bull and a calf.
The Mishnah rules that if one specified from animals but forgot, they bring all types: bull, calf, ram, goat, kid, and lamb.
The Mishnah begins the case of one who specified but forgot entirely, to be continued in the next section.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows for unspecified offerings and the dispute about substituting size
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows for unspecified offerings and the dispute about substituting size
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists cases where a person vows an offering without specifying the animal, and must bring all possible types. It then addresses cases where the vow specifies a price or color, and concludes with a dispute: if one vowed a small animal and brought a large one, Rabbi says he has not fulfilled his vow, while the Sages say he has.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by listing that one adds a dove and a pigeon to the unspecified vow, and then details the animals brought for a vow of a thanksgiving or peace offering.
The mishnah continues with cases of unspecified vows from cattle or beasts, requiring all possible types of animals.
The mishnah specifies the value of the animal and its libations for vows of a bull, calf, ram, or lamb.
The mishnah clarifies that when the vow specifies a price, the libations are separate.
The mishnah rules that if one vowed a bull for a maneh and brought two for a maneh, he has not fulfilled his vow.
The mishnah concludes with the dispute: if one vowed a small animal and brought a large one, the Sages say he has fulfilled his vow, but Rabbi says he has not.

items.text: Gemara: Clarification of the dispute's basis
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarification of the dispute's basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the two opinions in the mishnah are not actually in conflict, as each follows the custom of their own locale regarding the value of coins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent dispute in the mishnah by explaining that the two opinions are not in conflict, as each follows the custom of their own locale regarding the value of coins.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of a baraita and attribution to Rabbi and the Sages
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of a baraita and attribution to Rabbi and the Sages
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited about a vow for an olah costing a sela, and the Gemara questions why one must bring both a bull and a calf when the vow is from cattle. It identifies the baraita as following Rabbi's view that a small animal cannot fulfill a vow for a large one. The Gemara then resolves an apparent contradiction by showing that the baraita's beginning and end follow Rabbi, while its middle follows the Sages, and concludes that the entire matter is a dispute between Rabbi and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who vows an olah for a sela brings a lamb, and if unspecified, brings from any animal that costs a sela.
The Gemara questions why the baraita requires both a bull and a calf when one specified cattle but forgot which, arguing that a bull alone should suffice either way.
The Gemara identifies the baraita as following Rabbi's view that one who vowed a small animal and brought a large one has not fulfilled the vow.
The Gemara objects that the end of the baraita, which says one who vowed a small animal and brought a large one is exempt, contradicts Rabbi's position that he is not exempt.
The Gemara resolves that the beginning and end of the baraita follow Rabbi, while the middle follows the Sages.
The Gemara confirms that the entire matter is a dispute between Rabbi and the Sages.

items.text: Gemara: Debate about the six shofar chests for donations
items.text_en: Gemara: Debate about the six shofar chests for donations
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about six shofar chests for freewill offerings and presents three opinions: Hezekiah says they correspond to six priestly watches to promote peace; Rabbi Yochanan says they were instituted because donations were abundant; and Ze'iri says they correspond to six types of animals, following Rabbi's view. Bar Pada adds that they correspond to bulls and rams.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah about six shofar chests for freewill offerings and asks what they correspond to.
Hezekiah answers that the six chests correspond to six priestly watches, instituted by the sages to promote peace among them.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that because donations were abundant, they instituted many chests to prevent the money from spoiling.
Ze'iri answers that the six chests correspond to six types of animals (bull, calf, ram, lamb, kid, goat), following Rabbi's view that a small animal brought for a large one does not fulfill the vow.
Bar Pada answers that the six chests correspond to bulls and rams (plural forms, implying multiple types).

items.text: Rejection of earlier opinions on surplus funds
items.text_en: Rejection of earlier opinions on surplus funds
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Tanna of the Mishnah does not hold like Chizkiya, Rabbi Yochanan, Ze'iri, or Bar Pada regarding the handling of surplus funds from various offerings. Each opinion is rejected because the Tanna does not worry about certain factors or does not establish a minority view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishnah's list of surplus items (lambs, goats, surpluses, and the half-shekel coin).
The Tanna does not hold like Chizkiya because he does not worry about the possibility of a delay (אינצויי), since each offering is brought on its own day.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Yochanan's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Yochanan's view
sub.desc_en: The Tanna does not hold like Rabbi Yochanan because he does not worry about the possibility of adding funds (איעופושי).
The Tanna does not hold like Ze'iri because he does not establish a minority view (יחידאה) as decisive.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of Bar Pada's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of Bar Pada's view
sub.desc_en: The Tanna does not hold like Bar Pada because all the listed items are surpluses (מותרות), not just the explicitly named ones.

items.text: Dispute over the destination of the half-shekel surplus (Ma'ah)
items.text_en: Dispute over the destination of the half-shekel surplus (Ma'ah)
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the surplus of the half-shekel (ma'ah) goes to the shekel fund according to Rabbi Meir, but to voluntary offerings according to Rabbi Eliezer. Then Shmuel and Rabbi Oshaya each list the types of offerings whose surplus is used for communal sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about the destination of the ma'ah (premium), citing the dispute between רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) and רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer).
שמואל (Shmuel) lists six types of offerings whose surplus coins correspond to the six collection horns.
רבי אושעיא (Rabbi Oshaya) gives an alternative list of six offerings whose surplus coins correspond to the collection horns, replacing the High Priest's tenth of an ephah with pairs of birds.

items.text: Why Shmuel and Rabbi Oshaya differ in their lists
items.text_en: Why Shmuel and Rabbi Oshaya differ in their lists
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Shmuel did not include the surplus of bird offerings (kinin) like Rabbi Oshaya, and answers that Shmuel's Tanna already taught kinin separately. It then clarifies that Rabbi Oshaya taught both kinin and surplus of kinin as distinct categories.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Shmuel did not include the surplus of bird offerings (קינין) in his list, unlike Rabbi Oshaya.
The Gemara answers that Shmuel's Tanna already taught a separate horn for קינין (bird offerings) in the first clause of the mishna.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Oshaya's version of the mishna omits קינין, given that he explicitly teaches it.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Oshaya distinguishes between a horn for קינין (bird offerings) and a separate horn for מותר קינין (surplus of bird offerings).

items.text: Why Rabbi Oshaya omitted the High Priest's tenth-ephah
items.text_en: Why Rabbi Oshaya omitted the High Priest's tenth-ephah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Oshaya holds that the surplus of the High Priest's tenth-ephah must rot, citing a baraita. Rav Chisda and Rabbah debate whether the surplus of the tenth-ephah goes to voluntary offerings or rots, and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar is recorded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Oshaya omitted the High Priest's tenth-ephah from his list of surpluses that go to voluntary offerings.
Rav Chisda explains that the baraita means: surplus of a sin-offering meal-offering goes to voluntary offerings, but surplus of the High Priest's tenth-ephah must rot.
Rabbah objects that even the surplus of the High Priest's tenth-ephah goes to voluntary offerings, and only surplus of thanksgiving bread must rot.
The Gemara records the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says the surplus goes to voluntary offerings, Rabbi Elazar says it must rot.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding the tenth-ephah's surplus
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding the tenth-ephah's surplus
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that surplus of the tenth-ephah goes to voluntary offerings, challenging the view that it rots. The Gemara deflects by interpreting it as referring to the sinner's meal-offering, not the High Priest's. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports the view that it rots, citing a verse and Rabbi Yehuda's teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing surpluses that go to voluntary offerings, including 'surplus of the tenth-ephah', challenging the view that the High Priest's tenth-ephah surplus rots.
The Gemara infers that the baraita's 'surplus of the tenth-ephah' refers specifically to the High Priest's tenth-ephah.
The Gemara deflects by interpreting the baraita as referring to the surplus of a sinner's meal-offering, not the High Priest's tenth-ephah.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that the view that the High Priest's tenth-ephah surplus rots is logically correct.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda derives from a verse that only the sinner's meal-offering is called 'חטאת' (sin-offering), implying the High Priest's tenth-ephah is not, so its surplus rots.

items.text: Mishnah: Substituting animals for designated sacrifices that became blemished
items.text_en: Mishnah: Substituting animals for designated sacrifices that became blemished
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a person designated an animal as a sacrifice and it became blemished. If he designated one ox as a burnt-offering, he may use its value to buy two; if two, he may buy one. Rabbi Yosi (or Rabbi) prohibits. Similar rules apply for substituting a ram for a lamb or vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of one who designated a bull as a burnt-offering and it became blemished: he may bring two bulls with its redemption money, but Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) prohibits this.

The Mishnah continues with parallel cases: if one designated a ram and it became blemished, he may bring a lamb with its redemption money; if one designated a lamb, he may bring a ram; Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) prohibits substituting one species for another.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's first case and Rabbi's position
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's first case and Rabbi's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah distinguishes between a case where an animal becomes blemished and a case where it is lost, and explains that Rabbi argues on the entire Mishnah, waiting for the Sages to finish before stating his dissent.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah's later cases
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah's later cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from the Mishnah's cases of a ram or lamb that became blemished, where Rabbi prohibits substitution, confirming that Rabbi argues on the entire Mishnah.

items.text: Inquiry about substitution between different species
items.text_en: Inquiry about substitution between different species
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether one may substitute an animal of a different species for a blemished one, and resolves it with a baraita that allows bringing two rams instead of one ox, but notes a contradiction resolved by positing two Tannaitic versions.

items.text: Rabbi's reasoning and a contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbi's reasoning and a contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi prohibits substitution because there is no mixture (ביללה), implying that if there were mixture it would be permitted, but a Mishnah contradicts this, so the Gemara posits two Tannaitic versions of Rabbi's opinion.

items.text: The case of unblemished animals
items.text_en: The case of unblemished animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for unblemished animals, substituting a calf for an ox or a lamb for a ram is valid, and this anonymous ruling follows the Sages.

items.text: Rav's distinction regarding the donor's wording
items.text_en: Rav's distinction regarding the donor's wording
items.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Zevid quotes Rav that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when one says 'this ox is an olah', but if one says 'this ox is upon me as an olah', the animal is designated; the Gemara refines this to require 'this ox and its value upon me as an olah' for designation.

items.text: Mishnah: Designating one animal from a group
items.text_en: Mishnah: Designating one animal from a group
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one says 'one of my lambs is consecrated' and has two, the larger is consecrated; if three, the middle one; if one forgets what he designated, the largest is consecrated.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's principles
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's principles
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the first and second clauses regarding generous vs. stingy eye, and resolves it with Shmuel's explanation that the middle animal is considered generous relative to the small one. It then discusses how to effect the consecration, and distinguishes between different phrasings of dedication, citing various Amoraim and a baraita.

items.text: Clarification of the previous Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Clarification of the previous Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a lost document is not validated by witnesses who saw it fall, and explains that the buyer's hand is on the bottom, so the document is presumed to be written after the sale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the seller can automatically give the fallen house or dead slave; let him see which one fell or died.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a purchaser, and the principle is that the owner of the document is at a disadvantage, so the seller can claim he sold the fallen house or dead slave.
The Gemara adds that now that this explanation is reached, even if one says the attic is the worst house, the principle that the owner of the document is at a disadvantage applies.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows for the Temple of Onias
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows for the Temple of Onias
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one vows to bring an olah or be a nazir without specifying, it must be done in the Temple; if specified for the Temple of Onias, it is valid there, but Rabbi Shimon disagrees.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one vows an olah without specifying, it must be brought in the Temple; if specified for the Temple of Onias, it is valid there.
Rabbi Shimon disagrees, stating that such a conditional vow does not consecrate the animal as an olah at all.
The Mishnah rules that if one vows to be a nazir without specifying, he must shave in the Temple; if specified for the Temple of Onias, it is valid there.
Rabbi Shimon disagrees, stating that such a conditional vow does not make one a nazir at all.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can be exempt from liability for a sacrifice offered at the Temple of Onias. Rav Hamnuna suggests it is like stipulating no liability, but Rava objects regarding the nazir, and explains that the person intended to fulfill the vow with less effort.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can be exempt from liability for a sacrifice offered at the Temple of Onias, since it is merely a slaughter, not a valid sacrifice.
Rav Hamnuna suggests that the person is considered to have stipulated that he would not be responsible for the animal, so if it is killed, he is exempt.
Rava objects that the same logic cannot apply to a nazir, because a nazir cannot complete his term without bringing the required offerings, so a condition of non-liability is impossible.

Rava explains that the person intended only to bring a gift, not to consecrate the animal, and was willing to exert himself only if the sacrifice could be done in the Temple of Onias, not in Jerusalem.

Rava extends the same reasoning to the nazir: the person intended only to practice abstinence, not to fully accept naziriteship, and was willing to shave only if it could be done in the Temple of Onias.

items.text: Support for Rav Hamnuna and Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.text_en: Support for Rav Hamnuna and Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna distinguishes between the olah and nazir cases. Rabbi Yochanan supports Rav Hamnuna, stating that one who vows to bring an olah at the Temple of Onias but brings it in the Land of Israel is exempt but liable for karet, and a baraita confirms this.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna responds to Rava's challenge by distinguishing the nazir case (as Rava explained) from the olah case, where the speaker is considered to have said 'on condition that I not be responsible for it.'

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports that Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Rav Hamnuna: one who vows to bring an olah at the Temple of Onias but sacrifices it in the Land of Israel fulfills his obligation but is liable for karet.
A baraita is cited to support the view: one who vows to bring an olah in the wilderness but sacrifices it on the east bank of the Jordan fulfills his obligation but is liable for karet.

items.text: Mishnah: Priests who served at the Temple of Onias
items.text_en: Mishnah: Priests who served at the Temple of Onias
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that priests who served at the Temple of Onias may not serve in the Jerusalem Temple, but they may eat from the sacrifices like blemished priests.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that priests who served at the Temple of Onias are disqualified from serving in the Jerusalem Temple, but they may partake of the sacrifices like blemished priests.

items.text: Debate on a priest who slaughtered for idolatry
items.text_en: Debate on a priest who slaughtered for idolatry
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that a priest who slaughtered for idolatry may still offer sacrifices. Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi cites a verse, and the Gemara discusses whether slaughter is considered service. Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet debate whether an unintentional error in sprinkling disqualifies the priest.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that a priest who slaughtered for idolatry may still offer sacrifices.
Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi cites a verse to show that only actual service (שירות) disqualifies a priest, not slaughter.
The Gemara presents a dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet regarding a priest who erred unintentionally in the sprinkling (זריקה) of blood for idolatry.
Rav Sheshet derives from the verse that 'מכשול' (stumbling block) refers to an unintentional act, while 'עון' (iniquity) refers to intentional, so an unintentional sprinkler is disqualified.
Rav Nachman rejects Rav Sheshet's interpretation, arguing that 'מכשול' is a modifier of 'עון' (a stumbling block of iniquity), not a separate category.

items.text: Proofs and dispute about intentional slaughter
items.text_en: Proofs and dispute about intentional slaughter
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman brings a baraita that a priest can atone for himself through an unintentional sin, implying it refers to sprinkling. Rav Sheshet counters that it could refer to slaughter, and they follow their respective positions on intentional slaughter.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a baraita that a priest can atone for himself through an unintentional sin.
Rav Nachman argues that the baraita must refer to sprinkling, not slaughter, because slaughter would be valid even intentionally.
Rav Sheshet counters that the baraita could still refer to slaughter, because intentional slaughter disqualifies the priest as a servant of idolatry.
The Gemara notes that Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet follow their respective positions on intentional slaughter.
The Gemara concludes with the reasoning: Rav Nachman permits because slaughter is not service, while Rav Sheshet disqualifies.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and debate on a priest who served idolatry
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and debate on a priest who served idolatry
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman infers from a baraita that a priest who intentionally slaughtered for idolatry may still offer sacrifices if he repents, since the act of slaughter is not a 'service' that disqualifies him. Rav Sheishet counters that the baraita refers to an unintentional act, and only if he repents immediately.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with the case of a priest who became a priest for idolatry.
Rav Nachman infers from a baraita that a priest who intentionally slaughtered for idolatry may still offer sacrifices if he repents, since slaughter is not a 'service' that disqualifies him.
Rav Sheishet counters that the baraita refers to an unintentional act, and only if he repents immediately.

items.text: Dispute on prostration and gratitude to idolatry, with a צריכא
items.text_en: Dispute on prostration and gratitude to idolatry, with a צריכא
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Sheishet argue whether prostration or verbal gratitude to idolatry disqualifies a priest's sacrifice. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary to teach: each case highlights a different aspect of the dispute, such as whether the act constitutes a 'service' or a 'deed'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rav Nachman permits the sacrifice of a priest who prostrated to or thanked idolatry, while Rav Sheishet disqualifies it.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis: the צריכא (necessity) for both cases
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis: the צריכא (necessity) for both cases
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both cases (prostration and verbal gratitude) are necessary: without the first case, one might think Rav Sheishet only objects to a service (שירות) but not to slaughter.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis: second limb of the צריכא
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis: second limb of the צריכא
sub.desc_en: The Gemara continues: without the slaughter case, one might think Rav Sheishet only objects to an actual service (עבודה) but not to prostration, which is not a service.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis: third limb of the צריכא
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis: third limb of the צריכא
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: without the prostration case, one might think Rav Sheishet only objects to a deed (מעשה) but not to mere verbal gratitude (הודאה), so both cases are necessary.

items.text: Inference from the Mishnah's phrase 'אין צריך לומר דבר אחר'
items.text_en: Inference from the Mishnah's phrase 'אין צריך לומר דבר אחר'
items.desc_en: The Gemara deduces from the Mishnah's wording that the Temple of Chonyo is not considered idolatry, since the Mishnah says 'no need to mention another matter', implying that the case of Chonyo is not idolatrous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'אין צריך לומר דבר אחר' (no need to mention another matter) that the Temple of Chonyo is not considered idolatry.

items.text: Baraita: The story of Chonyo and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Baraita: The story of Chonyo and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that after Shimon HaTzaddik's death, his son Chonyo was appointed High Priest, but his brother Shim'i tricked him and caused him to flee to Alexandria, where he built an altar. Rabbi Meir says he built it for idolatry, while Rabbi Yehuda says he built it for the sake of Heaven, citing a verse from Isaiah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that it supports the view that the Temple of Chonyo is not idolatry, and begins the story of Shimon HaTzaddik's death.
The baraita recounts that after the festival, Shimon HaTzaddik fell ill for seven days and died, and the priests refrained from blessing with the Tetragrammaton.
Shimon HaTzaddik appoints his son Chonyo as successor, but his brother Shim'i tricks Chonyo by dressing him in priestly garments and accusing him of a vow to his beloved.

According to Rabbi Meir, the priests sought to kill Chonyo, who fled to Alexandria and built an altar for idolatry, leading the sages to say that one who flees from idolatry is praiseworthy, and one who descends to it is even more so.
Rabbi Yehuda objects to Rabbi Meir's version, asserting that Chonyo did not accept the appointment, and that he built the altar for the sake of Heaven, citing the verse from Isaiah.
According to Rabbi Yehuda, the sages said that one who fled from idolatry is praiseworthy, and one who seeks to descend to it is even more so.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachyah's statement and the example of Shaul
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachyah's statement and the example of Shaul
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachyah says that initially he would punish anyone who said 'ascend to her' (i.e., to the land of Israel), but now he would punish anyone who says 'descend from her', because Shaul fled from the land and later sought to kill David.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachyah states his initial and later policy regarding encouraging or discouraging aliyah to the land of Israel.
The gemara provides the supporting example of Shaul, who fled the land and later sought to kill David, justifying Rabbi Yehoshua's shift.

items.text: Mar Kashisha's question to Abaye about Rabbi Meir's use of the verse
items.text_en: Mar Kashisha's question to Abaye about Rabbi Meir's use of the verse
items.desc_en: Mar Kashisha asks Abaye how Rabbi Meir interprets the verse that Rabbi Yehuda used to support his view. Abaye answers that it is needed for another teaching: after Sancherev's defeat, Chizkiyahu made the captive kings swear not to worship idolatry, as the verse says five cities in Egypt will speak the language of Canaan.

sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha asks Abaye how Rabbi Meir interprets the verse that Rabbi Yehuda used to support his view.

Abaye answers that the verse is needed for another teaching: after Sancherev's defeat, Chizkiyahu made the captive kings swear not to worship idolatry, as the verse says five cities in Egypt will speak the language of Canaan.

items.text: Opening: The altar in Egypt
items.text_en: Opening: The altar in Egypt
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by recounting that Jews built an altar in Alexandria, Egypt, and offered sacrifices for the sake of Heaven, citing the verse about an altar in Egypt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Jews built an altar in Alexandria, Egypt, and offered sacrifices for the sake of Heaven, citing the verse about an altar in Egypt.

items.text: Interpretation of 'city of destruction'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'city of destruction'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the phrase 'city of destruction' as referring to the city of Beit Shemesh, which is destined for destruction, and connects it to the word for sun.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'city of destruction' refers to.
Rav Yosef translates the phrase as referring to Beit Shemesh, one of the cities destined for destruction.
The Gemara proves that 'heres' means sun by citing the verse 'the one who says to the sun (חרס) and it does not shine'.

items.text: Interpretation of 'bring my sons from afar'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'bring my sons from afar'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna interprets the verse as referring to the Babylonian exile, whose inhabitants have settled minds like sons, and other exiles whose minds are unsettled like daughters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'Bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the ends of the earth'.
Rav Huna interprets 'sons' as the Babylonian exiles, whose minds are settled like sons, and 'daughters' as exiles from other lands, whose minds are unsettled like daughters.

items.text: Geographical boundary of Jewish recognition
items.text_en: Geographical boundary of Jewish recognition
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda or Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that from Tyre to Carthage, people recognize Israel and their Father in Heaven, but beyond that they do not.

sub.text: Rav Chisda / Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda / Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda or Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states a geographical boundary: from Tyre to Carthage people recognize Israel and their Father in Heaven, but beyond that they do not.

items.text: Challenge from Malachi about universal worship
items.text_en: Challenge from Malachi about universal worship
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiya challenges Rav with a verse stating that God's name is great among the nations and offerings are brought everywhere. Rav responds by calling him 'Shimi' and noting that they call him the God of gods.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiya challenges Rav by citing the verse from Malachi that God's name is great among the nations and offerings are brought everywhere.
Rav dismisses the challenge by calling Rav Shimi bar Chiya 'Shimi' and noting that the nations call God 'the God of gods,' implying the verse refers to idolaters, not legitimate worship.

items.text: Interpretation of 'in every place' and 'pure meal-offering'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'in every place' and 'pure meal-offering'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains that 'in every place' refers to Torah scholars studying Torah, which is considered like offering sacrifices. The 'pure meal-offering' refers to one who studies Torah in purity, after marrying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the literal meaning of 'in every place' in the verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains that 'in every place' refers to Torah scholars studying Torah anywhere, which God considers as if they offer incense and meal-offerings to His name.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: The 'pure meal-offering' refers to one who studies Torah in purity, meaning he marries a wife and then studies Torah.

items.text: Interpretation of 'standing in the House of God at night'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'standing in the House of God at night'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the verse refers to Torah scholars who study Torah at night, and Scripture considers them as if they are engaged in the Temple service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse means by 'at night' in the context of standing in the House of God.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the verse refers to Torah scholars who study Torah at night, and Scripture considers them as if they are engaged in the Temple service.

items.text: Interpretation of 'this is for Israel forever'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'this is for Israel forever'
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav says this refers to a built altar with Michael the great prince offering a sacrifice. Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to Torah scholars engaged in the laws of the Temple service, as if the Temple were built in their days.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav interprets the verse 'this is for Israel forever' as referring to a built altar with Michael the great prince offering a sacrifice.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the same verse as referring to Torah scholars engaged in the laws of the Temple service, as if the Temple were built in their days.

items.text: Reish Lakish and Rava on Torah study as sacrifice
items.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rava on Torah study as sacrifice
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish says that one who studies Torah is as if he offered all types of sacrifices. Rava objects to the wording and concludes that one who studies Torah needs no sacrifices at all.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that one who studies Torah is as if he offered all types of sacrifices.
Rava objects to the wording of the verse, arguing it should read 'עֹלָה וּמִנְחָה' (burnt-offering and meal-offering) rather than 'לָעֹלָה לַמִּנְחָה'.
Rava concludes that one who studies Torah needs no sacrifices at all.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak on studying the Torah of sin-offering and guilt-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak on studying the Torah of sin-offering and guilt-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that one who studies the Torah of the sin-offering is as if he offered a sin-offering, and similarly for the guilt-offering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that one who studies the Torah of the sin-offering is as if he offered a sin-offering, and similarly for the guilt-offering.

items.text: Mishnah: Equal merit for large and small offerings with proper intent
items.text_en: Mishnah: Equal merit for large and small offerings with proper intent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that the same phrase 'a fire-offering, a pleasing aroma' is used for animal burnt-offerings, bird burnt-offerings, and meal-offerings, to teach that one who offers much and one who offers little are equal, provided they direct their heart to Heaven.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the same phrase 'a fire-offering, a pleasing aroma' is used for animal, bird, and meal offerings, teaching that one who offers much and one who offers little are equal, provided they direct their heart to Heaven.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural support for the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural support for the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira and Rav Adda bar Ahavah provide verses to support the Mishnah's principle that the amount does not matter as long as intent is proper.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks for a scriptural source supporting the Mishnah's principle that the amount of offering does not matter as long as intent is proper.
Rabbi Zeira cites the verse 'מְתוּקָה שְׁנַת הָעֹבֵד אִם מְעַט וְאִם הַרְבֵּה יֹאכֵל' (Sweet is the sleep of the laborer, whether he eats little or much) as the scriptural support.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's alternative answer
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's alternative answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah offers a different verse, 'בִּרְבוֹת הַטּוֹבָה רַבּוּ אוֹכְלֶיהָ וּמַה כִּשְׁרוֹן לִבְעָלָיו' (When goods increase, those who eat them increase; and what advantage is there to the owner?), as the scriptural source.

items.text: Tosefta: The name used in sacrifices and the lesson of equal merit
items.text_en: Tosefta: The name used in sacrifices and the lesson of equal merit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai notes that in the section of sacrifices, only the Tetragrammaton is used, not other divine names, to prevent heretics from arguing. The Tosefta repeats the Mishnah's lesson about equal merit with proper intent.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai notes that in the Torah section of sacrifices, only the Tetragrammaton (ה׳) is used, not other divine names, to prevent heretics from arguing.
The Tosefta repeats the Mishnah's lesson that one who offers much and one who offers little have equal merit, provided they direct their heart to Heaven.

items.text: God does not need sacrifices; they are for your benefit
items.text_en: God does not need sacrifices; they are for your benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that God does not need sacrifices for food, as He owns everything. The purpose of sacrifices is for your own benefit, as the verse says 'for your acceptance you shall sacrifice it'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara anticipates a possible objection that God needs sacrifices for food, and refutes it by citing verses showing God owns all animals and does not eat.
The Gemara concludes that sacrifices are not for God's benefit but for your own acceptance, as the verse says 'לִרְצֹנְכֶם תִּזְבָּחֻהוּ' (for your acceptance you shall sacrifice it).
An alternative interpretation of the verse 'לִרְצֹנְכֶם תִּזְבָּחֻהוּ' is given: sacrifice according to your will and your intention.

items.text: Source that one engaged in sacred matters is invalid
items.text_en: Source that one engaged in sacred matters is invalid
items.desc_en: Shmuel asks Rav Huna for the source that one who is engaged in other matters while performing a sacrifice is invalid. Rav Huna cites the verse 'and he shall slaughter the son of the cattle' to require intent for the specific animal. Shmuel then asks for the source that this invalidates, and Rav Huna cites 'for your acceptance you shall sacrifice it' meaning with intent.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel asks Rav Huna for the source that one who is engaged in other matters while performing a sacrifice is invalid.
Rav Huna cites the verse 'and he shall slaughter the son of the cattle' to require intent for the specific animal.
Shmuel asks for the source that this lack of intent invalidates the sacrifice.
Rav Huna cites the verse 'for your acceptance you shall sacrifice it' to mean with intent, thus invalidating if done without intent.
